case_source: (From the judgment and order dated January 5, 1994 passed by the Administrative Appellate Tribunal in Appeal No. 34 of 1993).
full_judgment:
ATM Afzal CJ : This appeal by leave is from judgment and order dated 5 January, 1994 passed by the Administrative Appellate Tribunal, Dhaka in Appeal No. 34 of 1993 setting aside those of the Administrative Tribunal dated 23.2.1993 passed in Case No. 22 of 1992 and further dismissing the said case.

2. The appellants filed the aforesaid Administrative Tribunal Case No. 22 of 1992 under section 4(2) of the Administrative Tribunals Act 1980 (Act No. 7 of 1981), hereinafter called the Act, making respondent Nos.16-18 herein as opposite parties for a declaration that the notification dated 12.8.1991 (Annexure 'Ka' to the original application) issued by the Ministry of Home Affairs regularizing and confirming the service of the appellants in their posts of Assistant Superintendent of Police (ASP) with effect from 12.2.1990 in the case of appellant Nos. 1-3, 7 and 8 and in the case of appellant Nos. 5 and 6 with effect from 18-3-1991, i.e., from the dates of recommendation of the Public Service Commission is illegal and for an order regularizing and confirming their service with effect from the date of respective officiation by them in the said posts and further for a declaration that they are eligible for consideration for promotion to the post of Additional Superintendent of Police.

3. The appellants while serving as Inspectors of Police were promoted to officiate as Assistant Superintendent of Police on different dates between 17-4-1982 to 22-3-1984. They are thus 'departmental promotees, as it is called, as against 'direct recruits' as respondent Nos.1-15 are, who were appointed as ASP in the Bangladesh Civil Service (Police) having successfully qualified in the competitive examination conducted by the Public Service Commission in the year 1984 and onwards, respondent Nos. 8-15 being latest among them having been recruited in 1988. The appellants while in continuous officiation as ASP passed departmental and senior scale examination conducted by the Public Service Commission.

4. It is the appellants case that in 1984 and 1986 the Ministry of Home Affairs regularised the appointment of 97 ASPs with effect from the date of their officiating appointment between 1976-1981 but in the case of the appellants a discrimination was made by issuing the notification dated 12.8.1991 as referred to above although they stand in the same category as that of the said 97 ASPs. They have in the meantime become eligible for promotion to the post of Additional Superintendent of Police. The appellants are being treated in a discriminatory manner in violation of the Constitutional protection of equality. The appellants made representation to the authority against such discrimination but having got no relief filed the case before the Tribunal.

5. Respondent No.18, Inspector General of Police, who was opposite party No. 3 in the Tribunal contested the application of the appellants by filing a written statement. The allegations made by the appellants were denied and it was stated, inter alia, that the application of the appellants was barred by the proviso to section 4(2) of the Act, that the appellants appointment on promotion to the post of ASP was regularised on the recommendation of the Public Service Commission in accordance with the relevant provisions of law and that the authority could not consider the appeal preferred by the appellants as there was no legal ground. They are thus not entitled to any relief under the Act and their case is liable to be dismissed.

6. The Administrative Tribunal upon considering notifications dated 27.3.1984 and 4.5.1986 (Annexures 'Ga' and 'Gha' respectively) by which the appointment of 97 ASPs was regularised from the date of their officiating appointment came to the conclusion that glaring discrimination had been made in the case of the appellants whose service was regularised and confirmed not from the date of their officiating appointment but from a much later date as shown in the impugned notification dated 12-8-1991. It was violative of Article 27 of the Constitution. As regards claim for promotion it was held that promotion cannot be claimed as a matter of right. Accordingly, the application of the appellants was allowed in part. The portion of the impugned notification so far it relates to the regularisation and confirmation of appointment of the appellants in the post of ASPs, with effect from the date of recommendation of the Public Service Commission, was declared to be illegal and void on the ground of discrimination and it was directed that the appointment of the appellants to the post of ASPs be regularized with effect from the date of their respective officiating appointment. The prayer for declaration that the appellants have acquired the right to be promoted to the post of Additional Superintendent of Police was, however, dismissed.

7. None of the opposite parties in the original petition including opposite party No. 3, the Inspector General of Police, took any appeal against the judgment and order of the Administrative Tribunal. An appeal, however, No. 34 of 1993 was taken by respondent Nos.1-15 under section 6(1) of the Act who were not parties in the original application and who, as already noticed, were 'direct recruits' to the post of ASP. The said respondents raised several objections against the application filed by the appellants and contended that no illegality was committed in their case by regularising and confirming their appointment in terms of the notification dated 12-8-1991. The respondents contended that the relief prayed for by the appellants before the Administrative Tribunal affected their seniority and that of the other direct recruits. The respondents and others have been made junior to the appellants by reason of the judgment of the Administrative Tribunal and they did not get any opportunity to present their case as they were not made parties before the Tribunal and, as such, there was a flagrant violation of the principle of natural justice for which they are very much aggrieved. Among others, the respondents also contended that although the appellants sought relief against the Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh as persons employed in the service of the Republic but the Government of Bangladesh was not made a party in the Administrative Tribunal case and thus the case suffered from defect of party.

8. It appears from the impugned judgment of the Administrative Appellate Tribunal that besides merit of the case three legal points were taken up for consideration : (i) Is the case premature in the eye of law; (ii) Is the case bad for defect of parties; (iii) Is the appeal maintainable at the instance of the appellants (respondent Nos.1-15).

9. It was held that the case having been filed before taking of any decision on the matter by the higher authority it was barred under both the first and second proviso to section 4(2) of the Act. It was also found that the respondents were necessary parties in the case and they having not been made parties, the case was bad for defect of parties and that they had a right to file an appeal against the judgment of the Tribunal inasmuch as their seniority would be affected by reason of the said judgment. On the merit of the case it was found that the case of 97 ASPs whose appointment was regularized from the date of their officiating appointment stood on a different footing and that the appellants having been appointed subsequent to the Memo dated 8-3-1980 of the Ministry of Home Affairs putting condition to their officiating appointment, it could not be said that discrimination was made in the case of the present appellants by issuing the impugned notification dated 12.8.1991. Having made the above findings the Appellate Tribunal, as already noticed by the impugned judgment and order dated 5.1.1994, dismissed the case of the appellants.

10. Leave to appeal was sought for against the impugned judgment raising objection to all the findings made by the Appellate Tribunal, which, it was argued, bear on question of law, namely, competence of the application, defect of parties and competence of respondent Nos.1-15 to file appeal. As to the main question determining the appellants confirmation to the post of ASP/seniority, it was submitted that the established principle is that unless otherwise provided by any law seniority counts from the date of continuous officiation in a post. It was also submitted that rule 3 of the Bangladesh Civil Service Seniority Rules, 1983, hereinafter called the Rules, governs the case of the appellants but unfortunately, the said Rules could not be produced before the Appellate Tribunal. The learned Counsel for the appellants further submitted that the learned Appellate Tribunal wrongly made a distinction between the case of the appellants and those of the 97 other ASPs who were confirmed from the date of their officiating appointment and thus fell in error in holding that there was no discrimination made in the case of the appellants.

11. As to the finding of the Appellate Tribunal that the application before the Tribunal was barred under both the first and second proviso to section 4(2) of the Act, Mr. TH Khan, learned Advocate for the appellants, has submitted that the same was, in any view of the matter, wrong. The impugned notification was dated 12.8.1991 and the application before the Tribunal was filed on 12.2.1992, that is, within six months of the order as required under the second proviso. The appellants, however, stated in paragraph 11 of their application that they had made representations to the Inspector General of Police against the said notification but they received no reply. In the written statement it was stated that the opposite party could not take any step with regard to the representations as there was no legal basis for the same. Mr. Khan has submitted that the representations of the appellants were made not under any law or rule nor to any higher administrative authority, the impugned notification being that of the Government, so as to attract the first proviso. Even if it was attracted, Mr. Khan submits making reference to the order-sheet of the Tribunal that the decision of the authority was made known to the Tribunal before the judgment was delivered on 23.2.1993 and thus there was no bar for the Tribunal to give its decision. The Appellate Tribunal took the view that as the case was filed before taking of any decision on the matter by the higher authority, it was barred under the first proviso and even if the authority's decision was produced during the pendency of the case, the defect could not be cured as there was no provision in the Act to treat an incomplete application like the present as "a mature one" on production of the order of the authority afterwards and further as there was no paper to show that the order of the authority so produced was passed before the filing of the application to the Tribunal.

<u>12. The Appellate Tribunal does not seem to have appreciated the matter correctly and in its proper perspective. The first proviso to section 4(2) debarring an application to the Tribunal is attracted when there is a higher administrative authority "under any law for the time being in force" to take a decision in respect of an order, etc. to be impugned before the Tribunal and until such decision is taken. The impugned notification was made by the Government and it is nobody's case that there is a higher administrative authority under any law to set aside, vary or modify the same. The appellants representation to the Inspector General of Police were not certainly made to a higher administrative authority. Therefore, they were entitled to file application against the impugned notification straightaway within six months under the second proviso which was actually done. Even if a decision of the authority was necessary, the statement made in the written statement that the representations having had no legal basis could not be attended, clearly indicated that the authority had already taken a decision. The opposite parties themselves submitted report dated 14-1-1993/3-2-1993 informing the Tribunal about their decision even though the appellants were not made aware of the same before filing of the application. In such circumstances, the finding of the Appellate Tribunal as to the application being barred under the provisos to section 4(2) of the Act cannot be upheld in any case.</u>

13. The Appellate Tribunal seemed to be far from objective in holding that the case was bad for defect of party as the Public Service Commission, a necessary party in the facts of the case, was not made a party even though it was very much made a party in the case as opposite party No. 1 Mr. TH Khan was very critical about this finding, complained about lack of application of mind and went on to submit that the other finding that there was defect of party for not impleading respondent Nos.1-15 in the case was also wrong in as much as the appellants pray for no relief against them. Mr. Khan went on the offensive to suggest that the said respondents rather had no locus standi to prefer appeal against the judgment of the Tribunal as they were not rightly made parties in the case and the finding of the Appellate Tribunal that they had a right to prefer the appeal was wrong.

<u>14. We think Mr. TH Khan is half right and half wrong in his submission. As regards the necessity of making particular person or person’s parties in a case before the Tribunal, there appears to be no guidance either in the Act or in the Rules framed thereunder. The provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, including those of Order I, except as referred to in the Act and the Rules, do not seem to apply to the Tribunal. But it cannot be disputed that as a general rule all the necessary parties must be impleaded in a case so that a Tribunal may effectually adjudicate on the matter brought before it.</u>

<u>15. Now in the present case the appellants are not complaining about any seniority or gradation list nor claiming seniority for themselves as against respondent Nos.1-15 or others. All they are claiming is confirmation in the post of ASP since becoming officiating in the said post. To ask them to make all the persons parties in the case who are likely to be affected in the matter of seniority is neither practical nor easy. They are making a claim against the Government and it is for the opposite parties to answer/refute the same in accordance with law and to protect the interest of other employees who are likely to be affected in the case of the appellants success. So, it cannot be said in the facts and circumstances of the present case that it was bad for defect of party for not impleading respondent Nos.1-15. Even if it is held for argument's sake that they are necessary parties, the appellants case cannot now fail on the ground of defect of party because they (respondents No.1-15) have appeared in the appeal which is a continuation of the original proceeding. Respondents No.1-15 may not have been necessary parties for the appellants' relief but, nevertheless, it cannot be said that they had no right to file appeal against the judgment of the Tribunal. They are 'aggrieved' within the meaning of section 6(2) of the Act, in that the order of the Tribunal was likely to be prejudicial to them in the matter of seniority and particularly because the opposite parties in the case did not prefer any appeal to safeguard their interest. So, we are of the view that although the right of appeal cannot be denied to them, they cannot be considered as necessary parties in the facts of the present case and, at any rate, the appellants case cannot fail for defect of party as they (respondents No.1-15) are now before the Tribunal in course of the appeal.</u>

<u>16. In this connection Mr. Abdur Rab Chowdhury, learned Advocate for respondent Nos. 1-5, 7, 9, 11 and 12 has submitted that the appellants application before the Tribunal was otherwise defective because the Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh was not made a party against whose order relief was claimed. We think there is substance in the contention of Mr. Chowdhury. Besides the Chairman, Public Service Commission who is opposite party No.1, the appellants have made the Secretary, Ministry of Home Affairs and Inspector General of Police, opposite party Nos. 2 and 3 in the application. It is true that the notification issued by the Home Ministry has been impugned in the application but the fact remains that it is a notification of the Government and therefore relief has to be claimed against the proper party, namely, the Government. Article 146 of the Constitution provides that the Government of Bangladesh may sue or be sued by the name of Bangladesh. In a case like the present the correct opposite party should have been Bangladesh represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Home Affairs. The appellants were at liberty to make any other person opposite party in the case but in the absence of the Government, to be made party as stated above, the Tribunal might not be competent to pass a proper and effective order. It has been noticed that petitioners before the Tribunal are generally either careless or not properly advised in making/describing opposite parties in a correct legal manner. This negligence or lack of proper advice may prove fatal in a particular case. In the present case, we are not putting any emphasis on the defect as pointed out by Mr. Chowdhury as it was not raised heretofore and as the decision is going to turn on the merit of the case.</u>

17. The appellants succeeded in the Tribunal on the ground that they were treated differently from the 97 officers who were confirmed and regularized in their posts of ASP from the date of their officiating appointment. The Appellate Tribunal, however, distinguished the case of the appellants from those of 97 officers taking into consideration a Memo No. P3P-3/80 (1)MPA(Police-1)/285 dated 8.3.1980 of the Ministry of Home Affairs, Police Section-I, which reads as follows :

"Subject : Appointment of ASPs.

The undersigned is directed to refer to his memo No. 2 GA.4-79/109/A dated 19-1-80, No. GA /4-79/77A dated 12-1-80, No. GA/4-79/1480/A dt. 19-11-79 and No. GA/4-79/1181/A dt. 20-9-79 on the above subject and to request him to deal with matters relating to officiating promotion from the post of. Inspector of Police to the post of Dy. SP since redesignated as ASP. This officiating appointment, however, would not constitute an appointment to any service or cadre nor would it confer any right for consideration for such appointment by virtue of this officiating promotion.

Sd/ Md. Azizur Rahman

8.3.80

Section Officer."

18. The Appellate Tribunal observed that the officiating appointments of the appellants were made subject to the condition as mentioned in the above quoted Memo unlike the appointment of 97 officers who were not appointed subject to such condition. They were thus held to be not of the same class as the appellants and, as such, there was no question of making any discrimination between the two groups of officers. Mr. TH Khan pointed out from Annexures 'Gha' notification dated 4-5-1986 that out of the 68 ASPs who were confirmed from the date of their officiating appointment, many of them were appointed after 8.3.1980 and, as such, their case was not at all different from those of the appellants. Mr. Khan made a grievance that the Appellate Tribunal was completely oblivious of Annexure 'Gha', which, if considered by it, would have shown that there was no difference between the appellants and at least some of the ASPs mentioned in the said Annexure 'Gha' who were confirmed from the date of their officiating appointment. We shall consider the question of alleged discrimination lastly after disposing of Mr. Khan's more substantive argument based on the relevant Rules as advanced by him. The claim of the appellants, as it is revealed from the submissions made on their behalf, is really a claim for counting seniority from the date of officiating appointment as ASP which has been denied to them by the impugned notification. The main submission of Mr. TH Khan has been that the appellants' case is covered and will be governed by rule 3(c) of the Seniority Rules, 1983 already referred to above. Rule 3(c) reads as follows:

3. Principles of seniority inter se of the members of a Service Cadre:—The seniority inter se of the members of a Service Cadre of the Bangladesh Civil Service shall be determined in accordance with the following principles, namely:

(a).....

(b)......

(c) Seniority inter se of the members of a Service, which was earlier organised on junior and senior scale arrangements and under which the promotees were promoted to the junior scale, shall be counted from the date of continuous officiation in the junior scale.

(d) ...........

(e).........

(f).............

19. Mr. Khan submitted that the service called the Bangladesh Civil Service (Enforcement: Police) was constituted by the Bangladesh Civil Service (Enforcement: Police) Composition and Cadre Rules 1980 by notification dated 1st September, 1980. In the Schedule of the said Cadre Rules the post of ASP is included. Referring to Rules 2, 3 and 6 along with the schedule of the Cadre Rules Mr. Khan argued that the appellants have become 'members of service' and, as such, their case will be governed by Rule 3(c) of the Seniority Rules. Mr. Abdur Rab Chowdhury has pointed out that Rule 3(c) is not at all applicable to the appellants inasmuch as neither they were 'members of service' within the meaning and definition of the Seniority Rules 1983 nor have they been recruited even to the 'service' and appointed to a Cadre post under the Cadre Rules 1980 until the dates mentioned in the impugned notification. Mr. Chowdhury has elaborated his submission upon explaining the provisions of the aforesaid Seniority and Cadre Rules and the Bangladesh Civil Service Recruitment Rules, 1981 promulgated by notification dated 1st January 1981.

<u>20. In order to be governed by Rule 3(c) of the Seniority Rules 1983 one has, first of all, to be a member of a Service Cadre declared by the Bangladesh Civil Service (Reorganization) Order 1980 and constituted under the Cadre Rules 1980. Rule 3 of the Cadre Rules provides for constitution of Service and reads as follows:</u>

<u>3. Constitution of Service—(1) There shall be constituted a Service to be called the Bangladesh Civil Service (Enforcement: Police).</u>

<u>(2) the Service shall consist of—</u>

<u>a) persons who were members of the erstwhile Police Service of Pakistan and persons appointed to the posts of Deputy Superintendents of Police and above of the erstwhile East Pakistan Police Service on or before the 25th day of March, 1971;</u>

<u>(b) persons appointed on or after the 26th day of March 1971, on the recommendation of the erstwhile Central Public Service Commission or the East Pakistan Public Service Commission or the competent authority during the period of non-existence of the Commission or the Commission or ex-officers of the Armed Forces appointed by the Government against posts which would have been included in the cadre of the service had any such posts not been created as abolished after independence and whose terms and conditions are governed by the former cadre service rules and who were confirmed in a cadre post on or before the 1st day of January, 1979; and</u>

<u>(c) persons to be appointed to the Service in accordance with these rules.</u>

<u>21. Rule 5 provides that appointments to the Service shall be made by the President or an officer authorised by him. Rule 6 provides for the procedure for recruitment and the relevant portion of the said Rule is as follows:</u>

<u>6. Procedure for recruitment:—(1) The Service shall initially consist of the persons covered by rule 3(2)(a) and (b) and thereafter—</u>

<u>(a) by direct recruitment on the recommendation of the Commission; and</u>

<u>(b) by promotion from feeder posts in accordance with the provisions, if any, in the recruitment rules on the recommendation of the Commission.</u>

<u>(2) There may be one time lateral entry in the Service.</u>

<u>(3) ..................</u>

<u>(4) ..................</u>

<u>(5) ..................</u>

<u>22. Rule 3(2)(a)(b) admittedly does not apply to the appellants. The question is whether they were appointed to the service under Rule 3(c). Evidently the appellants were not recruited in accordance with the Recruitment Rules 1981. They were appointed by the Inspector General of Police and not by the President or any officer authorized by him as required under rule 5 of the Cadre Rules. Mr. Chowdhury submitted that there is nothing to show that their appointment had the approval of the President as required under the Rules of Business, 1975, vide Chapter II, rule 6(v) Schedule III. Mr. Chowdhury pointed out that appellant Nos. 1-2 were promoted by the Inspector General of Police on an officiating basis as ASP on 17-4-1982 from the feeder post of Inspector of Police without consultation with and recommendation of the PSC. Nor was the appointment approved by the President. The appellant Nos. 3, 4 & 7 were promoted as ASP on officiating basis by the Inspector General of Police on 27-7-1983. The appellant Nos. 3 and 6 were appointed on 23-3-1984 and the appellant No. 8 was appointed on 22-12-1982 by the IGP in misconception of law in purported exercise of powers under Regulation No. 735 read with the Appendix XLII of the Police Regulation Bengal 1943. The aforesaid officiating appointments were made without any jurisdiction and without any lawful authority, Mr. Chowdhury argued. He submitted that Regulation 735 provided for appointment of the Deputy Superintendent of Police (DSP) which was a class II gazetted post until 1.7.1973. On and from 1.7.1973 the post of the DSP was made Class I and redesignated as Assistant Superintendent of Police (ASP) and included in the BCS (Police) Cadre Service. The IGP thus ceased to have any authority to appoint an ASP whether on an officiating basis or otherwise. Under the Cadre Rules 1980 the power of appointment was vested in the President on the recommendation of the Public Service Commission. The aforesaid officiating appointments of the appellants were objected to by the PSC as would be clear from their letter No. SR 2/1 P-3/89/4259 dated 31-10-1992 and their Annual Report for 1993 and 1994 (produced by Mr. Chowdhury). The Commission pointed out that the officiating appointments made by the Inspector General of Police was not authorised by the Recruitment Rules of 1981; PSC was not consulted in the matter and reservation of quota for direct recruit and on promotion was not maintained. Promotion was made far in excess of the one-third quota available to the detriment of direct recruits. The Commission recommended for total stoppage of promotion by the IGP as it was not permitted under the BCS Recruitment Rules 1981.</u>

<u>23. The appellants were thus not members of the Bangladesh Civil Service (Enforcement: Police) Cadre prior to 12.2.1990 and 18.3.1991 until their officiating appointment was regularised on the recommendation of the PSC and they cannot claim seniority in the Cadre Service before that date.</u>

24. Then again 'member of service' as in Rule 3(c) has been defined in Rule 2(b) as follows:

2(b) "members of service" means members of an erstwhile constituted service;"

25. Mr. Khan argued that as the service was constituted by the Cadre Rules on 1st September 1980 the appellants became members of service within the meaning of the Seniority Rules 1983. That they did not even become member of Cadre service until 1990 has been seen above. On a reference to Rule 3 of the Cadre Rules it is found that reference was made to the erstwhile Police service of Pakistan etc. under sub-rule 2(a) and therefore 'members of service' as defined in the Seniority Rules must refer to erstwhile Police Service of Pakistan and not to the service as constituted under the Cadre Rules as argued by Mr. Khan. We have, therefore, no hesitation in accepting the submission of Mr. Rab Chowdhury that the appellants not being 'members of service' as defined in the Seniority Rules and not having been a member of the service Cadre until 1990, rule 3(c) will have no application in their case. Mr. Chowdhury, in our opinion, has argued with some justification that, if at all, rule 3(f) is applicable to the appellants prior to 1990. Rule 3(f) is as follows:

"3(f) Seniority inter se of the future appointees to a Service Cadre, where there is provision for lateral entry at higher levels, shall be counted from the date of appointment on regular basis to the relevant specified post."

26. From the Recruitment Rules 1981 it has been seen that the post of ASP is a specified one and the Cadre Rules in Rule 6(2) says that there may be one time lateral entry in the service. Rule 3(f) may or may not apply but it is clear that Rule 3(c) does not at all apply in the case of the appellants as claimed by Mr. Khan.

27. Leave was taken on a broad ground that the established principle is that unless otherwise provided by any law seniority counts from the date of continuous officiation in a post. Mr. Khan has not been able to show any clear authority in support of the said established principle. Our attention, however, has been drawn by Mr. Rab Chowdhury to the General Principle of Seniority vide OM No. 1/16/69-DII Rawalpindi, December 31st, 1970 which have been incorporated in the Seniority Rules 1983 by notification dated 15 August 1985. Amended rules 2(a) and 4 of the Rules read thus:

2(a) "general principles of seniority" means the principles contained in the annexure to the erstwhile Government of Pakistan Cabinet Secretariat (Establishment Division) office Memorandum No. 1/16/69-DII, dated the 31st December, 1970 and (b) for rule 4 the following shall be substituted, namely :

"4. Matters not covered by these rules—Matters not covered by rule 3 shall be governed by the general principles of seniority or, where such principles do not apply, by such other principles as the Government may, by order, specify in this behalf."

Under Rule B (Annexure to OM above) it is provided in B (iii) as follows:

B(iii) The seniority of departmental promotees to the higher grade shall count from the date of their regular promotion to the higher grade. The word regular implies; that the promotion to higher grades were made in vacancies reserved for Departmental promotion in accordance with the prescribed roster; and

(b) that the promotions to higher grades were made in accordance with the prescribed Recruitment Rules i.e. on the recommendation of the Departmental Promotion Committee or the Selection Board and in Consultation with the PSC where such consultation was necessary under the consultation Regulations and with the approval of the authority competent to make those appointment;

(c) the promotions to higher grade were kept within the maximum quota prescribed in the recruitment rules for Departmental Promotion. In the event of the Prescribed Departmental Promotion quota being exceeded in any particular case or cases, the seniority of the person or persons promoted in excess of that quota shall not count from the date from which the promotion or promotions were actually made, but from the date from which they would have been made, if the quota had been properly followed.

Mr. Rab Chowdhury submits that the appellants will be governed by the aforesaid general principles. In this connection Mr. Khan referred to the principle laid down in the case of Khushi Muhammad vs. GM, PW Rly 22 DLR (SC) (1970) 331 and pointed out that the same has been followed by the Appellate Tribunal in the case of AFM Badiur Raman & ors. vs. Shamsuzzaman & ors. (Appeal No. 30 of 1988) and approved by this Division in CPLA No. 255 of 1991 (decided on May 14, 1992). In the case of Khushi Muhammad, the appellants, who were departmental promotees as Railway Guards, grade II (later changed into Grade I) challenged the list of confirmation-cum-seniority of the personnel of their grade issued by the General Manager of the Pakistan Western Railway. Their grievance was that in the matter of determination of their seniority and confirmation vis-a-vis the directly-recruited Railway Guards, the impugned list was in violation of the basic principle that seniority between incumbents in the same grade is to be determined from the date of their entry in the grade and that confirmation takes place in the same order of seniority. Upholding the contention, it was held:

"We have not been shown any rule to uphold this method of determining seniority and none is discoverable on general principles (as was done in the impugned list). In fact, it is wholly against all notions of natural justice that persons who join service in a grade first should be relegated to a junior position as against those who join later, merely because they fill vacancies which were deemed to be reserved for them All the incumbents have to be treated at par in the matter of their seniority in the grade after they enter it."

28. The principle laid down in that case cannot be invoked in the present case because Mr. Khan himself argued that the appellants' case will be governed by the Seniority Rules 1983. It has been noticed that rule 4 of the said Rules has made the "General Principles of Seniority" applicable to matters not covered by rule 3. Mr. Khan has not been able to lay his finger either on any particular rule or on any established principle governing the case of the appellants as claimed by them. Rather B (iii) of the General Principles as quoted above shows that the seniority of departmental promotees to the higher grade shall count from the date of their "regular promotion" and the word "regular" has been explained. A direct recruit under the General Principles counts his seniority from the date of recommendation by the Public Service Commission or the date of joining the post, whichever is later. Admittedly, the General Principles of seniority or the Rules as are in force today were not there when the decision was made in Khushi Muhammad's case. Moreover, Mr. Rob Chowdhury has rightly pointed out that in the said case the question of seniority and confirmation was considered upon entry into a particular grade by the departmental promotees and direct recruits, but in the present case the appellants and respondent Nos. 1-15 are not in the same grade, the respondents having already been promoted as Additional Superintendent of Police. In view of the General Principles of Seniority which is now part of the Rules of 1983, the principle of Khushi Muhammad's case can hardly be applied, more so because the appellants and respondent Nos. 1-15 are not in the same grade.

<u>29. Now, the question of alleged discrimination. It will be seen from the Annexures 'Ga' and 'Gha' that 97 ASPs who were confirmed from the date of officiating appointment were all appointed before 24-1-1982 unlike the appellants who were all appointed by the Inspector General of the Police on and after 17-4-1982. It appears that the Government had made special provisions for regularization of ad hoc appointments made from 9-4-1972 to 24-1-1982 and their seniority under the Regularization of Ad hoc Appointments Rules 1982 vide SRO 157-L/83/ED/Reg-1/S-4/83 dated 12th May 1983 and Memo No. ME (R-H) S-34/84-78 (500) dated 22.4.84. The special circumstances in which the aforesaid legal dispensation was found necessary were noticed and upheld by this Division in Bangladesh vs. Md. Azizur Rahman reported in 46 DLR (AD) 19. The benefit of that special dispensation was available only for the period from 9.4.1972 to 24.1.1982. It appears that under the said dispensation 97 officiating appointments of ASPs made during that period were regularized (Annexures 'Ga' & "Gha'). But these officiating appointments of the appellants made after 24.1.1982 could not be regularized under the aforesaid provisions. As a general rule, regularization takes effect from the date of recommendation by the PSC. The appellants were recommended for regularization on 12.2.1990 and 18.3.1991 and they were regularized from the said date. The appellants did not have any regular appointment to the BCS (Police) Cadre until 12-2-1990 and 18-3-1991 and their claim for seniority from any earlier date is thus untenable in law.</u>

30. It may be debated how far it was right in applying the Regularization of Ad hoc Appointment Rules 1982 and the instructions in memo dated 22-4-1984 in the case of 97 ASPs but the appellants cannot get the benefit thereof because their appointment was after the terminal date mentioned in the said Rules and memo i.e. 24.1.1982. The appellants case could not be considered by the PSC as it did in case of 97 other ASPs. The PSC's memo No. SR-2/1P-3/89/4259 dated 31-10-1992 which was produced by Mr. Rab Chowdhury brings out the difficulties of regularizing the officiating appointments like that of the appellants in the manner it was done in the case of 97 ASPs and Mr. T H Khan had not much to say against the reasons given by the PSC. It will be useful to quote relevant portion of the said memo which clarifies the position of the appellants and the like:

মহোদয়,

বাংলাদেশ সরকারী কর্ম কমিশনের চেয়ারম্যান মহোদয়কে লিখিত আপনার ৮-১০-৯২ ইং তারিখের ৬৩৪ নং ডি, ও পত্র এবং উপরোক্ত বিষয়ে লিখিত পূর্ববর্তী বরাতে জানাইতে আদিষ্ট হইয়াছি যে, ২৪-০১-৮২ ইং তারিখের পরে পুলিশের এস এস পি পদে অফিসিয়েটিং নিয়োগপ্রাপ্ত পুলিশ অফিসারদের চাকুরী নিয়মিত করার প্রস্তাব বাংলাদেশ সরকারী কর্ম কমিশন সমীপে পুনরায় পেশ করা হইয়াছিল। সংশ্লিষ্ট সকল কাগজপত্র পর্যালোচনান্ততে  উক্ত বিষয়ে কমিশন অভিমত ব্যক্ত করিয়াছে যে, উক্ত তারিখ (২৪-১-৮২ইং) এর পরে নিয়োগপ্রাপ্তদের জন্য অফিসিয়েটিং/এডহক করনের প্রচলিত কোন বিধি নাই। কাজেই পুলিশের এ এস পি বা অন্য কোন পদে অফিসিয়েটিং/এডহক নিয়োগ স্বাভাবিকভাবে নিয়মিত করার কোন প্রশ্ন উঠে না। স্বাধীনতা উত্তর বাংলাদেশ বিভিন্ন কারনে অফিসিয়েটিং/এডহক ভিত্তিতে পুরনকৃত পদে নিয়মিত নিয়োগ বিলম্বিত হওয়ার প্রশাসনিক জটিলতা পরিহার কল্পে এবং মানবিক দিক বিবেচনায় ০৯-০৪-৭২ ইং তারিখ হইতে ২৪-০১-৮২ ইং তারিখ পর্যন্ত এডহক ভিত্তিতে নিয়োজিতদের চাকুরী নিয়মিত করার জন্য সরকার ১৯৮৩ সালে সরকারী নির্দেশ/বিধি জারী করেন। উক্ত সরকারী নির্দেশ ও বিধির আলোকে ১৯৮৩ সাল হইতে কমিশন বিভিন্ন মন্ত্রনালয়/বিভাগ/দপ্তর/পরিদপ্তরের এডহক নিয়োগপ্রাপ্ত অনেক কর্মকর্তা/কর্মচারীর চাকুরী নিয়মিত করার জন্য সুপারিশ করেন। এই সরকারী নির্দেশ /বিধির আলোকে কমিশন ১৯৮৪ ও ৮৬ সালে পুলিশের এ এস পি পদে অফিসিয়েটিং নিয়োগপ্রাপ্ত ১০৩ জন পুলিশ অফিসারের চাকুরীও  নিয়মিত করার জন্য সুপারিশ করেন। এইভাবে নিয়মিত করনকৃত কর্মকর্তা/ কর্মচারীদের জ্যেষ্ঠত্ব নিরুপনের বিষয়ে সরকার ১৯৮৪ সাল হইতে সরকারী নির্দেশ ও বিধিমালা জারী করিয়া আসিতেছেন। কাজেই নিয়মিত করনকৃত পুলিশ অফিসারদের জ্যেষ্ঠত্বও ঐ সকল সরকারী নির্দেশ ও বিধিমালা অনুযায়ী নির্ধারিত হইবে।

২। ১৯৮৯ সালে পুলিশের এ এস পি পদে অফিসিয়েটিং নিয়োগপ্রাপ্ত ৪৬ জন পুলিশ অফিসারের চাকুুরী নিয়মিত করার জন্য কমিশনে প্রস্তাব প্রেরন করা হয়। প্রস্তাবিত কর্মকর্তাদের অফিসিয়েটিং নিয়োগ ২৪-০১-৮২ ইং তারিখের পরে হওয়ায় তাহাদের ঐ নিয়োগ সরকারের এডহক নিয়োগকরন সংক্রান্ত নির্দেশ/বিধিমালার আওতায় পড়ে না তাই ১৯৯০ সালে কমিশন অফিসিয়েটিং নিয়োগ প্রাপ্তদের মধ্য হইতে প্রথমে ২৫ (পঁচিশ) জনের নাম এ এস পি পদে পদোন্নতির জন্য সুপারিশ করেন। মন্ত্রনালয়ের পরবর্তী  প্রস্তাবের পরিপ্রেক্ষিতে আরও ২৮ (আটাশ) জন কর্মকর্তার নাম পদোন্নতির জন্য সুপারিশ করা হয়।

৩। অফিসিয়েটিং  নিয়োগ করার জন্য স্বরাষ্ট্র মন্ত্রনালয়ের বারংবার অনুরোধের পরিপ্রেক্ষিতে কমিশন  প্রচলিত সকল নির্দেশাদি ও বিধিমালা সমূহ পরীক্ষা করিয়া দেখিয়াছেন সকল কাগজপত্র পর্যালোচনান্তে কমিশনের অভিমত এই যে, ২৪-১-৮২ ইং তারিখের পরে পুলিশের এ এস পি পদে অফিসিয়েটিং নিয়োগ প্রাাপ্তদের চাকুরী নিয়মিত করার কোন অবকাশ নাই।

বিনীত

স্বাক্ষর

(এ এইচ এমনুরুদ্দিন)

সচিব।

31. In view of what has been stated and quoted above, it cannot be said that the appellants were treated differently from those 97 other ASPs without any basis. The Appellate Tribunal's reason for rejecting the plea of alleged discrimination is not all but we have seen as above that there are further grounds.

32. In the result, therefore, the appeal is dismissed without any order as to cost.

End.

case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 11th June 1998 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 2588 of 1993)
full_judgment:
Md Fazlul Karim J: This appeal by leave at the instance of the preemptee is directed against the judgment and order of the High Court Division passed on 11-6-1998 in Civil Revision No. 2588 of 1993 making the Rule absolute setting aside those dated 20-6-1993 of the Court of appeal below passed in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 12 of 1989 affirming those dated 28-2-1989 passed by the Court of Subordinate Judge, Narsingdi in Pre-emption Miscellaneous Case No. 28 of 1985.

2. The facts leading to the present appeal briefly, are that, the respondent No. 1 as pre-emptor filed the above pre-emption case No. 28 of 1985 for pre-empting the land described in the schedule to the plaint on the allegations, inter alia, that one Abdul Gafur was the owner of the land of the case jote who sold some land to one Akram Uddin on 26-2-1949 who in turn sold 21 decimals of land to the appellants and his two brothers on 4-5-1949 and thus the appellants became a co-sharer by purchase in the case jote. The said Akramuddin sold some other land of the case jote to one Habib Bhuiyan, predecessor of Mizanur Rahman, Sukri Bibi and Akmulennessa and the heirs of Akramuddin sold 21 decimals of land to Khandakar Anwar Hossain, predecessor of the appellants by a deed of sale dated 12-3-1975. Further case of the respondent No. 1 is that after completion of the registration of the said deed under section 60 of the Registration Act a notice under section 89 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act was served on him on 28-1-1981 and that Khandakar Anwar Hossain being a stranger-purchaser to the case jote, respondent No. 1, as a co-sharer by purchase, is entitled to pre-empt the said land.

3. The appellants contested the case by filing a joint written objection denying the material allegations. Their case is that the pre-emptor is not a co-sharer of the case jote and the case is bad for defect of parties and that the case is barred by limitation. Their further case is that the suit land is adjacent to the house of the pre-emptor-respondent No. 1 and from the very date of purchase the pre-emptee purchaser entered into possession of the case land and since then they are possessing the same by cultivating the case land openly and to the knowledge of others including the pre-emptor. Their further case is that pre-emptor knows about the transfer from the very beginning and he did not exercise his right of pre-emption within the prescribed period of limitation and, as such, pre-emption case is liable to be dismissed.

4. The learned Subordinate Court dismissed the case on ground of limitation. The Court of appeal below affirmed the same. The High Court Division made the Rule absolute allowing the Miscellaneous Case.

5. Leave was granted in the appeal to consider that:

"the learned Judge of the High Court Division committed serious error in disturbing the, concurrent finding of facts relating to limitation of filing pre-emption case since both the Courts below with specific observations held that the pre-emption case was barred by limitation and the sale was within the knowledge of the pre-emptor and hence in exercise of revisional jurisdiction illegally interfered with the concurrent finding of the Courts below by the High Court Division. He further submits that both the Courts below gave specific observation and finding that the notice under section 89(4) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act shown to have served is a subsequent creation for the purpose of filing pre-emption case and there remains variations in the document filed before the Court and both the Courts below held the same as fraudulent document but the said finding of facts have been interfered with by the High Court Division in revisional jurisdiction which is not sustainable in law."

6. Mr Mahbubey Alam, the learned Counsel appearing for the appellants, submitted that the learned Judge of the High Court Division committed serious error in disturbing the concurrent finding of fact relating to limitation of filing pre-emption case since both the Courts below with specific observations held that the pre-emption case was barred by limitation and the sale was within the knowledge of the pre-emptor and hence in exercise of revisional jurisdiction interfering with the concurrent finding the High Court Division committed error in the decision. The learned Counsel further submits that the learned Judge of the High Co in Division failed to consider that trial Court d the Court of appeal below gave specific observation finding that the notice under section 89(4) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act shown to have been served is a subsequent creation for the purpose of filing pre-emption case and there remains variation in the documents filed before the Court and both the Courts below held the same as fraudulent document but the said finding of facts have been interfered with by the High Court Division in revisional jurisdiction which is not sustainable in law.

7. It appears from the impugned judgment of the trial Court that the trial Court held the case to be barred by limitation disbelieving the knowledge of the pre-emptor, as according to it, it found discrepancy as to date bearing in the notice under section 89(4) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act with the date of service thereon. The Court of appeal below, however, concurred with the finding as to limitation but illegally relied upon the statement of the learned Advocate in Court at the time of argument together with the fact that the respondent No. 1 had filed an application under Order XXXIX rules 1 and 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure against the appellant not to change the nature and character of the suit land and not to dispose of the suit pending disposal of the case. Thus erroneously arrived at a finding that the respondent No.1 had knowledge of the transfer together with the notice under section 89(4) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The High Court Division, however, allowed the pre-emption case holding that the notice under section 89(4) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act was issued on 21-1-1981 and the respondent No. 1 filed the Miscellaneous Case on 24-3-1981 which is within the period of limitation prescribed under section 96(1) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and that though the purchase was dated 2-5-1975 but the same was entered into volume under section 60 of the Registration Act on 24-3-1981 and, as such, the case is not barred by limitation under section 89(4) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act.

8. Section 89(4) of the Act reads as under:

89(4). If the transfer of a portion or share of such a holding be one to which the provisions of section 96 apply, there shall be filed notices giving particulars of the transfer in the prescribed form together with process fees prescribed for the service thereof on all the co-sharer tenants of the said holding who are not parties to the transfer and for affixing a copy thereof in the office of the Registering Officer or the Court House or the Office of the Revenue Authority, as the case may be."

9. Thus every transfer of a holding or a portion or share of it belonging to a raiyat shall be made by a registered document under the Registration Act and the deed of transfer must be accompanied by a notice giving particulars of the transfer together with deposit of the process fee for dispatch of the notice to the Revenue Officer and in case of transfer of a portion of a share or share of a holding having co-sharers, there must be filed in the Registration office notices bearing particulars of the transfer together with the process fee for service of such notices on all co-sharers who are not parties to the transfer and also for affixing copy of the notice to the Registration office and the Registering officer shall not accept the document for registration unless the above condition are fulfilled.

10. Thus, a notice under section 89 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act has to be issued in the prescribed form intimating the transfer of a portion or share of such holding to the co-sharer tenants to which the provisions of section 96 apply, giving particulars of the transfer in the prescribed form and under sub-section (5) thereof the Court, Revenue Authority or the Registrar, as the case may be, shall serve the notice as aforesaid on the co-sharer tenants.

<u>11. Section 96(1) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act provides that if a portion of a holding of a right is transferred, one or more co-sharer tenants of the holding may, within four months of the service of the notice given under section 89, or, if no notice has been served under section 89, within four months of the date of the knowledge of the transfer, apply to the Court for the said portion or share to be transferred to himself or themselves.</u>

<u>12. In the instant case, admittedly, the respondent No. 1 being a co-sharer by purchase was entitled to pre-empt the transferred land by either filing an application under section 96(1) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act within 4 months of the service of the notice given under section 89 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act or if no notice has been served as aforesaid, within 4 months of the date of knowledge of the transfer.</u>

<u>13. In view of the above, the respondent having filed the case within 4 months from the date of issuance of the notice dated 21-1-1981 was entitled to pre-empt the case land inasmuch as the issuance of the notice dated 21-1-1981 having the presumption that the official act has been done regularly in the absence of any evidence to the contrary carry a presumption of regularity to hold that the notice was issued on 21-1-1981.</u>

On scrutiny, there being no substance in the submissions of the learned Counsel for the appellants for the ground on which the leave was granted, this appeal is accordingly dismissed without any order as to costs.

End.

full_judgment:
Mohammad Ismailuddin Sarker J: This appeal by the contesting defendants is against the judgment and decree dated 30th November, 1985 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, Naogaon, in Title Suit No. 457 of 1983 decreeing the suit.

2. The plaintiff-respondent Nos. 2-36 instituted Other Class Suit No. 373 of 1979 in the Court of the learned Subordinate Judge at Rajshahi for declaration simpliciter with the following prayer :

"That upon grounds stated in the plaint a decree be passed declaring that the whole proceedings in exchange case No. 1/Naogaon of 1968-69 was tainted with fraud and that the power of Attorney set up by defendants 1 to 8 in respect of the properties of schedule "A" of the plaint was forged and fabricated and, as such, deed No. 29982 of 1968-69 executed by the Deputy Commissioner, Rajshahi is void and of no legal effect."

3. The case of the plaintiffs, in short, is that the lands described in Schedule ''A'' to the plaint belonged to (1) Khagendra Nath Roy, (2) Hemendra Nath Roy both sons of late Krishna Charan Roy, (3) Manindra Nath Roy, (4) Somendra Nath Roy, (5) Satyendra Nath Roy and (6) Ramendra Nath Roy all sons of late Debendra Nath Roy of village and Police Station Badalgachi, District Rajshahi, that the aforesaid owners of the properties of schedule ''A'' went to India leaving behind the properties in the care and custody of their employees, that after the promulgation of the Defence of Pakistan Rules the aforesaid properties were declared as enemy properties, that the plaintiffs were adhiars in respect of the land described in schedule "B" which is part of land covered by schedule ''A'' and they took lease of the properties from time to time from the Sub-Divisional Office, Naogaon, that the remaining land of schedule "A" were also leased out in the same manner to a large number of other bonafide cultivators; that with a view to grab the properties described in schedule ''A'' defendant Nos.  1 and 2 and Kazi Moshitullah, predecessor-in-interest of defendant Nos.  1 to 8, hatched up a plan in collusion with other principal defendants to claim ownership over the properties by creating some fictitious, forged and collusive documents of exchange of the properties, that the said Kazi Moshitullah and defendant Nos.  1 and 2 and defendant No. 9 forged and fabricated a power of attorney and other documents and they filed an application before the Deputy Commissioner, Rajshahi for permission to have a document of exchange executed in favour of defendant Nos.  1, 2 and the said Moshitullah on the allegation that the original owners Khagendra Nath Roy and others have exchanged the ''A'' schedule properties with them in exchange of some properties situated in India; that the said application was numbered as Exchange case 1/ Naogaon /1968-69; that coming to know about the aforesaid application the plaintiffs raised objections before the concerned authorities but defendant Nos. 1, 2, 9 and the said Kazi Moshitullah managed to influence some officers of Government, defendant No. 13 and succeeded in persuading the Deputy Commissioner, Rajshahi to execute a deed of transfer of the properties described in Schedule ''A'' on 3-8-78 in favour of defendants No. 1 to 6 and the said document was registered by the Sub-Registrar, Rajshahi Sadar being deed No. 29982 of 1976; that thereafter the plaintiffs made representation to the Deputy Commissioner, Rajshahi and the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Rev), Rajshahi submitted a report on 18-1-78 to the effect that there was no substance in the objection; that on further objection raised by the plaintiffs the matter was again enquired into by the Additional Deputy Commissioner (General), Rajshahi who submitted a report on 12-4-78/14-4-78 stating that the exchange set up by the alleged exchanges was not genuine; but the Deputy Commissioner, Rajshahi took no step; that thereafter on the application of the plaintiffs the Divisional Commissioner, Rajshahi Division sought advice from the Ministry of Land Administration and Land Reform and the Minister-in-Charge by his order dated 31-10-78 agreed with the views taken by the Deputy Commissioner, Rajshahi; that the original owners Khagendra Nath Roy and others never exchanged their properties with the principal defendants and that the said Khagendra Nath Roy and others never executed power of Attorney set up by the defendants and the certified copy of the alleged deed of exchange is a forged and fabricated document; that the said Kazi Moshitullah and others had no property in India; that Roushan Ara Begum (Defendant No. 1) was never an Indian national and Kazi Moshitullah was a poor man who had been serving as a constable in the then East Pakistan; that Khagendra Nath Roy and others never appointed defendant No. 9 Chowdhury Moharrimad Ali as their attorney for executing the deed of exchange; that the power of attorney set up by the defendants was alleged to be executed in June, 1964 and the same was restamped at Rajshahi on 8-12-72; that after the death of Kazi Moshitullah defendant Nos.  1 and 2 in collusion with defendant No. 9 practised fraud upon the Officers of the Government and managed to have reports in their favour and the Deputy Commissioner, Rajshahi acting on those fraudulent reports passed an order for regularising of the exchange case; that the whole proceedings for regularisation of the exchange set up by the defendant Nos.  1 to 9 has been tainted with fraud and collusion and the orders passed in that proceeding and the deed of exchange executed by the Deputy Commissioner, Rajshahi are void and without any legal effect; that the plaintiffs who have been in possession of the land of schedule "B" for more then 20 years were granted lease of those lands by the government; that had the deed of exchange been not executed by the Deputy Commissioner, Rajshahi the properties could be leased out to the plaintiffs as usual and that the plaintiffs have indefeasible right over the properties and the defendants have no right to destroy their right, as defendants have no legal right to claim title over the properties on the basis of void document. The suit was ultimately transferred to the court of Subordinate Judge, Naogaon and renumbered as Original Case Suit No. 457 of 1983.

4. The suit was contested by defendant Nos.  1 to 12, by the Government of Bangladesh, Defendant No. 13 and by defendant Nos.  23 to 32 and 38 by filing 3 separate written statements. Defendant Nos. 1 to 12 contested the suit by denying the material averments made in the plaint and contending, inter alia, that the plaintiffs have no cause of action for the suit, that the plaintiffs have got no locus standi to file the suit, that the suit was not maintainable in its present form and that the plaintiffs were not entitled to the reliefs prayed for. Their case, in short, is that the properties described in schedule ''A'' to the plaint previously belonged to the Hindu owners Khagendra Nath Roy, Mohendra Nath Roy, Manindra Nath Roy and his three brothers; that those owners of the properties left for India for good some time before 1964 and while in India they intended to exchange the said properties with suitable properties in India; that pursuant to negotiation between the parties for exchange of the said properties described in schedule ''A'' to the plaint with the Indian properties of Kazi Moshitullah, Kazi Badiuzzaman and Roushan Ara Begum described in schedule ''B'' of the power of attorney, the said Khagendra Nath Roy and others executed a power of attorney in June, 1964 for the purpose of completion of exchange document in this country in respect of the properties of schedule ''A'' to the plaint and they appointed defendant No. 9 Chowdhury Mohammad Ali as their constituted attorney and the said Kazi Moshitullah, Kazi Badiuzzaman and Roushan Ara Begum executed and registered a deed of exchange in India in favour of the said Khagendra Nath Roy and others in respect of their Indian properties; that the said power of attorney was duly re-stamped and revalidated; that the said exchangee Kazi Moshitullah died in 1971 leaving behind defendant Nos.  1 to 8 as his heirs; that for regularisation of the exchange between the parties, Exchange case No. 1 /Naogaon/ 1968-69 was started and after due inquiry and report regarding the genuineness of the exchange by competent officers of the Government, the exchange in question was regularised and the transfer deed relating to the said exchange was executed and registered by the Deputy Commissioner, Rajshahi; that the other defendants are transferees from the exchangees; that some of the land out of theland described in Schedule ''A'' to the plaint were wrongly listed as enemy properties in the office of the Sub-Divisional Officer, Naogaon but as a matter of fact those were not taken in possession by the SDO and the plaintiffs obtained some lease documents purporting to show lease in their favour in respect of "B" schedule properties; but those documents were simply paper transactions and that the plaintiffs have instituted the suit without any subsisting interest whatsoever in the suit properties only to harass the defendants on false and concocted allegations.

5. Defendant No. 13, the Government of Bangladesh, by filing a separate written statement contested the suit stating that the plaintiffs have no cause of action for the suit, that they have got no locus standi to file that suit as they have or had no right, title, Interest or possession in the suit land or in any portion thereof; that the properties in question belonged to Hindu owners Khagendra Nath Roy and others, that the said owners while in possession of the said properties intended to exchange the properties with suitable properties in India, that there was negotiation of exchange with the Indian properties of Kazi Moshitullah, Badiuzzaman and Roushan Ara Begum and they executed a general power of attorney in June, 1964 in favour of Chowdhury Mohammad Ali for the purpose of completion of the exchange document in this country in respect of the properties described in schedule ''A'' to the plaint and in lieu thereof the said Kazi Moshitullah and Kazi Badiuzzaman and Roushan Ara Begum executed and registered an exchange deed in India in favour of the said Khagendra Nath Roy and others in respect of their Indian properties: that for regularisation of the exchange, Exchange case No. 1/Naogaon/1968-69 was started and after verification, enquiry and report regarding the genuineness of the exchange by competent officers of the Government the exchange in question was regularised and a transfer deed relating to the said exchange properties was executed and registered by the Deputy Commissioner, Rajshahi in accordance with law.

6. Defendant Nos.   23 to 32 and 38 also contested the suit by filing a separate written statement supporting the case of contesting defendants and stating further that they have purchased some land from the aforesaid exchanges.

7. At the trial the plaintiffs examined 7 PWs including plaintiff No. 3 and plaintiff No. 5 and the defendants examined 2 witnesses including the Attorney , Chowdhury Mohammad Ali PW 1. Abdul Latif Khan is a Law Clerk of Naogaon Collectorate who produced the record of Exchange case No. 1/Naogaon/1968. PW 2 Md. Azimuddin Sarder is plaintiff No. 3 who deposed on behalf of the plaintiffs; he stated that the plaintiffs used to possess the "B" schedule land as borgader and the remaining lands of schedule ''A'' were also cultivated by other Borgaders; that the plaintiffs used to deliver the borga crops to the employees of the owners of the land and then to the Chairman, Union Parishad, Badalgachi. The lands were treated as vested properties and they took lease of ''B'' schedule properties from the office of the Sub-Divisional Officer, Naogaon. He further stated that the exchangees had no properties in India and asserted that the exchange document was a fraudulent one. PW 4 Abdur Rahman Sarder stated that the plaintiffs possessed the suit land by taking lease from the Enemy Property Authorities. But in his cross-examination he could not say the names and numbers of the plaintiffs nor he could say about the area of land or plot number of the land possessed by the plaintiffs. PW 5 Jasimuddin Ahmed stated that PW 2 and PW 3 along with other plaintiffs possessed the suit land. But in his cross-examination he could not say the number of the plaintiffs except 2 nor could he say in which mouza or plot number the plaintiff possessed. PW 6 Amir Ali Khondker has produced a document alleged to be executed by Debendra, Jogendra, Hemendra and Rabindra on 8-1-51 in favour of his father Abbas Ali. He stated that the plaintiff Azimuddin (Plaintiff No. 3) and a few Hindus possessed the suit land. In his cross-examination he submitted that he did not know the plot number of the land in possession of Azimuddin. PW 7 Md Shah Jahan Ali is the Tahsildcr of Badalgachi in respect of enemy properties; he stated that some of the properties were released from the enemy properties but lease in respect of some other properties are continuing. But he did not bring any document in support of his statement and he filed a document relating to order of release Ext.B(1). In his cross-examination he admitted that in view of memo No. 131 dated 19-3-79 those properties were released and thereafter no lease was granted in respect of those properties. DW 1 is Chowdhury Mohammad Ali (defendant No. 9), the constituted attorney for execution of exchange document. He stated that the properties belonged to Hemendra Nath Roy and others and he knew Kazi Moshitullah and defendant Nos.  1 and 2 who had these properties in India.
