8. The learned Subordinate Judge found that the plaintiffs have got right to challenge the exchange in question on the basis of their possessory right. The learned Subordinate Judge noticed that it is a fact that the concerned authority executed and registered the deed of transfer confirming the exchange in question. But the learned Subordinate Judge found that the exchange in question was not a genuine one.

9. Mr Lutfor Rahman Mondal, the learned Advocate appearing for the defendant-appellants, has taken us through the plaint, written statements, deposition of the witnesses and the relevant documentary evidence and submitted that the learned Subordinate Judge was wrong in holding that the exchange in question was not genuine. The learned Advocate has also submitted that the suit was not maintainable at the instance of the plaintiffs inasmuch as they have no right, title, interest and even possession in the land described in schedule ''B'' to the plaint. The learned Advocate further has taken us through the different circulars issued by the Government from time to time to regularise exchange document and submitted that after proper inquiry the Deputy Commissioner, Rajshahi certified the transaction as a genuine exchange and pursuant to that the exchange deed in question was executed and registered.

10. Mr Maksudor Rahman, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the plaintiff-respondents, on the other hand, has contended that the plaintiffs have locus standi to file the suit inasmuch as they were borgaders under the Hindu owners and subsequently they took annual lease from the enemy property authorities and they are thus in possession of the ''B'' schedule land which is part of ''A'' schedule land. Mr Rahman has secondly, contended that the cause of action for the suit arose because of the execution of the exchange deed by the Deputy Commissioner, Rajshahi in favour of exchangees as the same has affected plaintiffs' right to possess that suit land.

11. It appears from the impugned judgment that the learned Subordinate Judge came to the finding that the exchange transaction was not genuine not on the basis of the evidence adduced by the plaintiff but on surmises and conjecture.

12. As to the maintainability of the suit, it appears from the plaint that the plaintiffs, numbering 35, claimed their possession in the ''B'' schedule-and measuring 32.50 acres of land out of the land of schedule ''A'' measuring 269.53 acres. Mr Lutfor Rahman Mondal, the learned Advocate for the appellants, has taken us through Ext.2 series the lease documents and Ext.3 series the Duplicate Carbon Receipts and pointed out that out of the 35 plaintiffs only 17 of them have lease orders and out of the 17 plaintiffs 4, namely, plaintiffs 3, 11, 13 and 15, have lease orders covering an area of 4.25 acres of land out of ''B'' Schedule land and out of the Duplicate Carbon Receipts filed by the plaintiffs Exts. 3(a18), 3 (a9), 3(a7), 3, 3(a), 3(d) and 3(e) are relating to the aforesaid 4.25 acres of land. The learned Advocate further pointed out that out of 32.50 acres of land of schedule ''B'' only an area of 10.27 acres is covered by the land of schedule ''A''. Mr Moksudor Rahman, the learned Advocate did not dispute these facts. Thus, it appears that only 4 of the plaintiffs out of 35 took lease of 4.25 acres of land from the enemy property authorities out of the total land of 269.53 acres of land covered by the exchange. The relevant lease orders out of Ext.2 series and relevant duplicate carbon receipts out of Ext.3 series show that those 4 plaintiffs took annual lease up to the year 1978. The transfer deed Ext. A(5) was executed by the Deputy Commissioner, Rajshahi on 3-8-76. Thereafter the Enemy Property authorities by an order dated 19-3-79 Ext. B (1) directed the Sub-Divisional Officer, Naogaon to note that the said exchange properties were transferred by a registered deed in favour of defendant Nos.  1 to 8 pursuant to Exchange Case No. 1 /Naogaon /1968-69 and asked him to avoid leasing out any property covered by the said document. The present suit was instituted on 29-6-79 after the said order of release and, as such, the plaintiffs, for that matter the 4 plaintiffs ceased to have any annual leasehold right in any portion of the properties in question. It may be mentioned that the lease orders Ext. 2 series contained a stipulation that the annual lessee shall not acquire any right of occupancy on the land and shall not be entitled to hold over after the expiry of the period of lease. This stipulation is in accordance with Article 4(4) of the East Pakistan Enemy Property (Lands and Buildings) Administration and Disposal Order, 1966.

<u>13. As to possession, the plaintiffs asserted that they are in possession of ''B'' schedule land. But PWs 2 and 3 failed to give the particulars of the land in their possession. On the other hand, DW 1 Chowdhury Mohammad Ali although admitted that some of the plaintiffs possessed some land by taking lease from the Enemy Property authorities, stated that after execution of the transfer deed Ext.A(5), the exchangees got possession of 60/70 bighas of land through a Magistrate and apart from those lands late Moshitullah was in possession of the remaining land. From the above evidence it is clear that the plaintiffs or any one of them had no possession in any portion of the property in question since 1979 when the portion of the property taken over as enemy properties was released.</u>

<u>14. The plaintiffs also asserted that they were borgaders under the previous Hindu owners and subsequently became annual lessees under the enemy property authorities. Plaintiff No. 3, deposing as PW 2 on behalf of all the plaintiffs, alone stated that the plaintiffs were borgader in respect of ''B'' schedule properties. But no other witness corroborated him on the point of borga cultivation, not even plaintiffs No. 5 who deposed as PW 3. PW 3 simply stated that the suit land was declared enemy property and they individually took lease; but he admitted that after 1384 BS (1977-78) he would not renew his lease. Thus, although the plaintiffs asserted that they were borgaders in respect of ''B'' schedule land they failed to establish that they took lease of 32.50 acres of land of ''B'' schedule. On the other hand, the relevant lease orders and duplicate carbon receipts show that only four of the plaintiffs took annual lease of 4.25 acres of land out of schedule ''B'' and, for that matter, out of the lands of schedule ''A'' and that too came to an end in 1979. We, therefore, find no merit in the contention of the learned Advocate for the plaintiffs-respondents that the plaintiffs are still in possession and the suit at their instance was maintainable.</u>

15. The learned Subordinate Judge relying upon a Single Bench decision in the case of Jinnat Ali Muktear vs Abdul Majid reported in 27 DLR 385 held that the suit at the instance of the plaintiffs claiming their possessory right as borgadar was maintainable. In that case the plaintiffs claimed possession in the suit property by virtue of a power of attorney in his favour on behalf of the exchange and also claimed possession of the suit land as a borgadar of the said exchange. The defendants threatened the plaintiff with dispossession on the basis of a fraudulent deed of exchange and at his instance the suit land was attached under section 145 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and a Receiver was appointed and the parties were directed to get the matter decided by a Civil Court. Thereafter, the plaintiffs filed the suit for a declaration that he was entitled to get possession of the suit land. The trial Court dismissed the suit but on appeal lower appellate Court decreed the suit and on second appeal the learned Single Judge upheld the decree passed by the lower appellate Court. The question raised there was, whether the suit was maintainable without the prayer for declaration of title and in that context the learned Single Judge held that the plaintiff was in possession of the suit land as a borgader as well as by virtue of the power of attorney executed by the recorded owners. The plaintiff in that case did not claim any title for himself or possessory ownership in the suit land. The above principle is not applicable in the instant case inasmuch as the plaintiffs have challenged the exchange transaction having no title in the land. We have already found that since 1979 they have no possession in any portion of the property in question. The learned Subordinate Judge was not, therefore, justified in holding that the suit was maintainable at the instance of the plaintiffs.

16. In this connection Mr Moksudor Rahman, the learned Advocate has referred to the case of Aminul Islam vs Kilburn & Co Ltd, reported in 18 DLR 691, wherein it has been held that if a person takes possession of a property which belonged to another he does not become the owner thereof; but his possession is good as against others except the true owner and if the possessory owner is wrongfully dispossessed by person other than the true owner he can recover possession. But in the instant case before us the plaintiffs have not instituted the suit for recovery of possession or protections of their possession. Moreover, in this case the defendant Nos.  1 to 8 are the true owners by virtue of their exchange which was regularised by execution of the transfer document in their favour before the institution of the suit. Furthermore, the plaintiffs have no right, title, interest or possession in any portion of the land of schedule ''A'' and, as such, their suit for the above declarations is not maintainable.

<u>17. It may be mentioned that the plaintiffs are neither parties to the exchange nor privies of the Hindu owners nor they acquired any right, title and interest in any portion of the land in question from the said owners. As such, their prayer for declaration that the power of attorney dated 18-6-64 executed by the Hindu owners and the regularising of the exchange by execution and registration of the transfer deed Ext.A(5) cannot be maintained.</u>

18. The learned Subordinate Judge noticed that the concerned authorities executed and registered the deed of transfer confirming the exchange in question. But on perusal of the order sheet of the exchange case Ext.B(2) he noticed that the concerned officials lost sight of certain matter and pointed out that the deed of exchange executed and registered in India marked ''Y'' was executed by one Kazi Abul Kashem as constituted attorney of Kazi Moshitullah, Kazi Badiuzzaman and Roushan Ara Begum; that the exchangees did not file khatians showing title in Indian properties and that after the registration of the deed of transfer the plaintiffs made prayer to the authority to cancel the instrument. The learned Subordinate Judge also found that Kazi Badiuzzaman was minor at the time of execution of the exchange deed in India; that Chowdhury Mohammad Ali the constituted attorney of Khagendra Nath Roy and others was not contacted by the executants of the power of attorney and that the constituted attorney had no possession over the suit land. Upon these findings the learned Subordinate Judge concluded that the exchange in question was not a genuine one.

19. It appears that the learned Subordinate Judge without considering the relevant law and the Government circularsis sued from time to time for regularisation of the exchange case of the Muslim refugees from India with the immovable properties of the Hindu migrants of the then East Pakistan, fished out from the order sheet of the exchange case, that no khatians in respect of the Indian properties were filed but failed to notice that the rent receipt in respect of these properties were filed in the case. He also noticed that certain officials in course of the exchange proceeding made some adverse remarks but failed to notice that the Deputy Commissioner, Rajshahi after proper inquiry issued the necessary certificate of genuineness of the exchange which is the prerequisite for regularisation of such an exchange by execution and registration of deed of transfer. It may be mentioned that the exchange deed was executed by the Muslim refugees for their Indian properties though their constituted attorney Kazi Abdul Kashem and it is apparent from the endorsement made in the exchange deed, certified copy marked ''Y'', by the Sub-Registrar that the execution of the deed is admitted by the attorney Kazi Abul Kashem on behalf of the executants. This goes to show that the Sub-Registrar was satisfied about the authority of the said attorney to execute the document on behalf of the executants thereof.

<u>20. It may be noted that restriction and transfer of immovable properties by the members of minority community was imposed by section 6A of the Disturbed Persons (Rehabilitation) Ordinance, 1964 (East Pakistan Ordinance No. 1 of 1964) with effect from 10-10-64. Then the Indo-Pak war of 1965 took place and Defence of Pakistan Rules 1965 came into operation from 6-9-65 giving rise to enemy property and by the general notification No 1399 dated 3-12-65 all lands and buildings which were declared as enemy property under Rule 182 of the Defence of Pakistan Rules vested in the Deputy Custodian of Enemy Property for the purpose of regularising exchange between Muslim refugees from India and Hindu migrants from the then East Pakistan and detailed instructions from the Government were issued from time to time and those were included in Chapter IX of the Land Administration Manual under the head 'exchange cases'. The first such instruction was issued on the 15th November, 1968 regarding exchange of migrants' immovable properties with bonafide Muslim refugees from India wherein government decided to consider the case of exchange made prior to the 6th of September, 1965 for regularisation; and divided the exchange cases into two categories; namely, (1) those made before the 10th October, 1964, where the properties have become enemy properties under the Defence of Pakistan Rules and (ii) those made between the 10th October, 1964, and the 5th September, 1965, where the properties stand forfeited to the Provincial Government under section 6A of the East Pakistan Disturbed Persons (Rehabilitation) Ordinance, 1964. The exchange in question was made on 18-6-64 and falls under the first category. The following instruction was made in the said circular:</u>

<u>"(5) For satisfaction as to the genuineness of a case of exchange, where the refugee/expellee transferred his property in India to the migrant by a registered deed of exchange, with or without any power of attorney, the following should be considered adequate :</u>

<u>(i) that the examination of the documents produced establishes a prima facie case of genuineness :</u>

<u>(ii) that the exchangee is a bonafide refugee expellee; and</u>

<u>(iii) that the property involved in East Pakistan belongs to the migrant exchanger.</u>

<u>(b) In a case where there is no such registered deed of exchange in respect of the Indian property, enquiries may be held requiring the production of such proofs as may be considered necessary for ascertaining the genuineness of the transfer".</u>

21. In the circular dated 29-11-73 it is directed that in both the categories of exchange the Deputy Commissioner was to receive the application for regularisation of exchanges. In the first category of cases when the Deputy Commissioner is satisfied about the genuineness of the exchange, he should issue a certificate to that effect and the Assistant Custodian Enemy Property (Lands and Buildings) would on the basis of such certificate of genuineness give effect to the exchange by execution of the necessary deed of transfer in favour of refugee on behalf of migrant. By the circular dated 18-11-69 it was directed that the certificate of genuineness granted by the Deputy Commissioner, being very important, should be preserved as a permanent document and it is to form part of the deed of transfer. By memo No. 1245 (18) EP-374/69 dated 21-9-79 the Deputy Custodian of Enemy Property authorised the Deputy Commissioner of the Districts to execute the deed of transfer of the first category of exchange cases.

<u>22. In the instant case it appears from certified copy of the exchange deed executed by the Muslim refugees in respect of their Indian properties dated 18-6-64 (Marked ''Y''), that the Exchanges Kazi Moshitullah and others have exchanged their Indian properties with those of the Hindu migrants Khagendra Nath Roy and others and the said deed contained both the Indian properties and the suit properties. It further appears that the said Hindu migrants Khagendra Nath Roy and others executed a power-of-attorney on the very same day marked ''X'' (18-6-64) in favour of DW 1 Chowdhury Mohammad Ali authorising him to transfer their properties in this country in favour of the exchangees. Thereafter the said attorney filed Exchange Case No. 1 /Naogaon/ 1968-69 before the Deputy Commissioner, Rajshahi on behalf of Kazi Moshitullah and others as attorney of Khagendra Nath Roy and others and the matter was enquired by the Circle Officer (Rev), Mohadevpur, Rajshahi and by an order dated 15-10-69 it was noticed that the exchange in question was a genuine one; but there were further inquiries at the instance of the plaintiffs and it appears that ultimately the required certificate of genuineness was issued by the Deputy Commissioner, Rajshahi on 10-7-76 and thereafter the Deputy Commissioner, Rajshahi executed the deed of transfer on 3-8-76. The said deed of transfer also contained the certificate of genuineness granted by the Deputy Commissioner, Rajshahi on 10-7-76 and thereafter the Deputy Commissioner, Rajshahi executed the deed of transfer on 3-8-76. The said deed of transfer also contained the certificate of genuineness granted by the Deputy Commissioner Rajshahi. Thus, we find that the deed of transfer in question was executed by the concerned authority in conformity with the government instructions and the learned Subordinate Judge was wrong in holding that the exchange was not a genuine one.</u>

23. In the result, the appeal is allowed with cost. The judgment and decree passed by the learned Subordinate Judge are set aside and the suit is dismissed with cost.

Kazi Ebadul Haque J : I agree with my learned brother to allow appeal. But I like to add the following observations in view of the President's Order 98 of 1972 and the submission of the learned Deputy Attorney-General that court should take notice of the law in force in deciding a case.

<u>25. It appears from the order sheet of Exchange Case No. 1 of 1968-69 Ext.(2) that question arose whether entire 269.53 acres of the suit properties could be transferred to the defendant Nos.  1 to 8 by way of regularisation of the alleged exchange in view of the provisions of President's Order 98 of 1972 imposing a ceiling of 100 bighas of retainable land per family as in the meantime Kazi Moshitullah died in 1971 and whether the same could be transferred to Roushan Ara Begum and minor Kazi Badiuzzaman, widow and son respectively of the said Kazi Moshitullah. After much deliberation and seeking advice from the government pleader and instructions from the Ministry concerned and relying on the decision in the case of Province of East Pakistan vs Biroju Sundari reported in 18 DLR 554 it was decided in the said exchange case that the suit lands could be transferred to the said Roushan Ara Begum, late Kazi Badiuzzaman and other heirs of late Kazi Moshitullah on their furnishing an undertaking to surrender the lands in excess of 100 bighas. But curiously enough after such decision made by the Deputy Commissioner by his order dated 3-7-73 in the said exchange case Exchange Officer passed an order approved by the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Rev.) on 17-4-76 to distribute the entire suit lands amongst the defendant Nos. 1 to 8 showing 125 acres in the share of Roushan Ara Begum, 125 acres in the share of Kazi Moshitullah distributing the same in different quantum amongst his widow, sons and daughters and 19.53 acres in the share of Kazi Badiuzzaman and certificate of genuineness of exchange dated 10-7-76 was issued and deed of transfer dated 3-8-76 Ext. A(5) was executed showing such quantum of the suit properties in their respective share. But I find no basis either from the said power of attorney dated 18-6-64 and exchange deed dated 18-6-64 or in law for distributing the suit land in the respective share of the defendant Nos. 1 to 8.</u>

26. The Bangladesh Land Holding (Limitation) Order 1972 (President's Order 98 of 1972) came into operation with effect from 15-8-1972 when the said President's Order was made and published in the official Gazette. The said President's Order 98 of 1972 was amended subsequently by President's Order No. 138 of 1972, 154 of 1972 and President's Order No. 6 of 1973. After such amendment under the provision of article 2(b) "family" in relation to a person includes such person and his wife, son, unmarred daughter, son's wife, son's son and son's unmarried daughter except an adult married son, his wife and children living in separate mess independently of his parents continuously since five years before 20th February 1972. In the instant case defendant No. 1 is the wife and defendant No. 2 is the son of said Kazi Moshitullah and defendant No. 2 was a minor at the time of the alleged exchange in 1964 and they all together constituted a family. After the death of Kazi Moshitullah in 1971 defendant Nos.  2 to 8 were minors and none of them claimed to be major and living in separate mess independently of their mother defendant No. 1 and thus they constituted one family even at the time of execution and registration of the said deed of transfer in their favour by the Deputy Commissioner on 3-8-76 Ext.A(5).

27. Let me now see whether the Deputy Commissioner was authorised under the law to transfer entire suit land showing different quantum of lands in the respective share to defendant Nos. 1 to 8. The decision of the then Dhaka High Court in the said case relied on by the Deputy Commissioner was on the interpretation of the provision of section 20(2) (b) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 wherein there was no definition of the family. Accordingly, it was held that wife could retain khas land within the limit separately from her husband. It may be mentioned that the Deputy Commissioner by order dated 8-4-70 before coming into operation of President's Order 98 of 1972 held that wife could retain land separately from her husband relying on the said decision. So, the said order lost its force after coming into operation of President's Order 98 of 1972. In view of the definition of family in article 2(b) of President's Order 98 of 1972 already noticed the said decision has/had no manner of application at the time of execution of the said deed of transfer in favour of the defendant Nos. 1 to 8 by the Deputy Commissioner. It is also true that a minor can own land but the question is whether he could retain land in excess of the limit as a member of a family. We have already found that defendant No. 2 Kazi Badiuzzaman was a member of the same family with his father and mother and after death of his father with his mother and other heirs of his father.

28. Defendant Nos. 23 to 32 and 38 in their written statement and DW 2 Ahmed Ali Sardar, son of late Abdur Rahman Sardar, in his deposition claimed that late Abdur Rahman Sardar and his brother Abdul Hamid Sardar purchased 23.10 acres of the suit land from Kazi Moshitullah on the basis of sale deeds dated 18-1-1971 and the said deed was burnt in the Sub-Registrar's office in 1971. He further stated that Kazi Moshitullah then died and defendant No. 1 executed nadabi deed dated 22-1-1979 (Ext. A(2). He also stated that defendant Nos.  1 and 2 sold 18.42 acres of land to his father by sale deed dated 17-7-73 (Ext.A) and 13.77 acres of land to his uncle Abdul Hamid by sale deed 17-7-93 (Ext.A(4) and minor sons of defendant No. 1 executed and registered nadabi deeds dated 19-1-79 Ext.A(1) & A(3) confirming the aforesaid sales after they attained majority. Though in nadabi deed dated 22.1.1979 Ext.A(2) it has been admitted that late Abdur Rahman Sardar purchased 23.10 acres of land from Kazi Moshitullah and Roushan Ara by a registered sale deed dated 18-1-71 and the said sale deed was burnt in the Sub-Registrar Office during the war of liberation in 1971 but nothing has been produced to show that, in fact, such a deed of sale was executed and registered as claimed. The best evidence would have been the receipt granted by the Sub-Registrar Office after presentation for registration of the deed, for taking back the document after completion of registration in support of such a claim. In the absence of reliable proof of execution and registration of such a deed and burning of the Sub-Registrar Office in question and destruction of the alleged sale deed were admission in the said nadabi deed by one of the heirs of late Kazi Moshitullah cannot create any interest in the said land in favour of Abdur Rahman Sardar and his brother Abdul Hamid. It is well settled that a nadabi deed is not a deed of transfer and it alone cannot create any interest in favour of the recipient of the nadabi deed in respect of the land mentioned in the nadabi deed. I, therefore, find no basis for the claim that 23.10 acres of the suit land was sold to late Abdur Rahman Sardar and Abdul Hamid Sardar. Moreover at that time alleged exchange was not regularized.

<u>29. Article 5 of President's Order 98 of 1972 provides that a family shall be deemed to be holding land in excess of 100 standard bighas if the aggregate of total quantity of land held by all members of the family on the date of submission of statement under article 7 together with the total quantity of land, if any transferred by them after the 20th day of February 1972 and before the date of submission of such statement exceeds one hundred standard bighas. Article 5A of President's Order 98 of 1972 provides that all transfers of land made by any member of a family, holding land in excess of one hundred standard bighas within the meaning of article 5 after the 15th day of August 1972 and before the date of submission of such statement under article 7 and also all such transfers, on or before that date without any registered deed shall be void. Article 6 gives option to such a family to select the lands to be surrendered and article 7 provides that head of such family shall submit statement by 31st January 1973 and government may extend the time limit. Article 8 provides that if the head of the family fails without any reasonable cause to submit the statement required under article 7 within the time he shall be punishable with imprisonment and/or fine and the land for which no statement has been made may be forfeited to the government and article 10 provides that excess land surrendered by a family shall vest in the government subject to the provision of article 11 providing for appeal and revision and under article 13 owner of such surrendered land will get compensation.</u>

<u>30. From the above provisions of President's Order 98 of 1972 it is clear that no family can hold land in excess of 100 standard bighas and all transfers made by such a family after 15 August 1972 and all transfers, made before that date without a registered deed shall be void. Though the defendants Nos.  1-12 in their written statement stated that defendant Nos.  1-8 transferred some land to defendant Nos.  9-12 without any particulars but no documents were produced or proved in court in support of such claim. Any such transfer if comes within the mischief of President's Order 98 of 1972 shall also be void. In that view of the law already noticed all the transfers by the defendant Nos.  1-8 by the deeds of sale Ext.A and A(1) and all the transfers admitted in the nadabi deeds Ext.A(1), A(2) and A(3) are void and those did not create any interest in the suit land in favour of late Abdur Rahman Sarder and defendant No. 23, Abdul Hamid or Abdur Rahman's heirs defendant Nos.  24-32 and 38.</u>

<u>31. Suit lands were vested properties and after regularisation, of the alleged exchange entire suit lands measuring 269.53 acres could not be transferred in favour of the defendant Nos. 1-8 contrary to the aforesaid provisions of President's Order 98 of 1972 and, in my view, executive instruction of the government to transfer the entire suit land in favour of defendant Nos. 1-8 after taking an undertaking from them to surrender the excess land is not in conformity with the above provisions of law. It appears from government circular Nos. 7-85 (Part) AB/571(64) dated 30-7-87 issued by the Ministry of Land that Deputy Commissioner shall transfer land after regularisation of exchange subject to the provisions of President's Order 98 of 1972. This shows that the government also realised the mistake of its earlier instruction. I, therefore, find merit in the submission of the learned Deputy Attorney-General.</u>

<u>32. In the above facts and circumstances, evidence on record and the law involved in the matter I hold that the Deputy Commissioner was not justified in law to transfer the entire suit land to defendant Nos. 1-8 showing specified quantum of land in their individual share after regularisation of the alleged exchange. Above observation is necessary so that our decision to allow the appeal does not stand in the way of the concerned revenue officer taking action under section 10 of President's Order 98 of 1972.</u>

<u>33. Learned Advocate of the appellants submitted that the defendant Nos. 1-8 did not file any statement surrendering the excess land in pursuance of the undertaking furnished by them before the execution and registration of the deed of transfer in their favour by the Deputy Commissioner due to pendency of litigations. Their failure to submit statement to the appropriate revenue officer within the specified time brings them within the mischief of article 8 of President's Order 98 of 1972 and the entire land in question is liable to be forfeited. In view of the anomaly created in the said deed of transfer and in view of the fact that litigation is going on in respect of the suit property and in view of the fact that defendant No. 1 is a lady and other defendant Nos.  2-8 are her children and were minors at the relevant time and they all constituted one family and they were entitled to retain 100 standard bighas of land at the relevant time they should be allowed to retain 100 standard bighas of land and the appropriate revenue officer shall resume the balance quantum of suit ''A'' schedule land already vested in the government after giving an opportunity to the defendant Nos.  1-8 for expressing their option to select the lands to be surrendered and 100 standard bighas of land to be retained by them. Let a copy of this judgment be sent to the Deputy Commissioner Naogaon to take steps to comply with the aforesaid direction.</u>

Mohammad Ismailuddin Sarker J : I do not agree with the observation made by my learned brother which are not necessary in the disposal of the appeal as nobody including the government of Bangladesh raised this question in the pleading. There is no issue for deciding how much land the exchangees were entitled to retain. Further, the transaction was of 1964 and the deed of transfer executed by the Deputy Commissioner, Rajshahi was only to regularise the exchange which was effected by the parties in 1964. There is also no scope in their appeal for deciding that the documents Ext. A series are void. In my view, the direction to the Deputy Commissioner, Noagaon to resume the balance quantity of land of schedule ''A'' allowing to retain 100 bighas, is uncalled for in this proceeding.

35. Although we agreed to allow the appeal, we could not agree on the scope of deciding the question of limit of land holding of the Exchanges or on the direction to the Deputy Commissioner, Noagaon to resume their excess land or declaring the documents Ext.A series void in this appeal. Hence let this matter be placed before the learned Chief Justice for favour of orders.

High Court Division

(Civil Appellate Jurisdiction)

AM Mahmudur Rahman J

Appeal from Original Decree No. 70 of 1986.

Roushan Ara Bewa and others  ------  Appellants

Vs

People's Republic of Bangladesh, represented  by the Deputy Commissioner and others  ------  Respondents

Judgment: December 5th, 1993

Dr Rafiqur Rahman with Lutfor Rahman Mondal and Md Abdus Samad Kamal, Advocates — For the Appellants.

Moazzem Hossain, Deputy Attorney-General — For the Respondent No. 1 (Bangladesh) Maksudor Rahman, Advocate — For the Respondents.

Judgment

AM Mahmudur Rahman J : This appeal was allowed after hearing by a Division Bench consisting of Ismail Uddin Sarkar and Kazi Ebadul Huq, J J. The learned Judges agreed with the result but as they took contrary view of article 8 of the President's Order No. 98 of 1972 insofar as it relates for holding maximum quantity of land, it went to the learned Chief Justice for order and the learned Chief Justice on 18-8-93 ordered "A M Mahmudur Rahman J will dispose of it as 3rd Judge." Thereafter this appeal is heard by me.

37. Dr Rafiqur Rahman with Mr Lutfor Rahman Mondal appeared for the appellant. Mr Moazzem Hossain, appeared for Bangladesh, Respondent No. 1 and Mr Md Moksudur Rahman appeared for other respondents.

38. The respondent Nos.   2-36 as plaintiffs instituted the Other Class Suit No. 457 of 1983 in the Court of the Subordinate Judge,Rajshahi for declaration that the proceedings in Exchange Case No. 1/Naogaon of 1968-69 was tainted with fraud and the power of attorney executed in respect of the properties of Schedule ''A'' of the plaint being forged the deed No.  29982 of 1968-69 executed by the Deputy Commissioner, Rajshahi is void and of no legal effect. The suit was contested. The trial Court decreed the suit. The Division Bench on appeal from that decision set aside the decree of the trial Court and dismissed the suit holding that are same was not maintainable at the instance of the plaintiffs.

39. Dr Rafiqur Rahman referring to the order of the learned Chief Justice submits that I am to confine my decision of the observation of the learned Judges of the Division Bench on the applicability of Article 8 of President's Order 98 of 1972. He submits that both the learned Judges having had allowed the appeal the observation made by Kazi Ebadul Huq, J on the application of article 8 of President's Order 98 of 1972 in that case is uncalled for and that has correctly been observed also by Ismail Uddin Sarkar, J. He argues that the right, title and interest of the plaintiffs accrued on registration of the deed of exchange after holding investigation and an enquiry under the provision of President's Order 98 of 1972 and as soon as the Revenue Authority accepted the same and registered the deed the same took effect from the date of execution of the deed of exchange and the power of attorney. It is settled principle of law that a deed of transfer, where registration is compulsory, takes effect from the date of its execution on registration. A deed of exchange in the case is a deed of transfer of immovable property. He further argues that President's Order 98 of 1972 is prospective in its operation and in 1964 when the deed of exchange and the power of attorney were executed the family in question was in existence and so far as the present case is concerned it has undergone a tremendous change giving rise to more families in place of one. Therefore, according to him, the original family having had been split up into several families there is hardly any scope for application of Article 8 of President's Order 98 of 1972 in the instant case. He further submits that in view of the frame of the present suit, the question of applicability of Article 8 does not arise for consideration and the observation made by Kazi Ebadul Huq, J seems to be irrelevant and Ismail Uddin Sarker, J had aptly observed that the observation made by Kazi Ebadul Huq, J is uncalled for.

40. Mr Moazzem Hossain vigorously canvassed that President's Order 98 of 1972 no doubt is prospective in its operation but the law is to be applied on the facts of the given case. He submits that as soon as the exchange deed was registered by the Deputy Commissioner and there is President's Order 98 of 1972 the law must take its effect and as the defendants on the basis of the deed of exchange become owners of the disputed land they can not escape from the rigour of President's Order 98 of 1972. I have gone through the preamble of this Order. From reading Article 8 of this Order I am clear in my mind that provision of Article 8 is prospective in operation and covers the disputed land.

41. But, the question is whether mere existence of law will call for an observation from this Court as has been made by my learned brother Kazi Ebadul Huq, J. The question has to be resolved taking into consideration the fact of this case.

<u>42. Mr Deputy Attorney-General submits that a question of law can be raised at any stage of the proceeding and application of Article 8 of President's Order 98 of 1972 is a question of law. There is no doubt about this proposition of law. This brings me again to the questions whether the observation made by Kazi Ebadul Huq, J is relevant for the purpose of disposal of this appeal. My answer is in the negative. The reason is simple. In spite of such observation the Revenue Authority has got every power to take action as per mandate of the law in dealing with the cases of the present nature. The law is there. And it is for the Revenue Administration to apply this law in a given case who is under the mandate of legislation to do so. As my learned brother Ismail Uddin Sarker, J has observed that as the present suit of the plaintiffs failed on the ground of maintainability and as the appeal has been allowed setting aside the decree it seems to me that the observation made by my learned brother Kazi Ebadul Huq J on Article 8 of President's Order 98 of 1972 in this case is redundant. In my view, when a suit fails on the ground of maintainability the law court need not travel further to propound a principle of law or interpretation of a provision of law to examine its applicability. But this has been done here and with due deference to my learned brother Kazi Ebadul Huq, J. I am unable to agree with his view in that regard and I share the view of my learned brother Ismail Uddin Sarker, J. Further, provision of Article 8 of President's Order 98 of 1872 speaks about retention of land and not on the power of transfer by the Deputy Commissioner as has been done in the present case. Transfer of land and retention of land are two distinct and different concepts. To make a transfer a different set of procedure is to be adopted from that of retention. Retention of land more than the maximum ceiling as contemplated in Article 8 of President's Order 98 of 1972 has no legal consequence on the authority to transfer by the Deputy Commissioner in a case like the present one. If anybody retains land in his possession more than the maximum ceiling a different legal issue ensues which is to be dealt with in a different manner and the Revenue Administration is to be geared up by the machinery provided in the legislation itself. Again, it seems to me, Article 5A refers to transfer by a member of a family holding land in excess of the quantum prescribed under President's Order 98 of 1972 and it has no role to play which is made by the authority.</u>

Therefore, the appeal is disposed of with the aforesaid observation.

End.

full_judgment:
AK Badrul Huq J: By this application under Article 102 of the Constitution of the People''s Republic of Bangladesh petitioner, Mr. Obaid Jaigirdar, Settler and Chairman of the Board of Trustees of OJ Trust called in question the Telex Message No.VIII-267/84 /9-J. 3(A) dated 29-1-1990 issued by the respondent No. 2, Deputy Secretary, Ministry of Land, Government of Bangladesh whereupon a Rule Nisi was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the action said to have been proposed to be taken against the petitioner vide Annexure-M to the petition should not be declared to have been made without lawful authority and is of no legal effect and further why they shall not be directed to cancel, rescind or withdraw from taking such action. 
2. Fact relevant for the purpose of disposal of the Rule is as follows: 
Petitioner by a registered deed of Trust dated 3-12-79 created a Trust for welfare and charitable purposes. The trustees of the Trust decided to undertake a Housing Estate Scheme for the purpose of utilizing the income therefrom for the welfare and charitable purposes of the Trust. In the month of January, 1980, the petitioner approached the then Minister-in-Charge of the Ministry of Land Administration and Land Reforms for allotment of Government Khas land for the said Trust. Petitioner on 16-1-80 submitted an application for settlement of Government khas land to the said Minister who on the body of the application passed on order for submission of enquiry report. Respondent No. 4, the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue), Sylhet on 13-2-1980 submitted report. The Minister on consideration of the report passed an order for settlement of 31 acres of khas land of plot No. 1 of Mouza Debpur, PS Kotwali, Dist. Sylhet in favour of the OJ Trust at a salami of Taka 1,50,000.00. Respondent No. 4, Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue), in obedience to the said order of the Minister, allotted the said land in favour of OJ Trust, which paid the salami and Government Tahsilder delivered possession of the said land on 20-2-1980 to the Trust and, thereafter, on 22-2-1980 respondent No. 4, executed and registered lease deed in favour of OJ Trust. 
3. It is the further case of the petitioner that the Superintendent of the Government Cattle Breeding-cum-Dairy Farm put forward claim on the said land and approached the Government for not allowing the said Trust to utilize the land. It transpired, subsequently, that 228 acres of land including the disputed land were acquired for Cattle Breeding- cum-Dairy Farm in the year 1932 in Land Acquisition Case Nos. 220-240 of 1930-31. The said land was not recorded in the name of the said Farm but recorded as Government khas land. The Ministry of Land Administration and Land Reforms requested the Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries and Livestock’s to give up the claim over the said land and the Ministry of Fishery and Livestock had been pleased to agree to surrender the said 21 acres of land in favour of OJ Trust and the said decision was communicated by a Memo dated 5th of January, 1986 (Annexure-''H''). Subsequently, the Ministry of Land Administration and Land Reforms by a Memo dated 21-5-86 (Annexure-T) cancelled the allotment granted in favour of OJ Trust and asked the Deputy Commissioner, Sylhet to revoke the deed of lease and find out khas land elsewhere for the Trust. The petitioner''s prayer dated 31-5-86 addressed to the Government for revision of the said decision stood rejected and the petitioner was asked to submit proposal for lease of alternative Government khas land. Thereafter, the said Ministry revoked the earlier decision dated 21-5-86 and the Deputy Land Reforms Commissioner by a Memo dated 24-12-88 (Annexure-''K'') conveyed the decision of the Ministry to the Deputy Commissioner, Sylhet. 
4. It is also the further case of the petitioner that the trustees of the Trust proceeded with the work of Housing Estate in full swing, built a mosque with the help of the local people and established a Bazar nearby and took all preparations for constructing Housing Estate. The respondent No. 2, all on a sudden, sent the impugned Telex Message dated 29-1-1990 (Annexure-M) to the Deputy Commissioner, Sylhet communicating the decision that the allotment of said land to OJ Trust be kept in abeyance. In the meantime respondent No. 3 filed frivolous Title Suit No. 18 of 1990 in the Second Court of Subordinate Judge, Sylhet against the petitioner and others for declaring the lease in favour of the petitioner as illegal, inoperative, motivated, collusive and without jurisdiction and in that suit plaintiffs prayer for temporary injunction has been opposed by the petitioner and the matter is pending for decision. 
5. The petitioner challenged this Telex Message in this writ petition and obtained the present Rule. 
6. In answer to the Rule the respondent No. 1, Government of Bangladesh, represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Land entered appearance and filed affidavit-in-opposition. Thereafter the respondent No. 3, Secretary to the Ministry of Fisheries and Livestock also entered appearance and filed Affidavit-in-opposition. In both the Affidavits-in-oppositions the material allegations made in the writ petition have been stoutly denied. 
7. In the Affidavit-in-opposition filed on behalf of the respondent No. 1, it is stated that the said 31 acres of land of plot No. 1 of Mouza Debpur, PS Kotwali, District, Sylhet was acquired in Land Acquisition Case No. 235 of 1930-31 for Government Cattle Breeding-cum-Dairy Farm, Sylhet and the said Farm has been in possession of the said land since 1932. The said land was recorded as khas land by mistake in the khas khatian. The Khatian illegally prepared in the name of OJ Trust with respect to the land in question was cancelled by the Revenue Authority on 6-1-87. It is further stated and asserted that the Ministry of Land had no interest in the land in question as the same was acquired for Government Cattle Breeding-cum-Dairy Farm. The Government in Memo No. V-239/84/559 dated 23-8-84 addressed to the Deputy Commissioner, Sylhet categorically stated that the land in question belonged to Government Cattle Breeding-cum-Dairy Farm, Sylhet and the land was wrongly leased out to OJ Trust and asked the Deputy Commissioner to do the needful. 
8. In the Affidavit-in-opposition filed on behalf of the respondent No. 3, It is stated that 228 acres of land including the land in question was acquired in LA Case Nos. 220-240 of 1930-31 for Government Cattle Breeding-cum-Dairy Farm, Sylhet and since the year 1932, the land is under the possession of Government Castle Breeding-cum-Dairy Farm under the Ministry of Fisheries and Livestock’s bounded by RCC posts and barbad wire fencing. The Ministry of Livestock’s and Fisheries is the rightful owner and possessor of the said land and the Ministry of Land Administration and Land Reforms got no legal authority to lease out the said land in favour of the petitioner and the leasing out of the land is absolutely illegal, without lawful authority and void a ab-initio. The Ministry of Land Administration and Land Reforms by the order dated 21-5-86 cancelled the allotment in favour of OJ Trust. The land in question having been in exclusive possession of the Sylhet Cattle Breeding-cum-Dairy Farm since 1932, there arose no occasion on the part of the petitioner to get into possession over the said land. It is further stated that in reply to the letter dated 16-1-85, this respondent informed the respondent No. 1 by the letter dated 27-1-85 that the business and functions of Government Cattle Breeding-cum-Dairy Farm has been increasing day by day and, as such, the question of giving up 31 acres of land from 228 acres of land of the Farm did not arise at all and the order, if any, was obtained from the Ministry of this respondent, that was done by some officers of the Ministry being gained over by the petitioner. It is the further case of respondent No. 3 as stated in the Affidavit-in-opposition that the order dated 24-12-88 got no force of law as because this respondent is the owner of the land in question since the year 1932 and the respondent No. 1 got no lawful authority to deal with the said land in any way. 
9. Affidavit-in-reply was filed on behalf of the petitioner denying the averments made in both the Affidavits-in-opposition and reiterating the facts stated in the writ petition. 
10. Mr. Mahmudul Islam, learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner, challenged the legality of the impugned Telex Message Annexure-M, on the ground that the Government as the owner of the land in question having settled the same in favour of petitioner''s OJ Trust by registered deed of lease and the petitioner having acquired indefeasible title to the land, the Government cannot unilaterally revoke the said settlement and the impugned Telex Message suffers from clear illegality. 
11. Mr. Mahmudul Islam also contended that the Ministry of Fisheries and Livestock’s having consented to the surrendering of the land and handing over the possession to the petitioner''s OJ Trust and intimating the same to the petitioner, the respondent No. 3 is estopped from denying the right, title and interest of the said Trust in the said land and the denial of the right, title and interest of the petitioner''s Trust is volatile of Fundamental Rights guaranteed under Article 31 and 42 of the Constitution. 
12. Mr. KM Saifuddin Ahmed, learned Deputy Attorney-General appearing for both the respondent Nos. 1 and 3, on the other hand contended that the land in question along with other land had been acquired in the year 1931-32 for Cattle Breeding-cum-Dairy Farm and the said Farm is under the control of the Ministry of Fisheries and Livestock and that Ministry is the absolute owner and possessor of the said land and the Ministry of Land Administration and Land Reforms having got no legal authority to deal with the affairs of any other Ministry, got no authority to lease out any land owned and possessed by the Ministry of Fisheries and Livestock’s and the lease in favour of the petitioner OJ Trust is absolutely illegal, without any lawful authority and same is void ab-initio. Learned Deputy Attorney- General while developing his argument further contended that the acquired 228 acres of land including the land in question is well bounded by RCC Pillars and barbed wire fencing and the same is in exclusive possession of the Sylhet Cattle Breeding-cum-Dairy Farm since 1932 and the possession as alleged by the petitioner is nothing but a pretended delivery of possession by persons not competent to give delivery of possession of the land in favour of OJ Trust and it was never actual delivery of possession and was a mere paper transaction. 
13. In reply to the argument advanced by the learned Advocate for the petitioner that the Ministry of Fisheries and Livestock is estopped from challenging the right, title and interest of the petitioner over the said land Mr. KM Saifuddin, with all vehemence at his command, argued that there is no legal existence of any paper or document evidencing the alleged consent given by the Ministry of Fisheries and Livestock’s. In advancing his argument he contended that the Office Memorandum Annexure-H to the petition might have been managed by the petitioner by gaining over some corrupt officers of the said Ministry and that Office Memorandum cannot be deemed to be a legal document of consent and no reliance can be placed on the said Office Memorandum and the principles of estoppel is not at all attracted in the instant case. 
14. In this Rule we are to consider whether the Telex Message Annexure-M to the petition is liable to be declared to have been made without lawful authority and of no legal effect and also whether a direction in the nature of mandamus now codified in Article 102(2)(a)(i) of our Constitution can be issued by this Court upon the respondents to cancel/rescind or withdraw the same. 
15. Learned Deputy Attorney-General produced relevant files before us for our perusal and consideration. 
16. The admitted position is that 228 acres of land had been acquired in LA Case Nos. 220-240 of 1930-31 including 31 acres of land in question for Cattle Breeding-cum-Dairy Farm at Sylhet. The said Cattle Breeding-cum-Dairy Farm is admittedly under the control and management of the respondent No. 3, Ministry of Fisheries and Livestock of the Government of Bangladesh. It is not denied by the petitioner that the said 228 acres of land including 31 acres of land in question had not been acquired for Cattle Breeding-cum-Dairy Farm at Sylhet. It is the positive common case set up by both the respondent Nos. 1 and 3 that Sylhet Cattle Breeding-cum-Dairy Farm had been and has been in possession of the entire acquired 228 acres of land including 31 acres of land in question since the year 1932. The respondent No. 1, the Ministry of Land Administration and Land Reforms in the affidavit-in-opposition categorically stated that the land in question belonged to Sylhet Cattle Breeding-cum-Dairy Farm which is under the control of the respondent No. 3''s Ministry of Fisheries and Livestock. In the backdrop of this categorical assertion made by the respondent No. 1 as to the respondent No. 3''s control over the land in question, the point became manifestly clear that it was only respondent No. 3''s Ministry who had the exclusive jurisdiction and competence to lease out the land in possession of the Sylhet Cattle Breeding-cum-Dairy Farm. The respondent No. 1''s Ministry did not have any authority, whatsoever, to lease out the disputed land in favour of the petitioner OJ Trust, merely because, they said land was not recorded in the name of the Cattle Breeding-cum-Dairy Farm but wrongly recorded in the khatian as Government khas land. 
17. Perused the writ petition and the documents annexed thereto, the two affidavits-in-opposition filed by respondent Nos. 1 and 3 and the documents annexed thereto. We also perused the relevant Government files produced before us by the learned Deputy Attorney-General. On consideration of all these papers and documents we find that the process leading to the execution and registration of the lease deed had been done in a hot haste. OJ Trust was created on 3-12-79 by a registered deed of Trust with the sum of Taka one lac as its fund. Annexure-B is the deed of Trust. The Trust was created for the purpose of performing various charitable purposes, such as relief of the people in general and specially for the poor in regard to their education, health, medical treatment and for general cultural and social activities and other amenities of life and also for various research and scientific projects and religious and charitable purposes. The deed of Trust authorizes the trustees to invest the Trust Fund in any business, industry, security, etc. as the trustees may decide. In the month of January, 1980, petitioner met the Hon''ble Minister-in-charge of the Ministry of Land Administration and Land Reforms for allotment of khas land in favour of the said Trust. An application had been filed before the said Minster on 16-1-80. Annexure-C is the said application. We perused the said application. In the application, nowhere it was stated, that the income of the Housing Estate would be utilized for the purposes of the Trust. The prayer for allocation of Government khas land at Sylhet was for a Housing Estate Scheme for the expatriation living in Britain. The Hon''ble Minister on the body of the application passed an order in the following words: "ADC (Rev.), Sylhet will please enquire and report positively within 2 weeks whether the lands are vacant khas lands and could be leased out to the petitioner trust on long term basis. To 7-2-80 for orders." Enquiry report was submitted on 13-2-80. The Hon''ble Minister on 16-2-80 passed an order for settlement of the land in favour of petitioner OJ Trust at a salami of Taka 1,50,000.00. The possession of the allotted land was allegedly given to the petitioner on 20-2-80. Deed of lease was executed and registered on 22-2-80. Annexure-F is the Photostat copy of the certified copy of the deed of lease. In the said deed of lease, there is no mention at all that the income of the Housing Estate would be utilized to materialize the purposes of the Trust. In the deed of lease there is no recital that the possession had been handed over to the lessee OJ Trust though the possession was allegedly delivered to the lessee on 20-2-1980. The deed of lease was executed within a period of two months and sixteen days of the creation of Trust Deed. 
18. Annexure-D to the affidavit-in-opposition filed on behalf of the respondent No. 3 is Memo dated 12-4-1980 sent by the then Sub-Divisional Officer, Kotwali, Sylhet addressed to the Deputy Commissioner, Sylhet. That Memo is nothing but an Enquiry Report. In the said Report, the Sub-Divisional Officer stated that he personally visited the spot and found that the land in question was part and parcel of the acquired land and the land is well demarcated by barbed wire fencing with RCC pillars which appeared to be as old as the age of the acquisition. The Sub-Divisional Officer further reported that many attempts were made for getting settlement of the said land and in all the Enquiry Reports submitted by the Circle Officers, (Revenue), Kotwali it was stated that the land in question was in possession of the Dairy Farm and the area is covered by RCC posts and barbed wire fencing and being used for grazing purpose. It was further reported that the Circle Officer (Revenue), Kotwali by suppressing facts reported that the land in question was khas land and the same could be settled in favour of Obaid Jaigirdar. 
19. Annexure-A to the affidavit-in-opposition of the respondent No. 3 is a letter dated 7-5-1980 addressed to the Ministry of Land Administration and Land Reforms by the Deputy Commissioner, Sylhet. In the said letter, the aforesaid Enquiry Report of the Sub-Divisional Officer had been referred to. The Deputy Commissioner opined that the land in question was in possession of the Cattle Breeding-cum-Dairy Farm. In the said letter the Deputy Commissioner stated that he for the first time came to know of the illegal settlement matter in favour of OJ Trust from the Superintendent of the Farm when he approached him and intimated of the alleged settlement. Thereafter, the respondent No. 3''s Ministry made a series of letters and correspondences with the respondent No. 1''s Ministry for cancelling the lease granted in favour of OJ Trust. It appears to us that in the backdrop of the letters and correspondences and the actual state of affairs, the Memo dated 21-5-1986 had been issued. Annexure-C to the writ petition is the Memo dated 21-5-1986 by which the respondent No. 1''s Ministry cancelled the allotment in favour of petitioner OJ Trust with the decision that the Dairy Farm was a very important Government Project and no land of the Farm should be given to an individual on the plea that the same was recorded in collector''s khatian as khas land and the Government Dairy Farm could not be penalised for wrong recording of the land as khas land. The Ministry in the said Memo asked the Deputy Commissioner to take appropriate step to revoke the lease deeds and to find out land elsewhere for settlement to OJ Trust and send proposal to the Ministry for consideration with copy to the petitioner. But neither the Deputy Commissioner nor the petitioner appears to have taken any further step in the matter. 
20. Annexure-1 to the Affidavit-in-opposition filed on behalf of respondent No. 1 is Memo dated 23-8-84 from the Board of Land Administration to the Deputy Commissioner Sylhet stating that the land as sought for by OJ Trust belonged to the Government Cattle Breeding-cum-Dairy Farm, Sylhet and the land was wrongly leased out to the said Trust. In the said Memo, the Deputy Commissioner was advised to ask the applicant, OJ Trust, if it wanted alternative land, it might come up with such proposal and also directed the Deputy Commissioner to take the staff responsible in the matter to task. It appears from the Government file that proceeding has been started against the officer responsible in the matter, Mr. Abul Hashem, the then Circle Officer (Rev.) Sadar, Sylhet.
From the Government file we find two letters, one sent by the Secretary, Ministry of Fisheries and Livestock addressed to the Secretary, Ministry of Land Administration and Land Reforms requesting the said Secretary to cancel the illegal order of settlement with respect to land in question in favour of OJ Trust on recalling the order dated 24-12-88 by which the order of cancellation of the lease had been withdrawn and another letter from the Hon''ble Minister, Ministry of Fisheries and Livestock addressed to the Hon''ble Minister, Ministry of Land Administrative and Land Reforms requesting him to pass necessary orders to cancel the illegal lease granted in favour of petitioner OJ Trust.
21. From plethora of letters and correspondences annexed as annexures and also letters and correspondences from the Government file, it becomes evidently clear that the respondent No. 3''s Ministry had been pursuing the respondent No. 1''s Ministry for cancelling the illegal lease granted to OJ Trust. From all these annexure and letters, we find that the entire acquired 228 acres of land including the land in question since the year 1932 has been in possession of Cattle Breeding-cum-Dairy Farm and the land was illegally leased out to OJ Trust on the basis of the Enquiry Report submitted by the Circle Officer (Revenue), Kotwali, Syihet falsely showing the land in question as Government khas land by suppressing the fact that the same was in possession of the Dairy Farm. Thus, lease in favour of the petitioner OJ Trust was the result of fraudulent misrepresentation of facts to the respondent No. 1''s Ministry. 
22. It appears from the letter dated 20-2-80 (Annexure-E), written by the Government Tahsildar to the Circle Officer (Rev.) that he delivered possession of the land in question to the petitioner who accepted the same. But there is nothing in that letter how possession was delivered to the petitioner. On the other hand, it appears from the admission of the Deputy Secretary of the Ministry of LA & LR made in his letter dated 16-1-85 (Annexure-G) that possession could not be delivered to the petitioner as the land was within the boundary of the Government Cattle Farm. Though in the office memorandum dated 5-1-86 (Annexure-H) relied on by the petitioner and seriously challenged by the respondents as fortuitous, the Ministry of Fisheries and Livestock agreed to surrender and hand over possession of the land in question to the petitioner, there is nothing to show that possession was, in fact, made over to the petitioner by the respondent No. 3 in pursuance of assurance made in the said office memorandum. On the other hand, petitioner''s assertion in para 15 of the writ petition that an officer of the Ministry of Fisheries and Livestock went to the said Farm and told the people of that Farm that the land in question would be possessed and enjoyed by OJ Trust has been stoutly denied in para 12 of the Affidavit-in-opposition of the respondent No. 3 as nothing but downright falsehood. Even in that assertion, there is no name or designation of the Officer or the date and time when he went there to say so to make the assertion credible. In view of the above, we find that there is nothing to show that petitioner got actual delivery of possession in the land in question. Petitioner''s assertion of making constructions has also been denied by the respondent No. 3. Even, there is no such assertion in petitioner''s representation dated 4-12-88 (Annexure-J) for withdrawal of the order of cancellation of the allotment. Thus, we have no option but to hold that the delivery of possession of the land in question to the OJ Trust by the Tahsildar on 20-2-80 is a mere paper transaction and never an actual delivery of possession. 
23. From the facts and circumstances of the case as noticed and discussed above, we find that lease in favour of the petitioner was the result of fraudulent misrepresentation of facts and respondent No. 1 though offered alternative land, the petitioner did not care to take advantage of that offer and at his insistence, the order of cancellation was withdrawn and ultimately the said order of withdrawal has been kept in abeyance by the impugned Telex Message. We have also noticed from the materials on record that the petitioner had easy access to the then concerned Minister and taking advantage of the same he exerted undue influence on the officers of the concerned Ministry and was able to manipulate things in his favour by obtaining false report within a very short time. We find that the whole transaction was vitiated by fraudulent misrepresentation. No one can take advantage of fraud relying on technicalities of law. Thus, we find no merit in the contention of the learned Advocate for the petitioner that OJ Trust acquired indefeasible title in the land in question by virtue of the lease deed and the impugned Telex Message is without lawful authority. Merely because the lease deed in question has not been revoked it cannot be said that the petitioner acquired title in the land in question by obtaining the lease deed from respondent No. 4 on fraudulent misrepresentation of facts by unduly influencing the concerned Government staff under order of the Ministry of Land which had no control and management of the land in question. Had there been no order of stay from this Court the Deputy Commissioner would have taken steps to revoke the lease deed as directed in the letter dated 21-5-86. 
24. Let us now consider the soundness of the second contention of Mr. Mahmudul Islam that as the Ministry of Fisheries and Livestock consented to the surrendering of the land in question, the said Ministry is estopped from denying the right, title, interest of the petitioner in the land in question. 
25. Annexure-H to the petition is a Memo dated 5-1-86 allegedly issued by a Section Officer, Ministry of Fisheries and Livestock in the name of Office Memorandum. Said Office Memorandum is quoted below: 
"Government of the People''s Republic of Bangladesh Ministry of Fisheries and Livestock 
No.9/Misc-1 /85/8                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Dated 5-1-86 
Office Memorandum
The undersigned is directed to say that the Government in this Ministry have been pleased to agree to surrender the 31 acres of land currently in possession of the Dairy Farm, Sylhet for handing over the same to the possession of one Mr. OR Jaigirdar as per the request of the Ministry of LA & LR made under its Memo No.Vlll-267/84/53 dated 16-1-85. 
Sd/-Section Officer 
Ministry of Fisheries and Livestock
Phone: 235111/3030 
Secretary 
Ministry of LA & LR 
Bangladesh Secretariat, 
Dhaka 
No.9/Misc-1/85/8/1 
                                                                   dated 5-1-86 
Copy forwarded for information to: 
1. Mr. O R Jaigirdar, Chairman, OJ Trust, 34,F, Road-7, Banani, Dhaka-12. 
Sd/-A Majid Molla
5-1-86 
Section Officer 
Phone: 235111/3030".
26. The contents of the Office Memorandum is that Government in the Ministry of Fisheries and Livestock has been pleased to agree to surrender 31 acres of land currently in possession of the Sylhet Cattle Breeding-cum-Dairy Farm for handing over the possession in favour of Mr. Obaid Zaigirdar as per the request of the Ministry of LA and LR dated 16-1-85. It is the contention of the learned Deputy Attorney-General that there is no legal existence of any such Office Memorandum and the said Office Memorandum might have been obtained by illegally gaining over some corrupt Officers of the said Ministry. It appears from the government file that a letter dated 5-10-89 was sent to the Secretary, Ministry of Land Administration and Land Reforms by the Secretary, Ministry of Fisheries and Livestock. Paragraph-3 of the letter is very significant and the same is extracted below: 
“৩।  পরবর্তীতে আমার ১৬-১-৮৫ ইং তারিখে ডেইরী র্ফাম কর্তৃক জমির উপর উপযুক্ত সদ্ব্যবহার ও তদারকী না হওয়ায় অজুহাত তুলে আপনার মন্ত্রনালয় কর্তক মেসার্স ও, জে ট্রাষ্টের অনুকূলে ইতিপূর্বে প্রদত্ত চিরস্থায়ী বন্দোবস্ত বহাল করার লক্ষ্য বর্ণিত ৩১.০০ একর জমি আপনার মন্ত্রণালয়ের অনুকুলে ন্যস্ত করার জন্য আমাদের মন্ত্রনালয়কে অনুরোধ করা হয় (সংযোজনী ‘র’ )। কোন না কোন ভাবে দীর্ঘদিন পর ৫-১-৮৬ ইং তাবিখে আমাদের মন্ত্রণালয় থেকে উক্ত জমি আপনার মন্ত্রনালয়ের অনুকুলে প্রর্ত্যাপনের একটি চিঠি জারী করা হয় (সংযোজনী ‘ড’)। কিন্তু এরুপ প্রর্ত্যাপণ আপনার মন্ত্রণালয় কর্তক গৃহীত হয়নি। বরং ২১-৫-৮৬ ইং তারিখে সরকারী দুগ্ধ খামারের গুরুত্ব এবং এর জন্য জমির প্রয়োজনীয়তার কথা উল্লেখ করে ভূল রেকর্ডের ভিত্তিতে প্রদত্ত চিরিস্হায়ী বন্ধোবস্থ বাতিল করা হয়(সংযোজনী ‘চ’)।
27. From the contents appearing in paragraph-3 of the said letter we see that the Secretary is not at all aware of the issuance of any Office Memorandum dated 5-1-86 and the words কোন না কোন ভাবে দীর্ঘদিন পর ৫-১-৮৬ ইং তারিখে আ���াদের মন্ত্রণালয় থেকে উক্ত জমি আপনার মন্ত্রনালয়ের অনুকুলে প্রর্ত্যাপনের একটি চিঠি জারী করা হয় are very much significant for the reason that many things happen behind the back of the highest executives. From the above, it seems to us that the said Office Memorandum had been obtained in an irregular manner. However, let us see whether assurance made in the said office memorandum was acted upon or not. Learned Advocate for the petitioner did not annex any paper nor could produce any paper to show that the respondent No. 3''s Ministry, in view of the said Office Memorandum, surrendered and handed over the possession of the said 31 acres of land in favour of OJ. Trust and also that the petitioner OJ Trust took over the possession of the land from respondent No. 3''s Ministry at any time after that date. 
28. On the other hand, even in his representation dated 4-12-88, petitioner stated that Government Tahsildar handed over possession on 20-2-80. There is no assertion in that representation that in pursuance of office memorandum dated 5-1-86, Ministry of Fisheries and Livestock handed over possession to OJ Trust and the said trust made improvement or construction in the said land. Thus, it is clear that the assurance made in the said office memorandum was not acted upon. On the other hand, the allotment in favour of OJ Trust was cancelled on 21-5-86 about 4 months after. In view of the discussions made above and also the facts and circumstances of the case, we are of this view that the principle of estoppel is not at all attracted here. Thus, we do not find any substance in the second contention of Mr. Mahmudul Islam. 
29. Finally, Mr. Mahmudul Islam, referring to a decision in the case of Official Assignee of the High Court of West Pakistan and others vs. Lloyds Bank Ltd. and others reported in 21 DLR, (SC) 177, argued that viewed from the principles of rule of equity, it is in favour of the petitioner. In the cited case the defendant''s deposit money with the Lloyds Bank Ltd. was attached under the order of the court and the Bank was prohibited to make any payment contrary to such attachment. The order of attachment stood vacated on the basis of a forged order purported to have been issued by the court and the Bank, on the basis of that forged order made full payment to the defendant. The order vacating the attachment being found to be forged, the question arose whether the Bank would be held responsible for action on a forged document or the innocent plaintiff would suffer. 
30. Their Lordships of the Supreme Court of Pakistan held; 
"This is one of those cases wherein, even if it were assumed that the bank has acted innocently, there is another innocent party involved in the transaction whose interest has to be put into the balance and safeguarded. In such case, one that could prevent the loss must suffer. The rule of equity which applies as between the two innocent persons in such case is that the one who could prevent the loss must suffer and not the other who was powerless to do so. While the bank in this case could prevent loss by a little more care and caution, the plaintiff who was completely in the dark as to how the transaction went through the bank, could do nothing in the matter." 
31. The facts and circumstances of the cited case is quite distinguishable and got no manner of application in the fact and circumstances of the present case. In our view, the said decision cannot be of any assistance to the petitioner who is not an innocent party in the transaction. Petitioner can take advantage of respondent No. 1''s offer of lease of Government khas land elsewhere but he cannot insist on asserting title on the land of respondent No. 3 
32. Regard being had to the facts and circumstances of the case and the discussion made above, we are of the considered view that the writ petition is devoid of any merit and the same is liable to be discharged. 
33. In the result, the Rule is discharged without any order as to cost. 
The order of stay stands vacated. 
End.

Nahid Mahtab, Assistant Attorney-General—For Respondent No. 1.

Vs

full_judgment:
Syed Amirul Islam J : The petitioner company is engaged in the business of indenting, importing and marketing foreign drugs and medicines and surgical goods and for the purpose of clearing their imported goods they have authorised C&F Agent Mr. Md. Badruddoza, managing partner Messrs Al-Afsar Traders the proforma respondent No.4 and it is stated that all payments are made through that agent for the purpose of clearing different consignments imported by them including the consignments which are involved in this writ petition, namely 18(eighteen) consignments, imported through different Letters of Credit. It appears that the goods were duly assessed on submission of the relevant bill of entries and thereafter the clearing agent took delivery of goods and handed over the same to the petitioner. The case of the petitioner is that thereafter while clearing consignments of the petitioner under Letter of Credit No. 19/WF/14660/01 dated 22-4-2001 for US$ 1,51,174 AWB No. 176-8195-3491 and B/E No. C90626 dated 10-5-2001 it was detected that the petitioner's clearing agent, the proforma respondent No.4, attempted to release the consignment in the name of Messrs Royal Trading Corporation on the reduced invoice value and the same was seized at the delivery point on 13-5-2001. The matter was brought to the notice of the petitioner by the L/C opening Bank on 14-5-2001 and subsequently, on 27-5-2001 the goods were released in favour of the petitioner after payment of the balance duty on 16-5-2001 by the said C&F Agent. After detection of the said fraud and forgery the Assistant Commissioner of Customs Air Freight Unit vide letter No. 5 /Cus/8(40) Freight/Miscellaneous 12000/ 274, dated 28-5-2001 asked the petitioner to supply the relevant papers and documents in respect of import during the period from 1-1-2000 to 27-5-2001 and accordingly, the petitioner supplied the relevant documents vide their letters dated 12-6-2001 and 1-7-2001 and along with those documents the papers showing payment of duties were also supplied. Thereafter, the Assistant Commissioner, Customs, issued show cause-cum-demand notice dated 1-8-2001 against the petitioner which was duly replied to by the petitioner on 14-8-2001. It is stated that from the show cause notice the petitioner came to know for the first time that two other C&F agents, namely, Messrs Royal Trading Corporation and Messrs Helping Hand are also involved in the clearance of the goods but the petitioner had never appointed them as their clearing agents for clearing the consignments in question and no documents can be produced by the Customs Authority showing that Messrs Royal Trading Corporation and/or Messrs Helping Hand were ever engaged by the petitioner. Ultimately, the respondent No. 1 issued a demand notice dated 3-9-2001 as evidenced by Annexure 'E' to the petition arising out of the aforesaid 18 consignments. In this case also the petitioner usually replied to the demand made by the respondent No. 1 submitting all the relevant documents but the respondent No. 1 did not pay any heed to it. Again, the respondent No. 1 demanded payment of Taka 3,24,30,348.27 vide notice dated 27-11-2001 as evidenced by Annexure 'F' to the application against which the petitioner company filed an appeal before the Appellate Tribunal, Customs, Excise and VAT, Dhaka, on 26-12-2001 vide Sl. No. 257. In the said appeal the petitioner made a prayer to admit the appeal and hear and dispose of the same without any deposit on the ground that before clearing the goods in question they have made payment of the entire amount to their C&F Agent and therefore, if now along with the Memo. of Appeal they are required to pay all the disputed amount this will cause economic hardship and it would not be possible on their part to carry on their commercial activities. The petitioner in their memo of appeal in paragraph 4.4 took a ground that they should be exempted from the payment of the disputed amount and also they filed a separate application before the Tribunal on 26-12-2001 praying for the same but in spite of that the Tribunal did not pass any order on that application as a result of which the petitioner out or their desperation moved the National Board of Revenue seeking the same relief for giving a direction upon the Tribunal accordingly, but without any effect whereupon the petitioner company moved this court and obtained the instant Rule.

2. The respondent No. 1 entered appearance and filed an affidavit-in-opposition wherein their main contention is that mere filing of a memo of appeal cannot be treated as an appeal without due compliance with the provisions of section 194 of the Customs Act and therefore, their contention is that although this court is competent to issue a direction upon the Tribunal on any matter but in the instant case it is for the Tribunal to consider this aspect and this court has no jurisdiction in the instant case to pass any such direction.

3. Mr Rafique-ul Huq, the learned Advocate, appearing for the petitioner company, has taken us through the application and the affidavit-in-reply along with, the papers annexed therewith and also the affidavit-in-opposition filed by the respondent No. 1. We have heard the learned Advocates of both the sides at length both on merit as well as on the point of maintainability. On a perusal of the Rule which was issued in terms of prayer (a) of the writ petition it appears that the only relief sought by the petitioner before this court through this application is nothing but a direction for staying the impugned demand till hearing of the appeal.

4. Mr Rafique-ul Huq, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner, submits that from the materials on record it is apparent that the petitioner company has duly paid the entire amount to its C&F Agent and it appears now that the C&F Agent in collusion with some dishonest officials of the Customs Department and two unauthorised C&F Agents managed to clear the goods by defrauding the Government and that matter should duly be enquired into by the law enforcing authority including the National Board of Revenue.
