The learned Advocate further submits that since it is found that the petitioner company prima facie paid the entire amount to its C&F Agent it would be unreasonable to demand a portion of the disputed amount to be deposited along with the memo of appeal and if the petitioner company is required to pay that it would cause great hardship and they would not be able to carry on their normal business and considering the economic hardship of the petitioner the respondent No. 3 should be directed to admit the appeal without any deposits and dispose of the same on merits. He also made submissions on merits of the writ petition. Mr Huq during the course of his submissions also urged upon us to give a direction upon the respondent No. 2 to initiate an enquiry to unearth the fraud committed in respect of the aforesaid 18 consignments imported by the petitioner in the relevant period and the National Board of Revenue should also refer the matter to the law enforcing authority for making an enquiry independently. Mr Rafiq-ul Huq further submits that it is clear from Annexure to the affidavit-in-opposition that there has been a series of frauds committed in respect of the aforesaid consignments and therefore, the National Board of Revenue should also take note of the aforesaid documents in dealing with the matter. Mr. Huq submits that the impugned demand is illegal and without jurisdiction and the Customs Authority cannot press the demand so long the matter is pending before the Tribunal.

5. Ms Nahid Mahtab, the learned Assistant Attorney-General appearing for the respondent No. 1, on the other hand, frankly concedes that this court sitting in its writ jurisdiction can issue any direction upon a person who is in the service of the Republic but in view of the facts and circumstances of the case the admitted position is that the appeal in question has been filed without complying with the provisions of section 194 of the Customs Act and therefore, it cannot be treated as an appeal pending before the Tribunal and in the fitness of thing at best this court can direct the Tribunal to dispose of the application filed by the petitioner on 26-12-2001 praying for admitting the appeal without any deposit. She further submits that since there is no appeal in the eye of law the respondent No. 1 can demand the payment at this stage.

6. Before the transcript was ready, the petitioner filed an application on 3-7-2002 and it was heard on 6-7-2002. It was heard in presence of both the parties.

7. Mr Rafiq-ul Huq, the learned Advocate for the petitioner, submits that from various documents which are annexed with the writ petition it is clear that the entire amount of money demanded by the respondents has been paid by the petitioner to its C&F Agents but it appears that the C&F Agents fraudulently and in collusion with the customs officials manufactured a second set of documents for the purpose of clearing the goods on payment of much lesser amount of taxes and duties and therefore, it is a fit case in which the Tribunal should admit and hear the appeal without deposit of the amount demanded otherwise it will cause quite hardship to the petitioner and it will not be possible for the petitioner to carry on its business. The learned Advocate further submits that the petitioner has made the entire payments of Taka 3, 26, 83,000 more than the demand made by the Customs Authority and, as such, the petitioner is not liable to pay for the second time any amount as demanded by Customs Authority, more so when the respondent No. 1 has clearly expressed his inability to produce any delivery document in support of the claim of Taka 3, 24, 30,348.27. The learned Advocate further submits that on 30-6-02 the petitioner went to the Tribunal with a prayer to admit and hear the appeal without any deposit in view of the facts and circumstances of the case but the Tribunal indicated that it would not waive any deposit unless the High Court Division so directs and the petitioner was further informed that in normal case the Tribunal would reject such prayer and the petitioner may get the order of waiver from the High Court Division. Mr. Huq, therefore, finally submits that in such situation for ends of justice and equity the Customs, Excise and VAT Appellate Tribunal may be directed to admit and hear the appeal without deposit of demanded amount and if no such direction is given it would not be possible on the part of the petitioner to make such deposit and the rejection of the appeal on that ground will cause irreparable loss and injury to the petitioner and considering the aspect of hardship this court may giver the direction to the Tribunal.

8. Mr Md Shamsul Huq, the learned Assistant Attorney-General appearing for the respondent No. 1, submits that he has nothing to add to the earlier submissions made by Ms Nahid Mahtab, the learned Assistant Attorney-General, who argued the case earlier.

<u>9. We have considered the submissions made by the learned Advocates for the respective parties. It appears that section 194(1) of the Customs Act empowers the Tribunal to exempt the payment of any portion of the demanded duty or penalty if it is of the opinion that the payment of the same will cause undue hardship to the appellant. In the instant case the appellant has taken the point of economic hardship both in the Memo of Appeal as well as through a separate application filed before the Tribunal and the admitted position is that the Tribunal till today did not dispose of that application filed by the petitioner company on 26-12-2001 as evidenced by Annexure 'H-1' to the application whereupon the petitioner moved the National Board of Revenue but did not get any relief therefrom. In the instant case from the papers annexed by the petitioner, prima facie, it appears that they have made payment of entire duties and other charges to their appointed C&F Agent and it appears that a fraud had been committed by the C&F Agent, the proforma respondent No. 4, in collusion with some customs 'officials who were entrusted to deal with the matter and a second set of documents were manufactured by them for the purpose of releasing the goods on payment of much lesser amount of taxes and duties. Moreover, the respondent No. 1 has clearly expressed his inability to produce any delivery document in support of the claim. Since it is prima facie established that the petitioner company has made payment to their appointed agent and the said agent in collusion with the customs officials and others defrauded the Government it would cause undue economic hardship to the petitioner if they are to pay statutory deposit along with the appeal. From the materials on record it is crystal clear that the petitioner had paid the entire amount of duties and taxes to their C&F Agent and there is proof also to show that the entire amount was duly received by the C&F Agent. From the averments and the materials it is also clear that a fraud has been committed and that fraud has been committed by the proforma respondent No. 4 in collusion with Customs Officials who were dealing with the clearing of the goods. That the dishonest Customs Officials manufactured a second set of papers is also evident from the materials on record. In that view of the matter it would be against the principle of justice and equity if the petitioner is asked to deposit the amount demanded. If the appeal is not heard without any deposit that will cause, in our opinion, immense hardship to the petitioner and the petitioner may be forced to go out of business which is not good for anybody. If the petitioner survives, both the petitioner and the Revenue will be benefited. Therefore, it appears to us that in the instant case the Tribunal and the National Board of Revenue without any reasonable ground have been sitting over the matter till today without disposing the application dated 26-12-2001 and it further appears that during the pendency of the appeal before the Tribunal the respondent No. 1 has issued the impugned Annexure 'A' dated 2-1-2002 suspending the commercial operation of the petitioner company under section 202(1) of the Customs Act read with section 56 of the VAT Act, 1991. It is clear from Annexure 'F' which is the impugned order before the Tribunal that there is no due on account of VAT but in spite of that in Annexure 'A' the respondent No. 1 has issued a direction upon the Customs and VAT Authorities under the aforesaid sections which appears to be illegal and without jurisdiction. Moreover, an appeal is pending before the Tribunal on the selfsame demand and therefore before the disposal of the said appeal the Customs Authority cannot issue any order either under section 202(1) of the Customs Act or under section 56 of the VAT Act. Therefore, the impugned memo Annexure 'A' is illegal and without jurisdiction and must be struck down.</u>

<u>10. In our opinion it appears to be a fit case where the Tribunal ought to have admitted the appeal after exempting the payment of the statutory requirement. Therefore, we think that it is a fit case where a direction should be issued upon them to admit and dispose of the appeal without any deposit made by the petitioner. Ms Nahid Mahtab strenuously argued that it is for the Tribunal to decide as to whether they would, in view of the facts and circumstances of the case, dispose of the appeal without complying with the statutory requirement of depositing the demanded amount and we have no jurisdiction to give any direction to admit the appeal and to hear the same without any deposit. We have carefully considered her submissions but we find it difficult to accept her submission, more so, in view of the observation given by the Appellate Division in Mizanur Rahman's case reported in 52 DLR (AD) 149, paragraph 36.</u>

11. If we accept the submission of the learned Assistant Attorney-General, it will lead us up a blind ally and yield no fruitful result. If we accept her submission then what happens? She agrees that we can issue a direction upon the Tribunal to dispose of the application dated 26-1-2001. As has already been indicated, the Tribunal will reject the same and the petitioner will be compelled to come to this court again against that order whereupon this court, in view of the facts and circumstances of the case, will, in all probability, issue a direction upon the Tribunal to admit and hear the appeal. This will unnecessarily spoil time and money of both the parties rather; if we give the direction right now on the ground of hardship it would be conducive to justice. Therefore, we are of the opinion that justice demands that we should issue a direction as prayed for.

12. The petitioner earlier filed two applications, namely, one application for addition of parties and the other for claiming for certain documents but at the time of hearing, the learned Advocate for the petitioner did not press these applications as the same could be placed before the Tribunal if they so desire.

<u>13. Accordingly, the Rule is made absolute. The impugned order dated 2-1-2002 (Annexure 'A' to the petition) is declared to have been passed without any lawful authority and is of no legal effect and the respondent No. 3 is directed to hear and dispose of the appeal within 6 (six) months from the date of receipt of this order without realising any portion of the disputed amount from the petitioner under section 194 of the Customs Act.</u>

<u>14. Since in this case there is a serious allegation of fraud and forgery against the Customs Officials, the NBR is directed to institute an independent enquiry to ascertain the truth and to bring to book the real culprits. Let a copy of the judgment be sent to the Chairman, NBR, for his perusal and necessary action.</u>

There will be no order as to costs.

End.

caseno:
Civil Revision No. 27 of 1989 (Barisal)
Civil Revision No. 2938 of 1991 (Dhaka)
lawyer:
Abdul Quayum, Advocate — For the Petitioner. 
Chandi Charan Paul, Advocate — For the Opposite Party Nos 1 and 2.
parties:
Abdul Malek Majhee ------ Petitioner
Vs.
Apser Ali Howlader and others ------ Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
A.K. Badrul Huq, J: Feeling aggrieved by a judgment passed by the appellate Court allowing appeal on reversing the judgment passed by the trial Court dismissing pre-emption case under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, the pre-emptor approached this Court in an application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure whereupon Rule was issued calling upon the opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 to show cause as to why the impugned order dated 10-9-88 passed by the Subordinate Judge, Pirojpur in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 22 of 1986 should not be set aside.

2. The only question which falls for determination in this Rule is whether clause (a) of sub-section 10 of section 96 of State Acquisition and Tenancy Act stands as a bar for the pre-emptor to preempt the land under the deed of transfer in favour of the pre-emptee who became a co-sharer in the tenancy by way of inheritance not on the date of transfer but subsequent to the date of transfer.

3. For the purpose of determining the point posed, the factual canvass of the matter may be adverted to which is as follows:

The petitioner as pre-emptor instituted Miscellaneous Case No. 6 of 1984 in the Court of learned Assistant Judge, Kowkhali Upazila under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act for pre-empting the land under the deed of sale dated 1-7-1978 on the ground that he is a non-notified co-sharer by inheritance and he for the first time on 2-10-79 became aware of the kabala under the miscellaneous proceeding and thereafter filed the case.

4. The opposite party Nos.1 and 2 being pre-emptees resisted the case by filing written objection taking the ground that the application for pre-emption was not maintainable as because they became co-sharers by way of inheritance. It was pleaded that the transferor opposite parties who were co-sharers by inheritance having died subsequent to the kabala deed under the pre-emption proceeding, they became co-sharers by way of inheritance and they were protected under section 96(10)(a) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and the pre-emption case was not maintainable.

5. The trial Judge allowed the pre-emption case with the decision that the pre-emptor was a co-sharer by inheritance and the co-sharer transferors were alive on the date of kabala deed dated 1-7-78 and pre-emptee could not acquire the status of co-sharership by way of inheritance on the death of their predecessor co-sharer transferors, subsequent to the said transfer and they were strangers to the proceeding land. The learned trial Judge further held that the case was not barred by limitation.

6. The pre-emptees felt aggrieved by the said decision and sought setting aside the same through a medium of appeal before the learned District Judge, Pirojpur. The appellate Court although concurred with the finding arrived at by the trial Court that the petitioner was a co-sharer by way of inheritance and that the case was not barred by limitation, set aside the judgment of the trial Court with the findings that the pre-emptees acquired the status of co-sharership by way of inheritance on the death of their predecessor Hamejuddin and Alikjan, the transferors and hence they were protected under section 96(10)(a) of State Acquisition and Tenancy Act.

7. The pre-emptor being aggrieved by the judgment of the appellate Court, approached this court in an application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure and obtained the present Rule.

8. Mr Abdul Quayum, learned Advocate for the pre-emptor petitioner appearing in support of the Rule, contended that the pre-emptee opposite parties were not co-sharers on the date of the deed of transfer and in the event of any change of status of co-sharership of the pre-emptees, the right of pre-emption accrued to the pre-emptor would not be affected. The further contention of the learned Advocate is that, the acquisition of interest by the pre-emptees subsequent to the impugned kabala cannot take away the right of pre-emption of the pre-emptor and the lower appellate Court misdirected itself in its total approach of the matter and committed a substantial error of law in finding that in view of the bar under section 96 (10)(a) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, the pre-emption case was not maintainable against the pre-emptess. In support of the contention reliance had been placed in the case of Abdul Baten vs. Abdul Latif Sheikh and others reported in 45 DLR (AD) 26. In the said case the Appellate Division held that the right of pre-emption accrued to the pre-emptor is not affected by the subsequent acquisition of co-sharership by the pre-emptor.

9. Learned Advocate for the pre-emptor petitioner next submitted that although the right of preemption accrues when all the formalities as required under section 60 of the Registration Act is complied with but the right of the party vests when the deed is executed. Referring to section 47 of the Registration Act, it is argued by the learned Advocate that the status of a party relates back to the date of execution of the deed of transfer, though the deed is completed when the same is copied out under section 60 of the Registration Act. In advancement of the said contention, Mr. Abdul Quayum, further, contended that, although, for the purpose of exercising a right of pre-emption, the said right accrues on the compliance of the provision of section 60 of the Registration Act but status of the party and the vesting of title will be governed by section 47 of the Registration Act.

<u>10. Mr Chandi Charan Paul, learned Advocate representing the pre-emptee opposite parties, on the other hand, submitted that the question of vesting of title from the date of the execution of a deed of transfer is not the material issue, rather the material issue is when the right accrues in exercising the right of pre-emption. The right to pre-empt a land under transfer accrues when the deed is copied out on completion of all formalities as required under section 60 of the Registration Act, learned Advocate, then argued. The pre-emptee opposite party acquired the status of co-sharership by inheritance from the death of their predecessors who were co-sharer transferors of the case holding long before the deed of transfer was copied out under section 60 of the Registration Act, Mr Paul, further submitted. In support of the said contention, the decision in the case of Abdur Rahman vs. Baser Ali and others reported in 21 DLR 599 has been referred to. In the said case it was held by the High Court that the right of pre-emption accrues not on the date of execution of the deed but on the date of its registration. The principle of law enunciated in the said case is not at all disputed and that is the correct proposition of law.</u>

11. To appreciate the rival contentions advanced by the learned Advocates of both the sides, it will be appropriate to notice the provisions of section 96(10)(a) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and sections 47 and 60 of the Registration Act which read as follows respectively :

Section 96(10) (a) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act.

Section 96(10) Nothing in this section shall apply to (a) a transfer to a co-sharer in the tenancy whose interest has accrued otherwise than by purchase. Sections 47 and 60 of the Registration Act :

"47. Time From Which Registered Document Operates-A registered document shall operate from the time from which it would have commenced to operate if no registration thereof had been required or made, and not from the time of its registration.

60. Certificate of Registration—(1) After such of the provisions of sections 34, 35, 58 and 59 as apply to any document presented for registration have been complied with, the registering officer shall endorse thereon a certificate containing the word "registered", together with the number and page of the book in which the document has been copied.

(2) Such certificate shall be signed, sealed and dated by the registering officer, and shall then be admissible for the purpose of proving that the document has been duly registered in the manner provided by this Act, and that the facts mentioned in the endorsements referred to in section 59 have occurred as therein mentioned.

12. Clause (a) of sub-section 10 of section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act lays down that a transfer to a co-sharer whose interest in the land transferred has accrued by inheritance is not liable to pre-emption.

13. Section 47 of Registration Act provides that a registered document shall operate from the time from which it would have commenced to operate if no registration thereof had been required or made and not from the time of its registration.

14. Section 60 of the said Act provides that a document can be said to be registered only when the Registering Officer after completing the preliminary formalities enjoined under sections 34, 35, 57 and 59 of the Registration Act has endorsed thereon the certificate.

15. From a plain reading of the aforesaid provisions it appears that the presentation of document for registration and admission of its execution are merely preliminary steps towards registration.

16. The deed of transfer under the pre-emption proceeding is dated 1-7-78 and the said deed was copied out under section 60 of the Registration Act on 11-6-79. The pre-emption Miscellaneous case was filed on 22-10-79. It is admitted by both the parties that Hamejuddin, the transferor, died on 20th Ashar, 1385 BS which is after four days of the date of the execution of the kabala deed and for presentation of the same for registration. Hamejuddin is the father of pre-emptee opposite party No. 2 Zibannessa. Alikjan Bibi, another transferor, died in the month of Ashwin, 1385 BS which is about 2½ months after the execution of the said deed of transfer. Alikjan Bibi is the mother of pre-emptee opposite party No. 1, Apser Ali Howlader. The admitted position is that the transferors Hamejuddin and Alikjan Bibi died long before the date 11-6-79 when the deed of transfer was copied out under section 60 of the Registration Act. Law is well settled that the right of pre-emption accrues not on the date of execution but on the date of registration, meaning thereby not on the date when the deed is presented for registration but on the date when the deed is copied out under section 60 of the said Act on completion of all formalities. In the instant case before me, the right of pre-emption on the part of the pre-emptor accrued on 11-6-79 and before that the pre-emptees acquired the status of co-sharership by inheritance on the death of their predecessors who were co-sharer transferors.

17. Section 47 of the Registration Act governs from which point of time the title will vest with a party and got no bearing on the question of accrual of the right of pre-emption. In the case of Abdul Baten vs. Abdul Latif Sheikh and others, 45 DLR (AD) 26 referred to by the learned Advocate for the petitioner, the interpretation of clause (a) of sub-section 10 of section 96 of State Acquisition and Tenancy Act came up for consideration before their Lordships of the Appellate Division. The Appellate Division held: "The right of pre-emption accrued to the pre-emptor is not affected by subsequent acquisition of co-sharership by the pre-emptee". In deciding the said case application of section 47 of the Registration Act along with clause (a) of sub-section 10 of section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act did not come up for consideration before their Lordships.

18. This question came up for consideration before their Lordships of the Appellate Division in the case of Ayesha Khatun (Musammat) vs. Musammat Jahanara Begum and others reported in 43 DLR (AD) 9 wherein interpretation of both the sections 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and 47 of the Registration Act was involved. The observations of their Lordships of the Appellate Division are covered in the following terms : "It is now a settled principle of law that the cause of action under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act accrues on the date of registration of the deed of sale, when registration is compulsory. This is because the right of pre-emption arises on the completion of the transfer. It could not be said to have been completed earlier by reason of section 47 of the Registration Act though there-under the instrument of transfer commences to operate from earlier date. "Mr Abdul Quayum with all fairness submitted before me that in view of the said decision of the Appellate Division, he cannot now say that he got a point to be decided in favour of the pre-emptor.

19. In view of the discussion made hereinabove and also viewed in the light of the aforesaid principle of law enunciated by our Appellate Division I am of the considered view that clause (a) of sub-section 10 of section 96 of State Acquisition and Tenancy Act stands as a bar on the part of the pre-emptor to maintain his application against the pre-emptee who acquired the status of a co-sharership by way of inheritance before the deed of transfer under the pre-emption proceeding was registered. The judgment of the appellate Court is well founded on law and the same does not warrant any interference by this court in the exercise of the power under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The Rule is devoid of any substance and the same, thus, is liable to be discharged.

20. In the result, the Rule stands discharged. The judgment passed by the lower appellate Court in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 22 of 1986 is maintained.

21. Having regard to the facts and circumstances of the case I make no order as to costs.

Let the lower court''s records be sent down at once.

End.

lawyer:
Faruque Ahmed, with Quamrunnessa, Advocates — For the Petitioners.
Mahbubey Alam, with A M Amin Uddin, Advocates — For the Opposite Party No.1
parties:
Shahjahan Mizi and others ------ Petitioners
Vs.
Md Shamsul Hoque Mizi and others ------ Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
By this application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the concurrent decisions of the courts below have been called in question whereupon Rule was issued calling upon the First and Second Opposite Parties to show cause as to why the judgment and decree complained of in the petition moved in court should not be set aside.

2. Facts leading to issuance of this Rule may be summarised which are as follows: The First and Second Opposite Parties as plaintiffs instituted a suit being Title Suit No. 32 of 1980 in the Third Court of Subordinate Judge at Comilla for declaration of title and recovery of possession of the suit land. The suit on transfer to the court of the Subordinate Judge, Chandpur was re-numbered as Title Suit No. 172 of 1981. Case of the plaintiffs, in short, is that Chandra Mohan Chowdhury was the owner of the suit land comprising of an area of 0.01 acre of land situated at Mohamaya Bazar. Chandra Mohan Chowdhury settled the same with structures standing thereon in favour of Abdul Jalil Mizi, defendant No. 8 who executed and registered a kabuliyat dated 23-8-1951 on his behalf as well as his full-brother Abdul Jabbar Mizi, the predecessor of defendant Nos.  1 and 2 Abdul Jalil Mizi, acquired the suit land out of the joint family fund for his own benefits and also for the benefit of his full-brother Abdul Jabbar. On amicable partition Abdul Jabbar Mizi used to own and possess northern half of the suit land with the structure described in schedule 1(ka) to the plaint and Abdul Jalil Mizi, used to own and possess the remaining southern portion of the land with the structure described in schedule 1(kah) to the plaint. During Revisional Settlement Operation the suit land was recorded both in the names of Abdul Jalil Mizi and Abdul Jabbar Mizi in Revisional Settlement Khatian No. 134 in equal shares. Abdul Jabbar Mizi transferred his portion of land with structure standing thereon to Serajul Islam Mizi, the defendant No. 9 by registered sale deed dated 16-9-1970 and possession was handed over to the transferee Serajul Islam Mizi. During the War of Liberation Abdul Jabbar Mizi died leaving behind two sons defendant Nos.   1 and 2 who approached their cousin defendant No. 9 in the year 1972 to permit them to start tea stall in ''Ka'' schedule land and permission was accordingly accorded by the defendant No. 9 and the defendant Nos.   1 and 2 since then remained there as licensees under defendant No. 9. Abdul Jalil Mizi also transferred his portion of land with structures thereon in favour of defendant No. 9 by a registered deed of conveyance dated 1-2-1977 and parted with possession. Defendant No. 9 allowed his uncle defendant No. 4 to run a business in the southern half of schedule ''Ka'' land as a licensee. The defendant Nos.   5 and 6 are the sons of defendant No. 4. The defendant No. 9 being the absolute owner over the suit land and the structures standing thereon, transferred the same in favour of the plaintiffs by way of two registered sale deeds dated 23-6-1979. The plaintiff, after purchase asked the defendant Nos.1-6 to hand over the vacant possession of the suit property in his favour. The defendants got no right, title and interest in the suit land. They having declined to give vacant possession of the suit property, the plaintiffs have been constrained to institute the suit for the reliefs stated above.

3. The defendant Nos.   1 and 2 contested the suit by presenting joint written statement which was thereafter supplemented by Better Statement. In the written statement it is stated that the suit land was self acquired property of Abdul Jalil Mizi, defendant No. 8 and while in possession allowed his full-brother Abdul Jabbar Mizi to start business on the northern half of the suit land. Abdul Jabbar Mizi having fallen in great financial distress, with the permission of Abdul jalil Mizi, transferred the schedule 1 (ka, land with structure thereon in favour of Serajul Islam Mizi, defendant No. 9 by registered sale deed dated 16-9-1970 and the said sale deed was accompanied with a contemporaneous registered deed of agreement for reconveyance. During the War of Liberation of the year 1971, the structure on the suit land was set on fire by Pakistan Occupation Army and Abdul Jabbar Mizi was also killed by the Army. It is also averred that defendant No. 8 made an oral gift with respect to schedule 1(ka) land in the middle part of the year 1972 and defendant Nos. 1 and 2 after reconstruction of the but started a Tea Stall. It is also pleaded that the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 let out a portion of their but to defendant No. 3, Kalu Patwary as a monthly tenant on 18-7-1979. It is again asserted that the defendant No. 8 in confirmation of the earlier oral gift registered a deed of gift in favour of defendant Nos.   1 and 2 and the defendant No. 9 purchased the northern half of the suit land subject to an agreement of reconveyance and the land of schedule 1(ka) by operation of law stood redeemed in the year 1977 being the said deed a usufructuary mortgage.

4. The defendant No. 6 also filed a written statement taking the stand that the defendant No. 9 acquired no title on the basis of a purchase from Abdul Jabbar Mizi and Abdul Jalil Mizi. The further plea is that, the plaintiff acquired no legal right on the suit land on the basis of purchase from defendant No. 9 and their kabalas are illegal and void.''

5. Over the pleadings of the parties five issues have been framed which are as follows :

1. Is the suit maintainable in its present form?

2. Have the plaintiffs right, title interest in the suit land?

3. Are the plaintiffs entitled to get khas possession of the suit land?

4. Is the impugned deed dated 18-7-79 liable to be declared void, illegal, collusive and not binding upon the plaintiffs.

5. To what relief, if any, are the plaintiffs entitled to?

6. Both the parties adduced evidence both oral and documentary in support of their respective contentions/pleas.

7. The learned Trial Judge on a consideration of the legal evidences and other materials on record recorded the finding that the suit land belonged to the two brothers Abdul Jalil Mizi and Abdul Jabbar Mizi in equal shares. The learned trial Judge further recorded the finding that the story of oral gift in favour of the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 is false and the deed of gift dated 18-7-79 in favour of the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 is collusive one. The learned trial Judge held that the defendant No. 1 purchased the entire suit land and the defendant Nos. 1, 2 and 4 are in permissive possession of the suit land under the defendant No. 9 and the plaintiffs acquired valid title by purchase from defendant No. 9. With the above findings the trial Judge decreed the suit.

8. The defendant Nos. 1, 2 and 6, against the said decisions of the trial Judge, carried an appeal to the court of District Judge, Chandpur but without any success. The learned District Judge concurred with the decisions arrived at by the trial Judge who in agreement with the decisions of the trial Judge held that the story of oral gift is absolutely false and the plaintiffs acquired valid title on the suit land by purchase from defendant No. 9 in the year 1979 on the basis of two sale deeds. The learned District Judge also found that the deed of gift in favour of defendant Nos. 1 and 2 is a collusive document created by defendant No. 8 who ceased to have any subsisting interest on the suit land long before the execution of the deed. The learned District Judge also recorded the finding that the plaintiffs instituted the suit within 12 years from 1972 when the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 first went into possession admittedly as licensees and entitled to the reliefs sought for subject to the right of redemption of schedule 1(ka) land by the legal heirs of late Abdul Jabbar according to law laid down in section 95(4) of State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The learned Judge, thus, dismissed the appeal and affirmed the judgment and decrees passed by the trial Judge subject to the modification that the plaintiffs'' title to the disputed 1(ka) schedule land be declared subject to the right of redemption by the legal heirs of late Abdul Jabbar Mizi.

9. Feeling aggrieved by the aforesaid decision of the appellate Court, the defendant Nos. 1, 2 and 6 challenged the propriety of those decisions before this Court in an application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure and obtained the present Rule.

10. The plaintiff-opposite-parties appeared and opposed the Rule by filing an Affidavit-in-opposition. In the Affidavit-in-opposition it is stated that the Redemption Case No. 3 of 1987 filed by the defendant-petitioners has been allowed by the Upazila Revenue Officer on 8-6-1987 and on appeal preferred by the plaintiff-opposite-parties, the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) being the appellate Authority allowed the said appeal. The order allowing the Redemption Case by the Upazila Revenue Officer and the order allowing the appeal on setting aside the order of redemption passed by the Upazila Revenue Officer are annexed in the Affidavit-in-opposition as Annexures-1 and 2 respectively.

11. The findings that the oral gift and the subsequent registered deed of gift by defendant No. 8 in favour of defendant Nos. 1 and 2 are collusive and that the plaintiffs acquired valid title in the suit land by way of purchase from defendant No. 9 by two sale deeds and that defendant Nos. 1, 2 and 4 are in permissive possession have been concluded by concurrent finding of fact. On going through the judgments and also on examination of the reasons given by both the courts below it is not at all possible to hold that the conclusions are perverse or even that those are against the weight of evidence on record. It is a case of reasonably possible factual appreciation and proper assessment of the entire evidence, materials and circumstances brought on record. It is well recognised that this Court in exercising Revisional Jurisdiction under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure cannot interfere with a finding of fact. A finding of fact is immune from attack in revision unless it is shown that the finding is based on gross misreading of evidence or non-consideration of material evidence or it has been founded on misconception or misapplication of law or misinterpretation of any material document or otherwise it is perverse being contrary to the evidences on record. From the judgments of the courts below it is not at all possible to hold that the finding is based on misreading of evidence or non-consideration of material evidence or the same has been founded on misapplication or misinterpretation of any material document. It cannot be also shown that the decisions of the courts below are perverse being contrary to law and the legal evidence brought on record.

<u>12. Mr Faruque Ahmed, followed up by Quamrunnessa, learned Advocates, addressed me raising the only contention that the remedy that was open to the plaintiff-opposite-parties was in a suit for foreclosure as enjoined under section 67 of the Transfer of Property Act of 1882 and the suit praying for the reliefs of declaration of title and recovery of possession on the suit land is not at all maintainable. In support of the said contention reliance has been placed on Lal Nursing Pratap Bahadur Singh vs Mohammad Yeakub Khan and others, AIR 1929 PC 139 and Bishna Prasad Ram and others vs Anup Narayan Singh AIR 1949 Patna 166.</u>

<u>13. The contention so raised is no doubt a question of law. But it is to be remembered that question of law follows from the fact proved. The defendants did neither set up this plea/contention in their written statement nor in the Memorandum of Appeal presented before the appellate Court nor taken as a ground in the Revisional application. This contention for the first time has been pressed into service before this Court orally at the time of the hearing of this Rule. This plea/contention, if would have been raised in the written statement or in the Memorandum of Appeal before the appellate Court, the plaintiff-opposite-parties would have got an opportunity to meet or to resist the same. The plaintiff-opposite-parties could not get any opportunity to meet and resist this plea. This plea having been for the first time raised orally before this Court at the time of hearing of the Rule, in exercising discretionary power under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, it is difficult for me to take into consideration of the said contention. The authorities cited from the side of the petitioners having been quite distinguishable in the facts and circumstances of the present case, the petitioners cannot get any benefit from those authorities. It is to be borne in mind that each and every judgment is to be made applicable in the facts and circumstance of each and every case and there cannot be any general application of the principles of law enunciated in any decision.</u>

14. Let me now turn to a legal aspect of the matter which is a substantial question of law and is of a great public importance. The question is the redemption of the schedule 1 (ka) property by the legal heirs of Abdul Jabbar Mizi, the defendant Nos. 1 and 2. The learned District Judge came to the decision that the plaintiffs title to the schedule 1(Ka) land is liable to be declared subject to the right of redemption by the legal heirs of Abdul Jabbar Mizi. Admittedly, the sale deed dated 16-9-70 was accompanied by a contemporaneous agreement of reconveyance executed by the transferee Serajul Islam, defendant No. 9 in favour of Abdul Jabbar, the predecessor-father of defendant Nos. 1 and 2. In the said agreement of reconveyance it is stated that in the event of payment of consideration money fixed in the deed of sale within the period of 5 years from 1377 BS to month of Poush 1382 BS the transferee would be bound to deliver the possession of the said property to the transferor Abdul Jabbar Mizi. The certified copy of the agreement of reconveyance has been exhibited as Exhibit-C for the defendants. It appears from Annexure-1 annexed in the Affidavit-in-opposition filed by the plaintiff-opposite-parties that after the pronouncement of the judgment by the appellate Court, the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 by filing a Redemption Case got an order of redemption from the Upazila Nirbahi Officer. From Annexure-2 it further transpires that the said order of redemption passed by the Upazila Revenue Officer stood set aside on an appeal being Redemption Appeal No. 1 of 1987-88 preferred by the plaintiff-opposite-parties before the Additional. Deputy Commissioner (Revenue), Chandpur who was the appellate authority.

15. It, thus, appears that the defendant Nos. 1 and .2 being encouraged with the decision of the learned District Judge approached the Upazila Revenue Officer to get the schedule 1 (Ka) property redeemed on the strength of section 95A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act though no attempt was ever made by the defendant Nos.   1 and 2 to get the land redeemed earlier possibly they being in possession of the Schedule 1(Ka) property. The Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) in his order dated 15-8-88 observed that since the matter in dispute remains pending before the High Court Division in Civil Revision Case, the decision of the High Court Division would be final.

16. Now the question comes whether the schedule 1(ka) property is liable to be redeemed under the purview of section 95A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act.

17. For the purpose of answering to the said question relevant provisions of law of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act (hereinafter referred to as SA Act), The Transfer of Property Act (hereinafter referred to TP Act) and Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act (hereinafter referred to NAT Act) may profitably be noticed.

18. Under section 95A of State Acquisition and Tenancy Act a transfer of a holding or of portion or share thereof either by way of an out and out sale with an agreement to reconvey or where the transferor receives from the transferees any consideration or the transferee acquires the right to possess, and to enjoy the usufruct of, such holding or portion or share thereof for specified period in lieu of such consideration is deemed to be a complete usufructuary mortgage for a period not exceeding 7 years and the provision of section 95 had been made applicable to such transfer whether made before or after the date of commencement of the Act (Second Amendment) Order, 1972 (President's Order No. 88 of 1972).

19. Section 95 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act provides that a Raiyat could not enter into any form of usufructuary mortgage other than the complete usufructuary mortgage as defined in section 2 (6) of the Act and every such complete usufructuary mortgage is subject to the limitation of section 90 of the Act and the period for which such complete usufructuary mortgage may be entered by a Raiyat shall not exceed seven years.

20. "Mortgage" is defined in section 58 of TP Act which enjoins that it is a transfer of an interest in specific immovable property for the purpose of securing the payment of money advanced or to be advanced by way of loan, an existing or future debt or the performance of an engagement which may give rise to a pecuniary liability. The transferor is called a mortgagor and the transferee is mortgagee. The instrument by which the transfer is effected is called a Mortgage deed and the principal money and interest of which payment is secured is called the Mortgage money.

21. Usufructuary Mortgage is defined in section 58(d) of the Transfer of Property Act which provides that where the mortgagor delivers possession or expressly or by implication binds himself to deliver possession of the mortgaged property to the mortgagee and authorises him to retain such possession until payment of mortgage money, and to receive the rents and profits accruing from the property or any part of such rents and profits and to appropriate the same in lieu of interest, or in payment of the mortgage money or partly in lieu of interest or partly in payment of the mortgage money, the transaction is called an usufructuary mortgage and the mortgagee an usufructuary mortgagee.

22. The right given to Mortgage is a right conferred by section 95A of the SA Act which is a special statute.

23. A reading of section 95 of State Acquisition and Tenancy Act manifests that a usufructuary mortgage can be effected in respect of a holding or a portion or share of the said holding. Holding is defined in section 2 (13) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act which is as follows :

"2(13). Holding means a parcel or parcels of land or an undivided share thereof, held by a raiyat or an under raiyat and forming the subject of a separate tenancy".

24. "Land" is defined in section 2(16) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act which is quoted hereunder :

"2(16). "Land" means land which is cultivated, uncultivated or covered with water at any time of the year, and includes benefits arising out of land, houses or buildings and also things attached to the earth, or permanently fastened to anything attached to the earth".

25. On a plain reading of the definition of land it manifests that it is agricultural land which is cultivated, uncultivated or covered with water at any time of the year and includes houses or buildings and also things attached to the earth or permanently fastened to anything attached to the earth.

26. Raiyat is defined in section 82(2) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act which runs thus:

"82(2). "Raiyat" means a person who, by virtue of section 44 or otherwise, has acquired a right to hold land directly under the Government mainly for the purpose of cultivating it by himself or by members of his family or by, or with the aid of, servants or labourers or with the aid of partners or bargaders, and includes also the successors-in-interest of persons who have acquired such a right;".

27. Raiyat is thus a person who has acquired a right to hold land directly under the Government for the purpose of cultivating the land by himself or by members of his family or with the aid of servants, labourers, or partners or bargadars.

28. "Non-agricultural land" is defined in section 2(4) of the Non-agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949 which is as follows :

"2(4). "Non-agricultural land" means land which is used for purposes not connected with agriculture or horticulture and includes land which is held on lease for purposes not connected with agriculture or horticulture irrespective of whether it is used for any such purposes or not, but does not include—

(a) a homestead to which the provisions of section 182 of the Bengal Tenancy Act (VIII of 1885) apply,

(b) land which was originally leased for agricultural or horticultural purposes but is being used for purposes not connected with agriculture or horticulture, without the consent either express or implied of the landlord, if the period for which such land has been so used is less than twelve years, and

(c) land which is held for purposes connected with the cultivation or manufacture of tea."

29. Non-agricultural land, therefore, is a land which is not used for agricultural or horticulture purposes and the same will not include a homestead and a land originally leased for agricultural or horticulture purposes but is being used for purposes not connected with agriculture or horticulture.

30. "Non-agricultural Tenant" is defined in section 2(5) of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act which is extracted hereunder :

"2(5). "Non-agricultural tenant" means a person who holds non-agricultural land under another person with consent of that person and is, or but for a special contract would be, liable to pay rent to such person for the land and also includes the successors-in-interest of the former but does include any person who holds any such land on which any premises occupied by such person are situated if such premises have been erected, or are owned by the person to whom such occupier is, or but for a special contract would be, liable to payment for such occupation;

Explanation—In this clause "premises" mean any building such as a house, manufactory, warehouse, stable, shop or but whether constructed of masonry, bricks, concrete, wood, mud, metal or any other material whatsoever and includes any land appertaining to such building."

31. "Non-agriculture tenant" is also defined in section 2(17) of the SAT Act which is quoted thus:

"2(17). "Non-agriculture tenant" means a tenant who holds land for purposes not connected with agricultural or horticulture but does not include a person holding land together with any building standing thereon any necessary adjunct thereto under a lease other than a lease in perpetuity."

32. "Bazar" is defined in section 2(12) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act which is extracted hereunder :

"2(12). Bazar means any place where persons assemble daily primarily for the purposes of buying or selling agricultural or horticultural produce, livestock, poultry, hides, skins, fish, eggs, milk, milk-products or any other articles of food or drink or other necessaries of life, and includes all shops of such articles or manufactured articles within such place".

33. In P Remanatha Aiyar's "The Law Lexicon" Bazar is stated as a market, a daily market, a market place. To constitute a Bazar all that is necessary is a place where buyers and sellers congregate to sell and buy.

34. "Bazar", thus, is a place where persons assemble daily for the purposes of buying and selling of different articles of food and other necessaries of life and includes all shops of such articles within such place.

35. Exhibit-5 is the Deed of Settlement dated 23-8-1951 executed and registered by the original owner Chandra Mohan Chowdhury in favour of Abdul Jalil. The schedule-1 property has been described as Chandina Bhiti (চান্দিনা ভিটি) and in the said deed the schedule 1(ka) property is stated to be situated at Mohamaya Bazar.

36. Exhibit-3 is the Deed of Conveyance dated 16-9-1970 executed by Abdul Jabbar Mizi in favour of Md. Serajul Islam the defendant No. 9. In the said deed the schedule 1(ka) property is stated as ChandinaBhiti land and the house standing thereon and the same is also stated to be situated at Mohamaya Bazar. Exhibit-C is the agreement of re-conveyance dated 16-9-70 executed by Serajul Islam in favour of Abdul Jabbar Mizi. In the said agreement of reconveyance also the schedule-1(ka) property has been described as Chandina Bhiti and is stated to be situated at Mohamaya Bazar. Exhibit-8(a) is the certified copy of the Record of Right of the relevant khatian No. 134 wherein the tenancy is stated to be a Non-agricultural tenancy right (সেকস্তি প্রজা স্বত্ব) and the schedule-1(ka) property has been stated to be shop (দোকান).

37. Having regard to the above provisions of law as well as the definitions it is evidently clear that schedule-1(ka) property is a Chandina  Bhiti and the same is situated at Mohamaya Bazar under Lodhergaon Mouza, Police Station-Chandpur and the said property is not an agricultural land. The schedule-1(ka) property is not held or possessed by a Raiyat and the same property is neither cultivatable nor covered with water at any time of the year. The suit property is shop (Dokan) situated at Mohamaya Bazar where people assemble there for the purpose of buying and selling agriculture or horticulture produces, articles of foods and other necessaries of life. The schedule 1(ka) property is, thus, an out and out a non-agricultural property is a non agricultural tenancy right.

<u>38. Section 95A of State Acquisition and Tenancy Act is attracted only when a transfer of a holding or of portion of share thereof of an agricultural land either by way of an out and out sale with an agreement to reconvey takes place and since the schedule-1(ka) property is not an agricultural land and the same being a non-agricultural property, the agreement of reconveyance dated 16-9-70 cannot be deemed to be a complete usufructuary mortgage and the same cannot also stand redeemed tinder section 95A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. It is worthwhile to mention here that the Deed of Transfer and the agreement of reconveyance were executed on 16-9-70 before the amended section 95A of the said Act effected by President's Order 88 of 1972 and President''s Order 24 of 1973 came into force. President''s Order 88 of 1972 came into force on 3rd of August, 1972.</u>

<u>39. True it is that the deed of conveyance dated 16-9-70 having been accompanied with an agreement of reconveyance, by operation of law, on the strength of section 95A of the said Act, the said agreement of reconveyance can be deemed to be a complete usufructuary mortgage for a period not exceeding 7 years Provided the land is an agricultural land held by a raiyat and after the expiry of the said period of 7 years, the land in the Agreement of Reconveyarice can stand re-deemed. It has already been pointed out that since the redemption of the schedule 1(ka) Property does not come within the mischief of section 95A of the said Act, the question of redemption of the said property does not at all arise. The agreement of reconveyance having been contrary to law, the right or redemption cannot be enforced by invoking the provision of section 95A of the Act and the plaintiff-petitioners are not at all entitled to get the schedule-1(ka) property redeemed on the strength of the said section 95A of the Act. The title of the plaintiffs to schedule-1(ka) property is liable to be declared absolutely without any embargo and the decision of the learned District Judge to the effect that the plaintiffs'' title to the 1 (ka) schedule property is liable to be declared subject to the right of redemption by the legal heirs of late Abdul Jabbar Mizi stands set aside. The right of the plaintiffs to the schedule-1(ka) property is declared absolutely. The judgment and decree passed by the learned District Judge is maintained with the modification stated above.</u>

40. In view of the discussion made hereinbefore and the reasons stated I am of the considered view that the Rule is devoid of any substance and the same must be discharged.

In the result, the Rule is discharged.

Having regard to the fact and circumstances of the case there will be no order as to cost.

Order of stay stands vacated.

Send down the LCR at once.

End.

caseno: Second Appeal No.468 of 1974 with Civil Rule No. 401(s) of 1991
lawyer:
Syed Mokaddas Ali, Advocate— For the Appellants. 
Md Latifur Rahman, Advocate— For the Respondents.
parties:
Mander Sheikh and others ------ Appellants
Vs.
Sultan Ali Molla and others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
This Second Appeal by the defendants is directed against the judgment and decree dated 24-5-1974 passed by AKM S Uddin Additional District Judge of Khulna in Title Appeal No.28 of 1972 affirming the judgment and decree dated 29-4-1972 passed by Mr Afzalur Rahman, Munsif, Second Court, Bagerhat, in Title Suit No.235 of 1987 decreeing the suit.

2. Relevant facts are summarized as follows: Plaintiffs filed the aforesaid title suit for a declaration of title and confirmation of possession or in the alternative for recovery of khas possession of the suit land on the allegations that they as benamdar of the judgment-debtors auction purchased a jote which included 5.33 acres of tenanted land under Khatian No. 99 standing in the names of Panchy Sheikh, Kamaruddin Sheikh i.e. the father of defendant Nos. 1 and 2 and Ramjan i.e. the father of the defendant Nos. 3 and 4 in Rent Execution Case No.1035 of 1930 arising out of Rent Suit No. 607 of 1930 on 20-1-1931 and took delivery of possession thereof on 2-5-1931 after having annulled the encumbrance namely, the said under-tenancy by service of notice under section 167 of the Bengal Tenancy Act. Father of defendant Nos.1 and 2 late Kamaruddin Sheikh having admitted annulment of the said under-tenancy took fresh settlement of some of the said under tenancy by executing kabuliayat. But due to mistake 2.30 acres of land of the said under-tenancy was wrongly recorded in the names of the defendants during SA settlement and by taking advantage of such wrong recording the defendants threatened the plaintiffs with dispossession from the said land on 21st Chaitra 1373 BS. Hence the plaintiffs were constrained to file the suit.

3. Defendants contested the suit by filing a written statement asserting that their under-tenancy was never annulled and they were all along in possession. The defendants denied that late Kamaruddin or Samajuddin ever executed any Kabuliyat admitting annulment of their under tenancy or taking over Khas possession of the same by the plaintiffs stating that if there was any Kabuliyat by Kamaruddin that must have been manufactured for the purpose of the case. The defendants further asserted that since there was no annulment of the under-tenancy in question the suit land was recorded in the name of the predecessors-in-interest of the defendants during the petty and revisional settlement that took place after the purported auction-sale. Subsequently the suit land was recorded in the name of the defendants during the SA settlement.

4. Both the trial Court as well as the first appellate Court below decreed the suit on the finding that the plaintiffs succeeded in proving the service of notice under section 167 of the Bengal Tenancy Act annulling the under-tenancy in question and that they were in possession of the suit land holding that although the plaintiffs could not prove the service of notice of annulment of the under-tenancy in question in terms of section 167 of the Bengal Tenancy Act by producing any paper, but admission of late Kamaruddin i.e. the father of the defendants Nos.1 and 2 and Mominuddin i.e. the defendant No.6 (not an under-tenant) and the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 sufficiently proved service of notice. Being aggrieved the defendants preferred this Second Appeal.

5. Mr Syed Mokaddas Ali, the learned Advocate for the appellants, submits that both the trial Court as well as the appellate Court below earred in law in holding that the plaintiffs as auction-purchasers annulled the under tenancy in question by serving notice on the under-tenants in terms of section 167 of the Bengal Tenancy Act, although they (plaintiffs) failed to prove the service of notice as required in law. Learned Advocate also submits that the courts below also erred in law in failing to appreciate that since the plaintiffs as benamdars of the judgment-debtors were debarred under section 173 of the Bengal Tenancy Act from auction purchasing the suit land no notice under section 167 of the Act was served by the Court which held the auction-sale.

6. Mr Md Latifur Rahman, the learned Advocate for the respondents, on the other hand, submits that although the respondents Could not adduce any documentary evidence including the notice itself in order to prove the service of notice of annulment under section 167, but the very admission of the appellants and their father late Kamaruddin as well as the admission of defendant No. 6 Mominuddin was enough to prove the service of notice of annulment and possession of the suit land by the plaintiffs. The learned Advocate relied on the case reported in 37 DLR 126 in this connection. Learned Advocate for the respondents contends that even if the respondents failed to acquire any title to the suit land by auction-purchase, since both the Courts below have found them in possession on the suit land for more than 12 years the respondents must be held to have acquired title thereto by adverse possession.

7. The moot question requiring determination is whether the respondents succeeded in proving the annulment of the encumbrance, namely, the under-tenure of the appellants, by serving notice under section 167 of the Bengal Tenancy Act. The question whether notice under section 167 of the Bengal Tenancy Act was duly served in this case is a question of law. Hence the concurrent finding of the Courts below on this point is liable to be interfered with by this Court in case such finding is bad in law.

<u>8. A sale in execution of a rent decree will ipso facto cancel an encumbrance. Until an encumbrance namely, the under-tenancy, as in this case, is annulled by notice as required under section 167 of the Bengali Tenancy Act the under-tenancy subsists vide AIR (1929) Cal. 392. If an auction-purchaser in a rent sale desires to exercise his power of annulment of any encumbrance he is required to strictly comply with the requirements of section 167 of the Bengal Tenancy Act as regards service of notice and such notice must be served within one year from the date of confirmation of sale or from the date of knowledge thereof whichever date is later.</u>

<u>9. Section 167 confers on the purchaser the power to extinguish an encumbrance without any obligation to pay for it. Since the power of annulment conferred by this section operates very harshly on the encumbrancer strict proof of service of the notice is required vide AIR (1928) Pat 459.</u>

<u>10. Purchaser is under obligation to show that the notice under section 167 has been served in the manner provided under this section, namely, that he made an application to the Court or the revenue officer in writing requesting him to serve on the encumbrancer a notice declaring that the encumbrance is annulled. Notice of annulment is to be served in the manner provided for the service of summons under Order 5, rules 11 and 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure as required by the Rules framed by the Government under sections 189 and 190 of the Bengal Tenancy Act. The case of Ananda Gopal vs Nafar Chandra reported in 18 CWN (PC) 259 is an authority on this point. The purchaser must prove service of notice by the production of the person who served it or by any other means recognized by law vide 7 CLJ 262. Even the entries in the order-sheet of the Court which caused the notice to be served on the application of the purchaser are not the prime evidence against the encumbrance that the notice was served.</u>

<u>11. In the instant case, respondents have admittedly failed to produce any paper in support of service of notice under section 167of the Bengal Tenancy Act. The finding of the Courts below, particularly the appellate Court below that service of such notice as well as possession of the suit land by the respondents have been proved by admission of the appellant Nos.1 and 2 and their father late Kamaruddin and also by admission of defendant No.6 Mominuddin is erratic and perverse being contrary to law and evidence. The decision reported in 37 DLR 126 is not applicable in the present case as the facts are distinguishable. The defendant No.6 is not an under-tenant but apparently a camp-follower of the respondents and accordingly, he deposed as PW 2 stating in his evidence that notice was served in his presence. Such admission by defendant No.6 cannot be a proof of service of notice as contemplated under Section 167.</u>

<u>12. Respondents are admittedly the benamdars of the judgment-debtors. Section 173 of the Bengal Tenancy Act debars the judgment-debtors as well as their benamdars from purchasing any defaulting tenure. A judgment debtor or his benamdar purchasing the defaulting tenure, even if the sale is allowed to stand, is not entitled to annul the encumbrance. The case of Fakir Chander Dutt and others vs Ram Kumar Chatterji reported in 8 CWN (PC) 721 is referred to in this connection. Since the service of notice under section 167 in this case has not been proved as proscribed by law the encumbrance in question still subsists. Accordingly, the finding of possession of the suit land in favour of the plaintiffs by the Courts below is not sustainable in law. Therefore, the contention that the plaintiffs have acquired title by adverse possession is not acceptable.</u>

13. In the result, this appeal is allowed without any order as to costs. Impugned judgment and decree dated 24-5-1974 passed by the Additional District Judge, Khulna in Title Appeal No. 28 of 1972 affirming , the judgment and decree dated 29-4-1972 passed by the Munsif, 2nd Court, Bagerhat, in Title Suit No.235 of 1967 are set aside.

Connected Civil Rule No. 401(s) of 1991 (Dhaka) /200(s) of 1988 is accordingly disposed of.

End.

caseno: Civil Rule 257 (fm) of 1997. FMA No. 109 of 1997
lawyer:
Khandakar Mahbubuddin Ahmed with Moudud Ahmed, Abdul Razzak, Mizanur Rahman Bhuiyan, Advocates—For the Petitioner. 
Amirul Islam with Rokanuddin Mahmud, Abdul Quayum, Bivash Chandra Biswas, Probir Haider, Advocates—For the Opposite Party.
parties:
Mowlana Delower Hossain Saydi ------ Petitioner
Vs.
Sudanshu Sakhar Halder ------ Opposite Party
full_judgment:
Md Sirajul Islam J: This Rule at the instance of the appellant was issued calling upon the opposite party Nos. 1-3 to show cause as to why the operation of the judgment and order dated 10-5-97 passed by the Election Tribunal, Pirojpur in Election Petition No. 1 of 1996, should not be stayed till disposal of First Miscellaneous Appeal No. 109 of 1997 pending before this court or such other or further order or orders passed as to this court may seem fit and proper.

2. The short facts giving rise to this Rule are that, the appellant-petitioner and the opposite party Nos. 1 and 7 others were the contesting candidates for election as member of the parliament from constituency No. 129 Pirojpur-1 comprising the areas of Pirojpur, Nazirpur and Indurkandi Police Stations which was held on 12-6-1996. There were 93 polling centres in that constituency. After completion of election, the appellant-petitioner was elected securing 55,717 votes defeating his nearest candidate, the opposite party No. 1 by a margin of 280 votes. The result was duly published in the Official Gazette and the petitioner took oath as a member of parliament and has been functioining as MP since then.

3. The opposite party No. 1 thereafter filed an election petition before the Bangladesh Election Commission against the appellant-petitioner and others on various grounds. The Election Petition was sent to the Election Tribunal of parliamentary election, Pirojpur (District and Sessions Judge, Pirojpur) for trial and disposal. The election petition was registered as Election Petiton Case No. 1 of 1996 in the Election Tribunal at Pirojpur. The appellant-petitioner contested the election petition case denying the allegations made in the election petition. Both the parties adduced evidence in support of their respective cases. The learned Tribunal after considering the facts, circumstances and the evidence of the case allowed the election petition in part and directed for holding fresh poll in Gharghata Government Primary School Centre vide his judgment and order dated 10-5-1997.

4. Being aggrieved by that judgment and order dated 10-5-97, the petitioner as appellant has preferred First Miscellaneous Appeal No. 109 of 1997 in this court and by filing a separate application has prayed for stay of operation of the impugned judgment and order passed by the Election Tribunal whereupon this Rule was issued with an ad-interim stay order. This Rule is opposed by the respondent-opposite party No. 1 by filing 2 counter-affidavits.

5. Mr Khandaker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the appellant-petitioner, submits that clause 3 of Article 62 of the Representation of the People''s Order, 1972 (President''s Order No. 155 of 1972) has provided that any persons aggrieved by a decision of the Tribunal may, within 30 days of the announcement of the decision, appeal to the High Court Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh. He submits that although there is no express provision in this law for granting stay of operation of the impugned judgment and order, yet this court while admitting the appeal under Order 41 rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure shall have the power to pass an order for stay operation of the impugned order under rule 5 of the same Code. He further submits that the right to appeal given by a statute carries with it a similar right to ask for an order of stay of the impugned order for proper disposal of the appeal. He submits that the appellate Court has at least an inherent power to grant an order of stay of the impugned order, otherwise the purpose of filing the appeal will be defeated.

6. In support of his contention that the power to entertain an appeal against the decision of the Tribunal carries with it the similar power to stay operation of the impugned order. Mr Khandaker Mahbubuddin Ahmed has referred to a few decisions in the case of MM Dharmadas vs. State Transport Appellate Tribunal of Kerala and others reported in AIR 1963, Kerala 73, the case of Deputy Conservator of Creats Hammara vs. KS Sarojini and another reported in AIR 1981 Kerala 44, and the case of Income Tax Officer, Cannanore vs. Mk Mohammad Kunhi reported in AIR 1969 (SC) 430. The common observations made therein are that the appeal is a creature of statute and where an Act confers a jurisdiction, it impliedly also grants the power of doing all such acts or employing such means, as are essentially necessary to its execution. The order of stay is a necessary corollary to the power to entertain an appeal or revision. Appellate Tribunal has power to grant stay as incidental or ancillary to its appellate jurisdiction to make the exercise of these jurisdiction fully effective.

<u>7. From the observations as made by their Lordships in the above cited cases, it will appear that in the absence of any express provision for granting stay in the statute creating a right to appeal, the appellate Court or Tribunal shall have the power to grant stay of the impugned order as an ancillary to its appellate jurisdiction. Thus, it appears that although there is no express provision for granting stay in our statute (President''s Order No. 155 of 1992), yet an implied power of granting stay will be there as a necessary concomitant with the power of entertaining such an appeal under clause 3 of Article 62 of the statute.</u>

8. Mr Amirul Islam, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the respondent-opposite party No. 1, on the other hand, submits that it has been laid down in clause 2 of Article 62 of the Representation of the People Order, 1972 that the decision of a Tribunal on an election petition shall be final and that it has further been laid down in Article 67(1) that an order of a Tribunal under Article 62 shall take effect on the date on which it is made. The contention of Mr Amirul Islam is that the order of the Tribunal is a final order as per clause 2 of Article 62 and shall take effect immediately on the date of its pronouncement as per Article 67(1) of the President''s Order and, as such, there is no power left for this court to grant stay of operation of the impugned order pending hearing of the appeal and that in such a position, the stay order, if granted by this court, will make the provision of effectiveness a nugatory one. In this connection Mr Amirul Islam referred to section 116(2) of the Representation of the People''s Act of India and said that it has been specifically laid down therein that where an appeal has been preferred against an order of the High Court made in an election petition under section 98, the Supreme Court may, on sufficient cause being shown and on such terms and conditions as it may think fit, stay the operation of the order appealed from. Mr Amirul Islam wanted to say that had there been any intention for stay of the impugned order of the Tribunal in the mind of our legislatures a similar specific provision would have been made in our law also and since there is no such express provision for stay in our law, this court of appeal shall have no power to grant stay of operation of the order appealed from.

9. In support of his contention that in the absence of any express provision for stay in our statute, this court in appeal cannot grant any order of stay, Mr Amirul Islam has referred to a decision in the case of Md Yousuf Khan Khattak vs. SM Ayub and 2 others reported in PLD 1972 (Peshawar) 151 wherein it has been observed that in the absence of a special power to stay operation of the order of the Tribunal, the appellate Court shall have no power to stay the order of the Election Tribunal. The facts of that case were that, the election of Mr Md Yousuf Khan Khattak was declared void by the Election Tribunal, Peshawar by an order dated 13-5-72 and then the Election Commission announced an election programme for holding a by-election to fill up that vacancy and thereafter by filing an appeal, Mr Khattak prayed that the implementation of the orders of the Election Tribunal be kept in obeyance. The High Court in appeal rejected his prayer on the ground that there is no specific provision for grant of such stay in exercise of its special jurisdiction. But the instant case before us is not a case for holding any by-election to fill up any vacancy, but that it is a case for fraud polling in one centre only out of 93 polling centres. So, the facts and position of the cited case being distinguishable, the decision therein above shall have no application in the instant case before us.

10. The learned Advocate referred to another decision in the case of Chowdhury Mohammad Ali vs. Government of West Pakistan and others reported in PLD 1966, Lahore 335. The facts of that case were that a writ petition was filed in the High Court challenging the election of Town Committee Chairman to be held on 16th May, 1961 under the Electoral College Act. The petitioner filed an application under section 151 CPC praying for maintaining a status quo and for restraining the respondent from holding election. That prayer for injunction was rejected on the ground that it will amount to interference with the carrying out of the public functions of the authority concerned. This position of the cited case has no relevance in the position of the instant case before us.

11. Mr Amirul Islam has referred to some more case in aid of his contention that this court has no power to grant stay of operation of the impugned order passed by the Tribunal. We have considered those cases and found that those relate to interpretation of statues and that the subject-matter of those cases are quite different having no relevance with the subject-matters of the instant case before us.

12. The main contention of Mr Amirul Islam is that the provision of clause 2 of Article 62 reading together with clause 1 of Article 67 of the President''s Order No. 155 of 1972 will mean that the order of the Election Tribunal is final and effective from the date of its pronouncement and, as such, this court shall have no jurisdiction to stay the final and effective order of the Tribunal.

<u>13. But it appears that the provision of clause 2 of Article 62 is that save as provided in Clause (J), the decision of a Tribunal on an election petition shall be final. Clause 3 has created a right to appeal for an aggrieved person against the decision of the Tribunal and it has been laid down therein that the decision of the High Court Division on such appeal shall be final. There cannot be two final orders at a time and therefore, our opinion is that the finality of the decision of a Tribunal as contained in Clause 2 of Article 62 must be subject to the decision of the High Court Division in appeal, if any appeal is filed under Clause 3 of Article 62 and that the decision of the High Court Division on such appeal shall prevail as the final order under Article 62 and then the effectiveness of an order under Article 62 as a whole shall be reached under Article 67 (1).</u>

<u>14. In view of the position of the law as spelt out above, we are of the opinion that the power to grant stay of operation of the impugned order passed by the Election Tribunal is incidental to and implicit in the appellate jurisdiction of this court created by the statute. We therefore, hold that this court of appeal has the power to stay the impugned judgment and order passed by the Tribunal pending disposal of the appeal.</u>

15. Apart from the above, an appeal is meant for scrutinising the order of the Election Tribunal by the superior court of appeal to see whether there is any error of law or of fact committed by the Tribunal in passing its order and if any error of law or of fact or of procedure is found therein then the impugned order passed by the Tribunal may be set aside or varied or modified. In that view of the matter also, it appears that it will be just and proper to stay the impugned order passed by the Tribunal until it is finally scrutinised by this court in appeal.

<u>16. Furthermore, it has been laid down in Article 27 of the President''s Order No. 155 of 1972 that every election petition shall be tried, as nearly as may be in accordance with the procedure for the trial of suits under Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 and it has further been laid down in Article 59 that the Tribunal shall have all the powers of a Civil Court trying a suit under the Code of Civil Procedure. Appeal is the continuation of a suit and hence the court of appeal shall have the power to stay the operation of the impugned order appealed from under Order 41 rule 5 of the Code otherwise the purpose of the appeal will be defeated. In that view of the matter also, we final that this court is competent enough to stay the operation of the impugned judgment and order passed by the Election Tribunal pending disposal of the appeal. We are satisfied that there is sufficient cause made out for us to stay the impugned judgment and order appealed from.</u>

17. It may, however, be mentioned here that the appeal should be disposed of as early as possible. Since it is a matter mainly between the petitioner and the opposite party No. 1 all necessary steps should be taken to make the appeal ready for disposal expeditiously.

For all the reasons stated above, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to costs. The impugned judgment and order passed by the Election Tribunal Pirojpur are stayed till disposal of the First Miscellaneous Appeal No. 109 of 1997 pending before this court.

End.

caseno: Appeal from Original Decree (FA) No. 29 of 1990.
lawyer:
Md Ohiullah with Md Al-Amin, Advocates---For the Appellants. 
Kamal-ul-Alam with AKM Abdul Hakim, Advocates ---For Respondent No. 1.
parties:
Mitsui OSK Lines Ltd & anothers  ----- Appellants
vs
Bangladesh Jatiya Matshayajibi Samabaya  Samity Ltd and others  ----- Plaintiff-Respondents
full_judgment:
Md Abu Tariq J: Only defendant Nos. 1 and 2 as appellants presented the above appeal against the judgment and decree dated 18-10-1989 passed in Money Suit No. 140 of 1988 in the 2nd Commercial Court of Subordinate Judge, Chittagong decreeing the suit against the defendant Nos. 1 and 2/appellants with cost and interest @ 10% per annum with effect from the date of filing the suit.

2. Short facts for disposal of the appeal are that the plaintiff, Bangladesh Hatiya Maitshayajibi Samabaya Samity Ltd imported two consignments of nylon twine consisting of 614 and 396 cartons from Japan per 'MV Victoria Peak' covered by bills of lading Nos.
