full_judgment:
The Rule was issued against the opposite parties calling upon them to show cause as to why the judgment and decree passed by the 1st Court of Subordinate Judge, Chittagong in Other Appeal No.66 of 1982 reversing the judgment and decree passed by the Munsif, in-charge, 2nd Court, Chittagong, Sadar in Other Suit No.111 of 1976 decreeing the suit should not be set aside and such other or further order or orders passed as to this court may seem fit and proper.

2. It appears that the present petitioner as plaintiff filed the Other Suit for a decree for declaration of title, confirmation of possession and permanent injunction in respect of 66 decimals of land appertaining to RS plot No.2071. The case of the plaintiff in short is that the suit land and other lands was part of Taluk Askhkar @ Akbar and belonged to his grand-father Mohammad Ali who possessed the same in khas during his life time. Mohammad Ali sold some property which was under his khas possession to the mother of the plaintiff named Arfan Bibi and the same was recorded in her name in RS Khatian No.894. The suit land and his mother's land are contiguous and stands on the eastern shore of the river known as Sandip Channel.

3. Further case of the plaintiff is that Mohammad Ali died before RS operation and after his death his son Mokbul Ahmed, father of the plaintiff inherited the same property and possessed the same in khas till his death in 1935 and since his death the plaintiff had been possessing the land. During RS operation in 1930, the suit land was under water but it again came to its original shape in 1931 and thereafter it never fully went under water though occasionally it used to be submerged under the water of the river as it stands by the shore of the river. As the land was under water during RS operation the same was not recorded in the name of Mohammad Ali in RS Khatian No.894 but in the remark column of the Khatian itself it was mentioned that it was part of Taluk Ashker and being under water jama was not fixed. During the operation, the Survey officials without vi ling the locality wrongly recorded the schedu land as river in PS khatan No. 58 under khas land.

4. The plaintiff also claims that his mother's land and the schedule land being contiguous land, the plaintiff possessed the same by bringing both land within a common boundary. The other surrounding lands also used to be submerged under water of the said river and the plaintiff together with the schedule land also used to cultivate those lands for which notices were issued by the Government upon him claiming compensation. The plaintiff accordingly paid compensation.

5. Further case of the plaintiff is that as the suit land suit land was excluded from jama in RS Khatian No.894 because it was under water of the river, he could not pay any rent. Moreover, being an illiterate man and for want of correct legal advice, the plaintiff also could not take proper steps to get the land recorded in his name. However, on the advice of the local Tahsilder he filed a case under section 143(b) for substituting his name in the PS khatian but the case abated as the time for filing an application under section 143(b) already expired.

6. The next case of the plaintiff is that the local chairman of the Union Parishad asked him to appear in the Union Parishad office in connection with a criminal case filed in the court of SDO Sadar North, Chittagong. The chairman was asked to hold an enquiry into a complaint filed by the petitioner (the defendant No. 1 of the present suit) of that case alleging that the plaintiff caused damage to the crops grown by the defendant No. 1 in the schedule property. After obtaining a copy of that complaint case, the plaintiff for the first time came to know that the defendant No. 2 illegally leased out the suit land to the defendant No. 1 in Settlement Case No. 95/72-73. The suit land was althrough under possession of the plaintiff and his predecessors. The Government has no right, title or interest in the suit land and as such the defendant No. 1 also acquired no interest in the suit land on the basis of his lease from the Government. The defendant has been trying to enter into possession of the suit and on the basis of his alleged lease and also tried to lay claim to the suit land by filing the above false criminal case against the plaintiff. Hence the suit.

7. The defendant No. 1 contested the suit by filing a written statement claiming that the RS khatian was correct and the suit land was under water for about 60 years before 1954 in which year it started re-appearing and completely re-appeared in 1960 when an embantkment by WAPDA was constructed to the west of the suit land along the western side of the suit land. His further case is that he being a poor cultivator he applied for lease of the suit land to the Government and accordingly after holding enquiry the suit landalong with other lands, was leased out to him and a separate khatian has also been prepared in his name and since then he has been possessing the suit land.

8. The learned lower Court, on the basis of the evidence on record, decreed the suit with a finding that the suit land originally belonged to Mehammad Ali, the grand-father of the father of the plaintiff and that there was no diluvion and the suit land was althrough under possession of the plaintiff. The defendant preferred an appeal against that judgment and decree of the trial Court before the court of the District Judge, Chittagong. The appeal was numbered as Other Appeal No.66 of 1982. It was heard and disposed of by the Subordinate Judge, First Court. The learned Subordinate Judge allowed the appeal on the grounds that the suit was not maintainable in view of the provisions of sub-section (3) of section 86 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950; that the suit was barred by limitation because it was not filed within 6 years from the publication of PS khatian and from the date of knowledge of the RS khatian; that the suit land was vague and that the suit was bad for defect of parties as all the co-sharers of RSPS and BS khatians were not made parties in the suit. The plaintiff, by filing this revisional application challenged the validity of the decisions arrived at by the learned appellate Court.

9. Mr. BK Das, with Mr. Omar Farook, the learned Advocates appearing on behalf of the petitioner have made elaborate submissions on the four grounds on which the learned appellate Court allowed the appeal. It will be convenient to discuss separately the submissions made by Mr. B K Das. At first, he has submitted that the provisions of sub-section (3) of section 86 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act is not applicable in the instant case. In this connection, he has invited my attention to the fact that Part V of the aforesaid Act came into force in the district of Chittagong on 1-8-63. He has also contended that the plaintiff did not admit anywhere that the suit land was under water of the river in the year 1930 or it remained under water of the river for a long time. So, according to him, the provision of section 86 is not applicable in the present case. On the other hand, Mr. Ahsanul Kabir, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the opposite party defendant has submitted that the suit land finally appeared in the year 1960 long after the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act came into force. According to him, the provision of sub-section (3) of section 86 of the Act is applicable in the present case and as such the suit land after its re-appearance vested in the Government.

<u>10. The question whether the provisions of sub-section (3) of section 86 will be applicable or not is dependant on the decision of the question whether diluvion took place long before the land re-appeared finally in the year 1960. On this question, the courts below came to a contradictory decision. The learned lower Court held that the suit land was never under water of the river whereas the learned appellate Court observed that the suit land was under water of the river for more then 50 years. The learned lower Court with reference to the statements of PWs 2 and 3 and also relying on RS Map Exhibit; (a) came to a finding that the suit land was not under water but was under water only for a temporary period during RS operation in the year 1930. On the other hand, the learned appellate Court without any specific reference to the statements of witnesses or without reference to any particular exhibit made a general observation which is as follows :</u>

<u>"It has been proved from the statement of PWs. and DWs. and the evidence on record of both sides that the suit property was under the deep river water for more than 50 years  The lower Court has referred to the statements of witnesses and also referred to an exhibit but the appellate Court reversed the finding by making a general observation. The appellate Court did not discuss anything about Exhibit 2(a) on which the lower Court relied upon. I do not understand how the appellate Court reversed the findings of the lower Court without giving its own reasoning".</u>

11. At the time of hearing, the learned Advocate on behalf of the opposite party with reference to RS khatian has submitted that the suit land was under water during RS operation and the entry in that respect as made in the RS khatian is correct. He has also referred to some of the statements of PW 1 and the statements made in the plaint itself. In this connection, he has also pointed out that the plaintiff as PW 1 has made some contradictory statements; for example the PW 1 said that during RS operation the suit land was not under water and same was under his cultivation but in the next moment he said that when survey officers visited the the suit land, the same was submerged due to tidal water and as such the survey officers did not take measurement of the suit land. Mr. Kabir has also referred to the statement made in paragraph 6 of the plaint wherein it is stated that at the time of RS survey in 1930 the schedule land was under water but it again came to its original shape in the year 1931. The inconsistencies pointed out by the learned Advocate for the opposite party are definitely inconsistencies on very material points. from these inconsistencies it appears that the plaintiff tried to suppress the fact that the suit land was under water during RS operation. In the RS khatian No.894 which has been marked Exhibit 1, the following entry has been made:

নিম্নলিখিত দাগ গুলি সিকন্তি হওয়রে পূর্বে অত্র স্বত্বভূক্ত ছিল । বিল্লু সিকস্তি হওয়ায় বর্তমানে ধার্ষকূত জমাহইতে বাদ দেওয়া হ্ইয়াছে ৷ দাগ নং- ২০৭১

Subsequently a separate khatian bearing No.58 was prepared wherein it has been also mentioned that the land of that Khatian was under river. From Exhibit 2(a), copy of the RS Map, it appears that plot No.2071 was shown in that Map and relying on this the learned lower Court came to a finding that it was not under water of the river at the time of actual survey. From the endorsement in this map by the Settlement Officer and Superintendent of Survey, it appears that it was made under the authority of the Government in 1926-27. From the statement of PW 1 we find that the RS operation took place in the year 1930 and final publication of RS khatian was also made in that year. It has been clearly stated by the plaintiff in the plaint in paragraph 6 that at the time of RS khatian in 1930 it was under water and came to its original shape in 1931. In his examination in-chief he has stated as follows:

জরিপ কর্মচারীরা যখন নালিশী জমি পরিমাপ করিতে আসিয়াছিল তখন জোয়ার আসিয়া জমিতে পানি প্রবেশ করিয়াছিল ৷ জোয়ার ২/১ ঘণ্টা থাকে ৷ জোয়ারের পানি থাকাকালীণ জমির আইল দেখা যায় না৷ জোয়ারেৱ পানি দেখিয়া জরিপ কর্মচারীরা জমির পরিমাপ করে নাই ৷"

So, it is clear that the plaintiff admitted that at the time of actual survey by the Survey Officers, the suit land was under water. If that is the position, it is not understood how by the same survey officers took measurement of the land and how the land was shown in the RS Map. The next question which remains to be decided are: when the diluvion took places and when it re-appeared.

12. The defendant did not specifically mention as to when the suit land went under water of the river but it has been mentioned that it started re-appearing in 1954 and before that for about 50 years it was under water. The defendant also claims the re-appearance competed in 1960 and in that year it became cultivable. The plaintiff on the other hand only admitted that it was under water for a temporary period during actual RS operation in the year 1930. The RS Khatian shows that it was under water during RS operation. Besides that RS Khatian, there is no documentary evidence to show that the suit land actually was under water of the river. The oral evidence on this point also is not sufficient, the defendant No. 1 while deposing as DW 1 has stated in his examination on-in-chief that from before 1900 the suit land was under water of the river. This witness has given his age as 48 and he deposed on 19-12-81. Obviously, he could not have any personal knowledge about what happened to the suit land before 1900 AD. The only other witness who deposed in support of the defendant is DW 2. He could not say as to when the suit land went under water of the river. So, we find that there is neither any documentary evidence nor oral evidence to show that the suit land went under the river about 50 years back or before 1900 AD as claimed by the contesting defendant. The only evidence before us to prove the diluvion is the RS Khatian. From the RS Khatian we do not get any light as to when diluvion took place. However, it is interesting to note that the learned appellate Court held that the suit property was under deep river water for more than 50 years, I do not understand how without any evidence on the point, the learned appellate Court could come to such a finding. I have mentioned that the only evidence before us is the RS Khatian. The other evidence is admission of the plaintiff that it was under water during RS operation. In the absence of any other evidence as to in what condition the suit land was before RS Khatian, it can be said that diluvion took place during RS operation.

13. Next question is when the suit land reappeared. The plaintiff claims that it was remaining under water only for one year i.e. during the year 1930 and it came to its original shape just after one year in 1931. On the other hand, the defendant claims that it started reappearing in the year 1954 and it became cultivable after construction of an embankment by WAPDA in 1960. The plaintiff stated that his father was alive at the time of RS operation but his father did not take any step for recording the suit land in his name. The plaintiff for the first time tried to get the land recorded in his name in the year 1972 by filing an application under section 143(b) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. If the suit land re-appeared after one year in 1931 as claimed by the plaintiff there is no reason why his father remained silent or why the plaintiff did not take any step for such a long time of 40 years. The learned appellate Court found that the plaintiff was in possession of the suit land in 1960. PWs 1, 2 and 3 all of them claimed that the suit land did not go under water after RS operation but as I have stated earlier about their silence for long 40/42 years, it appears to me that the suit land did not re-appear only after one year in 1931. So, on this point also we can come to a conclusion on the basis of the admission of the defendant that the suit land started appearing in the year 1954 and became cultivable in the year 1960. The learned appellate Court relying on the case of the defendants on this point held that the suit land was under river for more than 60 years and as such he applied the provision of sub section (3) of section 86. If we accept that the suit land completely reappeared in 1960 and became cultivable in that year in that case it is to be seen whether sub-section (3) of section 86 will be applicable.

<u>14. The learned appellate Court without giving any reasoning abruptly came to a finding that the right of the plaintiff extinguished in view of the provision of subsection (3) of section 86. It is not explained how the provision is applicable. Mr BK Das, the learned Advocate on behalf of the petitioner has contended that if reformation was complete in 1960, the provision of subsection (3) of section 86 will not be applicable because this provision which is in Part V of the Act, came into force in the Chittagong district on 1-8-63. In support of his view, he referred to the case of Abdul Mannan and others vs. Kulada Ranjan Mowali and others reported in 31 DLR (AD) 195 and the case of Padmabati Biswas vs. Bangladesh and others reported in 44 DLR 465. In the first reported case, the court considered the question of the effect of section 87 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act as enacted by President's Order 137 of 1972. It has been held that only such accretion as took place after Part V of the Act came into force are affected by the provision of section 87. It has been also clearly held that the accretion which took place before coming into force of Part V of Act shall be beyond the scope of sub-section (1) and (2) of section 87 and the rights of the owner shall not be affected. In this case it is also held that a person's right to a property is not destroyed or affected in any way if it merely goes under water of a sea or a river and in such a case, the owner shall be deemed to be in constructive possession of his property during the period of submergence and he can claim back the said property in his own right if it can be so identified after re-appearance. As regards the applicability of the provision of sections 86 and 87 of the Act similar view was also taken in the other cited case where it has been held that the provision of the above...sections can have effect only with respect to the land which re-appeared after Part V of the Act came into force. The principle laid down in the above cited cases as regards the application of the provisions of the above two sections may be applied in the present case also. The defendant himself claims that re-appearance was completed in the year 1960 and the suit land became cultivable in 1960. In view of the Notification No SA-1116/63/609 dated 18-7-63 published in the Dhaka Gazette on 1-8-63 Part V of the Act came into force in the district of Chittagong on the date of publication of that notification. As the reformation was complete before that date, provisions of the amended sub-section (3) of section 86 cannot be applied in respect of the suit land. I am also of the opinion that right of the owner, i.e. the plaintiff, has not extinguished or destroyed in view of the fact the suit land was under water till 1954. In this connection the legal position has been explained in the cited cases. In the first case the Court relied upon the principle laid down in the case of Felix Lopez vs. Muddun Mohan Thakor in which case the Judicial Committee observed as follows:</u>

<u>"This principle is one not merely of English law, not a principal law, but it is a principle founded in universal law and justice; that is to say, that whoever has land, wherever it is whatever may be the accident to which it has been exposed, whether it be a vineyard which is covered by lava or ashes from a volcano, or a field covered by the sea or by a river the ground, the site, the property remains in the original owner." 31 DLR (AD) 195 para-13</u>

<u>So, in view of the principle laid down in the above cases which was also followed in many cases in this sub-continent, I am of the opinion that the learned appellate Court committed an error of law in holding that the right, title and interest of the plaintiff extinguished because the suit land was under water for several years. I am also of the opinion that the appellate Court committed an error of law in deciding that the suit was not maintainable in view of the provision of sub-section (3) of section 86 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act.</u>

<u>15. Next, the question is about limitation. The learned appellate Court was of the view that the plaintiff and his father both were aware of the RS Khatian from the time of RS operation and as plaintiff did not file the suit within 6 years from the date of knowledge or from the final publication of the record, the suit was barred by time. Though it is not mentioned in the judgment itself, it appears that the appellate Court came to such a finding by applying Article 120 of the Limitation Act in the present case. The learned appellate Court also committed an error of law on the question of limitation. The question as to what will be the starting point of limitation in a case like this came up for consideration in the case of Rai Keshab Chandra Benerjee Bahadur and another vs. Madan Moham Poddar and Roy Bahadur and others vs. Tarak Nath Gango Padhyay and others. The cases are reported in 40 CWN page 22 and 566 respectively. The principle laid down in these cases is that if the plaintiff comes with a suit for declaration that the entry made in the record of right is wrong, in that case Article 120 will be applicable. It has also been held that the plaintiff is not bound to institute a suit for a declaration as the entry is wrong. He can wait and when an invasion on his rights is made on the basis of the entry, he can come and sue for a declaration of his title on the ground that the record is wrong. Such a suit will be in time if brought within six years from the date of threatened invasion. In the present case we find that the right, title and interest of the plaintiff did not extinguish or was not destroyed because the land was under water for several years. In view of this position, the plaintiff shall be deemed to be in constructive possession of the sub-merged land. In the present case, actual threat or invasion was made by leasing out the suit land to the defendant. Before that, there was no actual invasion or threat upon the right, title and possession of the plaintiff in the suit land. The lease was granted in the year 1975 and the suit was filed on 26-5-76. So, the question of the suit being barred by the time does not arise at all.</u>

16. The learned appellate Court also found that the suit was bad for defect of parties. The court came to this conclusion on the basis of Exhibit E and F (1). It has been observed that the suit jote measures 11 acres and the same land are under possession of different persons. Accordingly it was held that all the co-sharers of the CS RS PS and BS Khatians were necessary parties in the suit Mr. BK Das, the learned Advocate on behalf of the petitioner has invited my attention to the fact that the question was never raised by the defendant either in the trial Court or before the appellate Court. On perusal of the record, I find no Exhibits having marked Exhibit E or B or Exhibit F. It appears from the record of Other Appeal No. 66 of 1982 that the appellant like, the present opposite party filed an application under Order 41 Rule 27 read with section 151 of the CPC along with some documents on 23-9-89. The application and the documents were kept with the file. No formal order was passed nor was the documents admitted into evidence as additional evidence. From the lower Court record it appears that the defendant filed some document in the lower court and the documents were marked as A B C and D. In the lower Court, no documents were marked as Exhibit E and F. So, the exhibits referred to by the learned appellate Court are not before us nor these can be found in the record. Even the learned Advocate on behalf of the opposite party could not say anything about Exhibits E and F. So, I do not understand how the learned appellate Court on the basis of those exhibits came to a finding that the suit was bad for defect of parties. In this suit, the plaintiff prayed for declaration of title and confirmation of possession and a decree for permanent injunction against those who have challenged his title and threatened to dispossess him. I do not understand why all the co-sharers of CS RS PS and BS Khatians are necessary party in the suit. This is not a suit for partition. So, the question of making all the co-sharers of all those Khatians as parties in the suit does not arise. Thus I am also of opinion that the appellate Court committed an error of law in deciding that the suit is bad for defect of party.

<u>17. Lastly, the appellate Court observed that Local investigation was necessary for ascertaining the indentity of the land because according to him out of 11 acres of land, the plaintiff prayed for declaration of title in respect of only 66 decimals. While making this observation, the learned appellate Court again relied on Exhibits E and F which have no existence in the record. In this connection Mr. BK Das, the learned Advocate for the petitioners submitted that this question was also not traised before the trial Court. According to him, the defendant never challenged the identity of the land either in the written statement or while deposing as DW I. The question of identity of the land is a question of fact. The defendant did not challenge the identity of the land in the written statement. The defendant although stated that the suit land was under water for more than 60 years before 1954, that he took settlement of the suit land in settlement Case No.96/95-72-73 etc. The defendant also used the word suit land while describing his case. He did not say anywhere that the land claimed by him was not the land as described in the schedule to the plaint. He did not say that the description of the land as given in the plaint was not identical with the land described in the plaint. Moreover, from the statements of PWs we find that the two of the PWs described the boundary of the suit land. In view of the above position, I do not understand why the learned appellate Court came to a finding that the suit land was not identifiable and as such identification of the same by holding local investigation was necessary.</u>

<u>18. Mr. Ahsanul Kabir, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the opposite party, submitted that the plaintiffs or his predecessor did not pay any rent of the suit land after the RS record and as the suit land was recorded in the name of the Government, the plaintiff cannot claim any title therein. Only non-payment of rent cannot extinguish or destroy any right of a tenant. Moreover, from Exhibit 1 the published copy of the RS Khatian No. 894, we find that due to diluvion of the land the suit land was not included in the jama and it was excluded from the jama. In the remark column it has been mentioned that jama was tagged with the jama of Khatian No. 893. The plaintiff filed series of dhakilas showing payment of rent of the land of Khatian No. 893. So, in the instant case non-payment of rent of the suit land cannot affect the right of the tenant.</u>

19. Considering all the facts, circumstances, evidence and the legal position as discussed above, I am of the opinion that the learned appellate Court committed error of law in deciding that the suit was barred by time, bad for defect of parties, hit by provisions of section 86(3) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act which resulted in an error in the decision occasioning failure of Justice and those decisions of the learned appellate Court cannot be sustained in law. In the result, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to costs.

The judgment and decree of the appellate Court be set aside and those of trial Court be affirmed.

End.

caseno: Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 397 of 2005
lawyer:
JN Deb, Advocate, instructed by AKM Shahidul Huq, Advocate-on-Record—For the Petitioners. 
Md Nawab Ali, Advocate-on-Record—For Respondent Nos. 1-6. 
Not represented—Respondent Nos. 7-68.
parties:
Guljan Bibi and others ----- Petitioners
Vs.
Md Fazlu Miah and others ----- Respondents
case_source: (From the judgment and Order dated May 12, 2004 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 1835 of 1997)
full_judgment:
Md. Ruhul Amin J: Plaintiffs have filed this petition for leave to appeal against the judgment dated May 12, 2004 of a; Single Bench of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 1835 of 1997 making absolute the Rule obtained against the judgment and decree dated March 20, 1997 of the 3rd Court of Subordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge) Sylhet in Title Appeal No. 6 of 1993 allowing the same and thereupon setting aside the judgment and decree dated June 29, 1992 of the Additional Court of Senior Assistant Judge, Sadar, Sylhet in Title Suit No. 2 of 1992/295 of 1989 dismissing the same. The suit was filed seeking redemption of an usufructuary mortgage dated 26-12-1927.

2. The suit was filed on September 27, 1989. It was the case of the plaintiffs, that land measuring 2.53 acres belonged to 4 brothers, by name Himmat Khan, Rahmat Khan, Hanif Khan and Anis Khan, that Hanif Khan and Anis Khan mortgaged the land in suit by a registered deed of mortgage dated December 26, 1927 for an amount of Taka 48 and that it was stipulated in the mortgage deed that after one year the mortgagors would be entitled to redeem the mortgage in the month of Magh on payment of the balance of the amount, that said Hanif Khan and Anis Khan mortgaged the land of the heirs of Himmat Khan and Rahmat Khan to the predecessor of the defendant Nos. 1-11, Asmot Miah, and since mortgage said Asmot Miah was in possession of the land so mortgaged and that after the death of Asmot Miah, his heirs defendant Nos. 1-11 were possessing the mortgaged land, that in the first part of Magh, 1395 BS plaintiffs requested the defendant Nos. 1-4 to return the land but the defendants refused to do so, that to frustrate the claim of the plaintiffs defendant No. 9 in collusion with the defendant No. 12 created deed of exchange on June 11, 1989 in respect of 8 decimals of land of Plot No. 4346 and the defendant Nos. 5 and 7 in collusion with defendant Nos. 13 and 14 created a deed of sale dated August 31, 1989 for 3 decimals of land from the eastern part of plot No. 4344, that defendant Nos. 2 and 3 in collusion with the defendant Nos. 13 and 14 created a deed of sale on September 2, 1989 for 4 decimals of land from the western part of the plot No. 4346, that defendant Nos. 1, 8 and 11 created a deed in respect of 15 decimals of land of plot No. 4346 in favour of the defendant Nos.13-16, that the said deeds are collusive and fraudulent, that the plaintiffs are entitled to recover possession of the suit land as well as usufruct thereof.

3. The suit was contested by defendant Nos. 1, 8, 10 and 11, in one group as well as by defendant Nos.13 and 14 and by the defendant No. 12 separately by filing separate sets of written statement. The contesting defendants in their written statement denied the material overments made in the plaint. The case of the 1st group of defendants was that the land in suit belonged to their predecessor and that the same has been possessed by their predecessor for more than statutory period of limitation and thus predecessor of the defendants and they have acquired title by adverse possession, that defendant No. 1 upon amicable partition got the entire land of the plot No. 4354 and 9 decimals of land of plot No. 4344 and he sold 26 decimals of land from plot No. 4354 to Ibrahim Ali in 1981 and said Ibrahim Ali re-sold the land to the defendant No. 1, that defendant No. 1 sold 15 decimals of land on August 6, 1989 to defendant Nos.13 and 14 and their brothers Sirajul Islam and Safiqul Islam, that balance 3 decimals of land of the plot land of which was sold to defendant Nos.13 and 14 and their brothers, is possessed by defendant No. 9, that defendant Nos. 2-7's predecessor Eklas Mia got 8 decimals of land in his share from the land of plot No. 4346 and the heirs of Eklas Mia sold the said land by the kabalas dated August 31, 1989 and September 2, 1989 to defendant Nos. 13 and 14, that the land has been recorded in the name of 3 brothers namely, Babur Mia, Moyna Mia and Eklas Mia, that deed of mortgage was executed on 10th Poush, 1334 BS for one year and, as such, the same expired after one year and from the date of such expiry plaintiffs' right to redemption arose but the plaintiffs have filed the suit after lapse of 62 years and, as such, the suit is barred by limitation, that defendant Sufi Mia had not exchanged any land from plot No. 4346 with Shaista Mia on June 11, 1989 and that if any deed of exchange is produced the same is forged, false and fabricated, since at the relevant time Sufi Mia was not in the country and that his address shown in the exchange deed is not correct and that the plaintiff Motasir Mia in collusion with the father of Shaista Mia collusively brought into existence the suit for exchange deed, that the plaintiffs are not entitled to get khas possession and their suit is liable to be dismissed.

4. The case of the defendant Nos. 13 and 14 was that Asmot Mia by a registered deed dated 10th Poush 1334 BS became the absolute owner of the land in suit and was possessing the same, that Asmot Mia died leaving 3 sons by name, Babur Mia, Moyna Mia and Eklas Mia and by amicable partition heirs of Eklas Mia (defendant Nos. 2-4) got 8 decimals of land along with their sister in plot No. 4346 and 4344 and defendant Nos. 4-7 sold 32 decimals of land on August 31, 1989 and defendant Nos. 2 and 3 sold 42 decimals of land by the kabala dated September 2, 1989 to the defendant Nos.13 and 14 and that defendant Nos. 1, 8, 10 and 11 sold 15 decimals of land to these defendants and their brothers, Sirajul Islam and Shafiqul Islam on August 6, 1989, that by purchase these defendants and their brothers have acquired the entire land of plot Nos. 4344 and 4346, that plaintiffs never made any objection to the transfer so made by the heirs of Asmot Mia, that record of right has been prepared in the name of heirs of Asmot Mia without any objection from the plaintiffs' side, that plaintiffs have no right, title and interest in the land in suit.

5. The case of the defendant No.12 was that Asmot Mia purchased some land on 15-2-1928 and owned and possessed the same till his death and after his death said property amicably partitioned amongst his heirs, that on June 11, 1989 defendant No. 9 Sufi Mia son of Asmot Mia exchanged 8 decimals of land from plot No. 4346 with the land of defendant No. 12, that claim of the defendant Nos.13 and 14 that they purchased some land of plot Nos. 4344 and 4346 by kabalas dated (August 1, 1989 and September 2, 1989 is false and they have no possession in the land so claimed to have purchased.

6. The trial Court on consideration of the materials on record dismissed the suit on the finding that the suit was barred by limitation and plaintiffs have failed to establish their case and the suit is not maintainable that defendant No. 12 is not entitled to the land said to have got by exchange, that mortgage was made on 26-12-1927 for one year and, as such, on the expiry of the said one year the plaintiffs were required to file the suit prior to the expiry of 60 years on and from 26-12-1928.

<u>7. The plaintiffs went on appeal. The appellate Court upon allowing the appeal set aside the judgment and decree of the trial Court and thereupon decreed the suit in the finding that the suit is not barred by limitation since demand for return of possession was made within 60 years and, as such, the period for limitation shall be counted as per Article 143 of the Limitation Act, that plaintiffs made the demand for return of possession in the 1st part of Magh, 1395 BS since by that time the mortgage being an usufructuary mortgage, the land in question became free from mortgage, that in case of usufructuary mortgage period of limitation as per provision of Article 143 of the Limitation Act, 1908 runs from the date of refusal to return possession of the mortgaged land. Thereupon, the defendants moved the High Court Division in revisional jurisdiction and obtained the Rule.</u>

8. On behalf of the defendant-petitioners it was contended before the High Court Division that the suit was barred by limitation since the same was not filed within 60 years from 28-12-1928 as the mortgage which was made on 27-12-1927 become redeemable on and from 27-12-1928 but the suit was filed on September 27, 1989, Chat the Court of appeal below on misreading the evidence and misconstruing the document as well as the provision of law allowed the appeal upon setting aside the judgment and decree of the trial Court.

9. As against the contention of the defendant-petitioners it was contended on behalf of the plaintiff opposite parties that the admitted position is that there was a deed of mortgage dated 26-12-1927 and the mortgagors acquired the right of redemption after one year i.e. on and from 26-12-1928, and the suit as per provision of Article 148 of the Limitation Act was required to file within 60 years from aforesaid date and that suit was filed on 27.9.1989 while 60 years expired on 26-12-1988 and thus though apparently it appears that the suit was barred by limitation but because of the provision of Article 4 of the Bangladesh (Legal Proceedings) Order, 1972 (President's Order No. 12 of 1972) the suit was not barred by limitation since the period between the 1st day of March, 1971 and the 1st day of March 1972 (both days inclusive) shall be excluded and, as such, the suit so filed was not barred by limitation. It was also contended by the learned Advocate for the plaintiff-opposite parties that in case of ambiguity, inconsistency or conflict between the substantive provision of the statute and the preamble of the statute then in that case the provision of law in the relevant section of the statute shall be given effect. It was also contended before the High Court Division that because of the provision of Article 4 of the President's Order No. 12 of 1972, hereinafter referred to as the Order, there is no scope to mitigate the provision of said section upon making reference to the preamble of the Order.

<u>10. The High Court Division in the background of the Exhibit 1 deed of mortgage dated 26-12-1927, held that plaintiffs filed the suit on 27-9-1989 i.e. 9 months after the date of expiry of the period of limitation dated 26-12-1928 since the mortgagors' right of redemption accrued on 26-12-1928 with the expiry of one year from the date of mortgage dated 26-12-1927, and, as such, it appears that the plaintiffs waived their right of redemption, that provision of Article 4 of PO 12 of 1972 is applicable as regard a case where a person could not because of the abnormal situation from 1st of March, 1971 to 1st of March, 1972 institute or initiate legal proceedings and, as such, his claim or suit become barred by limitation and that plaintiffs' suit being not of that kind or in, other words, plaintiff's' suit is not of a kind which become barred by limitation in between 1st of March, 1971 and 1st of March, 1972, both days inclusive, rather his suit become barred on 26-12-1988 i.e. much long after the period as in Article 4 of the PO 12 of 1972 and, as such, provision of Article 4 of PO 12 of 1972 is not applicable to plaintiffs' suit. On the aforesaid findings the High Court Division made the Rule absolute.</u>

<u>11. The learned Advocate for the petitioner has reiterated the contention which he made upon referring to the provision of PO 12 of 1972 before the High Court Division. To appreciate the contention of the learned Advocate for the petitioners the preamble and the Article 4 of the President's Order 12 of 1972 are quoted below:</u>

<u>"The preamble—Whereas during the material period there was disruption of normal life and activities throughout Bangladesh;</u>

<u>And whereas due to the reign of terror perpetrated by the Pakistan occupation army people were not able to go to Courts or Tribunals either to institute legal proceedings or to defend them so as to comply with directions issued by Courts or Tribunals and as a result many claims and legal rights have become time-barred and many legal proceedings have been disposed of ex parte or in default of compliance with directions of the Court or Tribunals.</u>

<u>And whereas, for the ends of justice, it is necessary to provide for the saving of limitation for all legal proceedings and for the nullification of all judgments, decrees and orders passed ex parte or in default of compliance with certain directions in certain legal proceedings; and</u>

<u>"Article 4. Notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force, in computing the period of limitation prescribed for any legal proceeding by or under any law, the period between the 1st day of March, 1971 and the 1st day of March, 1972 (both days inclusive), shall be excluded".</u>

<u>12. It is not disputed that the mortgage was made on 26-12-1927 and it was the stipulation in the mortgage deed that the mortgagors would be able to redeem the mortgage after one year from 27-12-1927. In that state of the matter the right of redemption accrued on December 26 of 1928 and from that date within 60 years as per Article 148 of the Limitation Act the plaintiffs were required to file the suit for redemption by 26-12-1988 but they filed the suit on 27-9-1989 i.e. after expiry of the period of limitation or, in other words, after 9 months after the period prescribed by law for seeking the relief of redemption of mortgage. The learned Counsel for the petitioner, who also represented the petitioners before the High Court Division, has not disputed that the suit was filed after the time prescribed by the Limitation Act but it was his contention that because of the provision of Article 4 of the PO 12 of 1972 which provides that period between the 1st day of March, 1971 and the 1st day of March, 1972, both the days inclusive as shall be excluded in computing period of limitation and thus the suit is not barred by limitation. It has also been submitted by the learned Counsel for the petitioner that the provision of Article 4 of the PO 12 of 1972 being clear and free from ambiguity, as such, upon resorting to the preamble of PO 12 of 1972 the High Court Division was in error in holding that the suit was barred by limitation on the view since plaintiffs' suit was not of the kind which became barred between 1st of March, 1971 and 1st of March 1972 or, in other words, plaintiffs are not of the category of the person who because of the abnormal situation in 1971 and thereafter up to 1st day of March, 1972 could not initiate their proceeding seeking redemption of the mortgage and thereupon their right to seek relief by way of redemption of the mortgage became barred and, as such, the suit so filed by the plaintiffs is barred by limitation since the same has been filed after the lapse of the statutory period of limitation. The learned Counsel in support of his contention that in the absence of ambiguity, inconsistency or conflict between the preamble and the substantive provision in the statute the substantive provision of law in the statute shall be given effect to has referred to the case of Nurun Nabi Mondal and others vs Joynal Abedin Khondkar and others reported in 29 DLR (SC) 137. It appears to us the whole contention of the learned Advocate for the petitioner is that the preamble of PO 12 of 1972 shall not control or restrict the substantive provision in Article 4 of the PO 12 of 1972. We have no reason to take different view other than the proposition of law laid down in the reported case as to that "the preamble of an Act cannot control or restrict the substantive provision of the Act and that it can be of some guidance if there is an ambiguity in the sections or some doubt as to the true scope of the provisions of that enactment" and that preamble cannot curtail or restrict the scope of the Act. In the preamble of PO 12 of 1972 it has been stated " due to the reign of terror perpetrated by the Pakistan occupation army people were not able to go to courts or Tribunals" to institute legal proceeding "and as a result many claims and legal rights have become time barred  " and, as such, "for the ends of justice, it is necessary to provide for the saving of limitation for all legal proceedings  " The object of enacting the PO 12 of 1972 was for saving the limitation of claims and legal rights that became barred because of the situation in 1971 and some time thereafter. The sole object and purpose of the provisions in Article 4 of the PO 12 of 1972 was to give life to the claims and legal rights that became barred between 1st March, 1971 and 1st March, 1972 (both days inclusive). In Article 4 it has been provided that "in computing the period of limitation prescribed for any legal proceeding by or under any law, the period between the 1st day of march, 1971 and the 1st day of March, 1972 (both days inclusive), shall be excluded". So, from the reading of the provision of Article 4 of the Order it is seen that where a person could not go to "the Courts or Tribunals" in between 1st March, 1971 and 1st March, 1972 (both days inclusive) to institute legal proceeding "and as a result" claims or legal rights of such person have become time barred in that situation for attaining the object and for achieving the purpose of saving claim or legal right from being barred by limitation, as in the preamble, and keeping in view the object and purpose law as in Article 4 of the PO 12 of 1972 has been enacted for saving the claims and legal rights from being time barred. In Article 4 of PO 12 of 1972 provision has been made "for the saving of limitation for all legal proceedings" and for excluding specified period "in computing the period of limitation prescribed for any legal proceeding by or under any law" as regard the 'claims and legal rights that have become time barred' as one could not or was not able, for special reason as in the preamble of PO 12 of 1972, 'to go to Court or Tribunals' 'to institute legal proceedings'. The legal proceeding as to which the provision of Article 4 shall apply is very much explicit as to which kind of proceeding the said provision shall apply when read with the preamble of PO 12 of 1972. The provision of law as in Article 4 of PO 12 of 1972 has been enacted to meet 'the ends of justice' upon making provision 'for the saving of limitation for all proceedings' those have become time barred as because people could not initiate legal proceedings "due to the reign of terror perpetrated by the Pakistan occupation army" or, in other words, a new lease of life was given to time barred claims and legal rights as well as to the legal proceedings that became time barred upon excluding the specified period in computing the period of limitation i.e. "the period between the 1st day of March, 1971 and the 1st day of March, 1972 (both day inclusive) shall be excluded". So, it is seen that the provision of Article 4 of PO 12 of 1972 would be applicable to 'the claims and legal rights' as well as to a legal proceeding that had become barred by limitation as because legal proceeding could not be instituted because of the situation as spelt out in the preamble of PO 12 of 1972. To avail of the provision of law as in Article 4 of PO 12 of 1972 as regard claim and legal right as well as legal proceeding the same shall have to be time-barred one because of the situation as in the preamble of PO 12 of 1972 and then said claim and legal right as well as legal proceeding would be given life by excluding the period "between the 1st day of March, 1971 and the 1st day of March, 1972 (both days inclusive)". The suit filed by the plaintiff-petitioners was not the one that became time barred "during the material period" as they could not file the suit "due to the reign of terror perpetrated by the Pakistan occupation army". The 'material period' during which legal proceeding could not be instituted and consequently, became time barred has been mentioned in Article 4 of the Order. The provision of law as in Article 4 of PO 2 of 1972 has been enacted to exclude specified period "for all legal proceeding" those have become time barred between the period as has been mentioned in Article 4 of the Order. The whole object of the provision of Article 4 of PO 12 of 1972 is "for the saving of limitation for all legal proceedings" that have become time barred at a time as mentioned in Article 4 of the Order or, in other words, in computing the period of limitation in respect of a proceeding which has become time barred between the period as mentioned in Article 4 of the Order the same would be excluded and thereby one whose claim or legal right has become time barred or one who could not institute legal proceedings during the period as mentioned in Article 4 of the Order would be extended in computing the period of limitation or, in other words, class of legal proceedings or claim and legal right has become time barred during the material period as in Article 4 of the Order for further one year but after the expiry of period as in Article 4 of the Order i.e. the claim or legal right of a person would certainly become time barred. The legal proceeding too. We are of the view the provision of Article 4 of the Order has no application to the legal proceeding that did not become time barred during the material period as mentioned therein. In the instant case it is apparent that plaintiffs claim of redemption did not become barred by limitation during the period as mentioned in Article 4 of the Order. The plaintiffs' right to file suit seeking redemption became time barred on 26-12-1988. In that state of the matter we are of the view the contention of the learned Advocate of the plaintiff petitioners that plaintiffs' suit was not barred by limitation since he would get one year more from 26-12-1988 and thus the period for filing the suit seeking redemption was to expire in December, 1989 but the suit having been filed on 27th September, 1989 the same was not barred by limitation legally not well founded and sustainable.</u>

<u>13. In the background of our discussions, we are of the view the High Court Division was not in error in holding that the plaintiffs' suit was barred by limitation.</u>

<u>Accordingly the petition is dismissed.</u>

End.

lawyer:
AJ Mohammad Ali with JN Deb and Md Ekramul Haque, Advocates---For the Petitioners. 
Promila Biswas, Advocate---For the Opposite Parties.
parties:
Mridul Kanti Sarder alias Mridul Sarder and others   ----- Petitioners
Vs
Krishna Charan Sarder and others ----- Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
This Rule was issued calling upon the opposite party Nos. 1(1) to (3) to show cause as to why the impugned Judgment and decree dated 27-6-1993, decree signed on 4-7-1993 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, Patiya, Chittagong, in Other Appeal No. 555 of 1991, reversing the judgment and decree dated 22-8-1991, decree signed on 28-8-1991, passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, 1st Court, Patiya, Chittagong, in Other Suit No. 16 of 1990 should not be set aside.

2. Facts leading to the issuance of this Rule are that one Krishna Charan Sarder instituted the Other Suit No. 16 of 1990 on 20-1-1990 in the Court of the Assistant Judge, 1st Court, Patiya, Chittagong against Mridul Sarder and 6 others, praying for a decree for declaration of title and confirmation of possession of the suit land, measuring an area of 4 sataks, i-e, 2 gandas of land in RS Plot No. 1377 under the RS Khatian No. 418, in Mouza-Dengapara, together with a decree for declaration of the BS Khatian recorded in respect of the suit property, is void, baseless and wrongly recorded, stating, inter alia, that one Uma Charan Sarder was in the right, title and possession of the suit land and the RS Khatian stood recorded in his name and after his death, Mathura inherited the right, title, possession and interest in the suit land. Mathura died leaving behind his daughter Khemlata and Khemlata with her son, Arun Sarder, inherited the same. Both Khemlata and Arun Sarder sold out the suit property to the plaintiff and handed over its possession. The defehdants have no right, title and possession in the suit land, but they are threatening the plaintiff of dispossession. The suit land is contiguous land to the homestead of the plaintiff and the BS Khatian has wrongly been recorded in the names of the defendants.

3. The defendant Nos. 1 to 6 have contested the suit by filing written statements, stating that Uma Charan had his 'Chakran' interest in the suit land and on his death, the suit property was restored to the Zamindar Sita Sundari Dutta and while she was in her khas possession, settled the suit land with Hirendra Lal Sarder, the predecessor of the defendants on 22-8-1956 under a registered Patta and handed over possession thereof and Hirendra Lal Sarder made a cowshed upon the suit land as the same is contiguous to his homestead and upon his death, the defendants have inherited it as his heirs and are in continuous possession in the suit land. The BS Khatian has rightly been recorded in the name of their predecessor and the purchase deed of the plaintiff has not been acted upon nor has he acquired any right, title and possession in the suit land by virtue of that deed, Since the plaintiffs vendor had no right, title, possession and interest in the suit land, the plaintiff too, has not acquired any such interest. The dispute being a long standing dispute, a local Shalish took place on 28-9-1980 between the plaintiff and the predecessor of the defendants and all the Arbitrators made an unanimous award in this respect and, according to the award, the plaintiff had no interest in the suit land.

4. After conclusion of the trial, the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Patiya, has been pleased to dismiss the suit on his findings that the plaintiff has not disputed the registered Patta of the predecessor of the defendants and nothing has been mentioned about the Patta in the plaint and thus, the plaintiff has admitted the said Patta. The Patta was executed and registered on 22-8-1956 and the plaintiff claimed that it was not acted upon, and thereby also admitted that his vendors had no right, title and interest in the suit land and if, at all, the Patta made after 14-4-1956 was ineffective, in that case, the suit property will be khas land of the Government and, as such, the plaintiffs purchase is also not effective. The PW 1 has admitted in cross-examination that the BS record has rightly been prepared, which is Annexure-C, in the suit and, as such, the possession of the defendants has been proved in the suit land. Though the plaintiff claimed that he is in possession of the suit land from 8-9-1980, but could not mention the plot number of the suit land which is waste land and the PW 2 claimed possession of the plaintiff for 4/5 years, whereas the defendants claimed that they are possessing the same since the time of their predecessor having a cowshed and the Advocate Commissioner was examined in the suit as DW 2, who stated that he saw a cowshed in the suit land during his inspection made more than 7/8 years ago and from the Arbitration Award, Exhibit -F(1) also it appears that the defendants are in possession in the suit land. The plaintiffs with a view to prove his possession exhibited two rent-receipts, vide Exhibit-3-3(a) which are of much later time of the institution of the instant suit i-e, the suit was instituted on 20-1-1990 and the rent paid under these Dakhilas on 28-6-1990 and 10-6-1991 respectively and the defendants exhibited 6(six) rent-receipts vide Exhibit-E-E(5) and Chowkidari receipt, vide Exhibit-D in respect of the suit land showing that the defendants are paying rent right from 19-4-1974 and in view of the case reported in 35 DLR (AD) 217 the rent-receipts are evidence of the possession, also may be used as a collateral evidence of title, thereby proving that the defendants are in exclusive possession of the suit land and, for argument's sake, if the Patta is not considered, still the possession of the defendants is for more than 12 years, and thereby creating possessory rights in favour of the defendants. In view of the case reported in 3 DLR 484 that if any person possesses any lane for 12 years is vested with the title of it and the person in possession became an owner' and that the plaintiff without instituting a suit for recovery of possession, cannot maintain his suit in its present form. The possession of the plaintiff in the suit land has not been proved and the BS Khatian has rightly been recorded.

5. On the other hand, the learned Sub-ordinate Judge, Patiya, Chittagong has been pleased to allow the Other Appeal No. 555 of 1991, preferred by the plaintiff against the said judgment and decree passed by the learned Assistant Judge in Other Suit No. 16 of 1990 setting aside the said judgment and decree and also to decree the suit declaring the right, title and possession of the plaintiff in the suit land holding that at the time of hearing, the plaintiff appellant has produced the PS Khatian on 4-5-1993, which has also been considered in the appeal and the genealogy of Uma Charan given by the plaintiff has been proved and the plaintiff's purchase from Uma Charan's descendants, namely Khemlata and Arun Sarder, by a Saf-Kabala dated 8-9-1980 (Exhibit-2), is also proved, holding further, that since Uma Charan had his Chakran interest during the RS operation and subsequent PS record has also been recorded in the name of Uma Charan showing his Chakran interest, it is thus established, beyond reasonable doubt, that by operation of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, Uma Charan acquired his tenancy right under section 11 of the Act, since he was in possession of the suit land at the time when the said Act came into force and thus, became a tenant under the Government and the learned Assistant Judge has failed to consider this legal aspect of the case. The learned Appellate Court also held that the learned Advocates appearing for the defendants-respondents had admitted that the Patta in question has never been acted upon, since it was registered after 14-4-1956 and has argued on the right of the defendants by adverse possession, on the ground of possessing the suit land for more than 12 years. But the DW 3 Manindra Sarder has admitted the possession of the vendors of the plaintiff in his evidence admitting also that after the death of Mathura Sarder, Krishna Sarder is possessing the suit land and Krishna Sarder was the original plaintiff of this suit and since, the DW 3 himself admitted the possession of the plaintiff, the adverse possession of the defendants could not be held.

6. The defendants-respondents have thereafter preferred this application under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure and obtained the instant Rule with an order of maintaining status quo in respect of the suit property, on the grounds that the learned Appellate Court has committed a grave error of law in deciding the question of possession relying upon the confused statements of the DW 3 without noticing his clear evidence on record and the learned Appellate Court has wrongly construed the section 11 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 in view of the fact that Mathura died in 1943 and the Chakran interest was not heritable. The learned Appellate Court has erred in law in not holding that Khemlata and Arun Sarder did not acquire Chakran interest and also by relying upon the PS Khatian which was not filed and proved in accordance with law before the learned trial Court and the learned appellate Court has also committed an error of law in not holding that the plaintiff has failed to prove his title and possession in the suit land.

7. The Opposite Party has, on the other hand, filed an affidavit-in-opposition controverting the statements and submissions made and grounds taken by the petitioners and reiterating the points that have been decided by the learned Courts below.

8. Mr AJ Mohammad Ali, the learned Advocate, appearing with Mr JN Deb and Mr Md Ekramul Hoque, the learned Advocates for the petitioners, by placing his reliance upon the case of Sakina Bibi vs Matra Bibi, reported in 1985 BCR (AD) 37 submitted that since Chakran interest is not heritable, Khemlata or her son Arun cannot be treated as in possession of the disputed land in the capacity of Chakran interest after the death of Uma Charan and that section 11 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act gives protection only to those persons who are in possession of the lands in the capacity of Chakran interest at the time of operation. The learned Advocate thus submitted that the RS record tenant Uma Charan had his interest in the suit land as Chakran and so also in the unproved PS Khatian and since, according to law, the Chakran interest is not heritable, Khemlata and Arun Sarder have not inherited the interest of Uma Charan and, as such, they acquired no right, title interest and possession in the suit land to transfer it to the plaintiff.

The plaintiff has acquired no such right, title, possession and interest in the suit land by dint of his purchase deed and the deed is ineffective and inoperative and not acted upon and thus, the learned Appellate Court has arrived at an erroneous findings occasioning failure of justice.

9. Mrs Promila Biswas, the learned Advocate, appearing for the opposite party, has, on the other hand, placed her reliance upon the provisions of section 11 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 and submitted that the vendors of the plaintiff have acquired their right, title and possession in the suit land by operation of law. The possessors of the suit land, namely, Khemlata and Arun Sarder, became the tenants under the Government having their transferable interests.

10. Perused the application, heard the learned Advocates and considered their submissions.

11. From the RS Khatian No. 418, it appears that Uma Charan, son of Joyman Hori, got tenancy of 4 sataks of land under Chandra Mohan Dutta and Ramoni Mohan Dutta and others as “দখল কার চাকরান বাধ্যকর” and from the PS Khatian, produced before the learned Appellate Court, it also appears that 4 sataks of land was recorded in the name of Uma Charan, son of Joyman Hori, as his Chakran interest.

12. Exhibit-2 is the registered kabala No. 4230 dated 8-9-1980 under which Sree Krishna Kumar Sarder purchased 4 sataks of land from Sree Arun Sarder and Sreemati Khemlata which is the suit land and from the recital portion of the deed, it appears that the vendors stated that the property was Uma Charan's khas property and homestead and that Uma Charan died having no other heirs and his daughter the vendor No. 2 and grandson, the vendor No. 1 inherited it as his heirs. From Exhibit -3 series, it appears that Lalu Sarder has paid rent for this 4 sataks of land in the name of Uma Charan in the year 1990 and 1991.

13. From Exhibit-B of the defendants, it appears that the Patta No. 4844 was registered on 22-8-1956 in respect of these 4 sataks of land by Sreemati Sita Sundari Dutta for settlement of land with Sree Khirendra Lal Sarder and the BS Khatian No. 736 (Exhibit-C) stood recorded in the name of Khirendra Lal Sarder in respect of these 4 sataks of land, and Exhibits-D and E series are the rent-receipts, showing rent paid by Khirendra also in the name of Uma Charan from the decade of seventies and the Exhibit-F is the Arbitration Award, where it was held that the vendors of the plaintiff had no possession of the suit land and also that the first party Krishna Kumar Sarder (plaintiff) had no possession in the land of dispute. The plaintiff produced 3 witnesses, including himself (Lalu Sarder, son of Krishna Sarder) and the stated, in gist that after the death of Uma Charan his son Mathura Sarder inherited the property and after the death of Mathura, Khemlata and her son Arungot it and the Amanat Kha stated that the plaintiffs father would possess the suit land and now the plaintiff is possessing it and the defendants have no possession in the suit land. The PW 3 is Khemlata, daughter of Mathura Sarder, stating that she had no brother and she along with her son Arun sold the suit property to the plaintiff and delivered its possession and they were in possession in the suit land.

14. DW 1 is Mridul Kanti Sarder who supported their Patta got through their father from Zamindar Sita Sundari also supporting the BS Khatian and the Award asserting their possession in the suit land. DW 2 is Md Ishaque who held the local inspection and proved his report stating that he found a cowshed in the suit land. The DW 3 is Monindra Sarder stating that there is a cowshed in the suit property and plaintiff or his vendors have never possessed the suit land and he saw the suit land in possession of Krishna Sarder after death of Mathura. Khemlata is his daughter and Arun grandson. After Mathura, Khemlata did not possess it. He did not know that Khemlata sold it to Krishna Sarder. It is not a fact that the plaintiff is in possession in the suit land.

15. On perusal of the documentary and oral evidence on record. findings of the Courts below, it appears that the dispute in relation to the suit land has narrowed down to the point as to whether Khemlata and Arun Sarder and, for that matter, Khemlata's father Mathura or grandfather Uma acquired tenancy right under the Government by operation of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 and whether the defendants acquired any right, title and interest under the Patta which has allegedly been executed by the ex-Zamindar in favour of their father in the year 1956 or they acquired title by adverse possession.

16. Section 11 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 is as follows :

"11. Acquisition of Occupancy Rights. —

(1) Notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force or in any contract, any person who holds under another person any land, for agricultural or horticultural purposes or for the purposes of his homestead, free of rent in consideration of some service to be rendered, under the system locally known as Nankar, Chakran or the like shall, on and from the date of commencement of this Act, acquire a right of occupancy in all such lands so held by him subject to the payment of a fair and equitable rent to the person under whom he holds such lands and the provisions of the Bengal Tenancy Act, 1885 (VIII of 1885) or the Sylhet Tenancy Act, 1936 (Assam Act XI of 1936), as the case may be, so far as they apply to occupancy raiyats, shall apply to him.

17. The Special Committee, by their report dated 6-7-1949, said that Chapter III of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 is intended to give the service tenure holders the status of occupancy radiates.

18. By section 11 the service tenure holders, namely, the Nankar, Chakran or the like, have been given occupancy status in agricultural, horticultural or homestead land "on and from the date of commencement of this Act subject to the payment of fair and equitable rent to the person under whom he holds such lands "

19. The State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 came into force on the 16th May, 1951 (Latif vs Manwar, 6 DLR 326) and on and from 16-5-1951 the Nankar, Chakran or the like acquired their right of occupancy in such land on condition that:  Subject to the payment of a fair and equitable rent to the person under whom he holds such land'.

20. The Nankars or Chakrans were also given protection from ejectment by the East Bengal Service Tenants (Protection) Act, 1952, which came into force on 5-11-1952.

21. In view of the provisions of section 11 of the Act, the determining factor is; whether Uma has acquired a right of occupancy in the lands or whether he was holding it on the date of commencement of the Act, i.e. on 16-5-1951.

22. In the case of Sakina Bibi vs Nazira Bibi, 1985 BCR (AD) 38 their Lordships held that 'section 11 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act gives protection only to persons who are in possession of the lands in the capacity of a Chakran tenant."

23. In the light of the said decision, the present case is required to be examined.

24. Under the RS Khatian No. 418, Uma, son of Joyman Hori, had the Chakran interest in respect of the suit land.

25. The plaintiffs Sale Deed No. 4230 was executed by Arun Sardar, son of Barada Sardar and Khemlata Sarder, wife of Barada Sardar and daughter of late Mathura Sardar (original was not produced) on 8-9-1980 stating that the property was khas property of Uma and the vendors of the deed have thereafter stated as follows in the recital portion:

যেহেতু মিশ্র তপকালীর সম্পত্তি ২নং দাত্রীর (ক্ষেমলতা পিত্র সহ উমা চরনের দাস দাসী ভিটিভূমি ছিল আর, এস দরীপ চুড়ান্ত আছে, উচ্চ উমাচর পরলোক গমন করিলে তাহার অন্য কোন ওয়ারিশ না থাকার হিন্দু ধর্মমতে তাহার কন্যা আমি ২নং দাত্রী প্রাপ্ত হইয়াছি তৎপর উমাচরনের মৃত্যুর স্থলে তাহার নাতিন আমি ২নং দাত্রা ওয়ারিশ সূত্রে দৌহত প্রাপ্ত হইয়া থাকে দখলকার ও মালগুজার আজি এবং ১নং দাতার নানুদার, মথুরার দৌহর ও ২নং দাতার মথুরার কন্যা হিন্দু ধর্মমতে প্রাপ্ত হইয়া ফাসে দখলকার ও মালগুজার আজি।

26. In this portion, the vendor stated that at the time of death of Uma Charan, he had no other heir except the vendor No. 2, Khemlata and she was the granddaughter of Uma Charan. It also appears from the statement above, that her father Mathura Charan died some time before her grandfather, Uma Charan. Now if Uma Charan was alive on 16-5-1951, he acquired his right of occupancy in the land, recorded in the RS Khatian, If Uma Charan acquired the tenancy right, under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, only after then, the sale deed of Khemlata and her son Arun Sardar may be operative.

27. Khemlata appeared in the suit as PW 3. She admitted her sale to the plaintiff by making statements, though the kabala in question was not produced before her and she has not proved her thumb impression or the thumb impression of her son on the Kabala. She stated her father died in 1943, in her cross-examination, but no question was put to her when her grandfather Uma Charan died.

28. PW 1, stated in his examination-in-chief, that:

যহেনালিশী তপশীলের ভুমি উমাচরনের স্বত্ব ও দখলীয় ছিল। তৎমতে আর, এস খতিয়ান দাখিল করেছি। Exhibit-I. উমাচরন মরনে তৎপুত্র মথুরা সর্দার প্রাপ্ত হন। মথুরা সরনে তৎকন্যা ক্ষেমলতা প্রাপ্ত হন। মথুরা মরলে তৎকন্যা ক্ষেমলতা প্রাপ্ত হন। মথুরা সর্দারের কোন পুত্র সন্তান ছিল না। ক্ষেমলতার ও পুত্র ছিল অরুন সর্দার।

<u>29. In view of the serious contradiction between the evidence of the PWs and the deed itself (Exhibit-2) in respect of source of interest of the inheritors and also on the vague point of Uma Charan's acquiring the occupancy right under section 11 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and its legal implication, it cannot be held the vendors of the plaintiff inherited Chakran interest of Uma Charan or the plaintiff acquired any interest under his kabala, Exhibit-2.</u>

<u>30. By Notification No. 4839-LR dated 2nd April 1956, all lands other than retainable khas lands, have, in fact, been acquired by the Government in accordance with the provisions of section 3 of the Act, vesting the same in the Government, and, as such, on 22-8-1956 Sita Sundari had no right to settle with the father of the defendants under the alleged Patta. The Patta is void ab initio.</u>

31. In her evidence Khemlata, PW 3 stated that her father died in 1943 and she was about 7/8 years of age at that time. After 5 years of her father's death, her marriage took place. She has visited the suit land before one year for the last and her husband's house is 10 miles away from the suit land. This means, the PW 3 did not possess the land at the time of her alleged sale. PW 2 Amanat Kha stated that he saw the suit land under possession of Lalu's full sister for 6/7 years and then plaintiffs father for 5/6 years and then the plaintiffs for 4/5 years, Thus, the possession of the plaintiff in the suit land is not proved.

32. In her evidence the PW Khemlata stated that there was a case in the UP while the defendant's father was alive.

33. Exhibit-F(1) is the Arbitration Award given by the 13 No. Shu-Chakradandi Union Parishad on 28-9-1980 holding the possession of Khirendra Sardar and finding no possession of Krishan Kumar Sardar. The BS Khatian No. 736 was recorded in the name of Khirendra Lal Sardar evidencing his possession, Khirendra Lal Sardar paid rent in the name of Uma Charan from the year 1974, vide Exhibit-E (series) and Lalu Sardar also paid rent in the name of Uma Charan for the years 1990 and 1991, vide Exhibit-3.

34. The documentary and oral evidence on record proved possession of the defendants in the suit land.

35. But there cannot be any adverse possession against the Government, in law. The land in question has been vested in the Government by operation of law on 2-4-1956. The possession could be adverse against Khemlata and her vendee. The Government has admitted possession of the defendants by receiving rent and by publishing the BS Khatian.

36. In the case of Wan vs Joynal Abedin, reported in 35 DLR (AD) 216 their Lordships held that "Rent-receipts though not documents of title, but are important items of evidence of possession and may be used as collateral evidence of title since possession generally follows the title."

37. This collateral evidence may be taken with the BS Khatian for consideration.

38. In the case of Abdul Hamid vs Abul Hossain Mir, reported in 35 DLR 295 his Lordship held that "Presumption of Khatian loses its weight with the passage of time and that the entries in the subsequent khatian would be more acceptable to a Court than the entries in the earlier Khatian."

39. In view of the legal position. I am con-strained to hold that the defendant-petitioners have acquired title by virtue of their possession and have become tenants under the Government.

40. In the result, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to costs.

41. The Judgment and decree dated 27-6-1993, passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, Patiya, Chittagong in Other Appeal No. 555 of 1991 is set aside.

42. The Other Suit No. 16 of 1990 of the Court of the learned Assistant Judge, 1st Court, Patiya is dismissed without any order as to costs.

Send down the lower Court's Record at once.

End.

Ekramul Islam, Advocate--For Respondent No.1.
