full_judgment:
M Moazzam Husain, J : This appeal at the instance of the sole plaintiff, a company, is directed against the judgment and decree of dismissal dated 7-9-2000 passed in Other Suit No.316 of 1994 by the learned Subordinate Judge, 3rd Court, Tangail, dismissing the suit. The suit was for declaration of title in respect of 7.65½ acre of land appertaining to CS Khatian No. 309 in Gorai Moeen Nagar Mouza under Tauji No.10 in Mirzapur, District- Tangail.

2. The facts as alleged in the plaint, in short, are that the suit land comprising of 182.23 acre described in Tauji No.10 of the then Mymensingh Collectorate originally belonged to Zamindar Haider Ali Khan Panni and others and the same having formed the saham of Haider Ali Khan Panni was accordingly recorded in his name in the CS khatian. The suit land along with other land constituted a waqf estate and Haider Ali Khan Panni himself was appointed as Mutawalli. During his tenure as Mutawalli Haider Ali Khan Panni settled a total of 126.54 acre land out of the waqf estate with his two sons, namely, Mehdi Ali Khan Panni and Sayeed Ali Khan Panni, and his two grandsons, namely Bayezid Khan Panni and Daud Khan Panni by executing a Jote-Pattannama in the year 1353 BS and handed over possession to them. The lessees having taken pattan of the land as above had been enjoying the same by paying rent to the Zamindari Estate. Meanwhile, SA operation started in the area and except a portion of land that was earlier transferred by the lessees rest 118.34 acre was recorded in their joint names. Thus the lessees and their heirs, as the case may be, had been in peaceful possession and enjoyment of the land in the suit khatian by paying rent to the Government.

3. The plaintiff purchased the suit land from defendant Nos. 2-8 who happen to be two sons of Late Mehdi Ali Khan Panni and four sons of Late Sayeed Ali Khan Panni by eleven kabala deeds registered on different dates between 7-6-1981 to 21-10-1982 and accordingly went into possession. The plaintiff has thus been in possession of the suit land ever since its purchase. Towards the middle of Kartik 1400 BS the defendant No.1 all on a sudden disclosed that he had taken lease of the suit property from the Government. It is the further case of the plaintiff that the land in suit khatian was never a khas land of the Government, therefore, it has no lawful authority to grant lease of the land to anyone whosever. The title of the suit land being created in favour of the predecessor-in-interest of the plaintiff by way of prajapattan and the land being accordingly recorded in their names in the SA Khatian Government cannot acquire any lawful right, title or interest in the same. The suit land being barren and fallow in nature the suit valuation was fixed at Tk.1,50,000 over which the court fee is paid.

4. The Government as defendant No.9 contested the suit by filing a written statement. The simple case of the contesting defendant is that the suit land along with other lands was non-retainable khas land of the Zamindars. After the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, hereinafter referred to as the "SA&T Act, 1950" came into force the entire waqf estate in question was acquisitioned as non-retainable khas land as per the provisions of the said Act. After acquisition the same vested in the Government free from all encumbrances and was accordingly recorded in the name of the Government in its khas khatian. The alleged pattannama in the names of the predecessors-in-interest of the plaintiff is forged, fabricated and subsequently created for the purpose of the suit. The original Zamindars did neither give settlement of the land to nor did they receive rent from anyone in respect of the suit land or the estate. Thus no right title and interest was created by the so-called pattannama allegedly executed in favour of the predecessors-in-interest of the plaintiff. By the same token no right, title or interest was created in favour of the plaintiff by the subsequent sale deeds executed by the so-called pattanholders. The registered sale deeds under which title to the suit land is claimed are collusive, void and not acted upon passing no title or interest whatsoever in favour of the plaintiff.

5. The waqf estate being so taken over by the Government as non-retainable khas land of the rent-receivers the same vested in the Government as per law and it had no reason to and indeed never realized rent from anyone claiming under the Zamindars, be that he is a pattanholder or subsequent purchaser. The plaintiff and his predecessors-in-interest have althrough been aware of the acquisition and record of rights standing in the name of the Government in its khas khatain. Government while in possession of the suit estate in khas settled 5.43 acre land from plot No. 3183 of the suit khatian with the defendant No.1 in connection with Settlement Case No. 16/1 (XII) 84-85 and handed over possession of the same to him. Accordingly he has been in possession of the land on its southern side. The suit is, therefore, liable to be dismissed.

6. The suit was for declaration of title simpliciter in respect of a piece of land admittedly forming part of the waqf estate sought on the basis of purchase from a number of persons whose title in the land rested in pattan-settlement allegedly taken from the Mutawalli of the said waqf estate. Learned Subordinate Judge tried the suit on six issues and finally dismissed the same. The issues framed are as follows:

1. Whether the suit is maintainable in its present form and manner?

2. Whether the suit is barred by limitation?

3. Whether the suit is bad for defect of parties?

4. Whether the plaintiff has any right title and interest in the suit land?

5. Whether the plaintiff is entitled to a decree declaring his right, title and interest in the suit land?

6. Is there any other or further releifs the plaintiff may be entitled to?

7. The issues framed suggest that there was no issue framed on the crucial question of the authority of the Mutawalli to give such perpetual pattan settlement of the waqf estate or any part thereof. No issue is found either on another crucial question ie, whether the waqf estate was acquisitioned by the Government as per provisions of the SA&T Act, 1950. And, if so, whether the rent-receiver had any subsisting saleable interest in the estate after acquisition.

8. Be that as it may, learned Subordinate Judge has taken pains to go into extensive discussions of the facts and evidence on records and came to his findings essentially on facts. Learned Judge upon an elaborate analysis came to disbelieve the genuineness of the pattannama, the only source of title of the plaintiff's predecessors. Trial court found the suit, amongst others, bad for defect of parties, plainly undervalued and devoid of cause of action. It appears that four witnesses were examined on behalf of the plaintiff company. While one was examined on behalf of the Government. Several documents were proved by the plaintiff including the eleven registered deeds by virtue of which he claims title to the suit land; one rent-receipt (Exhibit 6) showing payment of rent to Zamindari sherista and the pattannama of 1353 BS (Exhibit 4), the basis of title of its vendors. P.W. 2 is one of the vendors of the plaintiff. There is nothing in his deposition indicating his personal knowledge about pattannama. He said in his cross-examination that Haidar Ali Khan dedicated some land as waqf and retained the rest under his personal ownership. He denies knowledge about the quantum of land taken by the individual pattan-holders. He said that 'they did not hand over the pattannama to the vendee.' To reproduce his own words: পত্তননামা আমরা চৌধুরী সাহেবকে দেই নাই। Sliding of pattannama into the hands of the plaintiff in the circumstances remains unexplained.

9. The pattannama itself on a glance does not inspire satisfaction of the court about its genuineness. One Md. Abdul Halim is examined as PW.4 who claimed himself as Tahshilder of the Waqf Estate. He is 78 years of age. He is examined for proving the pattannama. He identified the handwriting of one Kanailal Sarkar who is styled as Pradhan Karjakarak (Chief Executive). There is nothing more about said Kanailal. Nevertheless, PW.4 claims that the pattannama was written by Kanailal and he is acquainted with and identified the handwriting of Kanailal. He sought to prove the mutation in the name of the plaintiff effected in 1996 and said that one Mannan Naib did the mutation. There is nothing about the whereabouts of said Mannan Naib. None of the attesting witnesses of the pattannama was examined. There is no explanation either about non-examination of Abdul Mannan. There is no explanation how the huge estate survived the acquisition by the Government so as to empower the Zamindars to receive rent from raiyats or pattan-holders. More importantly, not a single contemporaneous dakhila against the pattan was produced in court except one of 1996 which is again suspected by the trial court as fabricated and indeed seems to be so created for the purpose of the suit. A pattannama sought to be proved by a single dakhila showing payment of rent in the Zamindari sherista 54 years after the pattan-settlement that too when the estate had already stood acquisitioned, as would transpire herein later, can hardly be credited with truth. So is the case with statements made by the supporting witnesses examined by the plaintiff.

10. PW 2, an alleged vender of the plaintiff said in his cross-examination that Sayeed Ali Khan Panni (one of the so-called lessees under the Mutawalli) died leaving five sons and two daughters but daughters are not made parties to the suit. As per admission of PW.1 there is also a cotton mill on a portion of the suit land but the cotton mill is not made a party to the suit. It is the case of the plaintiff that it has purchased the suit land from nine plots of CS khatian No. 109 but plot Nos.2778 and 3187 are not found in the khatian. The suit valuation is fixed at Tk. 1,50,000 but PW1 himself said on oath that he paid Tk. 4,00,000 against few of the deeds which suggests that the suit is clearly undervalued. In view of the discussion made above we do not find reason to take any view different from what is taken by the learned Sub-ordinate Judge.

11. Mr. Abul Quasem, learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the appellant submits that the appellant has successfully proved its title and possession in the suit land. The 11 registered deeds by which the land is purchased was duly proved as Exhibit 3 and 7 Series. Mr. Quasem added that the plaintiff company mutated its name in respect of the suit land and has been paying rent. During the current survey operation the draft khatian of the land has been prepared in its name to the extent of 7.00 acres wrongly leaving aside rest 0.65½ acre. A settlement appeal is also filed by the plaintiff against the wrong recording. So far as the title of the plaintiff's predecessors is concerned Mr. Quasem submits that the suit land along with other land belonged to Karatia Zamindari Estate recorded in CS khatian No. 309 in the name of Zamindar Haider Ali Khan Panni. Haider Ali Khan Panni gave jote-settlement in 1350 BS of the entire 182.23 acre land of the estate to his two sons and two grandsons as is stated in the plaint and handed over possession. Accordingly SA and RS records were made in their names. They having thus taken settlement of the land possessed the same by paying rent to the Estate. The CS and RS khatians, draft khatian, mutation khatian of the Zamindari Estate and rent receipts are duly proved in court in support of the continuous and unbroken chain of title of the plaintiff.

12. The second branch of argument advanced by Mr. Abdul Quasem is that the predecessors-in-title of the plaintiff took settlement long before the East Bengal Sate Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, came into being. Moreover, the plaintiff's predecessors were not rent receivers. It follows therefore, that the gazette notification under section 43(2) dated 13-3-1975 seeking to acquire the rent receiving interest of the Estate has no manner of application to this case and it has not affected the right title and interest of the plaintiff in the suit land.

13. Mr. Quasem finally tried to assail the findings of the trial court as to failure of the plaintiff in disclosing any cause of action of the suit as well as its failure to establish title and possession in the suit land. In support of his submission Mr. Quasem cited the cases of Surat Sardar vs Afzal Hossain, 49 DLR (AD) 99; Arfan Ali Sheikh vs Ead Ali Talukdar, 14 DLR 791; Shaha Md. Elias Shah vs Province of East Pakistan, 17 DLR 277 and Jalil Ahmed vs Province of East Pakistan reported in 19 DLR 106.

14. Mr. Gautam Kumar Roy learned Deputy Attorney General appearing on behalf of the Respondent No. 9 raised basically three contentions. He contended that law runs contrary to the power of Mutawalli in disposing of or creating charge or encumbrance on immoveable property held in waqf. The suit land, he insisted, is admittedly a part of a waqf estate, therefore, pattan, if any, given by the Mutawalli did not create any title or saleable interest in favour of the pattanholders. Mr. Roy next submits that the waqf estate was undeniably acquisitioned by the Government as "Haider Ali Khan Panni Wakf al-al-Aulad Estate" Karatia. The notification (Exhibit Gha), he insisted, issued under section 43(2) of the SA&T Act showing final stage of acquisition of the said estate was published in the official gazette dated 20-3-1975 which means abolition of any intermediate interest in the property or taking over by the Government non-retainable khas land to the extinction of saleable interest of the Zamindars and other land owners who turned into tenants under the state. He buttressed up his submission by reference to The Bangladesh (Legal Proceedings) (Third) Order, 1972 which bars, amongst others, suits, appeals, applications and other legal proceedings challenging the legality or validity of any provision of SA&T Act, 1950 or acquisition sought to be made therein. Mr. Roy finally submits that the question of law apart, the plaintiff miserably failed to prove the pattannama which is the only basis of its predecessor's title.

15. We have already expressed our opinion on the factual aspect of the case as decided by the learned Subordinate Judge. Before going into technical questions of law one peculiarity of the case can hardly be side stepped. The plaintiff is a limited company incorporated under the Companies Act, 1913. Name of Md. Nur Ahmed Chowdhury (PW 1) appears in the cause title of the plaint as one appearing on behalf of the plaintiff. Plaint does not disclose the relationship Nur Ahmed Chowdhury and the company mutually stand to. The deeds under which the company claims title to the suit land discloses that PW.1 Nur Ahmed is a Director of the company. Statemints of PWs given on oath, save an isolated sentence uttered by PW.1, do not bear the trace of company's involvement in the deal rather speaks of the acquisition of land by an individual in the name of a company. In any view the plaintiff's case is indicative of anything but a fair deal in the transaction.

<u>16. Back to the question of law raised by the learned Deputy Attorney General. Waqf , as meant in the Muslim personal law, is the dedication of property for religious, pious or charitable purposes which by necessary implication is the extinction of the appropriator's ownership in the thing dedicated and detention of the thing in the implied ownership of God in such a manner that its profit may revert to the benefit of the mankind. As pointed out by the Privy Council in Vidyavaruthi vs Balusami, 48 IA 302:</u>

<u>“-----the Mohamedan law relating to trust differs fundamentally from the English law. It owes its origin to a rule laid down by the Prophet of Islam; and means: tying up of property in the ownership of God the Almighty and the devotion of the profits for the benefit of human beings."</u>

<u>17. A waqf by implication, therefore, is perpetual in character. And the ultimate purpose of valid wakf is religious, pious or charitable. Under the Muslim law a property does not vest in the Mutawalli. He is, therefore, not a trustee in the technical sense. He is merely a superintendent or manager of the waqf property.</u>

<u>18. The extreme view that a private wakf is in no case valid was later departed from and a wakf for the benefit of the settler’s descendants ie, wakf-al-al aulad may now be made subject to some strict limitations. The restrictions were further relaxed by the Mussalman Wakf Validating Act, 1913. Under the Act it was lawful for a person professing Muslim faith to create a waqf which in all other respects is in accordance with the provisions of Muslim law, amongst others, for the maintenance and support wholly or partly of his family, children or descendant provided that the ultimate benefit is reserved for the poor or for any other purpose recognized by the Muslim law.</u>

19. The Mussalman Wakf Validating Act, 1913, section 3 says as follows:

"It shall be lawful for any person professing the Missalman faith to create a wakf which in all other respects is in accordance with the provision of the Miussalman law for the following, amongst other, purposes:

(a) For the maintenance of and support wholly or partially of his family, children or descendants, and

(b) Provided that the ultimate benefit is in such case expressly or impliedly reserved for the poor or for any other purpose recognized by the Mussalman law as a religious, pious or charitable purpose of a permanent character."

20. It is, to be seen that under the above law waqf for the benefit of the descendants is validated but the essential tenet of wakf ie, vesting its ownership in God, its eminent purpose and perpetual character are maintained. It follows, therefore, that no valid waqf can be created unless the corpus of the property is vested in God for the ultimate benefit of mankind. A kind of perpetuity is found to be ingrained in a wakf which runs contrary to unrestricted transfer of the corpus of the waqf property by anyone whosever let alone the Mutawalli.

<u>21. Muslim law literature is not free from the controversy as to what is and what not a valid waqf is. But there is hardly, if ever, any controversy about restriction on the power of a Mutawalli to make a permanent disposal of the wakf property completely dedicated to the religious or charitable purposes to the extinction of its underlying purpose. By logical corollary power of disposal of the corpus of the waqf should be and indeed is subject to restrictions.</u>

<u>22. Section 207 of Mulla's Principles of Mahomedan Law (19th Ed. Page179) by M. Hidayatullah & A. Hidayatullah says:</u>

<u>"A Mutawalli has no power, without the permission of the court, to mortgage, sell or exchange wakf property or any part thereof, unless he is expressly empowered by the deed of wakf to do so."</u>

23. Section 10A of the SA&T Act, 1950, inserted a bit earlier by East Pakistan Ordinance, 1960, put similar restrictions on the power of Mutawalli to transfer waqf property. Wordings of the relevant portion of the section ie, section 10A(3)(b) are (selectively) quoted below:

"No such Mutawalli, shebait or trustee shall be entitled to transfer, or create any encumbrance or charge on, any such interest in any khas land in any manner otherwise by temporary lease, but no such lease shall be given for a period exceeding one year at a time expiring on the last day of the agricultural year in which it is created except with the previous permission of the Collector....any lease given in contravention of the provision thereof shall be null and void ..."

24. Section 56 of The Waqf Ordinance, 1962, (short of the proviso), reads as follows:

"No transfer by a mutawalli of any immoveable property of a waqf by way of sale, gift, mortgage or exchange or by way of lease for a term exceeding 5 years shall be valid without the previous sanction of the Administrator."

<u>25. In the instant case title of the plaintiff is rooted into a piece of pattannama of 1343 BS by which its predecessors-in-title allegedly took settlement of the entire waqf estate from its Mutawalli. Put into the legal perspective as above the pattannama needs be tested in terms of its validity precisely for the reason that the plaintiff's case rises and falls with the fate of pattannama particularly in absence of any other case set out in its support. The pattannama allegedly executed by the Mutawalli himself, apart from the question of its genuineness, seeks to make permanent transfer by pattan the entire estate in favour of some of his descendants, ie, the vendors of the plaintiff. Legal position as examined above does not permit such permanent transfer of any waqf estate by any means to the total extinction of its basic purpose. It follows, therefore, that the pattan, if any, taken by the plaintiff's predecessors-in-title did not survive the period prescribed by law let alone creating any saleable interest in favour of them.</u>

26. Besides the question of the transferability of waqf estate and credibility of the pattannama the most vital question that lingers through is whether the waqf estate survived the wholesale acquisition of rent receiving interest and non-retainable khas land under the SA & T Act, 1950? If the waqf estate is found to have vested in the Government by operation of law can the deeds create any right title or interest in favour of the plaintiff?

<u>27. Wholesale acquisition of rent receiving interest and of the non-retainable khas land, for all practical purposes, started with the notifications issued under sub-sections (1) and (2) of section 3 of the SA&T Act, 1950 and passed through different phases until preparation and final publication of the compensation assessment rolls under section 42 of the Act. The interest of the rent receivers held under any waqf, waqf-al-al-aulad, debutter or other religious trust acquired under sub-section (1) or non-retainable khas land acquired under sub-section (2) of section 3 finally vested in the Government free from all encumbrances with the publication of the compensation assessment roll under section 42 and declaration about such publication under section 43(2) of the SA&T Act, 1950. Intermediate arrangements had to be made for administration and management specially of the land held in religious or other trust but not taken in possession by the Government till the date of commencement of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy (Amendment) Ordinance, 1960 by allowing the Mutawalli, shebait or trustee, as the case may be, to continue to manage such interest as the agent of the Government till the last day of the agricultural year in which notification under section 43(2) is published or till the Government exercises' its right of possession, whichever is later, After the deadline prescribed by law the Mutawalli ceased to have authority to manage the waqf estate even under the Government. From any point of view Mutawalli or the pattanholders under him cannot have any lawful claim of right or title in a waqf estate after completion of acquisition process with the declaration of final publication made under section 43(2) of the SA&T Act, 1950.</u>

28. The suit land admittedly forms a portion of the "Haidar Ali Khan Panni Wakf al-al-Aulad Estate" Karatia. The single dakhila dated 25-2-1996 (Exhibit 6) sought to be proved by the plaintiff showing payment of rent in the Waqf Estate Karatia is issued by " Mohammad Haidar Ali Waqf al-al-aulad Estate," Karatia. The mutation order dated 28.11.1996 (Exhibit 5) proved by the plaintiff is also issued by the same Haidar Ali Waqf al-al-aulad Estate, Karatia. Mr. Abul Quasem, does not deny the fact that the suit property originally belonged to Karatia "Haidar Ali Khan Panni Wakf al-al-Aulad Estate." No dispute, therefore, is there about the identity of the suit land as part of the "Haidar Ali Khan Panni Waqf al-al-Aulad Estate." Karatia.

29. It is found from notification published in the official gazette dated 14-3-1975 (Exhibit Gha) published under section 43(2) of the SA& T Act, 1950, that the said "Haidar Ali Khan Panni Wakf al-al-Aulad Estate" Karatia, was acquisitioned as 'waqf estate' and that the compensation assessment roll in respect of the same was finally published as per section 42 of the Act meaning thereby that all formalities of acquisition of the waqf estate was complete with publication of notification as aforesaid finally vesting the estate in the Government free from all encumbrances. The rent-receiver or the land owner concerned after acquisition of his interest in his estate, tenure etc. or non-retainable khas land cannot have any subsisting saleable interest so as to transfer the same to anyone. It follows, therefore, that the sale deeds executed after acquisition of the estate did not create any right or title of the plaintiff in respect of the suit land.

30. Furthermore, the Bangladesh (Legal Proceedings) (Third) Order, 1972, bars, amongst others, suits, appeals, applications and other legal proceedings challenging the legality or validity of any provision of SA&T Act, 1950 or acquisition sought to be made therein. Article 2 of the Order reads as follows:

"Notwithstanding anything containing in any other law for the time being in force, on the commencement of this order, all suits, appeals, applications and other proceedings pending or continuing in any court against the Government of People's Republic of Bangladesh in which the legality or validity of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 ....or of acquisition of any property made under any provision thereof is challenged or called in question shall abate... and no person shall bring, any fresh suit, appeal, application or other legal proceedings in which the legality or validity of any such law or acquisition is challenged or called in question."

The suit as framed, though made to look like a suit for declaration simplicities, is one seeking to challenge the acquisition by implication. A suit or proceeding which cannot be brought directly cannot be brought indirectly so as to defeat the purpose of the legislature as the maxim goes: Nemo potent facers per oblique quid non potent facers per director (No one can do indirectly what he cannot do directly.) The present suit, in that sense, cannot circumvent the bar put by law.

31. Reverting back to the cases referred to by Mr. Quasem. The case of Surat Sardar, 49 DLR (AD) 99, as referred to by Mr. Quasem, is all about cause of action of suits which is far removed from the basic point mooted here in this case. Arfan Ali Sheikh's case, 14 DLR 791, is concerned with nature of tenancy vis-a vis presumption of knowledge of the pre-emptor and estoppels in pre-emption. In Elias Shah's case, 17 DLR 277, it is held by a Division Bench of the then High Court of East Pakistan that without assessment of compensation of property the same cannot vest in the Provincial Government and Jalil Ahmed's case reported in 19 DLR 106, another Division Bench of the then High Court of East Pakistan ruled that notification dated 9-5-1956 did not exempt waqfs from acquisition. The cases sought to be relied upon by Mr. Quasem are plainly distinguishable from the facts of the instant case and are of no avail to him.

32. For all the reasons stated above we do not find merit in the appeal which must, therefore, fail.

In the result the appeal is dismissed without any order as to cost. The judgment and decree of dismissal passed by the Subordinate Judge, 3rd Court, Tangail, is hereby affirmed.

Send down the lower court record at once.

End.

caseno: Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 2001 of 2009
lawyer:
Syed Amirul Islam, Senior Advocate, instructed by Syed Mahbubur Rahman, Advocate-on-Record-----For the Petitioner 
None represented-----For Respondents
parties:
Md. Nazimuddin ----- Petitioner
Vs
Government of Bangladesh and ors ----- Respondent
case_source: (From the Judgment and order dated 26-7-2009 passed by the Administrative Appellate Tribunal, Dhaka in Appeal No. 186 of 2003).
full_judgment:
Syed Mahmud Hossain J: This civil petition for Leave to Appeal is directed against the decision dated 26-7-2009 passed by the Administrative Appellate Tribunal, Dhaka in Appeal No. 186 of 2003 reversing the decision dated 29-8-2003 passed by the Administrative Tribunal, Bogra in Tribunal Case No. 33 of 2002.

2. The facts, leading to the filing of this petition, in a nutshell, are as follows:

3. The petitioner was appointed as "workmistri" in the Railway Department and at the time of his appointment in service, he declared that his date of birth was 8-4-1952 and in support of his date of birth, he swore an affidavit and the same was accepted by the authority. In recognition of his meritorious service, he was promoted to the post of Sub-Assistant Engineer. When the petitioner was in service as Sub Assistant Engineer at Kushtia, respondent Nos. 7 and 8 visited his office and found that in the service book, his date of birth was written as 23-1-1952 on the basis of an affidavit sworn by him. Thereafter, the authority asked the petitioner to produce his Secondary School Certificate (in short, SSC). The Audit and Accounts Department raised objection against the affidavit. On 23-2-1997, the petitioner filed an appeal to respondent No. 7 and the matter was delayed in the Established and Audit Department. Respondent No. 4 rejected the appeal holding that the date of birth of the petitioner was 8-4-1947 and the same should be recorded instead of 4-8-1952 in his Memo No. St/604/31 dated 24-6-2002. After about 30 years the audit objection is not legal and proper and the petitioner sustained loss and injury because of the objection of the Audit Department.

4. The respondents filed written objection denying all the material allegations made in the petition before the Administrative Tribunal, contending, inter alia, that the case was not maintainable in its present form and that there was no cause of action and that the case was barred under section 4(2) of the Administrative Tribunal Act. The Petitioner Nazimuddin, was appointed as workmistri on 4-12-1972 and he wrote his date of birth as 8-4-1952 and swore an affidavit in support of his date of birth and accordingly his date of birth was written in his service book as 8-4-1952 instead of 8-4-1947 which was written in his SSC Certificate. The Railway Audit Department, Paksey raised an objection against the affidavit. Accordingly, the petitioner was directed to submit his SSC Certificate but the petitioner could not submit his SSC Certificate and filed an application stating that his SSC Certificate was lost. After that, DRM Paksey forwarded the petitioner's application, service book and copy of objection of audit report to the General Manager, Bangladesh Railway, West, Rajshahi to ascertain in the correct date of birth of the petitioner. The General Manager after perusing the necessary papers and affidavit came to the conclusion that the petitioner's date of birth was not 8-4-1952 but 8-4-1947 which was accordingly written in his service book now lying with the office of the CPO, West, Rajshahi, After that, the petitioner preferred an appeal to the General Manager, West, Rajshahi for recording his date of birth as 8-4-1952 shown in the affidavit. The General Manager sent it to the CPO, West, Rajshahi for proper action but the CPO informed the General Manager on 25-6-2002 that there was no scope for correcting the date of birth against which the petitioner filed the AT Case No. 33 of 2002 before the Administrative Tribunal, Bogra, under section 4 of the Administrative Tribunal Act, 1980 for declaration that his correct date of birth was 8-4-1952 instead of 8-4-1947.

5. After hearing learned Member, Administrative Tribunal, Bogra, allowed the case vide her decision dated 29-6-2003.

6. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the decision dated 29-6-2003 passed by the learned Member, Administrative Tribunal, Bogra, the respondents preferred Appeal No. 186 of 2009 before the Administrative Appellate Tribunal, Dhaka. The Administrative Appellate Tribunal, upon hearing the parties, by its decision dated 26-7-2009 allowed the appeal and set aside the decision dated 29-6-2003 passed by the learned Member, Administrative Tribunal, Bogra.

7. Against the decision dated 26-7-2009 passed, by the Administrative Appellate Tribunal, Dhaka, the petitioner has filed this instant civil petition, for Leave to Appeal before this Division,

8. Mr Syed Amirul Islam, learned Senior Advocate, appearing on behalf of the petitioner, submits that the 3rd proviso to sub-section 2 of section 4 of the Administration Tribunal Act provides that the application shall have to be filed before Administrative Tribunal within 6 months, from the date of making or taking the order, decision on action Concerned or making the decision by the higher administrative authority as the case may be and that the petitioner has filed the case before the Administrative Tribunal within that period and as such, the decision of Administrative Appellate Tribunal, should be set aside. He further submits that proviso 2 to sub-section 2 of 4 section has no manner of application on the facts and in the circumstances of the case of the petitioner and that the Administrative Appellate Tribunal relying on the 2nd proviso without taking into consideration the 3rd proviso erroneously allowed the appeal and set aside the decision passed by the Administrative Tribunal.

9. We have considered the impugned decision and other papers, on record. The Administrative Appellate Tribunal noticed that the petitioner filed an application /appeal to the higher authority on 23-2-1997 which was rejected on 25-6-2002 and that accordingly, the petitioner filed Administrative Tribunal Case on 4-8-2002 before the Administrative Tribunal; Bogra under section 4 of the Administrative. Tribunal Act, 1980 against the order, dated 27- 11-1996 passed by the Audit, Department for declaration that his correct date of birth was 8-4-1952 instead of 8-4-1947. The Administrative Appellate Tribunal also noticed that the 2nd proviso to section 4(2) of the Administrative Tribunal Act came into force on 19-11-1997 when the petitioner's appeal was pending before the authority and that according to the amended proviso, the appeal pending before the authority shall be deemed to have been rejected after expiry of 2 months from 19-11-1997 as the amended proviso came into force on that date. Therefore, the Administrative Appellate Tribunal came to a finding that after calculation, it appeared that the appeal be deemed to have been rejected on 19-11-1998 and that he would have to file the. AT Case Within 6 months from 19-114998, that is, on or before 19-7-1998, and that the petitioner filed the AT Case on 28-9-1998 long after the period of limitation.

10. The Administrative Appellate Tribunal also came to a finding that the petitioner could not submit his SSC Certificate as directed by the authority and that ultimately after perusing the necessary papers and the disputed affidavit the authority finalized the petitioner's date of birth as 9-8-1947.

11. The findings of the Administrative Appellate Tribunal are based on proper appreciation of law and fact.

12. We would like to give more explicit reply to the questions raised by the learned Advocate for the petitioner. It is important to note that amended proviso 2 was added before the original 2nd proviso and, as a result, the 2nd proviso was relegated to the 3rd proviso. The 1st proviso, in essence, provides that where there is a higher administrative authority having the power to set aside, vary or modify an order, decision or action to be challenged before the Administrative Tribunal; the Administrative Tribunal shall not entertain a case until such higher authority takes a decision on the matter.

13. The 2nd,proviso, in essence, provides that if the appellate authority does not take any decision on an appeal or application for review in respect of any order, decision or action referred to in the 1st proviso within 2 months, the appeal or application for review shall be deemed to have been disallowed after expiry of that period.

14. The 3rd proviso, in essence, provides that the Administrative Tribunal shall not entertain a case unless it is made within 6 months from the date of making or taking of the order, decision or action or making the decision on the matter by the higher administrative authority as the case may be.

<u>15. It is the cardinal rules of interpretation that interpretation of any provision in isolation without taking into consideration the allied provisions is not permissible.</u>

<u>16. If the 3rd proviso is considered in isolation then the 2nd proviso becomes redundant. It was never the intention of the legislature to incorporate a redundant proviso by amendment when the 3rd proviso was in existence. According to the 3rd proviso if an appeal or application for review is filed to higher administrative authority, and if such authority passes an order on such appeal or application for review after a long lapse of time, that is even beyond two months then the case before the administrative Tribunal can be filed within 6 months from the date of passing of that order.</u>

<u>17. According to the 2nd proviso, if an appeal or application for review is filed and if the higher administrative authority does not take any decision on such appeal or application for review within two months, then such appeal or application for review shall be deemed to have been disallowed after expiry of that period. If the word "disallowed" as mentioned in the 2nd proviso is construed as a decision or order by higher authority as contemplated under the 3rd proviso then there exists a harmonious construction between the 2nd and 3rd provisos and in fact, the legislature intended as such. In the event, the period of computation of limitation of six months as contained in the 3rd proviso will start running from the date when an appeal or application for review shall be deemed to have been disallowed as completed under the 2nd proviso. The legislature also intended to see that the 2nd and the 3rd provisos are complementary to each other otherwise the 2nd proviso would not have been added before the 3rd proviso by subsequent amendment. Haying considered all the 3 provisos in general and the provisos 2 and 3, in particular, we find that there is no conflict between the 2nd and the 3rd provisos; rather both the provisos are complementary to each other.</u>

18. According to Maxwell, "when possible, a construction should be adopted which will facilitate the smooth working of the scheme of legislation”—Interpretation of Statutes, 12th Edition at page 201.

19. In the case of Canada Sugar Refining Co VR (1898) AC 735, Lord Davy observed as under:

"Every clause of a statute should be construed with reference to the context and other clauses of the Act, so as, as far as possible, to make a consistent enactment of the whole statute or series of statutes relating to the subject-matter".

20. In the case of "Sultana Begum vs Prim Chand, AIR 1997 SC 1006 the Supreme Court of India held as under:

This rule of construction which is also spoken of as "ex uisceribus actus" helps in avoiding any inconsistency either within a Section or between two different Sections or provisions of the same statute.

On a conspectus of the case law indicated above, the following principles are clearly discernible: (1) It is the duty of the Courts to avoid a head-on clash between two Sections of the Act and to construe the provisions which appear to be in conflict with each other in such a manner as to harmonise them.

(2) The provisions of one Section of a statute cannot be used to defeat the other provisions unless the Court, in spite of its efforts, finds it impossible to effect reconciliation between them.

(3) It has to be borne in mind by all the Courts all the time that when there are two conflicting provisions in an Act, which cannot be reconciled with each other, they should be so interpreted that, is possible, effect should be given to both.  This is the essence of the rule of "harmonious construction."

(4) The Courts have also to keep in mind that an interpretation which reduces one of the provisions as a "dead letter" or "useless lumber" is not harmonious construction".

(5) To harmonise is not to destroy any statutory provision or to render it otiose.

21. The principles expounded in the cases referred to above apply to the facts and circumstances of the present case.

22. Therefore, the petitioner should have approached the Administrative Tribunal within 6 months from the date of decision on his appeal which would be deemed to have been disallowed by the higher authority after two months of its filing as contemplated under the 2nd proviso and the period of limitation of 6 months as mentioned in the 3rd proviso would be reckoned from the expiry of two months as provided under the 2nd proviso. But the petitioner failed to do so. Consequently, the Administrative Appellate Tribunal rightly came to the finding that the case before the Administrative Tribunal was barred by limitation.

Accordingly this Petition for Leave to Appeal is dismissed.

End.
