full_judgment:
Zubayer Rahman Chowdhury J: This is an application under section 42 read with section 43 of the Arbitration Act, 2001 for setting aside the Award dated 8-4-2006 passed by the Arbitral Tribunal in an arbitration proceeding between Saudi Arabian Airlines Corporation (the claimant) and Messrs Saudi-Bangladesh Services Company Limited (the respondent).

2. In the arbitration proceeding before the Arbitral Tribunal (hereinafter referred to as the Tribunal), the respondent, as claimant, made a claim of Taka 32,27,50,566.51, while the present petitioner, as respondent, not only denied the claim, but made a counter-claim for Taka 161,15,29,583 along with interest @ 16% per annum on the awarded sum.

3. The three-member Tribunal comprising of Mr Justice MH Rahman, a former Head of the Caretaker Government and former Chief Justice of Bangladesh, Mr M Amirul Islam, Senior Advocate, Supreme Court of Bangladesh and Dr M Zahir, Senior Advocate, Supreme Court of Bangladesh, upon hearing the parties, by a majority decision, made an Award of Taka 31,27,50,566 in favour of the claimant (the respondent herein) and dismissed the counter-claim of the respondent (the petitioner herein).

4. The dissenting opinion was given by Mr M Amirul Islam, who allowed the claim of the claimant for the amount of Taka 4,88,72,217.43 and also allowed the counter-claim of respondent No. 1 for Taka 57,26,92,897.67.

5. Since the instant application was filed challenging the legality and propriety of the Award on the ground of non-compliance as well as violation of the provisions of the Arbitration Act, 2001 by the Tribunal, and that too, at the stage of making and signing the Award, this Court is not inclined to enter into a discourse regarding the claims and counter-claims of the parties or, for that matter, the merit of the case.

6. Mr Ajmalul Hossain, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner, submits at the outset that he will not press ground numbers I, II, III, IV and V which relate to jurisdiction of the Tribunal, but would rely on the other grounds, particularly ground numbers VI, VII and XI stated in his application.

7. Giving a factual background of the entire arbitration proceeding, Mr Hossain submits that in the instant case, the majority decision of the Tribunal is not legal and binding upon the parties in view of the fact that one of the Arbitrators, namely, Mr M Amirul Islam (hereinafter referred to as the 3rd Arbitrator), was completely left out of the process of consultation before finalising and making the Award. Mr Hossain submits that the spirit and intent of the Arbitration Act, 2001 (hereinafter referred to as the Act) is to ensure that the arbitration proceeding including the making and signing of the Award is conducted by effective participation of all the members of the Tribunal, but in the instant case, there was a dear deviation therefrom. Mr Hossain accepts the position that there may be an Award by the majority, but contends that such an Award has to be made after taking due consideration of the views and opinion of the dissenting Arbitrator.

8. Referring to Annexures I and II, annexed with the dissenting opinion marked as Annexure-F, Mr Hossain submits that upon conclusion of the hearing on 5-4-2006, the 3rd Arbitrator had written to both the Chairman and the 2nd Arbitrator (Dr M Zahir) on the following day expressing his view that the Tribunal should meet and deliberate on the issues before making the Award.

9. Referring to the respective endorsements made by the Chairman and the 2nd Arbitrator on the letter sent by the 3rd Arbitrator, Mr Hossain submits that the 3rd Arbitrator was led to believe that the members of the Tribunal would meet at BILIA (the venue of the Arbitration proceeding) for holding deliberation before making the Award. However, when the 3rd Arbitrator went to BILIA at the appointed date and time, i.e. on 8-4-2006 at 10-00 AM, he was given a one hundred-page typed Award, which had already been signed by both the Chairman and the 2nd Arbitrator. Upon receiving the same, the 3rd Arbitrator put the following endorsement on the Award:

"I just now saw the opinion this morning at 10-20 AM. Since 1 differ with the opinion given herein I will submit my separate opinion."

Sd (M Amir-ul-Islam)

Barrister-at-Law, Senior Advocate

10. Mr Hossain contends that without paying any heed to the aforesaid request and without even affording an opportunity to the 3rd Arbitrator to participate in the deliberation and express his views before the Award was made, the Chairman and the other member of the Tribunal finalised and signed the Award. Therefore, on this ground, the Award is liable to be set aside.

11. Substantiating his argument, Mr Hossain has referred to the opening paragraph of the dissenting opinion given by the 3rd Arbitrator, as evidenced by Annexure-F, which reads as under:

"At the outset 1 express my discomfort with the statement in paragraph 45 of the award, opinion of my fellow co-arbitrators, Mr Justice MH Rahman, Chairman and Dr M Zahir that "Mr M Amir-ul-Islam, Barrister-at-Law, Senior Advocate, co-arbitrator, has been consulted " On the contrary, I wrote letters to both of my co-arbitrators on April 6, 2006 stating that our very brief discussion on the date of the close of the hearing was not enough and we should discuss at length with regard to each of the issues before we make up our mind, In response to my letters, both the learned co-arbitrators were pleased to fix a meeting on April 8, 2006 in the morning. But with utter surprise both my co-arbitrators, without allowing time for the proposed discussion, signed the award at 10-20 on the same date before 1 could even have a look at the award which was produced in a finished and conclusive form typed on a stamped paper, already signed by my two co-arbitrators."

12. Mr Hossain submits that it is evident from the aforesaid statement made by the 3rd Arbitrator that he was neither consulted nor was he given any opportunity, as was requested by him on the previous day, to discuss the issues before the Award was made.

13. Referring to section 43(v) of the Act, Mr Hossain contends that although the law requires the arbitration proceeding to be conducted in accordance with the agreement of the parties, there was a clear deviation from the agreement, inasmuch as, the 3rd Arbitrator was totally excluded from the deliberation process before making and signing the Award. In doing so, according to Mr Hossain, the Tribunal had not only acted in utter disregard to the requirement of section 23 of the Act, but had also acted contrary to the provisions of section 25 of the Act, Consequently, Mr Hossain submits, the Award is liable to be set aside.

14. Mr AJ Mohammad Ali, Senior Advocate appearing with Ms Verbeena Huda, Advocate for the respondent (Saudi Arabia Airlines Corporation) submits that the Award under challenge was passed by the Tribunal upon holding a lengthy hearing in presence of both the parties, who were duly represented by their Teamed lawyers. Mr Ali further submits that the arbitration proceeding lasted for about three years and, therefore, it cannot be said that the parties did not have adequate opportunity to place their respective case before the Tribunal. Mr Ali further submits that the agreement between the parties provides for an Award by the majority and in the instant case, the Award having been so made, it does not call for any interference by this Court.

15. Mr Ali submits categorically, that the entire proceedings took place before the Tribunal comprising of the Chairman and the two Arbitrators who had ample opportunity to discuss the issues amongst themselves when the hearing took place and, therefore, the allegation of excluding the 3rd Arbitrator from the deliberation process before making the Award is not tenable. Mr Ali further submits that if any member of a Tribunal decides to give a dissenting opinion, he can very well do so. Mr Ali lastly submits that if the instant application is allowed, it will open a floodgate and frustrate the purpose and spirit of the Act, which is primarily intended to settle disputes between the parties outside the Court.

16. Undoubtedly, there is a great deal of force in the contention of Mr Ali that the purpose of the Arbitration Act, 2001 is to minimise the duration of litigation between the parties by affording a forum for settling their dispute out-side the Court.

17. When an arbitration proceeding is conducted before an Arbitral 'Tribunal, there may very well be an Award by the majority. This is an undisputed position. At the same time, the arbitration proceeding must also conform to certain well established principles and norms of legal rules and conduct. Upon conclusion of hearing, the members of the Tribunal must hold proper deliberations amongst themselves covering all the issues of the proceeding before making and signing the Award. This is not an idle formality, but a judicial requirement designed to ensure that the matter is heard and deliberated by each and every member of the Tribunal before making and signing the Award.

18. Although a good number of cases have been cited by Mr Hossain, I shall only refer to those which are relevant for the purpose of disposal of the instant case. On the other hand, Mr Mohammad Ali has lightened the burden of the Court by not referring to any decision. In Sheik Abdulla vs MVRS Firm and Sons reported in 1924 Rangoon 153, both the parties nominated five Arbitrators and agreed that the Award of the majority of the Arbitrators would prevail. Nevertheless, the Court held:

"In this view of the reference each party was entitled to have the benefit of the opinion and decision of all the five arbitrators and not only some of them. From the fact that the three arbitrators who actually made the award happened to hold the same opinion it cannot be assumed that even if the other two had acted, the opinion of the former three would not have been affected. It is not impossible that a discussion among all the five might have produced a different award."

19. In another case, reported in 22 CWN (1917-18), 301 (Abu Hamid Zahira Ali vs Golan Samar), the Court held:

"…It is essential that there should be unanimous participation by the arbitrators in consulting and deliberating upon the award to be made; the operation of this rule is in no way affected by the fact that authority is conferred upon the arbitrators to make a majority award; even where less than the whole number of arbitrators may make a valid award, they can-not do so without consulting the other arbitrators."

20. Mr Hossain refers to the widely followed work of "Russell on Arbitration", 28th Edition, where it has been stated:"

All the arbitrators most act together. As they must all act, so they must all act together. They must each be present at every meeting; and the witnesses and the parties must be examined in the presence of them all.

All most make award together. Where there are two or more arbitrators, all should execute the award at the sometime and place. If they do not, the award may be invalidated, but as the objection is one of a formal character, if no other objection is shown, the Court may remit the award to the arbitrators for correction."

21. The aforesaid statement was cited with approval in the case of European Grain vs Johnston, reported in Lloyd's Law Reports (1982) Vol 2, 551, where the Court held:

"What I think the authorities show, as must be right, is that an arbitration conducted by a tribunal of several arbitrators necessarily requires a joint process of full and complete adjudication by all of them, so that the ultimate award represents the state of mind of all of them at the time when they sign it." (Per Lord Justice kerr).

22. It appears from Annexure I and Annexure II of Annexure 17, that upon conclusion of the hearing on 5-4-2006, the 3rd Arbitrator sent a letter on the following day to the Chairman and the 2nd Arbitrator of the Tribunal requesting for a meeting to discuss and deliberate on the issues before making the Award. It is perhaps, pertinent to quote the said letter in full, which reads as under:

"April 6, 2006

Dear Hon’ble Chairman Mr Justice Habibur Rahman and Co-Arbitrator Dr M Zahir

Ref Saudis Arabian Airlines Corporation vs Saudia Bangladesh Services Company Ltd.

I refer to our discussions yesterday after the close of the hearing. I thought this was not adequate to discuss the proposed award, not allowing any opportunity to discuss the issues and the underlying legal principles involved both on question of fact and law. While we accepted the obligation to hear and determine the dispute between the parties it will not be proper to rush for an award without discussing each of the issues. You proposed. Saturday, 8-4-2006. I hope you will not close your mind and take a view before we have had opportunity to share our thoughts and reasoning. I invite you to arrange a mutually convenient time when we can discuss the issues between the parties and deliberate our reasoning for resolution of those issues. You suggested Saturday but before signing the award there has to be enough time, opportunity and willingness to share the reasoning before taking a view and finalising the Award.

Since this matter is of the greatest importance to the parties, I feel that it is incumbent upon us to properly and judicially approach the issues with a view to resolving them and the material and legal principles have to be considered before the Award is finalised.

Kindly inform me of a convenient date and time for proper deliberations with adequate opportunity to deal with each of the issues before the award is made. If there is such an opportunity prior to finalising the Award, then, I shall certainly make myself available to deliberate upon these issues and consider the proper Award to be made in this case.

Yours sincerely,

M Amir-ul-Islam Co-Arbitrator"

23. Upon receiving the aforesaid letter, the Chairman of the Tribunal made the following endorsement:

“The matter was heard for days. The parties have given their written submission extensively. I shall be at the BILIA at 10-10 AM next Saturday."

Signed (ineligible)

6-30 PM 6-4-06.

The 2nd Arbitrator made the following endorsement:

"We have already exchanged opinions, pl contact Chairman. Friday 7th April, 06 we can meet. Alternatively, you can give your opinion later. But whatever the Chairman says is OK with me."

Signed (M Zahir)

6 April 2006

The following day, i.e., 7th April, was a holiday, being Friday. On 8-6-2006 (Saturday, when the 3rd Arbitrator went to BILIA at 10-00 AM, he was given the 100-page typed Award, which had already been signed by the Chairman and the 2nd Arbitrator.

Immediately thereupon, the 3rd Arbitrator made the following observation, which appears at page 100 of the Award:

"I just now saw the opinion this morning at 10-20 AM. Since I differ with the opinion given herein, I will submit my separate opinion."

Sd (M Amir-ul-Islam)

Barrister-at-Law, Senior Advocate.

Furthermore, at page 53 of the dissenting opinion, the 3rd Arbitrator made the following observation:

"Though it is a dissenting award, I wish I could share my views as expressed in this opinion with my co-arbitrators before they signed their award which I did not have the opportunity to see before they were signed by them."

24. From the sequence of events noted above, it is apparent that the 3rd Arbitrator was not provided with any scope or opportunity to deliberate on the issues with the other members of the Tribunal and express his views before the Award was made. Moreover, there is no indication in the endorsement made by the Chairman that he had already discussed the matter with the 2nd Arbitrator. Rather, from his endorsement, it appears that the 3rd Arbitrator was asked to be present at BILIA on Saturday at 10-00 AM in the morning thereby giving him an impression that there would be a deliberation before making the Award, as was requested for by the 3rd Arbitrator in his letter dated 6-4-2006.

25. At the penultimate page of the Award made by the two Arbitrators, there is a statement to the effect that the 3rd Arbitrator had been consulted. Paragraph 45 at page 99 of the Award reads as under:

"Mr Amir-ul-Islam (sic), Barrister-at-Law, Senior Advocate, co-Arbitrator, has been consulted, he differs from the above finding and has stated that he will give his opinion later on. This award is given on the basis of agreement between the Chairman and another arbitrator, that is, a majority of two in a panel of three arbitrators."

26. However, the endorsement made by the 3rd Arbitrator at page 100 of the Award as well as the opening and concluding remarks made by him in his dissenting opinion, quoted above, clearly demonstrate that the 3rd Arbitrator was neither consulted nor given any opportunity to deliberate on the issues with the other two Arbitrators before the Award was finalised and signed. In other words, the Award was made and signed by the Chairman and the 2nd Arbitrator without even the participation, let alone any input, of the 3rd Arbitrator. Evidently, there was an omission or failure on the part of the Chairman of the Tribunal to deliberate on the issues with the 3rd Arbitrator or, at least, provide an opportunity to him to express his views on the issues before making the Award, moreso, when he had expressed such intention immediately after conclusion of the arbitration proceeding, as is evident from the letter dated 6-4-2006, referred to above.

27. Having discussed the factual aspect and background of the matter, I now intend to deal with the legal aspect of the case. Section 23 of the Act, which deals with the general responsibilities of the Tribunal, stipulates that the Tribunal shall deal with the dispute submitted to it "fairly" and "impartially".

Section 25 of the Act provides that subject to the Act, the Tribunal shall follow the procedure "to be agreed on" by the parties in "conducting its proceedings.  A similar provision appears in the 'United Nations Commission on International Trade Law' (briefly UNCITRAL), Model Law on International Commercial Arbitration (hereinafter referred to as the 'Model Law'). Article 28(4) of the Model Law stipulates that in all cases, the arbitral tribunal shall decide in accordance with the terms of the contract.

28. Section 36(3) of the Act mandates that the Tribunal shall decide in accordance with the terms of the contract.

Upon a combined reading of the sections and articles referred to above, the conclusion that Sows therefrom is that the Tribunal, meaning all the members' and not just the majority, are not only required to act fairly, but are also required to follow the procedure that has been agreed by and between the parties "in Conducting the proceeding’s.

29. The term "proceeding" has not been defined in the Act. However, Article 32(1) of the Model Law provides that the arbitral proceedings are terminated by the final award. In my view, the term 'proceeding' includes the final deliberations/discussions that takes place between the members of the Tribunal before an Award is made and signed. Therefore, the duty to act fairly, as envisaged by section 23 of the Act, is not merely confined to the arbitration proceeding itself, but extends to the deliberations that is required to take place between the members of the Tribunal before an Award is made.

30. Section 37 of the Act provides that the decision of the Tribunal shall be by a majority of its members. Article 29 of the Model Law contains a similar provision.

An Award by the majority connotes an Award where each and every member of the Tribunal actively participates not only in the arbitration proceeding, but also in the deliberation that takes place among the members of the Tribunal before the Award is made and signed. There may very well be an Award by the majority, but that should only be made after there has been a proper and complete deliberation between the members of the Tribunal covering all the issues in dispute between the parties, However, if Award is made in violation of the aforesaid procedure, it would tantamount to a procedural impropriety and therefore, the resultant Award cannot be termed as an Award by the majority. In my view, this is certainly not the intendment of the parties.

31. In any event, whether the Award of the Tribunal is 'unanimous' or by a majority, it is imperative that there must be deliberation/ discussion among the members of the Tribunal prior to making and signing the Award. This is 'not an idle formality, but a legal requirement, as reflected in section 23 of the Act, which enjoins a positive duty upon the Tribunal to act fairly.

32. Furthermore, the Tribunal is not only expected to act fairly, but it must also act judicially in the discharge of its duty. If it does otherwise, that would be contrary to and violative of the principles of natural justice since judicial acts, by their very nature, are deemed to be amenable to the rules of natural justice.

33. In Dewan Singh vs Champat Singh, reported in AIR 1970 SC 967, the Supreme Court of India observed:

"The proceedings before the arbitrators are quasi-judicial proceedings. They must be conducted in accordance with the principles of natural justice."

In the case of SL Kamer vs Jagmohan, reported in AIR 1981 SC 136, it was held:

"Non-observance of natural justice by itself causes prejudice to a party and proof of prejudice to a party and proof of prejudice independent thereof is unnecessary"

34. In "Law and Practice of International Commercial Arbitration' (Alan Redfern and Martin Hunter, 3rd Ed page 257) it has been observed:

"A tribunal should act judicially. The duty to act judicially is a duty which extends to all aspect of the proceedings"

It has further been observed (at page 377):

"Where an arbitral tribunal is composed of more than one arbitrator, it is self-evident that there should be discussion among the arbitrators before the award is drawn up. Some systems of law contain mandatory provisions to this effect but, whether this is so or not, the principle that arbitrators must consult before issuing their award is well-recognised."

35. The aforesaid principle was endorsed by the International Centre for the Settlement of Investment Disputes (ICSID) in the matter of Klockner Industries vs United Republic of Cameroon, reported in (1986) XI Yearbook of Commercial Arbitration, 161.

36. As has been stated so aptly by Mahmood, J more than a century ago in the case of Nand Ram vs Fakir Chand, reported in ILR 7(1885) All 523:

"What the parties to a reference to arbitration intended is that the persons to whom the reference is made should meet and discuss together all the matters referred, and that the award should be the result of their united deliberations. This conference and deliberation in the presence of all the arbitrators is the very essence of the arbitration, and the sole reason why the award is made binding."

37. In the instant case, the parties had agreed to have their dispute settled by a Tribunal comprising of three members. Both the parties also agreed that the Award of the Tribunal shall be by a majority. It was therefore implied that the Award should be the outcome of the deliberation between each and every member of the Tribunal, even though at the end, the Award may either be unanimous or by a majority. However, in no circumstances can it be inferred that by agreeing to an Award by the majority, the parties had empowered the Chairman to deliberate on the issues with only one member of the Tribunal to the exclusion of the other member before making and signing the Award.

38. Although section 37(2) of the Act authorises the Chairman to decide "questions of procedure", if authorised by the parties or all the members of the Tribunal, it does not confer any authority on the Chairman to make the Award without undertaking a proper and detailed deliberation with the other members of the Tribunal. However, in the instant ease, the Tribunal or, in any event, the Chairman had acted in contravention of the terms of the agreement between the parties.

39. Despite having made a request in writing, the 3rd Arbitrator was not given any scope or opportunity to deliberate on the issues with the Chairman and the other member of the Tribunal before the Award was finalised and signed. On the contrary, he was merely required to append his signature on a one hundred-page typed Award which had already been signed by the Chairman and the 2nd Arbitrator. Even if there was any deliberation before the Award was made and signed, it took place between the Chairman and the 2nd Arbitrator, evidently, without the participation and input of the 3rd Arbitrator. In such premises, the Award in question cannot be termed as an Award by the majority. Consequently, it cannot be said that the Tribunal had either acted fairly or in accordance with the terms of the agreement between the parties, as it was required to do under the Act.

40. From a careful reading of the provisions laid clown in the Act as well as the Model Law, it appears that neither the Act nor the Model Law have considered the scenario where one of the Arbitrators is, in fact, excluded totally from the process of deliberation that is required to take place among the members of a Tribunal before an Award is made. Neither the Act or the Model Law contains any provision to that effect.

41. In my view, the provisions of section 43(1)(a)(v) of the Act as well as Articles 34(2)(a)(iv) and 36(1)(a)(iv) of the UNCITRAL Model Law are attracted in the instant case, both of which provides for setting aside an Award on the ground that the arbitral procedure was not in accordance with the agreement of the parties".

42. It has also been argued by Mr Hossain that the Award is liable to be set aside on the ground of being opposed to public policy.

43. In the case of Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Limited vs Environmental Engineers Ltd reported in (2001) 2 Comp 79 (Bom), it was held:

"As the expression is incapable of precise definition, those challenges would be available, if the Court finds the award obnoxious to its sense of justice, based on settled principles of law, whether as to the conduct of the arbitrator or arbitral proceedings or the award itself. Justice is the beginning and the end. Law must ultimately reach out to justice. Public policy contemplates that, Courts must reflect it."

44. In Murlidhar Agarival vs State of Uttar Pradesh reported in AIR 1974 SC 1924, the Supreme Court of India observed:

"Public policy, has been defined by Winfield as a principle of judicial legislation or interpretation founded on the cur-rent needs of the community."

45. In the case of Oil and Natural Gas Corporation Lid vs SAW Pipes Ltd, reported in AIR 2003 SC 2629, the Supreme Court of India held:

"In exercising jurisdiction, the Arbitral Tribunal cannot act in breach of some provision of substantive law or the provisions of the Act."

46. In the case referred to above, the Court further held:

"It can be stated that the concept of public policy connotes some matter which concerns public good and the public interest. What is for public good or in public interest or what would be injurious or harmful to the public good or public interest has varied from time to time. However, the award which is, on the face of it, patently in violation of statutory provisions, cannot be said to be in public interest."

<u>47. Evidently, the final deliberation that took place leading to the making and signing of the Award was only between the Chairman and the 2nd Arbitrator to the total exclusion of the 3rd Arbitrator, although the parties had referred the matter to a Tribunal comprising of three members. In my view, this is not what the Act or the Model Law contemplates and this is certainly not what the parties intended. Consequently, upholding the Award would be against the spirit and intendment of the Act and that, no doubt, would be contrary to public policy.</u>

<u>48. Having considered the submissions advanced by the learned Advocates of the con-tending sides and due deference to the decisions cited above, this Court is inclined to hold that the 3rd Arbitrator was neither consulted nor given any opportunity by the Chairman of the Tribunal to deliberate and express his views on the issues before making and signing the Award under challenge.</u>

49. In the premises noted above, I am of the view that there was non-compliance with the provisions of the Arbitration Act, 2001. Consequently, the Award dated 8-4-2006 made by the majority members of the Arbitral Tribunal is liable to be set aside,

50. Accordingly, the Award dated 8-4-2006 is hereby set aside.

There will be no order as to costs.

End.

lawyer:
M Amin Uddin with Arabinda Kumar Roy, Advocates—For the Petitioner. 
Shamim Khaled Ahmed, Advocate—For Respondent No. 1.
parties:
Provat Kumar Das ------ Petitioner
vs. 
Agrani Bank and others ------ Respondents
case_source: Above decision of the High Court Division has been affirmed by the Appellate Division vide CPLA 28 of 20।8. [Reported in ।5 BCC (AD) ।।3]
full_judgment:
Sheikh Abdul Awal J: This Rule Nisi has been issued at the instance of the petitioner on an application under Article 102(1) and (2) of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the impugned Order No. 56 dated 12-4-2004 vide Annexure-E passed by the respondent No. 2 Joint District Judge and Artha Rin Adalat, 3rd Court, Rajshahi in Money Execution Case No. 38 of 1995 passing an order of Civil imprisonment for 3(three) months against the petitioner should not be declared to have been pawed without lawful authority and is of no legal effect and/or such other or further order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

2. The facts relevant for the purpose of disposal of this rule are as follows:

The respondent No. 1, Agrani Bank instituted Artha Rin Suit No. 16 of 1992 in the Court of Joint District Judge and Artha Rin Adalat, 3rd Court, Rajshahi claiming amount of Taka 21,63,148 including interest as stood on 31-12-1991 against the 6(six) defendants including the petitioner. Ultimately the suit was decreed ex-parte vide Judgment and Decree dated 12-6-1994. In usual course the decree holder Bank filed Money Execution Case No. 38 of 1995 in the Court of Joint District Judge and Artha Rin Adalat, 3rd Court Rajshahi (herein after called "the Adalat") for executing the decree. Thereafter, the decree holder Bank (respondent No. 1) filed an application under section 34 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain 2003 (herein after called "the Ain 2003") on 12-4-2004. The learned Judge of the Adalat on consideration of the application awarding civil imprisonment for each of the judgment debtors for 3(three) months including the petitioner by his Order No. 56 dated 12-4-2004.

3. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the order of civil imprisonment, the petitioner has come before this Court and obtained the present rule.

4. Mr. M Amin Uddin, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner after placing the writ petition along with the monocle papers submits that the lamed Judge of the Adalat on misconception of law and facts and without appreciating the matter from a correct angle most illegally passed the impugned order of civil imprisonment against the petitioner and others. The learned Advocate next submits that the Adalat without complying the mandatory provisions of the section 33(1) and 34(9) passed impugned order awarding civil imprisonment and, as such, the impugned order is liable to have been passed without lawful authority and is of no legal effect.

5. Mr. Shamim Khaled Ahmed, the learned Advocate appearing for the respondent No. 1 Agrani Bank, on the other hand, by filing affidavit-in-opposition molested the rule. The learned Advocate after placing entire order sheet of the Money Execution case No. 38 of 1995 as contained in "Annexure-2" to the supplementary affidavit-in-opposition submits that the learned Judge of the Adalat committed no illegality in passing the impugned order of civil imprisonment which was, according to him, correct, just and proper. Mr. Ahmed next submits that the instant Writ Petition is incompetent and malafide one and filed by the defendant-petitioner with sole motive to hang the process of the realization of the Bank money for an indefinite period.

6. These are the points which were argued by the learned Advocates for the respective parties. Now, to deal with the contentions raised by the parties before us, we feel it necessary to quote the provisions of section 34 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 which read as follows:

৩৪ ৷ দেওয়ানী আটকাদেশ; (১) উপ ধারা (১২) এর বিধান সাপেক্ষে, অর্থ ঋণ আদালত, ডিক্রীদার কর্তৃক দাখিলকৃত দরখাস্তের পরিপ্রেক্ষিতে ডিক্রীর টাকা পরিশোধে বাধ্য করিবার প্রয়াস হিসাবে, দায়িককে ৬(ছয়) মাস পর্যন্ত দেওয়ানী কারাগারে আটক রাখিতে পারিবে ৷

(২) উপধারা (১) এর উল্লিখিত বিধান, মূল ঋণ গ্রহীতার মৃত্যুর কারণে পারিবারিক উত্তরাধিকার আইন অনুযায়ী স্থলাভিষিক্ত দায়িক ওয়ারির্শদের ক্ষেত্রে প্রযোজ্য হইবে না।

(৩) জারী মামলা কোন কোম্পানী (Company) যৌথ কারবারী প্রতিষ্ঠান (Firm) অথবা অন্য কোন নিয়মবদ্ধ সংস্থা (Corporate body) এর বিরুদ্ধে কার্যকর করিতে বিবাদী দায়িককে দেওয়ানী কারাণ্যার আটক করা আবশ্যক হইলে, উল্লিখিত কোম্পানী, যৌথ কারবারী প্রতিষ্ঠান বা নিয়মবদ্ধ সংস্থা আইন বা বিধি মোতাবেক যে সকল স্বাভাবিক ব্যক্তির (natural person) সমন্বয়ে পঠিত বলিয়া গণ্য হইবে, সেই সবপ্স ব্যক্তি এককভাবে ও যৌথভাবে দেওয়ানী কারাগারে আটকের জন্য দায়ী হইবেন ৷

(৪) উপ ধারা (৩) এর বিধান এইরূপ কোন ব্যক্তির বিরুদ্ধে কার্যকর হইবে না যিনি ডিক্রীর সত্শিষ্ট ঋণ গ্রহণের পরবর্তীতে উত্তরাধিকার সূত্রে উপরি উল্লিখিত কোন ব্যক্তি বা ব্যক্তিবর্গের স্থলাভিষিক্ত হইয়াছেন৷

(৫) উপ ধারা (১) বা (৩) এর অধীনে দেওয়ার্নী কারাগারে আটক কোন ব্যক্তি, ডিক্রীর দাবী সম্পূর্ণরূপে পরিশোধ না করা পর্যন্ত, অথবা ৬(ছয়) মাসের সময়সীমা অতিক্রম না হওয়া পর্যন্ত, যাহা পূর্বে হয়, দেওয়ানী কারাগার হইতে যুক্তি লাভ করিবে না, এবং ডিক্রীর সম্পূর্ণ টাকা পরিশোধ করার সংগে সংগে আদালত তাহাকে দেওয়ানী কারাগার ইেতে যুক্তির নির্দেশ প্রদান করিবে I

(৬) উপ ধারা (৫) এর বিধান সত্বেও, দেওয়ানী কারাগারে আটক দায়িক যদি ভিক্রীদারের অপরিশোধিত পাওনার ২৫% এর সমপরিমাণ অর্থ নগদ পরিশোধ করিয়া এই মর্মে বন্ড প্রদান করেন যে, তিনি পরবর্তী ৯০ (নব্বই)দিনের মধ্যে অবশিষ্ট পাওনা পরিশোধ করিবেন, তবে সেক্ষেত্রে আদালত দায়িককে মুক্তি প্রদান করিবে।

(৭) উপ ধারা (৬) এ উল্লিখিত বন্ডের শর্ত মোতাবেক যদি দায়িক অবশিষ্ট পাওনা পরিশোধ করিতে ব্যর্থ হন তবে তিনি পুনরায় গ্রেফতার ও দেওয়ানী কারাগারে পুনরায় আটকাদেশ হইলে, উহা ছয় মাস পর্যন্ত বহালযোগ্য নতুন আটকাদেশ হিসাবে গণ্য হইবে৷

(৮) এই আইনের অধীনে দেওয়ানী কারাগার আটককৃত ব্যক্তির ভরণ পোষণ খরচ সরকার কর্তৃক বিচারাধীন আসামীর অনুরূপ খরচের ন্যায় বহন করা হইবে, এবং পরবর্তীকালে সরকার ডিক্রীদারের নিকট হইতে সরকারি পাওনা হিসাবে উক্ত খরচের অর্থ আদায় করিতে পারিবে, এবং ডিক্রীদার দায়িকের নিকট হইতে মামলার খরচ বাবদ উক্ত অর্থ আদায় করিতে পারিবে।

(৯) এই ধারার অধীনে আদালত কোন দায়িককে দেওয়ানী কারাগারে আটক করার আদেশ প্রদান করিবে না, যদি না তৎপূর্বে অন্ততঃ একটি নিলাম বিক্রয় কার্যক্রম অনুষ্ঠিত হইয়া থাকে এবং উহার দ্বারা ভিক্রীদারের প্রাপ্য পরিপূর্ণভাবে আদায় হইয়া থাকে৷

(১০) যদি কোন কারণে উপ ধারা (৯) এর অধীন একটিও নিলাম বিক্রয় কার্যক্রম অনুষ্ঠান করা সম্ভব না হয়, তবে সেই ক্ষেত্রে দায়িককে সরাসরি গ্রেফতার ও দেওয়ানী কারাগারে অটিক করা যাইবে।

(১১) ১৮ (আঠার) বৎসরের কম বয়স্ক কোন ব্যক্তিকে এই ধারার অধীনে ডিক্রী কার্যকর করার নিমিত্ত গ্রেফতার এবং দেওয়ানী কারাগারে অটিক করা বা রাখা 'যাইবে না ৷

(১২) এই আইনের অধীনে কোন ডিক্রী বা আদেশ বাস্তবায়নের উদ্দেশ্যে পরিচালিত জারী মামলায়, জারী মামলার সংখ্যা একাধিক হইলেও, কোন একজন দায়িককে গ্রেফতার করিয়া পরিপূর্ণ মেয়াদের জন্য একবার দেওয়ানী কারাগারে আটক রাখা হইলে, তাহাকে পুনবরি গ্রেফতার করা ও দেওয়ানী কারাগারে আটক করা যইিবে না৷

(১৩) এই ধারার অধীনে কোন দায়িককে আৎশিক বা পূর্ণ মেয়াদের জন্য দেওয়ানী কারাগারে আটক রাখার কারনে তিনি দেনার দায় হইতে মুক্ত গণ্য হইবেন না, এবং এই আইনের অধীন নির্ধারিত তামাদি দ্বারা বারিত না হইলে, তাহার বিরুদ্ধে নতুন করিয়া জারী মামলা দায়ের করা যাইবে।”

<u>7. From a combined reading of those sub-sections of section 34 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 it transpires that the Adalat is empowered to pass an order of warrant of arrest/civil imprisonment directly when no auction sale is possible to be held for any reason.</u>

<u>8. We have carefully examined the writ petition, affidavit-in-opposition and supple mentor affidavit-in-opposition along with connected papers as filed therewith, it appears that the respondent No. 1, Agrani Bank filed Money Execution Case No. 38 of 1995 in the Artha Rin Adalat, Rajshahi on 12-8-1995 against the petitioner and other judgment debtors. The Adalat by order dated 24-11-2003 directed to publish notice under the provisions of section 33 of the Ain, 2003 and on that, the auction sale notice was published in the 'Daily Sonar Desh' on 19-2-2004 mentioning date of auction sale on 23-2-2004 at 3-00 PM but the property in question was not sold due to non-availability of the auction purchaser. Therefore, the contention of the learned Advocate for the petitioner that no attempt was made to sale the property as per mandatory provision of section 34(9) of the Ain, 2003 by the respondent No. 2 before passing the impugned order of civil imprisonment is wholly untenable.</u>

<u>9. So, in any view of the matter, the learned Judge of the Adalat committed no illegality in passing the impugned order of civil imprisonment rather, it appears to us that the impugned order is well founded in law. The learned Judge of the Adalat appears to have considered all the legal aspects.</u>

10. In view of our discussions made in the foregoing paragraphs vis-a-vis the law, it is by now clear that the instant Rule must fail.

11. In the result, therefore, the Rule is discharged with a cost of Taka 2,000 (two thousand) to be paid by the petitioner to the respondent No. 1 (decree holder Bank) immediately.

The Joint District Judge and Artha Rin Adalat, 3rd Court, Rajshahi is directed to proceed with the Money Execution Case No. 38 of 1995 is expeditiously.

End.

lawyer:
Shah Md. Ahsanur Rahman, Advocate ------ For the Plaintiff. 
M Hafizullah, with Fida M Kamal, Senior Advocates with Md Ohiullah, Advocate— For the Defendant Nos. 1, 2 and 4 .
parties:
S Alam Vegetable Oil Ltd and others ------ Plaintiffs
Vs.
MT Trompeteros and others ------ Defendants
full_judgment:
The Plaintiffs namely, (1) S Alam Vegetable Oil Ltd. (2) Al-Noor Edible Oils Ltd, (3) Bay Fishing Corporation Ltd, (4) MM Vegetable Oil Products Ltd, instituted the instant Admiralty Suit for realization of compensation in respect of short landing of crude degummed soyabean oil, in short CDSO, imported by them, against the carrier the defendant No. 1 'MT Trompeteros'. 
2. The Suit has been heard in presence of both the parties and now disposed off by this judgment. 
3. It has been asserted in the plaint that the plaintiff companies are Vegetable Oil refinery installations and it refine Crude Degummed Soyabean Oil for the purpose of selling the same in the local market for profit. It course of their business the plaintiffs jointly imported 24,000 MT of Crude degummed Soyabean Oil from Argentina. Six Letters of Credit were opened through the bank namely, Prime Bank Ltd, Agrabad Branch, Chittagong, Islami Bank Bangladesh Ltd, Khatungonj Branch, Chittagong, Dhaka Bank Ltd, Agrabad Branch, Chittagong, South East Bank Limited, Khatungonj Branch, Chittagong, Bank de Credit Agricole Indusnez and Standard Chartered Bank, Chittagong, being Nos. 155402010063, dated 17-11-2002, 086903020010, 144003010002, 1334/03/02/0001, 265603010006 and 2467030100056, for an amount of US $ dollar 1,48,233.66. The CDSO was imported from the supplier in Singapore Bunge Agribusiness Singapore Pte. Ltd. The said cargo was boarded in defendant No. 1 vessel 'MT Trompeteros' at the load Port of Sanlorenzo, Argentina. the Master of the vessel issued 9 (nine) bills of leading being Nos. 1 dated 27-1-2003, No. 2 dated 28-1-2003, No. 3 dated 29-1-2003, No. 4 dated 27-1-2003, No. 5 dated 27-1-2003; No. 6 dated 27-1-2003 No. 7 dated 27-1-2003, No. 9 dated 27-1-2003 and No. 9 dated 27-1-2003. The said vessel is a Panama Flag carrier which reached the outer anchorage of Chittagong Port on 8-3-2003, laden with 24,000 MT CDSO in bulk. 
4. The vessel started discharging the cargo on 8-3-2003 and completed the discharge on 17-3-2003. There was a joint inspection by the surveyor of the agent of the consignee, agent of the ship and Customs Preventive Officer, Chittagong, on 8-3-2003 and the report reveals that 201.699 MT of the CDSO at bond temperature were short landed for which the plaintiff incurred loss of US $ dollar 141,676.37 equivalent to Bangladeshi Taka 82,29,980.90. The defendants admitting the shortage issued P&I Club guarantee through James Finlay, Chittagong, in favour of the plaintiffs through securing an amount of US $ dollar 33,869 for anticipated custom penalty and for US $ dollar 1,12,897 for consignee's cargo claim at a total of US $ dollar 1,46,766 equivalent to Bangladeshi Taka 85,25,636 at the rate of, Bangladesh Taka 58.09 per one dollar. Subsequently the agent of the vessel Pacific Ocean Ltd demanded their claim against their principle to be secured by furnishing unconditional bank guarantee from the James Finlay as the vessel is going to be scrapped in Bangladesh. 
5. The plaintiff suffered loss and damage to the extent of US $ dollar 1,08,917.46 equivalent to Bangladeshi Taka 63,27,159.15, for short delivery of 201.699, MT of CDSO which were valued at the rate of US $ dollar 540 per MT and also on account of custom duty and Penalty to the extent US $ dollar 24,151.60 equivalent to Bangladeshi Taka 14,02,965.75. The plaintiff also claims to recover from the principal defendant compensation for business loss at the rate of 20% to be paid on the value of the claim and also interest at the rate of 16.50% on the amount of the total claim till actual realization of the claim. The plaintiff prays for a decree against the defendants for an amount of US $ dollar 141,676.37 equivalent to Bangladeshi Taka 82,29,980.90, with interest and cost of the suit. 
6. The aforesaid total claim of US $ dollar 141,676.37 equivalent to Bangladeshi Taka 82,29,980.80 has been inserted by the amendment of the plaint dated 27-2-2005. By this amendment the serial number of the plaintiff's in the cause title was re-arranged and accordingly the original plaintiff No. 3, S. Alam Vegetable oil Ltd, become plaintiffs No. 1 and original plaintiffs No. 1 Messrs Bay Fishing Ltd became plaintiff No. 3. . 
7. The suit is contested by the defendant Nos. 1, 2 and 4 being the vessel 'MT Trompeteros', the master of the vessel and the present local agent of the vessel Messrs RK Shipping Agency and the owners and parties interested in the vessel 'MT Trompeteros' by filing a joint written statement along with raising counter claim against the plaintiff.
8. It has been asserted in the written statement, after denying all the material allegations brought in the plaint, that the oil tanker 'MT Trompeteros' carried the imported CDSO of the plaintiffs from the load Port Sanlorenzo to the Chittagong port. The vessel arrived at Chittagong Port on 8-3-2003, with the cargo against bills of leading for an estimated quantity of 24,000 MT. After the arrival of the vessel and before discharge the same, a joint ullage survey was carried out on board the vessel 'MT Trompeteros' as a regular action and the surveyor found the cargo at a quantum of 24,873 MT of crude degummed Soyabean Oil on board the vessel and accordingly issued ullage Survey report on 8-3-2003. The said ullage survey was conducted in presence of and attended by the surveyor on behalf of the consignee and the carrier. Thereafter, the discharge was commenced and completed on 17-3-2003, when the vessel tanks were jointly inspected and checked by the Chief Officer of the vessel and surveyor of the cargo owner and found that the tanks of the vessel is empty and dry and accordingly a dry tank certificate dated 17-3-2003 was issued. There was no short landing of 201.699 MT of the cargo rather an excess quantity of 0.873 MT of the CDSO were discharged from the vessel. The plaintiff since most illegally threatened the vessel to be detained and arrested for some alleged short landing of cargo, the owners of the vessel, to avoid any unlawful arrest and the detention of the vessel, under compelling circumstances issued P&I club guarantee for US $ dollar 1,12,897.00 dated 18-3-2003, in favour of the plaintiff's for alleged cargo claim and another for US $ dollar 33,869.00, dated 18-3-2003, in favour of the Commissioner of Customs, Chittagong, for anticipated customs penalty through their P&I Club, the Standard Steamship Owners Protection and Indemnity Association (Bermuda) Limited. It was stipulated in the said guarantee that the plaintiff's will be refrained from arresting or otherwise detaining and harassing the vessel 'MT Trompeteros' and the defendant shall pay on demand to the plaintiff such some as may be found to the due by final judgment of the High Court in Bangladesh or in Arbitration or by agreement between the parties. But despite such receiving the P&I Club guarantee, the plaintiff instituted the instant suit and obtained an order of arrest of the vessel 'MT Trompeteros' on 29-3-2003, for which the owners of the vessel compelled to furnish bank guarantee being No. 864 /CG 6300483, dated 1-4-2003, issued by the Standard Chartered Bank; Dhaka, for an amount of Taka 85,25,636 in order to obtain the release of the vessel. 'MT Trompeteros' from arrest. Their is no short landing of the cargo CDSO from the carrier vessel 'MT Trompeteros', rather an excess of 0.873 MT of the cargo was received by the plaintiffs as discharged from the vessel. The plaintiff's suffering of loss and damage is not true. Moreover, the declaration regarding quantum of CDSO made by the agent of the vessel Messrs Pacific Ocean Lines Ltd, the defendant No. 5, to the customs authority is a liability of the ship owners as such the plaintiff being mere consignee suffered no loss for the alleged customs penalty made against the declaring agent and therefore the claim raised by the plaintiff on the said Court is also not tenable in the eye of law as there is the P&I Club guarantee issued in favour of the customs authority is still in existence. The plaintiff filed the instant suit for illegal gain and illegally detained and wrongfully arrested the vessel 'MT Trompeteros' and caused loss and injury to the defendant for which the defendant is entitled to recover a damage of US$ dollar 11,310.70, equivalent to Bangladeshi Taka 6,65,974.02, by way of counter claim on account of the illegal detention of the vessel at Chittagong Port for three days from 29-3-2003, up to 2-4-2003. 
9. After the amendment of the plaint on 27-2-2005, the defendant No. 1, 2 and 4 filed a additional written statement where the defendant reiterated the statement that the custom duty and penalty imposed by the custom authority against the declaring agent as alleged by the plaintiff for short landing of cargo, is directly recoverable by the customs authority from the carrier through the declaring agent and, as such, the plaintiff cannot claim any compensation in respect of the alleged customs penalty. The defendants prayed for dismissal of the suit, return of the bank guarantee furnished and as decree on the counter claim. 
10. Upon the aforesaid pleading of the parties, this Court framed issues to the following effect: 
1. Is the suit maintainable under the Admiralty Jurisdiction? 
2. What is the plaintiff's locus standi to file the instant Admiralty Suit against the defendant Nos. 1 , 2 and 4? 
3 Was the plaintiff entitled to arrest the vessel 'MT Trompeteros'?
 4. Has the plaintiff suffered any loss and damage? 
5. Is the plaintiff entitled to any other relief? 
6. Are the defendant Nos. 1, 2 and 4 entitled to a decree for the counter-claim against the plaintiffs?

13. Both the PWs and DWs were duly cross-examined by the adversary. 
14. The PW 1 Md Aslam in his examination in chief narrated the plaint case who has been authorized by Bay Fishing Corporation Limited, the plaintiff No. 3, to depose on behalf of all the plaintiffs. The said authorization letter has been exhibited and marked as exhibit No. 1. The PW 1 filed the letters of credit of the plaintiffs, the bills of leading issued by the defendant vessel and other related documents in order to substantiate the fact of quantity of the imported CDSO. He has also submitted the shore tanks terminal survey report, exhibit 9 series, to show the short landing of 201.876 MT at bond temperature. He has also submitted the custom adjudication documents, being exhibit No. 15 series. 
15. On cross-examination, the PW 1, upon seen the exhibit 8, stated that it is in writing in it that the vessel 'MT Trompeteros' arrived at Chittagong on 8-3-2003 at 04-12 hours and the cargo calculation was started at 14-20 hours and completed at 15-30 hours and the quantity of the cargo was found as per the ships figure i.e., 24,000.873 MT. The PW 1 also stated that the ullage survey was stated on 8-3-2003, at 14-20 hours and was completed at 15-30 hours which ascertained the quantity of the cargo at 24,000.873 MT. The PW 1 further stated in cross-examination that he attended the custom adjudication as representative of the local declaring agent of the vessel and the defendant No. 5 Pacific Ocean Line was the local declaring agent of the vessel 'MT Trompeteros', who further stated that the customs adjudication was directed against the local declaring agent Pacific Ocean Lines Ltd, Chittagong, the defendant No. 5. He further stated that the plaintiff was made a party to the custom adjudication. 
16. PW 2 Kamrul Ahsan, representing the plaintiff No. 4 MM Vegetable Oil Products Ltd, proved the L/C, Exhibit 7, the bills of leading Exhibit Nos. 2, 7, 8 and 9, dated 27-1-2003. He also proved the survey report issued by Summit United Tank Terminal Limited, Exhibit-9(2), who stated that 23,798.304 MT. Cargo was discharged in the said tank terminal at bond temperature, and 201.699 MT CDSO was short landed. He also proved the claim letters and the heads of claim as appears in the plaint. 
17. In this examination-in-cross the PW 2 stated that the bond temperature of the cargo was taken at the shore tank terminal of plaintiff No. 3, Bay Fishing Corporation and other tank terminal of the plaintiffs. He further stated that the custom authority had commenced proceeding against the defendant No. 5, Pacific Ocean Lines, Chittagong as the declaring agent of the defendant vessel. 
18. The DW 1 Md Halim Bhuiyan, in his examination-in-chief stated that the vessel 'MT Trompeteros' arrived at Chittagong Port on 8-3-2003, with the cargo of 24,000 MT of CDSO and a joint ullage survey was held on board the vessel prior to commencement of discharge of the cargo and the surveyor found 24,000.873 MT of CDSO on board the vessel and accordingly issued ullage survey report dated 8-3-2003, which he submitted and marked as Exhibit B. He stated that Port surveyor namely Captain AHM Khairul Anam appeared on behalf of the consignee and Captain QK Newaz, appeared on behalf of the owners P&I Club, Captain MN Kamal, appeared on behalf of the ships declaring agent and the Chief Officer of the vessel 'MT Trompeteros' were present at the ullage survey and all of them signed the ullage survey report. He further stated that despite the fact that there was no short landing yet the owners of the vessel through their P&I Club issued two letters of guarantee one in favour of the plaintiff with a condition that the plaintiff will be refrained from arresting and otherwise detaining and harassing the vessel. He further raised the counter claim against the plaintiff equivalent to an amount of Taka 6,65,974.00. 
19. In his examination-in-cross the DW reiterated the name of the local agent of the vessel 'MT Trompeteros' as Pacific Ocean Lines Limited and further stated that Messrs RK Shipping was the new local agent of the vessel 'MT Trompeteros', as shown in the birthing documents of the Chittagong Port Authority. He further proved, relying on Exhibit No. 8, the quantity of the discharged cargo from 10-3-2003 up to 15-3-2003 and further stated that after 15-3-2003, there was no mention of any discharge of the cargo in the said exhibit-8, but claimed that the vessel duly discharged the balance cargo. 
20. DW 2 Kazi Kamal Newaz, is a master mariner who is engaged in marine related survey including ullage survey of crude degummed Soyabean Oil from 1991. He, upon showing exhibit B stated that he was present at the ullage survey on behalf of the owner P&l Club and Captain AHM Khairul Anam, appeared on behalf of the consignee, Captain MN Kamal, appeared on behalf of the declaring agent of the vessel and the Chief Officer of 'MT Trompeteros' were present at the joint ullage survey carried on the tank of the vessel on 8-3-2003 and all of them signed the ullage survey report of Exhibit B. He stated that 24,000.873 MT of CDSO was found in the tanks of the vessel 'MT Trompeteros' at the time of ullage survey and after the completion of the ullage survey the cargo was discharged from the vessel in the lighterage tanker vessel and thereafter upon completion of the discharge carried the dry tank inspection on 17-3-2003 and issued Dry tank report showing that the tanks were dry. 
21. In his examination-in-cross the DW 2 stated that he could not recollect the name of the Captain of 'MT Trompeteros' who attended during the ullage survey. He further stated that during the ullage survey on 8-3-2003, the temperature shown in the sixth column of the report ranges from 27-30 degree Celsius. 
22. This is all about the evidence on record adduced by the parties. 
23. Upon hearing the evidence this Court has recasted the issues which are as follows; 
(1) Is the suit maintainable in this Admiralty Jurisdiction? 
(2) It the suit filed by the proper person as plaintiff ? 
(3) Is their short landing of 201.699 MT of CDSO from the defendant vessel 'MT Trompeteros' ? 
(4) Has the plaintiff suffered any loss and damage? 
(5) It is plaintiff is entitled to any others relief ? 
(6) Are the defendant Nos. 1, 2 and 4 is entitled to a decree on their counter claim? 
24. In this suit the learned Advocate Mr Shah Md Ahsanur Rahman, appeared on behalf of the plaintiffs while the senior counsel Mr Fida M Kamal along with the learned Advocate Mr Md Ohiullah, appeared on behalf of the defendants. 
25. We have heard the learned Advocates on every issue and accordingly we will now dispose off the issues as raised in between the parties in this suit upon considering the evidence on record as adduced by the parties in support of their respective case. 
Issue No. 1. 
26. The issue of maintainability of the instant Admiralty Suit on the point of law that it is not covered by the Admiralty Court Ain, 2000 has not been seriously pressed by the parties. But as the same goes to the root of the suit it must be examined at the very out set even not being pressed by the parties. The ground taken by the defendants that the instant suit is not maintainable as filed by fictitious person will be taken into consideration in the next issues since the same depends on the factual aspects .of the suit. 
27. The plaintiffs instituted the instant suit for recovery of compensation for short delivery of cargo by the sea carrier. The cause of the instant suit arose as mentioned in the plaint on the date of short delivery i.e. in the month of March, 2003. Therefore, the instant suit has been brought under the provision of Admiralty Court Ain, 2000. Section 3(2)(Cha) of the said Act provides that Admiralty suit shall be maintainable for recovery of compensation arising out of loss of or damage to goods carried in a ship. Therefore this Court finds that the cause of the plaintiff is squarely maintainable in this jurisdiction as such issue No. 1 is disposed off in favour of the plaintiff. 
Issue No. 2-5. 
29. These issues have been taken together for the sake of brevity and convenience. 
30. The learned Advocate Mr SM Ahsanur Rahman, appearing on behalf of the plaintiffs while taken this Court through the different Exhibits filed by the parties developed his argument on these issues in manifold Court upon relying the shore tanks survey report Exhibit 9 and argued that admittedly the plaintiff imported 24,000 MT of CDSO which was loaded at the load Port Sanlorenzo, in the tanks of the defendant vessel 'MT Trompeteros' and, as such, The defendant vessel is liable to discharge the same quantity of the cargo to the plaintiff. But the defendant since failed to deliver a quantity of 201.699 MT of CDSO, the plaintiff incurred loss mainly on three heads i.e. the price of the short landed goods, the customs Penalty and the business loss or the said quantity of the short landed cargo.
31. In elaborating the argument on these points the learned Advocate Mr SM Ahsanur Rahman, drawn the attention of this Court to the P&I Club guarantee and argued that by issuing the P&I Club guarantee the defendants admitted the short landing of the cargo which was ultimately found to be correct when the shore tank terminal survey was carried out. The learned Advocate Mr SM Ahsanur Rahman, refuted the claim of the defendant that 0.876 MT of CDSO was excess delivered to the plaintiff and argued that such claim of the defendant categorically proves that the defendants have not delivered the correct quantity of the CDSO as loaded in the vessel 'MT Trompeteros' which has been clearly proved from the customs survey which is more authentic survey report upon which the custom authority imposed Penalty upon the plaintiff for the short landing of the cargo through the adjudication order Exhibit No. 15(1). 
32. The learned Advocate Mr SM Ahsanur Rahman, next argued that the ullage survey report was not prepared properly as no agent of the importer, the plaintiffs, were present at the time of conducting the ullage survey, although the Provision of Article 3 Rule 6 of the carriage of goods by sea Act, 1925 requires a joint survey. Therefore the defendant cannot relay upon the ullage survey report in order to substantiate their claim that excess quantity of CDSO was discharged and there was no short landing. The learned Advocate Mr SM Ahsanur Rahman, argued that the contract of carriage in this case is the bills of leading and Section 74 of the Contract Act will come into play when the question of compensation arises. In this respect he relied on the case of Elsar Navigation Water. 
33. In his second Court of argument on the issue of locus standi of the plaintiffs to file the suit, the learned Advocate Mr SM Ahsanur Rahman, submits that the plaintiff's are not fictitious persons and the defendant has issued the P&I Club guarantee in favour of the plaintiff's which proves that the plaintiff's are the proper person to initiate the Admiralty proceeding against the defendants as a consignee of the cargo. He further argued that the counter claim as filed by the defendants are based on fabricated documents and, as such, the same cannot be considered by this Court. Upon such arguments the learned Advocate SM Ahsanur Rahman prayed for dismissal of the suit. 
34. On the other hand the senior counsel Mr Fida M Kamal, appearing on behalf of the defendants along with Mr Muhammed Ohiullah, emphasized on the ullage survey report, so far the discharge of the CDSO is concerned and argued that the long standing practice in the carriage of goods by sea established the principal that when the fact of correct quantity of discharge of Liquid Cargo is in question, the ullage survey is the appropriate method for ascertaining the quantity of the cargo and not any other survey conducted elsewhere after the discharge as the liability of the carrier terminates just after the point of passing of the liquid through the ships rail i.e. when the delivery hose of the vessel is disconnected from the vessel tanks. Therefore, the ullage survey which is conducted before delivery of the cargo is the appropriate method to be considered by this Court in order to come to a finding that 24,000 MT of CDSO was discharged from the vessel 'MT Trompeteros'. the learned Senior counsel Mr Fida M Kamal in this context referred the case of James Finlay PLC vs Member (Appeal & Revision) Ministry of Finance, reported in 1990 BCR 194 and the case of Haque and Sons vs National Board of Revenue reported in 5 BLC 579 and also un unreported case of this Court being CA No. 46 of 1999, and the case of Lever Brothers Bangladesh Limited vs Botany Bay Shipping Company (Aust) Pvt. Ltd reported in 9 BLC 280. 
35. The learned senior counsel Mr Fida M Kamal, while taken this Court through the plaint and the Vokalatnama executed by one Mr Shamsul Alam, appointing the learned Advocate SM Ahsanur Rahman to act on his behalf, argued that the instant suit has not been field by the proper person since the plaintiff's being the corporate bodies are juristic person which should file a plaint through their recognized agent i.e. the Managing Director or the chairman of the company and the plaint must contain the common seal of the company and unless such legal formalities is observed any plaint filed by a limited company is liable to be rejected as being not properly presented. The learned senior counsel further argued that the instant plaint has been signed by one Mr Shamsul Alam and he not being the chairman or managing Director of the plaintiff companies, the instant suit is liable to be dismissed on the ground and the same has been filed by the fictitious person. The learned senior Advocate Mr Fida M Kamal, concludes his argument praying for dismissal of the suit on the ground that there was no short landing of the cargo and plaintiff is not liable to pay the customs Penalty and also that the suit is not maintainable as filed by the fictitious person. 
36. The plaintiff brought this Admiralty Suit on the ground that 201.699 MT of CDSO was short landed out of 24,000 MT of imported CDSO from Argentina which was loaded on board the defendant vessel 'MT Trompeteros' which arrived at Chittagong Port on 8-3-2003 and discharged the said cargo up to 17-3-2003 in the lighterage tanker vessel which in turn discharged the same in the shore tank of the plaintiffs. Thereafter, a survey was conducted in the shore tanks terminal in order to ascertain the discharge quantity of the CDSO and it was found that the said quantity of 201.699 MT cargo was short landed for which the plaintiff was saddled with the customs penalty for short landed cargo. The plaintiff further incurred loss due to the business loss it faced for the short landed cargo. It is the contention of the plaintiffs that to ascertain the discharge quantity of liquid cargo i, e; CDSO the shore tanks terminal survey report is the appropriate report to consider and since the customs authority upon conducting the shore tanks terminal survey found the short landing of the cargo and imposed the penalty under the provisions of section 156(1)(24)(2) of the customs Act 1961, the defendants are laible to compensate the plaintiff in all those count. 
37. On the other hand, the defendants relied on the ullage survey report and argued that the only method of ascertaining the quantity of liquid cargo carried by a vessel is the ullage survey conducted at the port of discharge prior to commencement of the discharge of the liquid cargo. In this respect the reliance were made on the decision of the referred cases as decided by this Division. 
38. In the case of James Finlay PLC vs Member, (Appeal & Revision) and ex-Office Additional Secretary to the Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, Ministry of Finance, Dhaka reported in 1990 BCR 194 a Division bench of this Court in the writ jurisdiction while considering a question as to the mode of ascertaining the quantity of liquid cargo carried in a vessel held as under: 
"In the light of the provision of clause 24 (ii) of the table under section 156(1) of the Customs Act 1969 and in the light of definition of 'conveyance' as quoted above it can be said that the shortage, if any, has to be found in the conveyance which means that he shortage, if any, has to be found on board the vessel. Therefore, the tillage Survey Report on Board the vessel 'MT Botany Trojan' shall prevail against the shore tank survey report in case of any difference in respect of shortage of cargo between the ullage Survey Report on board the vessel and the Shore Tank survey Report and that in case the shortage, if any, found in the ullage Survey on board the vessel is covered by the 1% admissible Ocean allowance then the carrier will not be responsible for any shortage of crude oil found in the Shore Tank Survey Report which is not covered by 1% admissible Ocean allowance and in such case no penalty can be imposed on the carrier or his agent. The respondents have not applied their mind to this aspect of the case." 
39. In the case of Haque and Sons vs National Board of Revenue reported in 5 BLC 579 another Division Bench of this Court in the writ jurisdiction while considering the similar point held as under: 
"It appears that the ullage survey was carried out on board the vessel 'MT Atlantic Antares' on 1-4-1978 at the outer anchorage at Chittagong when the total quantity of cargo found on board at the time of survey was 40,445,53 crude oil as against the manifested quantity of 40,967 long tons of crude oil. Thus on the basis of ullage survey report there was shortage of 81.87 long tons of crude oil which was well within 1% Ocean allowance admissible. It has appears that the entire quantity of crude oil was discharged into the lightening vessels namely 'MT Banglar Alo' and 'MT Banglar Kheya' which was 'acknowledged by receipt of the total quantity of 41,024 long tons of crude oil. Therefore, it is evident that there was no shortage beyond the 1% Ocean allowance at conveyance, that is, when the crude oil was discharged by 'MT Atlantic Antares' into the aforesaid lightening vessels. Dip reading of the shore tanks which allegedly shown shortage of 1,211.38 long tons of crude oil cannot be relied upon for imposing penalty in view of the provisions of section 156(1) of the Customs Act, 1969. In view of the definition of the word 'conveyance' as made in the Customs Act, 1969 and for reasons as aforesaid when there is a conflict between ullage survey report and dip shore tank survey in respect of shortage of cargo the ullage survey report will prevail. Hence, all the actions taken by the respondents in imposing penalty in respect of shortage of cargo are without lawful authority and are of no legal effect". 
40. In the unreported case decided by their lordships on a Division Bench of this Court in the Civil Jurisdiction in the case of Errata Shipping Pte Limited vs Lever Brothers Bangladesh Limited in Civil Appeal No. 46 of 1990 on the similar question held as under: 
"It appears that an ullage survey was carried out prior to discharge of the cargo from the vessel 'MT Aktubinsk' and a quantity of 1,923.457 metric tons of tallow was found as per the ullage survey report as opposed to the shore tank survey report and after giving 1% ocean allowance there remains co shortage whatsoever. Having considered the plaint, written statement, both oral and documentary evidence adduced by the parties it appears that a quantity of 5.754 metric tons tallow was found short as per the ullage survey report, but such alleged shortage is well within 1% Ocean allowance allowed to carrier in the carriage of bulk oil trade. Moreso, from the reported cases reported in 9 BLC 218;11 BLC 83; 5 BLC 579; BCR 1990 (HCD) 194 supports the case of the Appellants/ Defendant Nos. 1 and 2 wherein the Hon'ble High Court Division has held that ullage survey must prevail over shore tank survey." 
41. It appears from the aforesaid decisions that the question as to the mode of ascertaining the quantity of Liquid cargo at the time of delivery has been held to be the ullage survey method since at the time of conducting such survey the cargo remains in the tanks of the vessel and the ullage survey is being conducted" before the commencement of discharge. It further appears that there is a logic behind such method of ascertaining the dischargeable Liquid cargo on the basis of ullage survey report since the cargo remains unbroken when the said survey is conducted. More so as the long line of decisions of this Court has already settled the point that the ullage survey report should be the basis of ascertaining the quantity of the dischargeable liquid cargo, this Court finds no scope to vary with the decisions as to such method of ascertainment of the quantity of the Liquid cargo. 
42. It appears that on 8-3-2003, DW 2 Kazi Kamal Newaz, was present at the time of ullage survey conducted at the tanks of the vessel 'MT Trompeteros' and in his examination-in-chief he disclosed that Captain AHM Khairul Anam was the surveyor appointed by the consignee and there are other surveyor namely Mr MN Kamal present as the surveyor for the declaring agent of the vessel and the chief officer of the vessel were also present at the joint ullage survey carried out, whereupon they have issued the ullage survey report. It has been alleged by the plaintiffs that the said ullage survey report has not been conducted in presence of the consignee or any of the representative of the defendants but this Court finds that such an allegation has no substance since the plaintiff failed to examine the surveyor AHM Khairul Anam who had been the only witness to negative the contention of the defendants that the ullage survey was conducted in this presence as a surveyor of the consignee. Therefore, this Court finds that the ullage survey was conducted in presence of the surveyor Mr AHM Khairul Anam appointed by the consignee as proved by the DW 2 Kazi Kamal Newaz. 
43. Accordingly, this Court finds that as the ullage survey report confirms that the vessel had the quantity of 24,000 MT of CDSO and the same quantity of CDSO was has been discharged by a the vessel in the lighterage tankers which carried the same to the shore tanks owned by the plaintiff and therefore the plaintiff's suffered no loss or damage on this Count. 
44. The second count of argument as advanced by Mr SM Ahsanur Rahman, appearing on behalf of the plaintiffs in regarding the customs Penalty imposed upon the plaintiff due to alleged short landing of the cargo from the vessel 'MT Trompeteros'. In this respect the plaintiff relied upon Exhibit No. 15(1), which is a document regarding customs adjudication and wherefrom it appears to this Court that the custom authority upon adjudicating the alleged short landing of the cargo from the vessel 'MT Trompeteros' imposed Penalty upon the declaring agent of the vessel Pacific Ocean Line. Section 156(1)(40) of the Customs Act, 1969 deals with the Penalty to be imposed upon a vessel in-charge of any vessel which unloads or suffers to be unloaded any goods not duly entered in the import manifest of the conveyance. 
45. Section 43 of the Customs Act, 1969 provides for delivery of import manifest in respect of a vessel which further provides that the primary liability of an incorrect manifest lies on the Master of the vessel who discharges his responsibility through the appointed declaring agent. Therefore, this Court finds that the liability of customs Penalty for declaration of incorrect quantity of liquid cargo primarily lies on the owner of the vessel and any penalty to be imposed upon the owners of the vessel has to be made through the declaring agent of the vessel, what has been done in this case as appears through Exhibit No. 15(1) which shows that the adjudication was made against the defendant No. 5, Messrs Pacific Ocean Lines who acted as a declaring agent of the vessel 'MT Trompeteros'. Therefore, the question of incurring loss by the plaintiff on this count does not arise at all.
46. It appears that the customs authority while adjudicating under Section 156(1)(40) of the Customs Act, 1969 considered the shore tank survey report Exhibit 9(1) and found that the vessel has delivered short of 201.699 MT of CDSO and accordingly imposed penalty under the said provisions of law upon the vessel declaring agent of the vessel, the defendant No. 5. This Court since already found that a long line of decision of this Court have decided as to the method of ascertaining the dischargeable quantity of the Liquid Cargo as the ullage survey report, this Court further finds that the customs authority upon misconception of law found that the vessel 'MT Trompeteros' made a short delivery of 201.699 MT of CDSO and adjudicated under Section 156(1)(40) of the Customs Act 1969 against the declaring agent of the vessel and, as such, the same has no legal effect. The Customs authority if have realized any fine, is liable to refund it to the defendant No. 5. 
47. The defendants have seriously assailed the initiation of this suit by one Shamsul Alam on behalf of the plaintiffs who signed the plaint by subscribing his hands on the plaint itself. Upon examination of the plaint it appears that the plaintiff's are the private limited company and the plaint has only been signed by one Mr. Shamsul Alam, without disclosing his identity as to his relation to the plaintiff's company. Mores, the verification attached to the plaint was not signed by said Mr Shamsul Alam, rather the learned Advocate Mr Md. Bashir Uddin Zindigir, signed the verification which not being an illegality but a irregularity, was required to be cured by the plaintiff. But no such attempt has even been taken by the plaintiffs at any point of time and, as such, it appears that statement made in the plaint as to the claim of the plaintiffs has not been verified. Moseso, when the signatory of the plaint Mr Shamsul Alam, has not deposed before this Court, any statement made in the plaint, not verified by him, cannot be taken as made by the plaintiffs. Therefore, this Court finds that the initiation of the suit has not been properly made before this Court and, as such, the plaintiff's cannot get any relief through such wrongly instituted suit. A plaint submitted by juristic person if not been properly signed cannot be said that it has been field by proper person. A Juristic person is always required to act through a natural person as required by the companies law. 
48. In view of the discussion and reasoning as above this Court finds that there being no short landing of the cargo from the vessel 'MT Trompeteros', the claim of the plaintiff as to incurring loss in respect of short landing has no substance to be considered by this Court. Moreover, since the adjudication made by the customs authority was not lawful, the plaintiffs have also not incurred any loss in respect of the customs Penalty which is not at all a liability of the plaintiff. Therefore, the question of business loss upon the alleged short landing does not come at all. 
49. As this Court finds that the plaintiff measurably failed to prove the vital aspects in this Court these issues are disposed off against the plaintiffs. 
Issue No. 6: 
50. The defendant Nos. 1,2 and 4 upon filing written statement raised counter claim and prayed for a decree against the plaintiff for realizing Taka 6,65,974.02 equivalent to US $ 11,310.70 along with interest @ 18% per annum for the loss it incurred due to illegal detention of the vessel 'MT Trompeteros' through the order of Arrest. 
51. It appears that the defendant vessel 'MT Trompeteros' was detained in the Chittagong Port through the order of arrest of this Court, issued on 29-3-2003, for which the vessel was detained for three days only in the Chittagong Port where after the defendant furnished the bank Guarantee on 2-4-2003 and obtained the release of the vessel. 
52. It appears that the vessel has come to Bangladesh on his eternal journey and the same was scrapped afterward from the release of the same from arrest. The detention of the vessel for three days only not having cast very serious and adverse effect upon the defendant, this Court finds that the counter claim as raised by the defendant as to the expense of the vessel for the three days has little substance and therefore, cannot be considered by this Court. The defendants not having alleged any loss due to interest paid to the Bank on Bank guarantee, this Court is reluctant to consider the same. Therefore, this issue is disposed off the favour of the plaintiff and against the defendants. 
53. As the plaintiff has failed to prove his case the suit is laible to be dismissed. 
54. The Court fee paid is sufficient. 
55. Hence, ordered. 
That the Suit be and hereby dismissed. The bank guarantee being No. 864/CG6300483, dated 1-4-2003, for an amount of Taka 85,25,636.00, issued by the Standard Chartered Bank, 18-20 Motijheel Commercial Area, Dhaka, 1000, now 67, Gulshan Avenue, Gulshan, Dhaka-1212, furnished by the defendants and the club letter of guarantee be returned at once of the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the defendants. The defendant No. 5 the Pacific Ocean Lines Ltd., is entitled to return of the money, if it paid as penalty, to the customs authority. 
The parties shall bear their respective cost of the suit. 
End.
