full_judgment:
What should be destiny of Petition, bestowed by the Plaintiffs-Petitioners for withdrawing suit over which Civil Revision has sprung with permission to sue afresh is the pivotal point which holds out for answer.

2. In resoluteness of doom of petition, laws and principles controlling and regulating withdrawal of suit enshrined in Rule 1(1), (2) (a)(b), 3 and (4) of Order XXIII of the Code of Civil Procedure (for short the Code) may profitably be ruminated, Judicial pronouncements on the subject may, also, be given an eye.

3. Provisions relating to withdrawal of suit engrafted in Order XXIII, rule 1-(1), (2)(a)(b) (3) and (4) of the Code reads thus:

1.-(1) At any time after the institution of a suit the plaintiff may, as against all or any of the defendants, withdraw his suit or abandon part of his claim.

(2) Where the Court is satisfied-

(a) that a suit must fail by reason of some formal defect, or

(b) that there are other sufficient grounds for allowing the plaintiff to institute a fresh suit for the subject-matter of a suit or part of a claim.

It may, on such terms as it thinks fit, grant the plaintiff permission to withdraw from such suit or abandon such part of a claim with liberty to institute a fresh suit in respect of the subject-matter of such suit or such part of a claim.

(3) Where the plaintiff withdraws from a suit, or abandons part of a claim, without the permission referred to in sub-rule (2), he shall be liable for such costs as the Court may award and shall be precluded from instituting any fresh suit in respect of such subject-matter or such part of the claim.

(4) Nothing in this Rule shall be deemed to authorise the Court to permit one of several plaintiffs to withdraw without the consent of the others.

4. Legislative policy behind Order XXIII of the Code is to prevent technicalities from defeating justice, Court shall allow withdrawal where it considers unjust and unequitable to deprive a plaintiff from laying a flesh suit to establish his lawful and legal right.

5. Sub-rule 1 gives an unqualified right to plaintiff to withdraw his suit at any stage of proceeding without any permission from Court for withdrawal only when he wants to sue afresh on the same cause of action and if no permission to file suit is sought under sub-rule 2 of Rule 1, he becomes precluded from instituting a fresh suit in respect of that subject matter.

6. Sub-rule 2 confers power upon Court to permit plaintiff to withdraw from suit or abandoning part of a claim with liberty to sue afresh for the cause of action. Permission under sub-rule 2 can be granted only where the condition set out therein are satisfied. Mere statement that there is formal defect in the form of the suit is not enough. Plaintiff asking for permission to sue afresh must make out a case within clause (a) or (b). The grant of leave envisaged in sub-rule (2) is at the discretion of Court which should be judicially exercised. A suit may fail on account of certain technical factors, though, plaintiff may have a good case on merit and the object of sub-rule (2) is to remedy the failure of justice in such a case. Court should be liberal in allowing withdrawal of suit with permission to file a fresh one if some formal defect, lacuna, inaccuracy or omissions are found in the plaint. Plaintiff in the interest of justice may be allowed to withdraw his suit with permission to file a fresh one. Procedural provisions should not be allowed to become a stumbling block in the way of doing justice. Technical knockout aimed at a party would not be conducive to interest of justice.

7. The expression "formal defect" occurring in Rule 1(2)(a) of Order XXIII has not been defined anywhere in the Code. The expression "formal defect" within the meaning of clause (a) of sub-rule (2) connotes defects of various kinds springing out of some error made by plaintiff in plaint in good faith. The expression "formal defect" should not be construed strictly but must be given a wide and liberal meaning and must be deemed to connote a kind of defect which does not affect the merit of the suit.

8. Some examples of "formal defect" may be taken note of:

i. Defect is not apparent on the face of the record but discovered on evidence being led.

ii. Defect with respect to form prescribed by Rules of Procedure: Kunji Jonabhai Kolecha vs Ambalal Kanjibhni Patel AIR 1972 Gujarat 63.

iii. Certain technical factors, though, plaintiff may have a good case on merit and object of Sub-Rule 2 is to cure defect only to remedy the failure of justice.

iv. Absence of prayer for a proper relief and non-payment of requisite Court Fee: Radha vs Dibakar, AIR 1989 NOC 193.

v. Proper relief inadvertently not asked for: Md Rahim vs Bakshi Khan, PLD 1983 Peshawar 115.

vi. Defect or such nature as to entail dismissal of suit: Nazir Mooraj vs Md Sultan Khan PLD 1966 (WP) Karachi 356.

vii. Wrong description of property: 1992 MLD 1301 (SCAJK).

viii. Non-identification of a property conveyed in a deed of conveyance with the property described in schedule to plaint.

ix. Failure on the part of plaintiff to bring all partible i.e. ejmali or joint properties in hotchpot.

x. Dismissal of suit for non-production of evidence in support of plaintiffs claim.

xi. Failure of plaintiff to give formal proof of a document which was essential for his success in the suit.

9. Sub-rule (2) of Rule 1 of Order XXIII speaks of "other sufficient grounds". "Other sufficient grounds" mean grounds other than and different from "formal defect" To put it differently, words 'other sufficient grounds" occurring in Order XXIII, rule 1(2)(a) are not ejusdem generis with words "formal defects" mandated in Rule 1(2)(a) of Order XXIII and are much wider in signification covering all those cases which appear to Court as affording such grounds. Expression "other sufficient grounds" in clause (b), thus, are not restricted to grounds related to "formal defects" and those words should be read independent of the words "formal defects" in clause (a) and Court has been given a wider discretion to allow withdrawal from a suit in the interest of justice, though, such prayer is not covered by clause (a) of sub-rule (2) of Rule 1. Permission to withdraw from a suit to institute a fresh one can be granted for "other sufficient grounds" in the interest of justice.

10. The words "may grant" appearing in clause (b) of sub-rule (2) of Rule 1 of Order XXIII may conveniently be taken into stock of Court "may grant permission" means that Court always enjoys power to permit withdrawal of suit or part of it against all or any of the defendants in order to bring a fresh suit to avoid a "formal defect" which may ultimately affect the result of suit or on account of some "other sufficient grounds." Such power is to be exercised keeping in view interest of parties to do complete justice.

11. This takes me to a legal aspect of public importance. The legal aspect is, whether in the Appeal or in Civil Revision a suit can be allowed to be withdrawn at the instance or on the request of plaintiff.

12. Suit/Appeal/Civil Revision are all "Civil Proceedings". "Proceeding" is a term of wide amplitude. "Proceeding" is a prescribed course of action for enforcement of legal right. The word "Proceeding" has been stated in Black's Law Dictionary, Sixth Edition Page 1204 in the following way.

"An act which is done by the authority or direction of the Court, agency, or tribunal, express or implied; an act necessary to be done in order to obtain a given end; a prescribed mode of action for carrying into effect a legal right. All the steps or measures adopted in the prosecution or defence of an action. Statter vs United States, CCA Alaska, 66 F 2d 819, 822. The word may be used synonymously with "action" or "suit" to describe the entire course of an action at law or suit in equity from the issuance of the writ or filing of the complaint until the entry of a final judgment, or may be used to describe any act done by authority of a Court of law and every step required to be taken in any cause by either party. The proceedings of a suit embrace all matters that occur in its progress judicially. In a more particular sense, any application to a Court of justice, however, made, for aid in the enforcement of rights, for relief, for redress of injuries, for damages, or for any remedial object."

13. The word "Proceeding" what it connotes came up before Full Bench of Madhya Pradesh High Court in Ratan Chand Darbari Lal Saina vs Rajendra Kumar Khoobchand AIR 1970 MP (14 FB) wherein it has been stated that a suit/appeal or second appeal can all be described as proceeding.

14. It is observed that Second Appeal embodied in section 100 of the Code, though stood omitted by Law Reforms Ordinance of 1978 which came into force on June 1, 1979 now stands replaced by section 115 of the Code. Before Law Reforms Ordinance, Judgment and Decree passed by Court of appeal were challenged in Second Appeal under section 100 and now those are being challenged under section 115 of the Code.

15. A suit, thus, can be very much withdrawn with permission to sue afresh in Civil Revision under section 115(1) of the Code.

16. In Mustafa Kabiruddin Ahmed vs Badrun Nessa Chowdhury, 54 DLR 416 it has been laid down that there is no legal bar in granting an application for withdrawal of a suit with liberty to file a suit afresh on the self-same matter even at the Revisional stage provided the other requirements of the law are complied with.

17. Portrayal of essential datums forming backdrop of petition for withdrawal of suit with permission to sue afresh:

Plaintiff-Petitioners laid a Suit being Title Suit No. 33 of 1989 in the First Court of learned Subordinate Judge now Joint District Judge. Sunamganj for a decree of Partition in respect of 2.40-3/4 acres of property which has been described in schedule to plaint. Plaintiffs-petitioners rested their claim on the strength of a registered kabuliyat dated 21-2-1919. Record of Right had not been fully prepared in the name of plaintiffs-petitioners but the same had been recorded in the name of defendants-opposite parties.

18. Second, Third and Fifth-Defendants contested claim of plaintiffs-petitioners on presentation of a written statement. Contesting defendants seriously challenged right, title and interest of plaintiffs over suit property and they asserted their own right, title and interest over suit property.

19. Learned Joint District Judge as Trial Judge by judgment and decree dated 13-4-2002 dismissed the suit. In dismissing suit learned Trial Judge rendered decision:

I. Property of Lakshmipur and Singua Mouza were measured and there had been no identity of the land conveyed in the kabuliyat with schedule property. In coming to decision, learned Trial Judge took into account evidence of PW 5, Advocate Commissioner who made disclosure in his evidence that he did not mention in his report that he did not find any similarity in respect of plots of Kabuliyat and, also, he did not mention the quantity of land conveyed in kabuliyat dated 21-2-1919.

II. Suit suffered from defect of hotchpotch and the suit is barred by defect of hotchpotch.

III. Plaintiff failed to prove their title and possession on suit property.

IV. Plaintiffs did not mention all lands noted in kabuliyat and deeds in schedule and plaintiff suit is barred by doctrine of hotchpot. In coming to said decision learned Trial Judge examined Kabuliyat and documents.

V. Plaintiffs in schedule had mentioned less land of the lands noted in kabuliyat and deed and no grounds had been assigned to that effect.

VI. It came to light from examination of testimonies of witnesses of plaintiffs that heirs of Tota Bibi, sister of Alekzan Bibi had not been made party in the suit and suit, thus, is bad for defect of parties.

VII. Plaintiff failed to prove title and possession of suit property and plaintiffs did not seek any relief and plaintiffs did, also, not file suit within the period of limitation.

VIII. Plaintiffs in support of title on the basis of Kabuliyat did not produce any documentary evidence and plaintiff did not produce any evidence in support of case tabled by them that landlords accepted them as tenants on granting Rent Receipts.

IX. Plaintiffs, through oral and documentary evidence could not characterise suit property and, as such, plaintiffs are not entitled to get any relief in the suit.

X. Plaintiffs could not prove their title and possession in suit property and plaintiffs simple suit for partition was not at all maintainable.

20. Plaintiff-petitioners could not reconcile to Judgment and Decree passed in Title Suit and carried an appeal being Title Appeal No. 53 of 2002 in the Court of District Judge, Sunamganj. Learned Additional District Judge, Sunamganj heard the appeal and by Judgment and Decree dated 16-5-2005 dismissed the appeal. In recording dismissal of appeal, learned Appellate Judge came in full agreement with the decisions rendered by learned Trial Judge.

21. Feeling still dissatisfied plaintiffs-petitioners knocked at the door of this Court on presentation of a Civil Revision Petition under section 115 of the Code.

22. In Civil Revision Petition plaintiff-petitioners on bestowing a petition under Order XXIII, rule 1 of the Code sought withdrawal of suit with permission to sue afresh on setting aside Judgments and Decrees of Courts below. Grounds pressed into service and contentions advanced in support of withdrawal of suit with permission to file fresh suit are catalogued hereunder.

I. Suit for simple partition without prayer for declaration of title and khas possession was not maintainable and there is "formal defect" in the suit and plaintiffs cannot succeed without removing "formal defect" and, as such, suit is liable to be withdrawn with permission to sue afresh.

II. Suit is bad for defect of parties and defects of hotchpotch and hotchpot and these defects are "formal defects" and plaintiffs-petitioners may be granted permission to withdraw suit with permission to sue afresh.

III. There are sufficient grounds for allowing plaintiff-petitioners to withdraw suit with permission to sue afresh.

In support of contention Kamta vs Gaya Prasad AIR 1972 Allahabad 143, AZM Khalilur Rahman vs Md Syed Hossain 25 DLR 485 and Abdur Rahman vs Kheru Malitha 50 DLR (AD) 71 have pressed into service.

23. Defendant-Second-Opposite Party and Defendant-First-Opposite Party resisted petition for withdrawal of suit on laying two (2) sets of counter-affidavits adopting almost similar stand and contentions surged forward in counter-affidavits have been, also, contentions advanced which are:

I. Petitioners has not alleged any "formal defect" in the application and all the defects stated could be amended because all those defects were pointed out in written statement.

II. Present application for withdrawal of suit after nineteen (19) years with permission to sue afresh is unjust and unreasonable.

III. If fresh suit is to be allowed to be instituted that would stand barred by limitation.

IV. Petition does not have any merit for consideration and suit and appeal had been dismissed on merit after careful consideration by Judges.

V. Defect of parties and defect of hotchpotch are not "formal defects" going to the root of case of plaintiffs-petitioners. Md Badruddin Moral vs Santosh Kumar Sen 41 DLR (AD) 156 has been relied upon in support of contention so surged forward.

24. Before adverting to judicial decision I am inclined to record an observation that a Judicial decision is only an authority for what it actually decides. It cannot be quoted for a proposition that may seem to flow from it. Every Judgment must be read applicable to the particular facts proved or assumed to be proved. The generality of expression that may be found cannot be intended to be the exposition of whole law but must be regarded as governed or qualified by the particular facts of the case in which such expression occurs. It is neither permissible nor desirable to pick out a word or sentence from the Judgment divorced from the context of question under consideration and treat it to be law declared by Court.

25. In Kamta and another vs Gaya Prasad and others (Supra) the principle laid down is:

Order XXIII, sub-rule (1) of rule 1 of Civil Procedure Code confers an unqualified right on the plaintiff to withdraw at any time. Since an appeal is continuation of suit, the right of the plaintiff to withdraw from the suit inheres even at the appellate stage. On the language of sub-rule 1 it is difficult to hold that the plaintiff had only a qualified right to withdraw from the suit. It had been held that the case of Kedarnath vs Chandra Kiran, AIR 1962 Allahabad 263 wherein it was stated that Order XXIII, rule 1, sub-rule (1) does not give an absolute right to the plaintiff to withdraw a suit at the stage of second appeal was held no longer a good law. Principle laid down in Hulas Rai vs KB Bass and Co, AIR 1968 SC 111 had been quoted in pronouncing the Judicial verdict. Observation of the Supreme Court of India had been couched in the following language:

"The language of Order XXIII, rule 1, sub-rule (1), Civil Procedure Code gives an unqualified right to a plaintiff to withdraw from a suit and if no permission to file a fresh suit is sought under sub-rule (2) of that rule, the plaintiff becomes liable for such costs as the Court may award and become precluded from instituting any fresh suit in respect of that subject-matter under sub-rule (3) of that rule. There is no provision in the Code of Civil Procedure which requires the Court to refuse permission to withdraw the suit in such circumstances and to compel the plaintiff to proceed with it I am in respectful agreement with enunciation of law decided by the Supreme Court of India and Allahabad High Court.

26. In AZM Khalilur Rahman vs Md Syed Hossain (Supra) the principles laid down is, that where an application for leave to withdraw a suit either with or without liberty to bring a fresh suit is made to the Appellate Court under Order XXIII, rule 1, read with section 107, clause (2) of the Civil Procedure Code, the proper procedure for the appellate Court to follow, if it is inclined to grant such leave, is to set aside the decree of the trial Court and then grant permission to withdraw. If the application for withdrawal is allowed and at the same time the decree passed by the Court below be allowed to stand, anomalous situation would crop up.

In the said case Mir Golam Kibria vs Raja Pramatha Bhusan Deb Roy 39 Calcutta Weekly Notes, 586 had been relied upon.

I am, also, in respectful obedience to the said Judicial verdicts propounded by RC Mitter, J and well approved by Nurul Islam, J who are Author Judges of the two Judicial verdicts.

27. In Abdur Rahman vs Kheru Malitha (Supra) observation of their Lordships of the Appellate Division is couched in the following terms:

We have considered the language of Order XXIII, rule 1(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure which clearly gives an unqualified right to a plaintiff to withdraw from the suit at any time. When the plaintiff withdraws from his suit without seeking permission to sue afresh as contemplated under rule 1(2), the plaintiff is precluded from instituting any fresh suit in respect of the subject-matter or the claim made in the suit so withdrawn. The withdrawal of a suit by necessary implication blots out the effect of the judgments and decree prior to withdrawal. If the application for withdrawal is allowed and at the same time the decree or decree passed by the Courts below be retained it would create a situation contradictory in terms. Therefore an order of setting aside judgments and decrees in the suit withdrawn should naturally follow.

AZM Khalilur Rahman vs Md Syed Hossain (Supra), Mir Golam Kibria vs Raja Promatha Bhusan Deb (Supra) and Kamta vs Gaya Prasad (Supra) have been taken into stock.

28. This drives me to Judicial Authority referred to from side of defendants-opposite parties. In Md Badruddin Moral and others vs Santosh Kumar Sen and others (Supra) the plaintiffs filed a petition for withdrawing the suit with liberty to bring a fresh suit on the ground that there were defects in the schedule and parties and other formal defects in the plaint due to incorrect description given at the time of drafting of plaint. Learned Munsif observed that it was not specifically stated as to what "formal defects" were and that the defects in schedule and as to the parties could be amended by filing a petition for amendment of plaint. Suit was an old one which was once dismissed for default and plaintiff took no step for amending the plaint during the long time the suit was pending. Learned Munsif rejected the petition for withdrawal of suit with permission to sue afresh. Revisional application preferred before High Court Division stood rejected summarily and Appeal preferred against Judgment of High Court Division was, also, dismissed. No exception can be taken to Judicial Pronouncement made by the Appellate Division but the fact and circumstances of the case in the cited case got no bearing in deciding the destiny of petition in hand and, as such, defendant-opposite parties cannot get any advantage on the said Judicial decision.

29. Pivotal point formulated is now being broached and riposted.

30. Admittedly, suit is for decree of partition in respect of 2.40-3/4 acres of property and the basis of claim of plaintiffs-petitioners is a kabuliyat dated 21-2-1919.

31. Learned Trial Judge in dismissing the suit considered evidence of PW 5 Advocate Commissioner who laid bare evidence that he on local investigation did not find the similarity with all the plots noted in kabuliyat and he, also, did not make any report. Advocate Commissioner PW 5, also, did not state the quantity of land transferred in the kabuliyat dated 21-2-1919. Learned Trial Judge found inconsistency and infirmity in respect of quantity of land converted by kabuliyat. Learned Trial Judge, also, took into account evidence of PW 5 Advocate Commissioner who laid bare in evidence that he was not at all aware of land converted in the kabuliyat. Learned Trial Judge taking into account the evidence of PW 5 Advocate Commissioner came to hold that land of Lakshmipur and Singua Mouza had been measured and there had been no identity of land conveyed in kabuliyat with the schedule land described in plaint and suit is barred by the defect of hotchpotch. Learned Appellate Judge concurred with findings reached by learned Trial Judge.

32. In order to attract the land of kabuliyat with the land described in schedule to plaint the identify of property was required to be relayed by a Survey-trained Advocate Commissioner and by relayment identity of the land noted in kabuliyat with schedule land could not be at all ascertained and established. Non-identity of land conveyed in kabuliyat with schedule land described in plaint is definitely a "formal defect" of fundamental nature and the suit must fail for this "formal and material defect."

33. Land described in schedule to plaint was not clearly ascertained and determined and learned Trial Judge, also, took into account this vital aspect of case and came to hold that Trial Court would not pass a decree if plaintiffs would fail to ascertain and determine their land correctly. Learned Appellate Judge came in full agreement with decision handed down by learned Trial Judge.

34. Suit was for a simple decree of partition and title of plaintiff-petitioners had been seriously challenged by defendants-opposite parties. Defendants, also, fired the case of plaintiffs-petitioner in putting forth case that plaintiffs-petitioners were and are out of possession of Suit Land. Plaintiffs-petitioners were, therefore, required to seek a proper relief i.e. declaration of title along with a decree of partition on suit land.

35. In a suit for partition all joint properties are to be brought on hotchpot i.e. all joint properties must be subject matter of partition. But plaintiff-petitioners did not make all joint properties subject matter of partition i.e. into hotchpot and learned Trial Judge, also, took into account this vital aspect. Failure on the part of plaintiffs-petitioners to bring all joint properties in the suit for partition brought about the collapse of suit and non-bringing of all joint/ejmali lands is a serious "formal defect."

36. This takes me to non-joinder of parties in suit for partition. Admittedly, heirs of Tota Bibi, who is another sister of Alekjan Bibi, had not been made defendants in the suit and learned trial Judge held the suit to be bad for defect of parties.

37. In the case in hand "formal defect" on defect of parties was not the sole ground taken for withdrawal of suit with permission to sue afresh. Basic ground pressed into service for withdrawal of suit is defect of hotchpotch and hotchpot. In Messrs Ilamuddin and Sons vs Asghar Ali 1970 SCMR 233 objection raised in written statement was taken as to defect of party and it was categorically stated that Mian Hamuddin representing the petitioner's firm was a necessary party to the suit. It was further alleged that a mere declaratory suit was not maintainable and that the prayer made in the suit was vague and indefinite. Their Lordship of Pakistan Supreme Court held that all pleas of written statement obviously refers to defects in the frame of the suit. Pakistan Supreme Court overruled the objection raised by defendant that necessary party was not impleaded. Permission granted to plaintiff by Trial Court to withdraw the suit with liberty to bring fresh suit on the cause of action was maintained by the High Court of West Pakistan, Lahore in Revision and against these Judgments High Court Petition for Special Leave to Appeal before the Supreme Court of Pakistan was dismissed and permission to withdraw the suit with liberty to institute fresh suit was maintained.

<u>38. Defects occurred could have been possibly remedied by way of an amendment in the suit and, in the event of allowing amendment, suit might relate back to initial stage of the suit, inasmuch as the defendant side got the right to lay additional written statement and would take other steps which would have definitely encumbered the suit. Moreover, by way of amendment "formal defects" of fundamental nature such as, identity of land conveyed in kabuliyat dated 21-2-1919 with the suit land could not be at all remedied. Even in the event of amendment, in the absence of identification of land conveyed in kabuliyat with suit land suit might fail for inherent defect. Amendment of plaint, thus, might not have been proper substitute and "formal defects" and all controversies can be solved if a fresh suit is instituted on curing all defects which is the spirit behind the provision engrafted in Order XXIII, rule 1 of the Code.</u>

<u>39. True it is that proceeding in hand took long nineteen (19) years and there had been wastage of time and money but ends of justice demands that all controversies involved in the suit are required to be laid at rest on removing "formal defects."</u>

<u>40. In the discourse made above, I am of this considered view that petition laid under Order XXIII, rule 1 of the Code for withdrawing of suit with permission to sue afresh is liable to be allowed.</u>

41. Defendant-opposite parties submitted that in the event of allowing the petition of plaintiffs-petitioners then defendants-opposite parties are entitled to cost.

42. Corollary thereof is that plaintiff's petition for withdrawing the suit with permission to sue afresh allowed. Plaintiffs-petitioners are granted permission to withdraw the suit with liberty to institute a fresh suit in respect of subject matter of the suit. Judgments recorded by Courts below are set aside.

<u>43. Plaintiffs-petitioners shall pay cost of Taka twelve thousand (Taka 12,000) to defendant-opposite parties.</u>

Lower Court's Records are sent down.

End.

Ahsanul Kabir, Advocate, instructed by Giasuddin Ahmed, Advocate-on-Record-For the Appellant. 
SR Khoshnabish, Advocate-on-Record-For the Respondents.

case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 4-5-2011 passed by the High Court Division Admiralty Suit No. 19 of 2009 heard along with Admiralty Suit Nos. 27 and 28 of 2009)
full_judgment:
Syed Mahmud Hossain J : This appeal, by leave, is directed against the judgment and order dated 4-5-2011 passed by the High Court Division in Admiralty Suit No. 19 of 2009 decreeing the suit against defendant No. 2, Kysco Shipping Co. Ltd. and dismissing the same against defendant Nos. 1, 3, and 4.

2. The facts relevant for the purpose of disposal of this appeal, in a nutshell, are:

The plaintiff company in course of its business as Ship Manager and Ship Managing Agent made a ship management agreement with defendant No. 2, the disposer owner/charterer regarding the Vessel MV Kunai (now renamed as MV BF Glory, i.e. defendant No. 1 Vessel) for the purpose of Marine operation, supply of bunkers, marine insurance, claims for seamen's wages, and for repair and new building of the vessel. Accordingly, the plaintiff Company supplied crews as per crew list to defendant No. 1 Vessel for which it was stipulated in the said Ship Management Agreement that the owners would remit the monthly management fee including seamen's wages to the Bank Account of the Manager by telegraphic transfer. The plaintiff also supplied bunkers to defendant No. 1 Vessel through Lubricants delivery receipt dated 19-10-2008 at the port of Masan in Republic of Korea.

3. The plaintiff also supplied necessaries to defendant No. 1 Vessel on 14-10-2008 and also on other dates at the owners/master disbursement. The plaintiff also completed electrical works to defendant No. 1 Vessel through POS Electric Company and supplied necessary Electrical items as per list dated 23-10-2008 for the period of 7-10-2008 to 23-10-2008. The plaintiff also made services as per service report to defendant No. 1 Vessel by the order of the disponer owner/charterer, defendant No. 2, which commenced on 30-9-2008 and further on 16-10-2008 and completed on 23-10-2008. The plaintiff submitted the statement of account to defendant No. 2 on different dates, that is, on 31-10-2008 for US $ 663211.33, on 30-11-2008 for US $ 88102.26, on 31-12-2008 for US $ 150728.52, on 31-1-2009 for US $ 149636.02, on 28-2-2009 for US $ 71829.51, on 31-3-2009 for US $ 49569.98 and on 30-4-2009 for US $ 44187.24 totaling an amount of US $ 15,90,442.76. Although the plaintiff appellant supplied the statement of account to the defendant for payment, the defendant did not settle the plaintiff's claim for which the plaintiff appellant is constrained to file the admiralty suit finding the Vessel within the territorial jurisdiction of this Court.

4. It has been asserted in the plaint that the owner of defendant No. 1 Vessel intends to quit the contract with the charterer, defendant No. 2 as the charterer has not paid charter hire for more than three months. The owner defendant No. 3, asked the charterer defendant No. 2, to re-deliver the vessel. As defendant No. 2, that is, the charterer is about to go into bankruptcy, the plaintiff has no other alternative but to institute the instant suit in Bangladesh for the recovery of its legitimate dues.

5. The High Court Division was pleased to admit the suit and also passed an order for arrest of defendant No. 1 vessel. Defendant No. 1 and 3 appeared in the suit and furnished the bank guarantee to the extent of US $ 15,90,442.76. The High Court Division subsequently released the Vessel by order dated 1-7-2009 by accepting such bank guarantee. The bank guarantee is still lying in the custody of the Marshall of this Court.

6. Defendant Nos. 1 and 3 contested the suit by filing written statements denying all the material statements of the plaint. Though in their written statements defendant/respondent Nos. 1 & 3 asserted that if there was any supply of crew members, spare parts, repairing works, supply of bunkers and any other service done to the Vessel the same would be business trans-actions between the plaintiff and defendant No. 2 and, therefore, the owner of the vessel is not responsible for such service. The plaintiff may realize his alleged claim of US $ 15,90,442.76 from defendant No. 2 in personam and since defendant No. 2 is bankrupt nothing may be realized from defendant No. 2. Defendant No. 3 is not at all liable to the plaintiff.

7. After hearing the suit, the High Court Division decreed the suit as liquidated debt only against defendant No. 2 and dismissed the suit against defendant Nos. 1, 3 & 4 holding that the plaintiff can only proceed against defendant No. 2 as an action in personam not as an action in rem against defendant Nos. 1 and 3.

8. Feeling aggrieved by and dissatisfied with judgment and order dated 4-5-2011 passed by the High Court Division, the plaintiff as the leave-petitioner moved this Division by filing Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 514 of 2012, in which, leave was granted on 27-11-2014 resulting in Civil Appeal No. 1 of 2015.

9. Mr Ahsanul Kabir, learned Advocate, appearing on behalf of the appellant, submits that the High Court Division committed error of law in not holding that sections 4(2) and 4(3) of the Admiralty Court Act, 2000 provide that supply of bunker, necessaries and costs of repairs create maritime lien upon the Vessel for which an action in rem is maintainable against defendant No. 1, Vessel, and as such, the impugned judgment should be set aside. He further submits that the High Court Division misread clause (a) of sub-section (4) of section 4 of the Admiralty Court Act, 2000 and most erroneously came to the finding that the plaintiff's claim is squarely against defendant No. 2, the Charterer, and as such, the impugned judgment should be set aside. He also submits that the plaintiff's claim is also enforceable as an action in rem under sections 3(2)(da) and 4(4) of the Admiralty Court Act, 2000 and, as such, the High Court Division erred in law in holding that defendant No. 2 was not the real owner and rather disponer owner particularly under the lease agreement and also failed to appreciate that defendant No. 2 is the beneficial owner of the Vessel by virtue of the lease agreement and that the plaintiff is not entitled to initiate an action in rem against defendant No. 1 Vessel.

10. Mr SR Khoshnabish, learned Advocate-on-Record, appearing on behalf of the respondents, submits that the High Court Division was fully justified in decreeing the suit against defendant No. 2 and as such, no interference is called for. He further submits that defendant No. 3 has been dissolved and as such, if any decree is passed against defendant No. 3 the same cannot be executed.

11. We have considered the submissions of the learned Advocates of both the sides, perused the impugned judgment and the materials on record.

12. Before entering into the merit of the appeal, it is necessary to go through the grounds, on which, leave was granted. The grounds are quoted below:

"The High Court Division erred in law in not holding that sections 4(2) and 4(3) of the Admiralty Court Act, 2000 provide that supply of bunker, necessaries and cost of repairs create maritime lien upon the vessel for which an action in rem is maintainable against defendant No. 1, vessel.

The High Court Division misread sections 4(1) and 4(3) of the Admiralty Court Act, 2000 and most erroneously came to the finding that the plaintiff's claim is squarely against the defendant No. 2 the Charterer. From a plain reading of section 3(2)(da) of the Admiralty Court Act, 2000, which widens the previous jurisdiction, the plaintiff is entitled to recover its just and lawful claim by initiating the proceeding as an action in rem against defendant No. 1 Vessel under section 4(2) of the same Act.

The supply was made on the credit of the vessel, and hence any disclaimer as to the creation of Maritime claim of the ship and/or limiting the authority of the ship's officers signing the receipts to bind the Vessel and owners, is null and void, as the claim has been made out in terms of conventions and also the bunkers and other necessaries were supplied on the faith and credit of the vessel. Thus it is clear from perusal of all exhibits in the instant suit and in pursuance of the requisition made, the supply was effected. The High Court Division ought to have held that the bunker and other necessaries have been supplied on the faith and credit of the Vessel and, therefore, a lien on the Vessel is thereby created.

The High Court Division erred in law in not holding that defendant No. 2 Charterer is a beneficial owner in respect of all shares during the existence of lease period and the plaintiff is entitled to bring the proceeding as an action in rem under section 4(4)(Ka) of the Admiralty Court Act, 2000 against defendant No. 1 Vessel and its owner defendant No. 3 who furnished the Bank Guarantee as security for the plaintiff's claim.

The plaintiff's claim is also enforceable as an action in rem under sections 3(2)(Da) and 4(2) of the Admiralty Court Act, 2000, and as such the High Court Division committed an error of law in holding that defendant No. 2 is not the real owner and rather the disponer owner particularly under the lease agreement and also failed to appreciate that defendant No. 2 is the beneficial owner of the Vessel by virtue of lease agreement and the plaintiff is entitled to proceed in an action in rem against defendant No. 1 Vessel."

14. The question to be resolved in the appeal is whether the plaintiff can file an admiralty suit in rem for realization for price of bunker, necessaries, wages of crew and the cost of the repairs and also ship management fees.

15. The High Court Division decreed the suit against defendant No. 2 and dismissed it against defendant Nos.1 and 3. The High Court Division came to a finding that defendant No.2 was not admittedly the real owner and rather the disponent owner, particularly under a lease agreement and that the debt incurred by it could not create a lien upon the properties not owned by it. The High Court Division further found that the Vessel MV BF Glory being the property of real owner, M/s. Dossan Capital Co. Limited (defendant No.3), could not be liable for the debt created by the lease user of the Vessel, liability of which always remained with the said company M/s. Kysco Shipping Co. Ltd. (defendant No. 2). The High Court Division held that the maritime claim of the plaintiff in respect of price of bunkers, necessaries and cost of repairs of the vessel could not create maritime lien upon the Vessel MV BF Glory and as such, could not be realized in Admiralty Jurisdiction through an action in rem and therefore, the claim of the plaintiff against the res as an action in rem could neither be maintainable against the Vessel itself nor against the real owner of the Vessel M/s. Doosan Capital Co. Limited (defendant No. 3).

16. The High Court Division also held the plaintiff rendered service in favour of Kysco Shipping Lines Ltd. (defendant No. 2) under the ship management agreement and supplied bunkers, necessaries to the Vessel and also rendered services in respect of the repair of the Vessel under the authority of defendant No. 2 and therefore, defendant No. 2 was liable to pay price due to the plaintiff. The High Court Division was of the view that the admiralty suit was maintainable as an action in personam against defendant No. 2.

<u>17. sub-section (1) of section 4 of Admiralty Court Act, 2000 provides that subject to the provision of section 5, the admiralty jurisdiction of the High Court Division may in all cases be exercised in personam. Sub-section (2) of section 4 provides that in relation to claims mentioned in clauses (ka) to (ga) and (da) of sub-section(2) of section 3 of Admiralty Jurisdiction of the High Court Division as the Court of Admiralty may be exercised through an action in rem against the ship or property in question.</u>

<u>18. Sub-section (3) of section 4 provides that where the amount claimed relates to any ship, aircraft or any other property over which there is maritime lien or other charge, the Admiralty Jurisdiction of the High Court Division as the Court of Admiralty may be exercised through an action in rem against that ship, aircraft or property.</u>

19. Sub-section (4) of section 4 provides that in relation to claims as mentioned in clauses-(Ga) to (Tha) of sub-section (2) of section 3 relating to any ship, the person who would be liable for the claim in an action in personam was, when the cause of action arose, as the owner or charterer of, or person in possession or in control of, the ship, whether the claim gives rise to a maritime lien on the ship or not an action in rem can be brought in the Admiralty Jurisdiction of the High Court Division as the Court of Admiralty against the following ships, namely, (a) if at the time when action is brought, the person has beneficial ownership over all the shares of the ship; or (b) if at the time when action is brought, any other ship is under the beneficial ownership of the said person.

20. sub-section (6) of section 4 of the Admiralty Court Act provides that notwithstanding anything contained in the preceding clauses of the section, an action in rem shall not be brought in the admiralty jurisdiction of the High Court Division as the Court of Admiralty for any claim mentioned in clause (dha) of sub-section(2) of section 3 unless the claim relates wholly or partly to wages.

21. Clause-(Tha) of sub-section (2) of section 3 provides for any claim in respect of the goods or materials supplied to a ship for her operation or maintenance. Clause-(Da) of sub-section (2) of section 3 provides for any claim in respect of construction, repair or equipment of a ship or dock charges or dues. Clause-(Dha) of sub-section (2) of section 3 provides for any claim for wages of a master or member of the crew of a ship or any claim for any money or property recoverable as wages of master or member of the crew under the Merchant Shipping Ordinance,1983.

<u>22. Having gone through section 4 of the Admiralty Court Act, in general, and clauses-(Tha), (Da) and (Dha) of sub-section (2) of section 3 and sub-section (6) of section 4 thereof, in particular, we find that the appellant is entitled to recover his claim in respect of clause-(dha) of sub-section (2) of section 3 according to the provision of sub-section(6) of section 4 of the Admiralty Court Act for realization of the wages of the crew. The claim of the appellant, however, does not come within the purview of sub-section (2), sub-section (3) and clause (a) of sub-section (4) of section 4 of the Admiralty Court Act.</u>

<u>23. Therefore, the plaintiff is entitled to bring a proceeding as an action in rem under section 4(6) of the Admiralty Court Act, 2000 for realization of wages of the crews as mentioned in clause (dha) of sub-section (2) of section 3 against defendant No. 1, the Vessel and its owner, defendant No. 3, although the plaintiff-appellant has not entered into any contract with defendant No. 3. It is of course true that there was no contract between the plaintiff-appellant and defendant-respondent No. 3 even then the plaintiff-appellant can sue the ship (defendant-respondent No. 1) and the owner of the ship (defendant-respondent No. 3) in an action in rem for realization of its dues in respect of wages of the crews above according to section 4 (6) of the Admiralty Act, 2000.</u>

<u>24. Respondent Nos.1 and 2 filed an additional paper-book stating that the plaintiff-appellant company, Kyung Hae Maritime Co. Ltd., had been dissolved in December, 2014. In support of their contention, the respondents filed an electronic copy of the plaintiff company, Kyung Hae Maritime Co. Ltd's Corporate Registry Certificate as well as its English translation. The appellant filed an additional paper-book dated 23-8-2015 stating that although the company was dissolved in December, 2014, subsequently, the same was reinstated by resolution of the share holders on 13th July, 2015 under article 520(2)(3) of the Commercial Act of Korea. In support of its contention, the appellant filed the minutes of the Extraordinary General Meeting of its share holders which is supported by a notarial certificate dated 30-7-2015. Therefore, we are of the view that the company is in existence which has the authority to proceed with this appeal.</u>

25. The plaintiff-appellant is entitled to recover the amount spent on account of wages of the crew. The amount spent for the payment of wages of crew is as follows:

Wages of the crew US $ 3,35,585.69

(at the relevant time US$1=Taka 69.35)

26. The detailed calculation of the amount spent by the plaintiff-appellant on the head of wages of crew appears to be correct.

27. In the light of the findings, we find substance in this appeal. Accordingly, the Admiralty Suit is decreed in part for US. $ 3,35,585.69 (at the relevant time 1 US $ equivalent to Taka 69.35) against defendant Nos. 1, 2 and 3.

Accordingly, the appeal is allowed in part. There is no order as to costs.
