full_judgment:
Ranadhir Sen J.:- This appeal at the instance of defendant No. 1 since deceased is directed against the judgment and decree of the learned Subordinate Judge in a suit for declaration of title and confirmation of possession and in the alternative for recovery of khas possession by evicting the defendants from the suit lands.

2. The plaintiff, erstwhile Province of East Pakistan, now Bangladesh, instituted a suit in the First Court of Subordinate Judge, Barisal claiming the following reliefs:-

"Ka. That the suit be decreed with a declaration that the disputed (amended) foreshore lands are Govt. lands and the defdts have no right, title and interest in the same.

(Kha) That the suit be decreed with the prayer for confirmation of possession in the disputed foreshores and the lands therein, or in the alternative, if found out possession then a decree for recovery of khas possession after evicting the defats from the disputed land and on demolition of the structures thereon.

(Ga) That prayer for temporary in-junction restraining the defdts from taking forcible possession in the disputed foreshore lands be allowed pending final disposal of the suit and that a permanent injunction be issued on the defdts restraining them not to possess or go upon the disputed lands.

(Gha) That it be declared that the alleged unregistered Arnaldari is a false, forged and fabricated document and the defdts have no right, title and interest in the disputed foreshore lands by virtue of this false and fraudulent Amaldari.

(Um a) That the cost of the suit be decreed against the defdts.

(Cha) That if any of the proforma defdts set up any claim on the disputed foreshore lands, a decree be passed against them as well.

(Chha) That the plaintiff Province be granted any other reliefs which the plaintiff Province is legally entitled to get."

3. The suit lands have been described in schedule A to the plaint in the following terms:-

"Within the district of Bakerganj under P. S, Kotwali in the town of Barisal and within Barisal Municipality, towards the east of the Barisal Bi-weekly market and contiguous east of R.S. No. 2027 J.L. No. 48 Mouza Amanatganj, are the disputed foreshore lands of R. S. No. 1670 J.L. No. 62 Mouza Char Badna, bounded on the south by the Barisal Jail Khal, on the east by the Barisal Kirtonkhola river, on the west by the tenanted and Govt. khas lands of Mouza Amanatganj on the north by lands of S. A. plot No. 2404 of Mouza Amanatganj and the straight line drawn eastward along northern boundary of the said S.A. plot No. 2404 right upto the river as in the S. A. map and the comparative map attached herewith. The total quantity of disputed foreshore lands is 6.66 acres only."

4. The allegations made in the plaint giving rise to the cause of action for the instant, suit have been stated in a lengthy plaint running over 44 paragraphs. We shall briefly state the plaintiff's case in the following term:- The suit land is the foreshore char land on the western bank of river Barisal known as Kirtonkhola which is a public navigable river. The Barisal bi-weekly market within the Municipality of Barisal situated in Mouza Amanatganj is adjacent to the west of the suit land. According to the plaintiff, Baisharashi Chowdhyrashi landlords of Bauphal Estate as they are popularly known were the owners in possession of the bi-weekly market. The plaintiff's specific case is that the disputed foreshore land is a char land which was under Kirtonkhola river and gradually appeared as an accretion to the hat since 1950. At that time part of the char was above water level and parts thereof were in process of formation. With the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act coming into operation, the interests of the landlords of Bauphal Estate were acquired and the plaintiff took possession of the aforesaid bi-weekly market. With the formation of the char land certain persons claimed interest in the foreshore land as an accretion to their karsha interest on the basis of settlement from the Bauphal Estate. The Government, however, did not recognise those persons in unauthorised occupation and after hearing their claims recognised only those who had valid settlement and rejected the claims of others. The Government while in khas possession of the foreshore char land by granting licences for construction of jetty, certain persons stealthily entered into the suit land and made certain unauthorised constructions. At the relevant time the char lands were gill soft and unfit for cultivation, The Government took notice of the possession of these unauthorised persons and served notice from them -in Miscellaneous case No. 18.S/55-56 under Act X of 1953 Government lands and Building (Recovery) Act. Thereafter defendant No. 1 Syed Hatem Ali put up certain unauthorised constructions which were also demolished and removed on 16-7-57. Meanwhile defendant No. 1 some how managed to get his name recorded in the S. A. khation but the entry in the record of right was struck off at the instance of the Government and record stood in the name of the Government. Defendant No. 1 Syed Hatem Ali moved the Dacca High Court in Writ petition challenging the legality of the notice under Act X of 1953. The High Court after hearing the matter allowed the petition and made the Rule absolute restraining the Government by an appropriate injunction from interfering with the possession of the defendant. This decision of the High Court gave rise to the cause of action for this suit. The plaintiff claims the suit land as foreshore land of river Barisal known as Kitton khola and also as an accretion arising from the river bed which belonged to the Government in a proprietary right as appertaining to Mouza Char Badna. The other basis of the plaintiff's claim appears on the basis of acquisition under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act of the interest of the Bauphal Estate landlords in the market situated in Mouza Anmatganj. It further appears that as an alternative case was sought to be spelt out that the suit land being adjunct to the bi-weekly hat, the Government acquired the same. For the purpose of establishing the claim over the suitland the plaintiff claimed that the bed of Kirton Khola river belonged to the Government, The plaintiff however, denied the claim of the defendants of the alleged settlement on the basis of Amaldari from Bauphal Estate and of possession therein. It is the consistent case of the plaintiff as available from the schedule to the plaint that the suit land appertains to Mouza Char Badna and not Amanatganj.

5. The suit was contested by defendant Nos. 1 to 4 by filing a written statement. Although some other defendants to filed written statement but they did not ultimately contest the suit. The case of the contesting defendants, briefly stated, is that the suit land appertains to Mouza Amanatganj and the Bauphal landlords were the owners thereof. The chat gradually reformed in situ since 1935 and the landlords, as proprietors of Mouza Amanatganj, were in possession- there-of. In 1940 the Char land became firm and hard, usable and capable for cultivation. Hash All Bepari, Rekat Ali Nigaban, Abdul Hasheni Howlader and defendant Syed Hatem Ali in the benami of Kazi Motaharuddin obtained lease of 8.86 acres of char land in raiyati right at a jama of Rs. 88/- on the basis of Amaldari and got possession. Since such settlement, the defendants have been continuing in possession by cultivating the land, growing paddy and pulses and by planting trees and thereafter by constructing several godowns and carrying on business there. According to the contesting defendants, their right, title and interest has not been acquired under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. Their further definite case is that the suit land does not appertain to mouza Char Badna. According to them, it is a reformation in situ of the land of mouza Amanatganj diluviated by river Kirtonkhola. The contesting defendants do not admit the proprietors khas possession of the suit land or that of the plaintiff on the basis of acquisition of Zarnindari interest. They were found in possession of the suit land in the Writ petition filed before the Dacca High Court and the action of the Government was held to be unauthorized and of no legal effect. Defendant No. 1 claims title on the basis of purchase by kabala’s from the original lessees.

On these pleadings the following issues were framed.

(1) Is the suit maintainable in the present form?

(2) Is the suit barred by res judicata?

(3) Is the suit barred by limitation?

(4) Is the suit land reformation in situ of mouza Amanatganj of toes No. 1721 and 1722 or reformation in situ of Char Badna?

(5) Has the plaintiff any right, title, interest and possession in the disputed land?

(6) To v, hat relief, if any, is the plaintiff entitled?

6. The parties adduced oral and documentary evidence in support of their respective claims. On behalf of the plaintiff P.W. 1 Hemanta Kumar Biswas, a surveyor of the Collectorate was examined. P.W. 2 is Haji Amjed Ali Mridha who has a. shop outside the suit land. P.W. 3 Golam Mohiuddin is an Aratdar having his gaddi Oar about 20/25 cubits from the suit land. P.W. 4 is Khadem Ali Sikdar, a Touzi Nabish and a Revenue Peshkar. He was also a jama Nabish in the State Acquisition Department. P.W. 5 is a clerk of S.A. Department, record room. In addition to the oral evidence, a large number of documents were also proved and marked exhibits in the suit. These are Exhibit No. 1 sketch map showing the foreshore land of the river Barisal in mouza Amanatganj. It was prepared by P.W. 1 H.K. Biswas on .13.1.53. This document was however admitted on objection by contesting defendants. Exhibit No. 2 is the original register VI. Exhibit No. 3 is certified copy of order sheet of Miscellaneous Case No. 167' of 1957 containing the order of the Settlement Officer. Exhibit 3A is the certified copy of order in Miscellaneous case No. 1 of 1958 by the Director of Land Records. Exhibit 4 is the order of A.O. Raziur Rahman, District Magistrate dated 22.2.56. Exhibit 5 is the petition dated 13.2.57 in Miscellaneous Case No. 167 of 1957. Exhibit 1(a) is a map of mouza Amanatganj. Exhibit 1(b) is another sketch map of the disputed land prepared by M. K. Biswas P.W.1. This map was admitted in evidence with objection of the contesting defendants. Exhibit 1(c) is the certified copy of Thak map. This was also admitted in evidence with objection. Exhibit 6 is the Written statement filed by Syed Hatem Ali in Misc. case No. 67 of 1957. Exhibit 7 is the S. A. Khatian No. 217 of mouza Amanatganj. Exhibit (d) is another sketch map. Exhibits 3(b) and 3(d) are two orders in Misc. case No. 4 of 1954-55 in S.A. proceedings. Exhibits 8, 8(a) and' 8(b) are certain petitions. Exhibit 9 is another objection petition of defendant No. 1 Syed Hatem Ali in Misc Case No. 167 of 1957. Exhibit 10 is the Talab bald register. Exhibit 11, 11(a) are the certified copies of demand register. Exhibits 12 and 12(a) are the certified copies of C.S. khatian No. 65 and 66 respectively. Exhibit 3(e) is the certified copy of the order in proceedings under section 19(1) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. Exhibit 1(e) is a blue-print map of I.W.T.A. Exhibit 13, 13(a) and 13(b) are certain information slips. Exhibits 12(b) are the S. A. khatian No. 413 of Mouza Amanatganj and Exhibit 10(a) is the original talab baki register. These documents are relied upon by the plaintiff.

7. On behalf of the defendants, Syed Hatem Ali, the defendant No. 1 was examined as D.W.I in the suit. Kadam Ali Fakir was examined as D.W. 2. Kali Pada Das, a timber merchant having his factory 'to the north of the suitland was examined by the contesting defendant as D.W. 3. Nurul Huq Bhuiya, defendant No. 16 was examined as D.W. 4. He has a business in the premises of Mati Sen for about 25 years and his premises is situated to the west of the disputed land. D.W. 5 Ayerali Mia is another businessman of Barisal bazar. D.W. 6 is Ahmad Ali Munshi, a merchant hating business for about 17 years at a place close to the disputed land. D.W. 7 is Chuni Lal Saha, a businessman of the locality. D.W. 8 is A.F.M. Delwar Hussain, a pleader of the local Court who was the Commissioner for the local investigation.

8. On behalf of the contesting defendants Exhibit A, the registered deed of release (Mukti Patra) executed by Kazi Motaharuddin in favour of Syed Hatem Ali was proved in support of defence claim of title to their leased land, Exhibit B series are rent receipts. Exhibit C series are the certified copy of the register of Rent Suit. Exhibit D series are the certified copy of Talab baki register. Exhibit E series are the copy of objection and orders of the Revenue officer. Exhibit F series are the Municipal receipt of Barisal Municipality. Exhibit G is the registered kabala executed by Abut Hashem in favour of Akkel Ali Sikdar. Exhibit is the another registered kabala executed by Rokat Ali and another in favour of Sahed Ali Negaban and another. Exhibit H is the certified copy of order in Writ Petition No. 149 of 1957. Exhibit I series are certified copy of judgments. Exhibit .1 is the certified copy of petition of complaint under section 476 Cr. P. C on behalf of the Sub-Divisional Officer, Sadar South, Barisal. Exhibit K series are certain R. S. Khatians of Mouza Amanatganj. Exhibit L is the copy of order of the Commissioner, Dacca Division passed in Appeal No. 108 of 1957.

9. On consideration of the aforesaid evidence the learned Subordinate Judge decreed the suit holding that the suit as framed was maintainable and was not bad for defect of parties. According to the trial court, the suit was not barred by limitation and the principle of res-judicata. The learned Subordinate Judge, however, held that "the defendants are now in possession of the disputed land where they have erected some godowns, one ice factory and other business concern, but I must observe that the defendants got that possession since 1956 and they had no title and possession before 1956."

10 Coming to the plaintiff's case the learned Subordinate Judge held that "the position, therefore, comes to this that in 1954-55 the hat and its adjuncts were acquired by the Government and further reformation of the char in its contiguity were accretion and adjuncts to the hat and therefore, the entire suit land became the property of the Government." The learned Subordinate Judge further held that "suit land is a hat and bazar land and its proprietorship Lies with the Government." The learned Subordinate Judge also took the view that under Article 146 of the Constitution of the Republic of Pakistan the land in suit vested in the Government and expressed himself in the following terms:

"If it at all be conceded that the Government did not acquire any proprietor right in the land under any provisions of the S.A. Act, the Government can still claim the land in proprietary right under Article 146 of Constitution of the Republic of Pakistan. Under this Article any land not belonging to any rightful person vests in the Government. At any rate, the plaintiff is entitled to the disputed property in their khas possession. They got possession and they possessed it on the formalities of char by permitting licenses for construction of jetties etc. and they were dispossessed by the defendants who have got no title and interest in the suit land."

Concluding, the learned Subordinate Judge observed that "the plaintiff has valued the property at Rs. 2 lakhs. The defence contention is that the property has been overvalued. 6.66 acres of land are the disputed property of which 3.00 acres submerged at high tide in the spring season reported by the Commissioner. Considering the above circumstance in my judgment, the proper value of the suit land is Rs. 1 lakh. Amend the plaint and suit register accordingly." In the ordering portion the learned Subordinate Judge directed that the Commissioner's report, field book and case map do form part of the decree. The learned Sub-ordinate Judge accordingly declared the plaintiff's title to the suit land and granted a decree for khas possession thereof by evicting the defendants therefrom.

11. Mr. S.R. Pal, the learned Advocate appearing for the defendants appellant, has taken us through the pleadings, the evidence and the judgment. According to Mr. Pal the plaintiff failed to prove the case as alleged in the plaint and sought to be made out in evidence. In his view, the plaintiff came with alternative grounds claiming title to the suit land and those alternative grounds were in-consistent and as such the learned Subordinate Judge erred in declaring the plaintiff's title in a misconceived suit. Mr. Pal also argued that the plaintiff failed to prove any of its claims.

12. Mr. Abdus Sobhan, the learned Additional Attorney General appearing for the plaintiff Government contends that the plaint disclosed a positive case and the relevant claims therein are consistent and there was no inconsistency in the plaintiff's case. The learned Additional Attorney General has further contended that the evidence on record is sufficient to lend support to the findings of the learned" Subordinate Judge who correctly decided the relevant issues raised between the parties in his view, the judgment of the learned Subordinate Judge is supported by the materials on record and calls for no interference by this court in appeal.

13. In order to appreciate the contentions raised by the learned Advocates, it is necessary to go into the genesis of the claim. We are' not oblivious as to the changes in the topographical position of the suit land during a period of about a century. We shall refer to such positions at the proper time. It is evident from the plaint that the plaintiff laid foundation for the claim on two-fold basis. One is that the suit land is a foreshore land of river Barisal known as Kirtonkhola and the same appertains to mouza Char Badna. The clear language and the expressions used in the plaint indicates that the plaintiff was sure as to the nature of suit land as foreshore land of river Kirtonkhola appertain to mouza Char Badna. Mr. Pal has also laid considerable emphasis on this part of the plaintiff's claim. There is no dispute that river Kirtonkhola lies to the contiguous east of the present suit land. We have been addressed by the learned Additional Attorney General relating to the topographical developments occurring from the time of Thak survey which was held in 1960 when the suit land was a part of mouza Amanatganj within the Thak line. In 1867-68 the revenue survey indicated some portion of mouza Amanatganj was diluviated and the plaintiff claimed that the river Kirtonkhola shifted its course to the west and diluviated certain areas reducing the total area of mouza Amanatganj. This is evident from the C. S. map of 190 P-2. In the C. S. map, however, the land of Char Badna was recorded in zero khatian and a portion of Amanatganj contiguous to the west of the river Kirtonkhola was recorded in plot No. 829. According to the learned Additional Attorney General, mouza Char Badna belonged to the Government in proprietary right including the river and its bed. There is nothing on record to indicate with the diluvion of certain portion of mouza Amanatganj the interest of the proprietors in the Tauzin were in any way affected. There is no evidence to show that the revenue of the touzi of the proprietors relating to mouza Amanatganj was reduced because of the dilution. One sided claim of the Government extending the limits of Char Badna mouza did not extinguish the lawful interest of the proprietors of the Taluk and, therefore, the proprietary interest of Bauphal Estate remained unaffected notwithstanding the diluvion of some land of mouza Amanatganj. During R. S. operation extending a period from 1941 to 1945 and thereafter in 1952, there was a notification as claimed by the plaintiff on 26.12.52 to swallow up the diluviated portion of mouza Amanatganj within the boundary of mouza Char Badna. In our opinion, this representation indicates that the suit land was not recorded in the R.S. operation as claimed by the plaintiff. In S.A. operation also, according to the evidence of P.W. 1, the suit land was not depicted as diluviated. The defence case, on the other hand, is that the process of diluviation started from 1935 with gradual reformation in situ around 1940 and the diluviated land of mouza Amanatganj belonging to the Bhuphal Estate reappeared in situ. The landlords took possession and thereafter granted settlement in terms of Amaldari at a rental of Rs. 88/- pepper year. The defence further case is that the settlement holders came in possession of the land which was partly fit fir cultivation and partly in the process of being fit. They did cultivation for certain years in some parts and when the soil became hard and fit for raising construction they made some constructions and had been continuing in possession till their structures were forcibly demolished pursuant to a notice under Act X of 1953. The High Court in a Writ petition at the instance of Syed Hatein Ali found possession of defendant No. 1 on the basis of some title and accordingly held that the possession was not unauthorized and that the defendants were not liable to be evicted in terms of 'the notice under Act X of 1.953. The High Court also noticed the respective contentions on the conflicting title. Considering these facts in the light of the pleading and the evidence, we may quoted here paragraph 29 of the plaint to indicate the plaintiff's basis of title as disclosed in the plaint. Paragraph 29 of the plaint runs as follows:-

"That Mouza Amanatganj and Mouza Char Badna are different and separate neighbouring mouzas, that during the C.S. operations of the year 1903-04, Mouza Amanatganj extended upto the western bank of the Kirtonkhola navigable river and the entire Kirtonkhola river fell in mouza Char Badna and this river Kirton khola was recorded in mouza Char Badna zero khatian during C.S. operation. The bed of the Kirton khola river belonged to Government. So lands formed out of the bed of the river Kirtonkhola are pure and simple Government lands in mouza Char Badna. The Chowdhyarashi Zaminders can have no claim of any right, title and interest in these newly formed lands of mouza Char Badna. The Chowdhyarashi Zaminders could not also therefore grant any lease of any land in mouza Char Badna."

14. This indicates that the Government's claim rests on the foundation 'that it had proprietary right in the lands of mouza Char Badna including river Kirtonkhola and its bed. It is also found in the claim that the suit land is a Char arising out of the bed of river Kirtonkhola. Therefore, there cannot be any alternative assertion that the suit land appertains to a mouza other than Char Badna. If we turn to the schedule as we have quoted earlier, the Government appears to have given out a definite case as set out in plaint paragraph 29 that the suit land appertains to Mouza Char Badna. We may also turn to the averments made in paragraph 7 of the plaint which runs as follows:-

"That the Government is the rightful owner of all the foreshore lands. That the entire area on the eastern side of the Barisal Bi-weekly market beyond the lands recorded in the names of the recorded tenants during S.A. operation was according to law a foreshore belonging to Govt. It appears that some portion of the foreshore lands were by the action of the river, being rapidly and gradually filled up. But to all intents and purposes the entire area according to the definition of foreshore and "spring tide" as in the Govt. Estate Manual, was clearly a foreshore. Some greedy people including some of the defendants considering that the foreshore lands might soon become high and firm lands, fraudulently attempted to set up some false and fictitious claims of right, title and interest in the foreshore lands and secretly and stealthily put up some unauthorised constructions under cover of darkness in the foreshore lands in early January, 1956. That the R. C. 0. Barisal on information started a Misc. case No. 18(S) 55-56. against the intruders and encroachers Mvi. Amjad Ali Mirdha and many others filed applications before the authorities about these encroachments. Govt. directed these unauthorised occupants to demolish and remove their unauthorised constructions but they did not pay any heed to these orders and directions made by the Government."

15. It appears that the Government attempted to make out a case that the suit land to all intents and purpose was a fore-shore land of Barisal river of Mouza Char Badna. Turning to the schedule as appended to the plaint, it is evident that the suit land appertains to mouza Char Badna and not Amanatganj. A graphic description of the suit land appears to have been made in Schedule A but within the defined boundaries the suit lands have not been described as appertaining to mouza Char Badna.

16. There was a local investigation at the instance of the contesting defendants. The Advocate Commissioner submitted a report holding that the suit land appertains to Thak mouza Amanatganj. Objections were raised against the report of the Commissioner which were heard and disposed of by the learned Subordinate Judge under Order No. 80 dated 23.1.65. The learned Subordinate Judge while disposing of the objections of the plaintiff expressed himself in the following terms:-

"The only objection against the Commissioner's map, report and field book taken by the plaintiff is that the learned Commissioner did not complete his traverse line and as such the scientific work cannot be accepted. I personally examined the map and found the traverse mentioned therein. The learned Commissioner started his work from the north-western corner of R.S. plot No. 2114. He, however, prepared the comparative map on the common basis of the puce building of Bina Singh, a tank represented by R.S. plots Nos. 1979, 1681 and another tank represented by R.S. plot No. 1705 and the Jailkhal or Nazir Khal. So, there was nothing wrong in his scientific work. The learned Commissioner also stated in his evidence that he did not close the traverse line at the starting point because his traverse line was connected with north-western corner of R.S. plot No. 2242 and north-western corner of R.S. plot No. 2179. In the Thak map the Jail Khal or Nazir Khal has been depicted and the position of the said khal did not change in the recent maps. I, therefore, hold that the work free from errors and the objection must be overruled."

<u>17. The Commissioner was examined as D.W. 8. He showed the dotted lines as representing the suit land in the map. At the time of survey the Government was represented by the Surveyor Hemanta Kumar Biswas P.W. I and the Sub-Divisional Manager, South, Barisal The defendant Syed Hatem Ali was also present. The Commissioner clearly stated in his report and map that the suit land appertains to Thak Char No. 53 of Mouza Amanatganj. He also relied upon the R.S. map of mouza Amanatganj and superimposed the same on the Thak map which coincided with the common objects of the That map. The objection raised by the plaintiff against the report of the Commissioner having been rejected, the report of the Commissioner with the map and field book formed a part of the evidence. This evidence, according to the established principles of law, is not to be lightly brushed aside. The learned Subordinate Judge, however, did not advert to the findings of the Commissioner. While considering issue No. 1, the learned 'Subordinate Judge mentioned the Commissioner's report and the finding but lost sight of the same while granting the declaration prayed for by the plaintiff. It is evident that the decree, as it stands, is in conflict with the report of the Commissioner and the map made by him which have been made part of the decree. Such a decree, in our opinion, is not executable in view of the fact that the suit land as determined and found by the Commissioner appertains to mouza Amanatganj and not to mouza Char Badna as alleged by the plaintiff and found by the learned Subordinate Judge.</u>

<u>18. Mr. Pal the learned Advocate for the appellants has drawn our attention to the decision in the case of Ranee Surat Soondree Debea v. Baboo Prosonna Coomar Tagore (1) and the decision in the case of Chandan Mull Indra Kumar and others v. Chiman Lal Girdhar Das Parekh and another (2) In both the decisions their Lordships of the Privy Council held that "it has been laid down that interference with the result of a long and careful local investigation except upon clearly defined and sufficient grounds is to be deprecated. It is not safe for a court to act as an expert and to overrule the elaborate report of a Commissioner whose integrity and carefulness are unquestioned, whose careful and laborious execution of his task was proved by his report, and who had not blindly adopted the assertions of either party."</u>

19. Leading the evidence of the Commissioner and the map, report and the field book in the light of the pleadings and evidence on record we hold that the suit land appertains to mouza Amanatganj and not to mouza Char Badna. Therefore, the plaintiff's case resting on the claim that the suit land appertains to mouza Char Badna coming out of the river bed of Kirtonkhola does not stand. Acordingl y, the plaintiff has failed to prove its case in that behalf. This conclusion of ours is based on a consideration of the plaint, the oral and documentary evidence on record and the law resting on the question. No doubt, the plaintiff can take alternative cases. It is difficult to conceive of a case where the alternatives do not co-exist but are mutually exclusive. The plaintiff, in our opinion, failed to prove a case that the suit land was foreshore land of river Kirtonkhola appertaining to mouza Char Badna. Therefore, the claim of the plaintiff on the ground that the suit land appertains to mouza Char Badna coming out of the river Kirtonkhola and is of the nature of foreshore must fail.

<u>20. The other case of the plaintiff is that the suit land being the khas land of the Bauphal land lords with accretion to their permanently settled estate and appertaining to mouza Amanatganj, having been acquired under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, the Government acquired title. While considering this case of the plaintiff, it is necessary to remember that the plaintiff is to succeed on the strength and proof of its own case and not on the weakness of the defence case. The learned Additional Attorney General repeatedly argued before us that the defendants having failed to prove their title to the suit land, the plaintiff has acquired good title. Such a proposition appears to be a clear departure from the established principles of law. The plaintiff is required to prove its case to the hilt. The plaintiff in this behalf appears to be shaky and could not spell out a definite and defined case. We are not oblivious of the principle that in the cases where char land is involved, the pleadings is not to be construed too strictly. Giving that allowance to the plaintiff, let us consider the case of acquisition of the suit land as excess khas land of the outgoing land-lords by the Government. Mr. Pal appears to have correctly pointed out that the proceedings in Exhibits 3(b) and 3(d) do not conclusively indicate that the suit land was acquired according to law and in terms of section 20 of the State Acquisition of Tenancy Act. We are, however, not directly concerned with the alleged title of the defendants based on their claim of settlement on the basis of an Amaldari and on payment of rent in terms thereof. In this suit, in our opinion, there is hardly any scope for determination of defendant's title. We are mainly concerned with the claim of the plaintiff as alleged in the plaint and sought to be proved in evidence. On scrutiny of the evidence, it appears that the witnesses fumbled to speak out any date or year when the suit land re-appeared. It is necessary to remember that the plaintiff's claim is that the suit land re-appeared after 1950. There is a significant gap between 1950 and 1954 when the Bauphal Estate was acquired by a notification under section 3(1) and 3(2) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. Unless it is shown that the suit land re-appeared before the Acquisition in 1954, the claim of the plaintiff that the suit land vested as excess khas land of Bauphal landlords cannot stand. It will have to be examined whether the suit land was the khas land of the landlords and in excess of the retainable quantity. The plain-tiff is also in a vacillating mood here. On this point no issue has been raised although this is one of the grounds of plaintiff's claim. No evidence of conclusive nature was adduced by the plaintiff to show that the suit land re-re-appeared in Amanatganj before Bauphal Estate was acquired. There is also no definite evidence to show that it was an accretion to the biweekly market. It is necessary to observe that different consequences will follow if either of the alternatives is proved, namely the suit land appertaining to mouza Amanatganj and belonging to permanently settled estate of the Bauphal Landlords if re-appeared before the acquisition under section 3 of the Act, in that case, the Government may acquire title upon a proper proceeding under section 20 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act upon proof that the same was excess khas land of the ex-proprietors. In the other case, if it is an accretion to the hat before the acquisition under section 3 of the Act, the Government cannot claim the suit land as an adjunct or .appendix to the hat. We have been taken through certain maps and also the oral evidence of the P.Ws. It is apparent that the hat and the suit land are intervened by strips of land which have been described as Chandina and in occupation of certain tenants evidently on the basis of settlement from the Bauphal Estate and recognized as tenants by the Government under the. State Acquisition and Tenancy Act The evidence on record does not indicate that the suit land is an accretion to hat. Therefore, these two contentions have to be kept in isolation and the plaintiff is required to prove its case relating to acquisition of title to the suit land as has been claimed by it. An accretion to the hat does not automatically vest in the Government within the meaning and scope of section 20 of the Act, if such accretion took place before the notification under section 3 of the said Act. Section 20 does not speak of acquisition of land adjunct or accretion to the hat. In the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, section 20 has clearly illustrated the nature of non-retainable land. Only those classes of non-retainable lands vest in the Government in the terms of section 20. Section 20 also prescribes the limit of retainable land. Therefore, there is no ground to conceive that an adjunct to a hat stood acquired with the hat under section 20 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. We are therefore, left with the only other conceivable case of the Government that the suitland was the excess khas land of the Bauphal Estate. In this regard, as it appears, due consideration should made as to when the land in suit re-appeared in situ. As painted out earlier, there is no conclusive evidence nor there is any clear indication in the Plaint and evidence as to the time when this land reappeared in view of the nitrate azalea we propose to make in this a appeal, we need not say anything more at this stage on the merit of the plaintiff's case in this regard. We have taken sufficient precaution in expressing our views on the questions which may require fur there considerate ion by the trial court.</u>

21. For the reasons stated above we hold that the plaintiff failed prove, its case far as the claim of foreshore land arising out of the bed: of river Kirtonkhola appertaining to mouza Char Badna is concerned wee therefore, conclude that the claim must on-this score; Turning to the other ground as indicated earlier, we are of the view that the plaintiff has, also failed to prove that the soiled stood acquired as an adjunct to the bi-weekly hat and such a claim is not 'maintainable according to section 20 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. We, therefore, Conclude these two points and hold that the 'suit land is not foreshore land arising out of river. Barisal known as Kirtonkhola appertaining to mouza Char Badna and that the same never stood acquired as adjunct to the bi-weekly hat Barisal. Yet the plaintiff may have a case that the suit land was an accretion. If it was in accretion, the same was an accretion to the land of mouza Amanatganj. In such circumstances question may arise as to when the suit land reappeared or whether the hat extended upto the river so as to embrace it within its folds as non-retainable lands or whether the suit and as a the permanently settled estate of Mouza Amanatganj belonging to the Bauphal Iandlords was the excess khas and aorta said landlords which were acquired under section 20 of State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. It is case that the suit land was a hat or 2, at the same was included within Barisal weekly market. If the accretion took place deform the of the hat, it will have one set of effects. If it was an accretion after the acquisition of the hat, it will have a different consequence. It may be observed that the Evince failed to prove possession of the sultan’s in consequence of its assertion of title. Before we conclude, it is necessary to say a few about the application for amendment of the plaint under Order 6 Rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure which has been filed on behalf of the plaintiff-respondent in this appeal. The amendment prayed for is in the following terms.

"Before the last sentence of as schedule of the plaint and after the words ending the comparative map attached herewith the Part of the suit land appertain to mouza Amanatganj per that survey.

22. This prayer for amendment appears to be misconceived. The learned .Subordinate Judge had to consider, an issue in the following terms:-

"Is the suit land reformation in situ of mouza Amanatganj of tauzin No: 1721 and 1722 or reformation in situ of Char Badna."

23. If the proposed amendment is allowed the complexion of the plaintiff's claim will be changed. Further in view of the Commissioner's report which was accepted by the Trial Court and to which we have no reason to take a different view, the amendment prayed for appears to be a subterfuge. Mr. Pal has opposed the petition for amendment contending that it will be inconsistent with I plaint the issues and the evidence on record. The learned Additional Attorney General however, contends that in terms of Rule 17, Order 6 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the court may allow the petition as it will help determination of the real controversy between the parties. We do not think that the proposed amendment will be of any, help in determining the real controversy between the parties. The plaintiff seeks to amend the plaint claiming that the suit land in part appertains to mouza Amanatganj After the evidence as led by the parties as to whether the suit land appertains to Mouza Amanatganj or Char Badna and the finding of the Advocate Commissioner the proposed amendment appears to be misconceived. For the reasons stated above we reject the application for amendment of the plaint.

24. For the aforesaid reasons, we are of the view that the learned Subordinate judge decided the issues upon misconception of facts and recorded inconsistent and erroneous findings without proper assessment, evaluation and appreciation of the evidence on record. The learned Subordinate Judge although accepted the report of the Commissioner and his finding but said nothing to brush aside the effect of the report, map, field book and the oral evidence. The learned Subordinate Judge appears to have failed to consider the incongruous nature of the plaintiff's claim. Indefinite and vague assertions with no conclusive evidence as to the time of reappearance of the suit land appear to have been overlooked by the learned Subordinate Judge. The finding of the learned Subordinate Judge that "the suit land is a hat and bazar land" is foreign to the pleadings and evidence.

25. In our considered opinion, the learned Subordinate Judge fell in error in recording his findings and in making the declaration as prayed for with the relief of recovery of khas possession. Accordingly, the judgment and the decree of the learned Subordinate Judge must be set aside and the appeal should succeed.

26. We are however, of the view that the plaintiff's claim on the basis of acquisition under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act or the effects of accretion to the hat needs further examination.

27. In the background of the observations made above, the matter is remitted to the trial Court for determination of only the questions mooted above on such further evidence as the parties may intend to adduce together with the evidence already on record and for disposal of the suit according to law and in the light of our observations made in the judgment.

28. In the interest of a fair trial and justice we refrain from expressing our views on the evidence on record which may have some bearing on the questions to be decided by the learned Subordinate Judge. Our observations, if any, relate to the disposal of the appeal and the determination of the questions we have clearly made.

29. For the reasons stated above the appeal is allowed with costs. The judgment and decree of the learned Subordinate Judge are set aside and the suit is remanded to the learned Subordinate Judge for disposal according to law in the light of the observations made above.
